context: A trade mark registration, once entered in the Register of Trade Marks and duly certified, shall be prima facie evidence of the absolute title of the proprietor to the trade mark, subject to any right arising from the use of a similar mark prior to the date of registration. Any certificate purporting to be a certified copy of an entry in the Register, or any extract therefrom, shall be received as evidence in any legal proceeding, and shall, until proved to the contrary, be presumed to be true. The Registrar may, at any time, require evidence to substantiate the continued use of the registered trade mark, and failure to provide such evidence may render the registration liable to be revoked. A registered trade mark shall remain valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration, renewable for further periods of ten years each, as provided herein, upon payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with all applicable conditions.

An applicant seeking to respect filing application for a layout-design shall submit Form LD-A along with a certified copy of the drawings constituting the layout-design. The Registrar may, upon receiving an application, issue a provisional registration certificate if satisfied that the layout-design is capable of being registered under this Act and does not conflict with any existing registered layout-designs. Provided that, the applicant shall declare in the application whether or not the layout-design incorporates elements derived from another source, and furnish details thereof as may be prescribed. Failure to provide such declaration will render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar shall maintain a register of applications received, noting the date of receipt and any correspondence relating thereto.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, copyright in a sound recording shall subsist until sixty years from the end of the year in which the work is first published. Provided that, where the ownership of the sound recording vests in a person other than the producer thereof, such copyright shall endure for a period not exceeding fifty years from the date of publication, unless a longer term is agreed upon in writing between the producer and the owner. The right to reproduce a sound recording shall be deemed an exclusive right, subject to any license granted under this Act or as provided herein. Any person infringing upon said rights may be liable for damages commensurate with the extent of commercial loss suffered by the copyright holder.

Any person against whom an order adjudicating officer is passed, pertaining to the revocation of a patent, shall have a right to seek a statement of reasons for such order within thirty days of the communication of the said order. The statement of reasons shall be furnished by the adjudicating officer within a further period of sixty days, subject to the condition that such furnishing does not prejudice ongoing investigations or reveal confidential information. Where the statement of reasons is deemed insufficient or unsatisfactory by the requesting party, an application for review may be made to the adjudicating officer, provided that such application is accompanied by supporting evidence demonstrating the inadequacy. Any review application shall be decided within ninety days of its receipt, and the decision of the adjudicating officer on review shall be final, unless an appeal is preferred as provided herein. Failure to comply with these timelines shall be considered procedural irregularity.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through the mechanism of the Madrid Protocol International, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by such registration against any person infringing the said trade mark within the territory of India. Any party seeking relief for infringement must demonstrate that the challenged use or activity falls within the scope of protection afforded under this Act and relates directly to the internationally registered trade mark as extended. Furthermore, a claim predicated on an international registration shall not preclude reliance upon prior conflicting rights existing in India, irrespective of the date of filing of the initial application. The remedies available for infringement, including injunctions and damages, are subject to principles governing patent litigation concerning novelty and inventive step, ensuring equitable balance between proprietors and potential infringers.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, the owner of an exclusive right in a layout design commercially may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating thereto. Such licenses may be granted on a non-exclusive basis, provided that the terms and conditions stipulated within clearly delineate the scope of permitted use and reproduction. Assignment of such rights shall require execution of a formal instrument witnessed by at least two witnesses and registered with the designated authority as prescribed herein. Any license or assignment purporting to transfer ownership of a layout design commercially must explicitly state whether it encompasses all or only certain aspects of the right, including but not limited to manufacture, import, sale, hire, or use. Further, any such transfer shall be subject to verification by the Controller and may be rejected if deemed contrary to public interest or detrimental to the promotion of innovation within India.

The term "entitled produce variety" shall mean a plant variety which has been formally registered under this Act and whose rights are vested in a breeder or other eligible person, subject to any conditions stipulated during registration. Any person claiming entitlement to an entitled produce variety may institute proceedings before the Appellate Board alleging infringement of their rights by another party cultivating, selling, or distributing propagating material derived from that variety without authorization. Provided that such claim must be substantiated with documentary evidence demonstrating prior registration and continued adherence to the terms outlined therein. The Board shall consider any counter-claims presented by the alleged infringer asserting bona fide use or customary cultivation practices predating the registration of the entitled produce variety, as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining ownership of copyright in cinematograph films, where such film is created under the direction of a director, the said director shall be deemed the author of the work only if the director’s creative contribution transcends mere supervision and demonstrably involves significant artistic decisions pertaining to script adaptation, character development, or musical composition. Provided that, if an agreement exists between the producer and the director specifying allocation of copyright ownership, such agreement shall prevail, subject to the condition that it is executed prior to commencement of principal photography and registered with the designated government authority. Further, where a work incorporates elements created by other individuals under the direction’s guidance, those contributions remain protected under this Act, notwithstanding the director's asserted authorship.

Any person who falsely applies a geographical indication prescribed under this Act to goods not originating in the territory associated with such indication, or who, with intent to deceive, uses a false geographical indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. The registrar, upon receiving credible information of such contravention, may initiate an investigation and, if satisfied, direct the cessation of the unlawful activity. Any aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the proceeding appellate board against any decision of the registrar concerning the imposition of penalties, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the decision. Failure to comply with an order of the appellate board shall attract a daily penalty of ten thousand rupees until compliance is achieved.

Any person who, without due authorization from the copyright owner, makes, distributes, imports into India, or offers for sale any article embodying an infringing copy of a work protected under this Act, and such article is demonstrably employed for industrial application, shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and with a fine which may extend to ten lakhs rupees. The right holder may, subject to the provisions herein, seek injunctive relief against any party engaged in such infringing activity. Further, where the infringement involves commercial reproduction intended for profit, enhanced penalties as determined by the relevant judicial authority shall apply. Damages recoverable shall be assessed based on demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner.

The registrar shall maintain a register of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs, and all applications for registration shall be made in the prescribed manner to the registrar. Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a layout-design may apply for registration, subject to the payment of the applicable fee as provided herein. The application shall include a detailed description of the layout-design, including supporting documentation demonstrating its originality. Upon receipt of a complete application, the registrar shall examine it for compliance with the requirements of this Act. Where the registrar is satisfied that the application meets all criteria, the layout-design shall be registered and an official certificate of registration issued. The registrar registration sub shall be open for public inspection, subject to reasonable restrictions to protect confidential information. Any objection to the registration may be filed with the registrar within the prescribed period.

Any process resulting in a commercially viable product, and claiming novelty as provided herein, shall be subject to examination for patentability. An invention shall not be considered novel if it lacks a distinct step from existing knowledge, or if it is obvious to a person skilled in the art. Where a product is patented, the patentee shall have the exclusive right to prevent others from making, using, selling, or importing that product. However, such exclusivity shall be subject to licensing provisions under this Act, particularly in cases of national emergency or public interest. 

A patented invention may be revoked if it is proven, through due process, that it was not truly inventive, or that essential details were concealed during the application process. Any person alleging infringement of a patented invention may seek redressal through established judicial procedures. The Controller of Patents shall maintain a public register of all granted and pending patents, accessible for inspection as prescribed.

For the purposes of this Act, the term "International Bureau" means the General Division of the World Intellectual Property Organization and includes any successor body designated under the Madrid Protocol. An application for registration of a trade mark may be made in accordance with the provisions of the Madrid Protocol, subject to such conditions as are prescribed herein relating to translation and representation of the mark. The trade proprietor registered under this Act shall be deemed the applicant for the purposes of an international application filed through the International Bureau, provided that all required fees have been duly paid.

For the purposes of this Act, "petition particulars contained" shall mean the specific details relating to a registered layout-design, as delineated in Schedule B annexed hereto. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the date of first fixation, the geographic location where the layout-design was initially made available, and a comprehensive description of the circuit elements comprising the integrated circuit. Failure to accurately reflect these petition particulars contained during registration proceedings may render subsequent claims of infringement registered less defensible under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record of all such particulars as provided herein.

Any person intending to establish a copyright society for the collective administration of rights in literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works may apply to the Central Government in the prescribed manner setting forth particulars as to its aims and objects, composition, area of operation and financial resources. The application shall be accompanied by a draft memorandum of association and rules and regulations governing the functioning of the proposed copyright society. Upon receipt of such application, the Central Government may, after making such inquiry as it deems fit, register the copyright society if it is satisfied that the applicant fulfils all requirements as provided herein. A registered copyright society shall act on behalf of its members in licensing their rights and collecting royalties for the use of their works, subject to terms and conditions determined by the society itself but consistent with this Act. The funds collected by a copyright society shall be distributed amongst its members after deducting administrative expenses, according to predetermined rules ensuring equitable distribution based on usage data. Any dispute regarding such distribution may be resolved through internal grievance redressal mechanisms established within the society.

The Registrar may refuse registration of a trade mark if it contains as a dominant feature the shape of goods, but such refusal shall only apply where that shape is dictated solely by factors including packaging efficiency, manufacturing processes, or aesthetic considerations intrinsic to the product's function. An appeal against this decision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the Registrar’s order. Provided that, if the applicant demonstrates a distinctiveness acquired through extensive use and consumer recognition subsequent to initial sale, the refusal may be reconsidered subject to evidence establishing such acquired distinctiveness outweighs any deceptive effect arising from the marks shape goods. The burden of proving this lies with the appellant.

The right of copyright under this Act in a cinematograph film shall extend to the producer thereof and where such film has been produced subject to a written agreement assigning to any person the exclusive right to reproduce the film, that person shall be deemed the owner for the purposes of infringement proceedings. Provided that, if the ownership of the underlying literary or musical work incorporated within the cinematograph film is disputed, the court may require evidence establishing the rightful claimant prior to adjudicating on the validity of the producer’s copyright claim relating to the entire film. Any appeal arising from a determination under this provision shall lie to the appellate forum as provided herein, subject to the satisfaction of conditions regarding deposit and costs.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered proprietor may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of their registered trademark for specific goods or services within defined geographical territories. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Trade Marks Registry, specifying the licensed rights, duration, and royalty structure. The grantor retains ownership of the underlying trade mark and may revoke a license upon material breach by the licensee, as provided herein. Further, a registered proprietor may assign their trademark, or any part thereof, to another person, either wholly or partially, subject to prior approval from the Registrar where such assignment involves use outside India. Any assignee shall be deemed the new registered proprietor with all attendant rights and obligations under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant documentation establishing prior publication, if any, and such documentation must clearly indicate the date and place of first disclosure. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding the manner applying appellate procedures in cases where the applicant claims priority based on an earlier foreign application. Provided that the applicant demonstrates diligent pursuit of the foreign right, the registration shall be deemed to have been filed on the priority date. Any appeal against a decision refusing registration, or imposing conditions thereof, must be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall follow the manner applying appellate jurisdiction as prescribed under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, a “geographical indication” means an indication which identifies such goods as originating from a place where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic thereof is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. An *indication use geographical* shall be deemed to qualify as a geographical indication only if such indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wine, spirits, beverages, herbs, spices, cereals, or manufactured articles having a distinctive name corresponding to a specific region or locality. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and their origin, provided that this requirement shall not apply where the connection is apparent from the geographical indication itself.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is descriptive of the goods or services for which it is sought to be registered, the Registrar may allow the registration if he is satisfied that, by reason of its use and reputation, the mark has acquired distinctiveness applicable to those goods. Such acquisition shall not preclude an appeal against the decision of the Registrar permitting such registration, wherein the appellant may demonstrate that the purported acquired distinctiveness is attributable solely to extensive advertising campaigns undertaken by the applicant and does not genuinely reflect consumer perception concerning purposes identifying goods. The burden of proving this lies upon the appellant, subject to a rebuttable presumption in favour of the applicant’s claim.

Where a patent applicant has submitted a provisional specification relating to an invention, and subsequently seeks to assign or license rights in respect of that invention prior to the filing of a complete specification, such assignment or license shall be conditional upon the timely submission of said complete specification as provided herein. The terms of any agreement granting a license may include provisions for royalty payments calculated on potential future sales based on projections derived from the provisional disclosure, subject to adjustment should the granted patent’s scope differ materially from that initially claimed. Further, an applicant who has entered into an assignment or licensing agreement predicated upon a provisional specification complete shall be obligated to notify all assignees and licensees of any material amendments made to the invention during the period preceding the filing of the complete specification. Failure to provide such notification may render the assignee or licensee entitled to damages.

Any person who falsely represents goods as originating from a specific geographical area, thereby creating a false geographical indication relation, shall be liable for prosecution under this Act. Such misrepresentation includes the use of any name, sign, or symbol which indicates a false provenance in connection with the sale or distribution of goods. Where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication proves that another party has engaged in such deceptive practices intending to mislead consumers regarding the true origin of the goods, the adjudicating officer may impose a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, any goods found to bear such falsely applied geographical indications shall be deemed contraband and subject to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Repeated offences shall attract enhanced penalties and potential imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, subject to investigation and proof of intent.

Where any question arises concerning whether a person is, or is not, entitled to be registered as a patent agent under this Act, the Controller may, subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, determine such question. An application for appeal against an order made by the Controller determining entitlement shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of that order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the applicant alleges the order to be erroneous in law or fact. Provided that if the appellant satisfies the Appellate Board that sufficient cause existed for the delay, the Board may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay. The Controller’s decision regarding registration as a patent agent shall be final pending such an appeal.

An application for rectification register may be filed by any person aggrieved by an entry appearing in the Designs Register, subject to compliance with the prescribed forms and fees. Such applications shall specify the particulars of the entry sought to be rectified and state the grounds on which such rectification is claimed, including instances where the design lacks novelty or originality as defined under this Act. The Controller may entertain any application for rectification register if satisfied that it involves a substantial question relating to the registrability of a design. Notice of the application shall be served upon the registered proprietor in the prescribed manner, allowing them an opportunity to file their response within a stipulated period. Any order made by the Controller concerning the rectification register is appealable before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any person who obstructs an officer authorized under this Act in the exercise of his powers, or disobeys any direction given by such officer, shall be deemed guilty of an offence and liable to a penalty of five thousand rupees for the first instance, and ten thousand rupees for subsequent instances. Failure to comply with a notice issued by the Agriculture Commissioner requiring submission of records pertaining to plant breeding activities will attract a daily penalty of one thousand rupees until compliance is achieved. Further, any entity found to be engaging in unauthorized commercialization of a registered variety without proper authorization from the Registrar shall face suspension of their registration and a fine not exceeding twenty-five thousand rupees, as provided herein. The Agriculture Commissioner may also initiate prosecution for wilful default.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall demonstrate, to the satisfaction of the Plant Variety Protection Authority, full compliance with the provisions relating to essentially derived varieties as provided herein. Such compliance shall include the maintenance of detailed records documenting the lineage and characteristics of the parent line from which the new variety is derived, and the provision of such records upon request by the Authority or any aggrieved party. Provided that, a breeder may also demonstrate compliance through the submission of a statutory declaration affirming adherence to all breeder complied provisions and a commitment to ongoing monitoring for genetic drift. Failure to maintain adequate records or to truthfully declare compliance shall constitute grounds for rejection of the application or revocation of any granted protection, subject to a reasonable opportunity to be heard. The Authority may, at its discretion, require independent verification of the breeder’s claims.

The trade mark registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration, conduct an examination to ascertain whether the mark satisfies the requirements of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Any deficiency in the application, including but not limited to incorrect classification of goods or services, or a failure to provide a clear representation of the mark, shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be granted a period of thirty days to rectify the same. Where the trade mark registrar is satisfied that the application meets all formal requirements, a notice of acceptance shall be issued, and the mark shall be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal. Subject to any opposition filed within the prescribed period, and provided that the applicant complies with all outstanding requirements, the trade mark registrar may proceed to register the trade mark. The registrar’s decision regarding acceptance or refusal shall be communicated in writing, and an appeal may be preferred as provided herein.

Every application for the registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by the prescribed registry fee, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government and notified in the Official Gazette. Failure to remit the full registry fee at the time of application shall render the application incomplete and liable to rejection, subject to an opportunity being given to the applicant to rectify the deficiency within thirty days of a notice issued by the Registrar. Any applicant who knowingly provides a false declaration regarding the payment of the registry fee, or attempts to evade payment, shall be punishable with a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees. The Registrar may, however, extend the time for payment in exceptional circumstances, provided that a late payment surcharge, calculated at ten percent of the original fee, is also submitted. All fees collected under this Act shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

Where a trade mark is registered in India and subsequently extended through an international registration process administered by the International Bureau, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred under this Act as if the international registration had been directly effected in India. Any person seeking to challenge the validity of such an internationally protected trade mark may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal, subject to demonstrating a lack of use within the territory of India for a continuous period exceeding five years following the date of extension. The proprietor shall be deemed to have knowledge of any conflicting prior rights existing in India at the time of application for international registration and shall remain liable for any damages arising from infringement occurring before such extension.

An application to register patents shall contain a specification describing the invention clearly and completely for enabling any person skilled in the art to make and use it. The applicant must also furnish details regarding priority, if claiming under a prior application. Upon receipt of an application, the court registrar shall verify compliance with prescribed formalities relating to form and execution. Further, the registrar may require the applicant to submit clarifications or amendments deemed necessary for proper examination. Any deficiency in these particulars will be communicated to the applicant, who shall have opportunity to rectify them within the time specified under this Act. Failure to comply with such requirements will result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

Where an investigation is initiated under this Act concerning alleged infringement of a registered layout-design, the Intellectual Property Office shall provide all relevant documentation pertaining to the registration, including technical specifications and design schematics, to the appointed judicial member technical. The judicial member technical may request further clarification or supplementary information from either the complainant or the respondent, provided that such requests are limited to matters directly impacting the determination of infringement. Any expert testimony presented must be accompanied by a written report detailing the methodology employed and the basis for conclusions reached; this shall be accessible to both parties under this Act. The Intellectual Property Office shall ensure compliance with procedural timelines as prescribed herein.

An application for a patent shall not proceed to grant unless the prescribed fees have been duly remitted to the office patent office and all required forms are completed in accordance with the regulations. Where an applicant has failed to respond adequately to any communication from the controller within the stipulated time, the application may be deemed abandoned; however, such abandonment is subject to review upon a written request demonstrating good cause for the delay. Any person aggrieved by the acceptance of a patent or the making of a patent grant may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the office patent office, provided that the grounds for opposition are clearly stated and supported by relevant evidence. The controller shall consider any such opposition registration in accordance with established procedures.

Any person aggrieved by the unauthorized reproduction of a work in which copyright subsists, as provided herein, may institute a suit for injunction restraining such infringement. The High Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all suits arising under this Act relating to copyright. Where a plaintiff proves that an act constitutes an infringement of copyright, the court may grant relief including damages or account of profits, at the option of the plaintiff. The amount of damages awarded shall be determined having regard to the nature and extent of the infringement, and any benefit accruing to the defendant by reason of such infringement. 

The Registrar of Copyrights shall maintain a register of copyrights, and all entries therein shall be *prescribed* in accordance with rules made under this Act. Any person desiring to obtain copyright in a work shall submit an application to the Registrar in the form so *prescribed*, accompanied by the necessary fee. Failure to comply with these requirements may render the registration invalid or subject to revocation, and no rights shall accrue until proper registration is effected as per the rules.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any disclaimers required under this Act. Where an applicant is recorded as the proprietor of a trade mark upon initial registration, subsequent alterations to ownership details shall necessitate notification to the Registrar within thirty days of such change. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the transfer or assignment and shall verify compliance with prescribed forms and fees. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence, or non-compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein, will result in temporary suspension of the application register proprietor’s rights until rectification is achieved. Any person aggrieved by such a decision may appeal under this Act.

Any person who, without due cause and with intent to deceive or injure the proprietor of a registered trade mark, uses an identical or deceptively similar mark relating to goods or services for which the said registered trade mark is registered shall be guilty of an offence under this Act. Such offender shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees, and may extend to two hundred thousand rupees. Where such use also infringes patent rights relating to the manufacturing process of those goods or services, the aggregate penalty shall be doubled. The proprietor may further seek injunctions preventing future infringing acts as provided herein.

Any person desiring registration of means invention technology shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by a detailed description of the technology, including its technical specifications and operational principles. The application shall also include a statement outlining the novelty and inventive step inherent in the proposed means invention technology, demonstrating a clear advancement over existing technologies. Supporting documentation, such as experimental data or simulations, may be furnished to substantiate claims of efficacy. 

An applicant may, subject to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein, claim priority based on an earlier application filed in a convention country. The Controller shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with procedural requirements and may require the applicant to amend the application if necessary. Registration shall be granted only upon satisfactory verification of the means invention technology’s patentability and payment of the prescribed fees.

Any person asserting a right to variety registration shall submit a detailed claim outlining the essentially derived variety, or the dependent variety, as the case may be, and shall provide demonstrable evidence of its distinctiveness, stability and uniformity, failing which the application shall be deemed incomplete and liable for rejection. Any false representation made in such registration claims purposes, including but not limited to the origin, characteristics, or breeding methods of the variety, shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. Furthermore, the Registrar may, subject to a reasoned order, revoke any registration obtained through fraudulent means. Repeated offences under this Act, or attempts to circumvent the provisions relating to registration claims purposes, may result in disqualification from future applications for a period of five years. The burden of proof regarding the veracity of any claim shall lie with the applicant.

Where a patent applicant submits an invention described in a provisional specification, and subsequently assigns or licenses the rights to that invention to another party prior to the furnishing of a complete specification, such assignment or license shall be subject to the conditions outlined herein. The assignor retains the right to file a complete specification within the prescribed time limit as provided under this Act; however, any subsequent assignment or further licensing agreement relating to the invention must explicitly acknowledge and incorporate the terms of the original provisional specification’s disclosure. Failure to do so may render such later agreements unenforceable in respect of aspects of the invention not adequately described therein. The Controller shall have the power to determine whether a complete specification sufficiently corresponds to the subject matter disclosed in the initial provisional specification, considering any subsequent assignments or licenses executed.

The Controller of Patents shall maintain an omission register detailing particulars of patents where the prescribed fees for maintaining the patent in force have not been paid. Any person desiring to inspect the omission register shall submit an application to the Controller in the manner as prescribed. The application shall clearly identify the patent in question, referencing at a minimum the patent number and the name of the patentee as recorded on the register of patents. Where a patentee seeks to restore a patent following omission from the register, they shall submit a request for restoration within the period stipulated under this Act, accompanied by payment of the prescribed restoration fee and any outstanding renewal fees. The Controller may, subject to verification of the request and payment, reinstate the patent and record the restoration in the omission register, noting the date of restoration for purposes identifying goods manufactured under the patent after such reinstatement. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the patent being deemed revoked.

For the purposes of this Act, "international trademark" means a trademark registered through an application originating in India and extended under the provisions of the Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks. Such international trademarks shall be deemed to have effect only as to the Contracting Parties designated in the international registration, subject to any limitations or conditions specified therein. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating compliance with the requirements of the Madrid Agreement before proceeding with an examination or acceptance of an application for extension of protection. Any opposition proceedings relating to an international trademark shall be conducted under rules consistent with those applicable to applications filed directly under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, where an act patent has been granted, any person aggrieved by a decision or order made under this Act relating to the grant, revocation, or infringement of such patent may appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall have the power to entertain appeals arising from orders passed by the Controller relating to compulsory licenses and to pass such orders as it deems fit, including setting aside or modifying any such order. Further, a party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The High Court shall have similar powers and jurisdiction in respect of appeals under this Act as it has in relation to suits relating to tortious infringement of patent rights, provided that costs may be awarded at the discretion of the court.

An applicant seeking registration of a geographical indication shall file an application with the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication as it is proposed to be registered, a description of the products for which the indication seeks protection, and the area of its origin. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any defects or ambiguities therein.

The Registrar shall publish particulars of the application in the Trade Marks Journal and invite objections from interested parties within the time specified under this Act. Any person alleging that the registration of the geographical indication would be contrary to law or prejudicial to the public interest may file an objection. The Registrar shall consider all such objections and, after affording the applicant and objector an opportunity of being heard, determine whether the application should proceed for registration in the registrar register title.

Where an application for patents has been refused under this Act, any person interested may appeal against such refusal to the Controller. The term “person interested” includes, but is not limited to, the applicant’s assignees, legal representatives, and those who have derived a right to make an application from the true inventor or their assignees. Such an appeal shall be filed within three months of the date of communication of the refusal order. Upon receiving such an appeal, the Controller may require the appellant to furnish security for costs, as provided herein. The Controller shall afford the applicant and any other person interested an opportunity to present their views in writing or orally regarding the merits of the application. Failure to comply with procedural requirements under this Act may render the appeal inadmissible.

The owner of a registered trademark may grant a license permitting the use of their mark in relation to specified goods or services, subject to conditions stipulated within the licensing agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar of Trade Marks in the prescribed manner and accompanied by the requisite fee. Where the licensed goods are imported, the importer shall comply with all applicable provisions under the Customs Act 1962 relating to declaration of trademarks and payment of duties. Any subsequent assignee of a trademark license retains the rights and obligations as if they were the original licensor, subject to any modifications agreed upon in writing by both parties. The Registrar may require production of documentation substantiating the chain of title for such assignments.

The Registrar shall consider any petition for rectification of the register relating to a registered trade mark, and shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, make an order for rectification if satisfied that the facts alleged in the petition are established. Provided that, where the petition alleges that a trade mark was not lawfully registered, or that it has been obtained improperly, the Registrar shall not make an order for rectification unless the petitioner proves that they have suffered damage as a result of the wrongful registration. Further, the Registrar may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the petitioner to furnish evidence of prior use of a similar mark, to demonstrate a genuine connection between the petitioner and the subject matter of the rectification. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may, within a period of two months from the date of the order, prefer an appeal to the High Court. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell, distributes, hires or displays any product containing a layout-design infringing the copyright in such layout-design shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the creation provided layout in whole or in part, whether temporary or permanent, and whether by means of printing, lithography, photography, electronic scanning, or otherwise. The registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings for damages sustained as a result of the infringement, subject to limitations prescribed herein regarding contributory infringement. Penalties for repeat offences shall be doubled, and any goods found infringing the layout-design are liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein.

For the purpose of this Act, "design" shall mean any wholly original artistic creation relating to the shape, configuration, pattern or composition of lines or colours applied to any article whether two-dimensional or three-dimensional, and capable of being reproduced in any material other than by an industrial process. A design shall not include a trade mark under this Act or a property mark as defined therein. The term "industrial application" with respect to a registered design signifies its use or exploitation for the manufacture of articles, subject to conditions prescribed herein regarding novelty and originality; provided that such application does not infringe upon any prior copyright existing in relation to the underlying artistic work.

Where the Registrar deems it necessary to seek clarification or additional information from an applicant regarding a layout-design registration, the Registrar shall issue notice to the applicant. The manner issuing notice shall be in writing and delivered by registered post with acknowledgement due to the address specified by the applicant in their application form, or at such other address as may subsequently be notified under this Act. Provided that, if the applicant fails to acknowledge receipt of the notice within thirty days, a further notice may be served through publication in a widely circulated national newspaper. The Registrar shall record the details of each notice issued and any responses received, forming part of the registration file.

Where a registered trademark is assigned or transmitted, the assignee or transferee shall be entitled to exercise all rights and privileges that were vested in the assignor or transferor immediately prior to the assignment or transmission. The Registrar may require proof satisfactory to the Registrar of such assignment or transmission before registering the new proprietor. Any person claiming right to the said trademark by way of subsequent assignment or transmission shall, subject to any agreement to the contrary, be deemed constructively noticee of all earlier assignments and transmissions. Failure to provide adequate documentation demonstrating a clear chain of title relating to an assignment transmission rights may result in the Registrar’s refusal to register the claim. The assignor shall remain liable for any infringement committed prior to the date of assignment or transmission unless expressly released by agreement.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any licensee granted rights under a license relating to a patent may, with the prior written consent of the patentee, assign such license, either wholly or partially, to any person or entity. Such assignment shall be recorded in the prescribed manner and shall take effect only upon such recording. Where a patent has been assigned, any subsequent dealings concerning the exploitation of the invention for which the means patent is granted shall be deemed to relate to the assignee as if they were the original patentee. The patentee may grant further licenses relating to the same invention, provided that such grants do not conflict with existing assignments or licenses and are consistent with the terms previously agreed upon under this Act. Any person acquiring an interest in a means patent by way of assignment shall be subject to all covenants and conditions contained within the original license agreement.

Where an application for a patent relates to a process for producing a substance and that substance is used as an ingredient or intermediate in the manufacture of another substance, the determination of novelty and inventive step shall be undertaken with due consideration given to the nature of the process itself. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish particulars relating to the working of the process claimed, including details concerning any equipment utilized and the yield obtained under standard conditions. Any objection raised by a third party regarding the validity of a patent for a process respect patent shall be adjudicated according to the prescribed procedures, with emphasis on demonstrating prior use or public knowledge undermining inventive step. The applicant bears the onus of proving that the claimed process is capable of being performed by a person skilled in the art and produces the desired result consistently.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is deceptively similar to a prior mark already uses trade mark in relation to identical or closely related goods or services, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations and counter-statements. The Registrar shall unconditionally registrar shall consider all such submissions, including evidence presented by both the objector and the applicant, and may direct the holding of hearings where necessary for clarification. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision, subject to payment of prescribed fees and compliance with procedural requirements as provided herein.

A variety shall be considered an essentially derived variety if it is not distinguishable from the initial variety in terms of characteristics relevant to its identification, while retaining the essential characteristics of that initial variety. The applicant seeking registration of such a variety shall submit evidence demonstrating a clear lineage tracing back to the parent or initial variety, and proof establishing that the essentially derived variety has been produced from the initial variety through successive propagation or hybridization. Provided that, if the production of the essentially derived variety requires repeated use of the initial variety, then consent of the breeder of such initial variety shall be mandatory for registration as provided herein. Any person alleging a variety to be an essentially derived variety may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority with supporting documentation and evidence of propagation history. The authority may require expert testimony or field inspections to verify the claim.

Subject to the provisions of this Patents Act, 1970, any person claiming title to an invention which is the subject matter of a patent application may grant licenses under that application to other parties, either wholly or partially, and such license agreement shall be in writing and specify the scope of rights granted. Assignment of patent rights, including all or any part of the patent, the benefit of the application, or the patent itself, may also be effected by written instrument, and registration of such assignment with the Controller is mandatory for it to be deemed valid against third parties. Further, where a license or assignment includes provisions relating to royalties or other considerations, these shall be clearly articulated within the agreement. The Central Government may, under this Act, prescribe conditions governing the transfer of patent rights to ensure equitable access and prevent anti-competitive practices related to patented technologies.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method for, in relation to, or concerning the manufacture or production of a substance, and such method involves one or more steps already known in the art, the Controller may allow the grant of a patent only if it is established that the claimed invention results in a technical effect which goes beyond the combination of the known steps. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act allowing or refusing a patent may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order, provided that the appellant shall demonstrate before the Board that the decision was manifestly erroneous in law and would materially affect his interests. The burden of proving said technical effect shall lie upon the applicant for the patent.

A complete specification filed under this Act shall disclose the invention in a manner sufficient for a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect, and shall define the scope of the invention for which protection is claimed. Where an applicant claims priority from one or more earlier applications filed in a convention country, such claim of priority shall be in writing and filed within the prescribed period from the date of the earliest such application constituting the basis for the claim. The priority date, when validly claimed, shall be the reference date for determining the novelty of the invention as disclosed in the complete specification. However, such a claim of priority shall not be valid if the earlier application was not a complete application as defined herein, or if the applicant fails to furnish, as required, certified copies of the earlier application within the stipulated timeframe. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the priority date shall be considered for the purposes of assessing the inventive step.

Any individual engaging in the design, manufacture, import, or distribution of semiconductor integrated circuits layouts shall maintain an entry register document detailing all practitioners employed by them, including their qualifications and areas of specialization. Failure to do so constitutes a violation under this Act and is subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees for the first offence, and one million rupees for subsequent offences. Any person found to be employing a practitioner without proper registration or verification as recorded in the entry register document shall also be liable to pay a fine of two hundred fifty thousand rupees. The Registering Authority may conduct inspections at any time to ensure compliance with these provisions; obstruction of such inspection is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months.

A person who, without being duly registered under this Act, offers to provide or provides services relating to the preparation, filing, prosecution, maintenance, or defence of applications for patents, or otherwise acts in the capacity of a *practise patent agent*, shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Any individual found to have engaged in such conduct is further subject to civil proceedings wherein any party demonstrably harmed by their actions may seek compensatory damages proportionate to the losses incurred as a direct result thereof. The Controller shall maintain a publicly accessible register of registered patent agents and may publish notices regarding individuals found to be acting contrary to the provisions herein. Further, an aggrieved party may apply to the relevant High Court for injunctive relief against any person engaging in unauthorized practice.

Application for registration shall be made to the Geographical Indications Registry in the prescribed form, detailing the characteristics of the goods originating from the specified territory, including but not limited to agricultural practices employed, traditional processing methods utilized, and unique qualities attributable solely to that origin. The applicant must demonstrate exclusive control over the quality and reputation of the goods as they relate to the geographical indication sought. Provided that the proposed name does not conflict with any existing trademark or prior right under this Act, and subject to verification by the Registrar regarding the authenticity of the claimed territorial boundaries, registration shall apply upon satisfaction that the application meets all requirements stipulated herein. Further, the applicant must provide evidence of widespread recognition amongst consumers associating the goods with the indicated geographical origin.

The right to use a registered trademark is, subject to any conditions specified in the registration, freely transferable. For the purposes of this Act, “transferable” includes, without limitation, assignment, pledge, license, and any other method by which ownership or rights pertaining to the trademark may be conveyed. A trademark shall be deemed transmissible even where such transfer involves a change in the goods or services for which it is registered, provided that the assignee undertakes to use the mark in accordance with the terms of registration and applicable law. Any agreement relating to the transmission of a trademark shall be void if it restricts the free assignability of the trademark under this Act.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for the transmission of the ownership of a trade mark already registered under this Act, verify that the proposed assignee is capable of satisfying all requirements for registration as if they were the original applicant. Such verification shall include confirmation of the assignor’s legal title and consent to the transfer, evidenced by a duly executed instrument. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the relationship between the transferor and transferee where unusual circumstances exist. Transmission is deemed effective from the date specified in the instrument of assignment unless otherwise stipulated, and notice thereof shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. Any subsequent dealings with the trade mark shall reflect the new ownership as recorded by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a proposed application registration mark may be filed with the Registrar, accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed under this Act. The applicant shall furnish details including but not limited to the representation of the mark, goods or services associated therewith, and the period of exclusivity sought. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish it in the Trade Marks Journal for public inspection and opposition. Any person possessing a relevant interest may file a notice of opposition within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. If an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence. The applicant’s right to the mark may be assigned subject to compliance with regulations governing such assignments under this Act; however, patent shall assigned only upon written consent from the Controller General of Patents, Designs, and Trademarks.

Where the copyright subsists in a literary work created under contract for services, the right to grant licenses and assign such copyright shall vest initially in the party commissioning the work, provided that the agreement expressly stipulates the terms governing subsequent exploitation. Such agreements may delineate specific rights granted to the creator, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, public performance, and adaptation of the literary work. Further, where an assignment of copyright is made, it shall be deemed a conveyance of all rights therein unless the instrument of assignment specifically reserves certain privileges for the assignor. The assignee shall have full authority to sub-license the literary work subject to any limitations outlined in the original contractual agreement or subsequent assignments. Any royalties derived from such licensing activities shall be distributed as per the terms agreed upon between the parties involved, reflecting their respective contributions and negotiated percentages.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark, aggrieved by any act which constitutes an infringement of their rights as provided herein, may serve a notice of intent to defend upon the alleged infringer, and simultaneously notify the Registrar of Trade Marks of such intent. Such notification shall include a detailed account of the alleged infringement, specifying the goods or services affected and the manner of infringement. Where a party receives a notice of intent to defend, they may, within thirty days of receipt, submit a counter-statement to both the registered proprietor and the Registrar, outlining grounds for disputing the claim of infringement. Failure to notify the Registrar within the prescribed timeframe may be considered an abandonment of the right to contest the infringement. The Registrar shall, upon receiving both the notice and any counter-statement, initiate a preliminary inquiry to determine if a prima facie case exists for further adjudication, subject to the provisions relating to rectification of the register.

The registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain whether the mark is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. The registrar may, if satisfied that the mark meets the requirements of this Act, proceed to advertise the application in the prescribed manner. However, the registrar shall refuse the application if the mark is deceptively similar to an existing trade mark, or if it is prohibited under the provisions relating to scandalous or offensive marks. Subject to the payment of the prescribed fees, the registrar may, at any time before the completion of the registration process, require the applicant to amend the application or furnish further information. Any decision of the registrar regarding refusal may be appealed as per the established procedure.

Applications for registration of designs shall be made to the Controller in such form and manner as may be prescribed. Every application shall contain a full and clear representation of the design, either by means of drawings or photographs, accompanied by a statement defining the nature of the article in which the design is applied or proposed to be applied. The Patent Office shall maintain a register of designs, open for public inspection during office hours. Any person may inspect such register and obtain copies thereof, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. An application once filed shall not be altered without the written permission of the Controller. The Controller may require any further information or clarification deemed necessary for processing an application under this Act.

Any person who creates a design, being an aesthetic feature of an article, shall be entitled to register such design under this Act, subject to novelty and originality requirements as may be prescribed. The right conferred by registration shall subsist for ten years from the date of registration. Where a semiconductor integrated circuit is embodied in an article, the layout-design thereof shall also constitute a registrable design provided it satisfies the criteria outlined herein. The exclusive right of the registered proprietor extends to reproduction or substantial imitation of the design, and any unauthorized act infringing such right shall be actionable. Remedies for infringement include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages accounting for lost profits, and delivery up of infringing articles for destruction as determined by a competent court. A person aggrieved by an incorrect refusal of registration may appeal to the High Court within ninety days from the date of such refusal, subject to prescribed procedures and fees.

Where any act or omission constituting an offence under this Act is committed by a department or unit within a public corporation, every officer of the said corporation who was responsible for the management, control, or supervision of the department or unit at the time when the act or omission was so committed shall be deemed to be guilty of a commission offence attributable to such department or unit. Such officers shall be liable to pay compensation as determined by the Controller, proportionate to their degree of responsibility in failing to prevent the infringing activity. The Controller may, upon receiving complaints regarding inadequate oversight, issue directives for improved internal controls within the corporation. Further, any person abetting or conspiring to commit an offence under this Act shall also be subject to penalties as provided herein, and such liability extends to those who knowingly benefit from the illegal activities.

A trade mark comprising a description of the characteristics, quality, or quantity of the goods or services sought to be identified shall not be registrable unless such description is distinctive and not merely descriptive of the goods or services themselves. However, a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through long and continuous use may, subject to the provisions of this Act, be registered. An application for registration of a description trade mark shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating a period of not less than five years of continuous use in commerce, and a clear showing that consumers primarily perceive the description as a brand identifier rather than a mere statement of fact. Any objection raised by the Registrar regarding lack of distinctiveness shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the appellant demonstrates a prima facie case of acquired distinctiveness based on evidence of extensive advertising and sales figures. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition.

For the purposes of this Act, "layout-design" means the three-dimensional representation of an integrated circuit, reduced to a physical form by any manufacturing technique and includes both the arrangement of elements on the semiconductor material and the interconnections between them. The term “element” shall include active and passive electronic components, semiconductors, interconnects, leads, pads, bonding wires, chips, or other functional units. An application for registration of a layout-design shall be filed with the registrar semiconductor integrated, who may require such particulars as are necessary to ascertain whether the layout-design is original and not contrary to public order or morality. The registrar semiconductor integrated shall maintain a record of all applications and registrations under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be deemed complete only when all prescribed fees have been remitted and the required documentation, including detailed schematics and topographical representations conforming to standards specified by the Controller General, has been submitted. The Controller General may reject an application if it contains any material which is contrary to public order or decency, or if the layout design does not meet the originality criteria as provided herein. A layout design registered under this Act shall confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights relating to the reproduction and commercial use of that layout design within the territory of India. Subject to compliance with these provisions, a registered layout design remains valid for a period of ten years from the date of registration or for the term of copyright subsisting in any element incorporated therein, whichever is longer.

A visual recording, whether expressed by means of any mechanical device or otherwise, shall be deemed to be a work in which copyright subsists, subject to the provisions of this Act. The author of a visual recording shall be the person by whom the recording is made, and in the case of a recording made on the direction of a person, that person shall be deemed to be the author. Where a visual recording is made as the result of a contract for work, the person who commissions the recording, subject to any agreement to the contrary, shall be the first owner of the copyright therein. 

Any person intending to make a copy of a visual recording for purposes other than private use shall obtain a license from the owner of the copyright, and such license may be subject to payment of a royalty as determined by mutual agreement. Failure to obtain such license, or contravention of the terms thereof, shall constitute an infringement of copyright as provided herein. The rights conferred by this Act in relation to visual recordings are subject to such limitations and exceptions as may be prescribed.

The Authority shall, upon receiving an application for registration as a registered breeder, verify that the applicant has contributed to the replenishment of the Gene Fund in accordance with the prescribed procedures. Such contribution may be made through the deposit of germplasm, data relating to plant genetic resources, or financial contributions determined by the Central Government. Applications from individuals who have not fulfilled their obligations regarding contributions to the Gene Fund shall be deemed incomplete and will not proceed for further consideration under this Act. The Authority may require additional documentation demonstrating compliance with contribution requirements prior to granting registration. A registered breeder is obligated to maintain records pertaining to any germplasm deposited into the Gene Fund, detailing its origin and characteristics, accessible to the Central Government upon request. Failure to comply with these record-keeping obligations shall render the registered breeder liable for penalties as provided herein.

Any invention developed as a result of research undertaken by a government undertaking, or to which the government undertaking has acquired ownership, shall be deemed to be an invention for the purposes of this Act, notwithstanding any prior public knowledge or use thereof, provided that such invention is not disclosed to the public without prior intimation to the Controller. Where a government undertaking seeks a patent for such an invention, it may, subject to fulfilling all statutory requirements as provided herein, proceed directly to grant, bypassing certain procedural delays ordinarily applicable to patent applications. Should a dispute arise regarding the ownership of such an invention between the government undertaking and any other person claiming interest, the matter shall be referred to the High Court having jurisdiction. The government undertaking shall be liable to pay prescribed fees, though a reduced rate may be considered in cases of inventions demonstrably benefiting national security or public health. Any revenue generated from the exploitation of a patented invention owned by a government undertaking shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to an integrated circuit may be opposed by any person claiming such right or interest as is provided herein. Such opposition shall be made within three months from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application under this Act. Where an opposition is filed, the Registrar shall forthwith direct the applicant and the opponent to submit their pleadings in a prescribed proceeding appellate before the designated authority. The form petition for opposition shall contain particulars as specified by the rules framed thereunder, including details regarding the claimed right or interest and grounds for objection. The authority shall afford both parties an opportunity of being heard and may order discovery of documents relevant to the dispute.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any patentee of a pharmaceutical substance may grant exclusive licenses authorizing specific acts relating to the manufacture, use, sale, or importation of the patented invention. Such licenses shall be assignable, both absolutely and conditionally, by instrument in writing duly executed and registered with the Controller. Where an assignment or license is made without disclosing the names of all reversionary interest holders, it shall be void unless such disclosure is subsequently rectified as provided herein. The patentee shall provide a copy of any licensing agreement to the Controller within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so may render the license unenforceable against third parties. Further, any licensee granted rights under this Act shall adhere to quality control standards prescribed by the relevant regulatory authority and be subject to inspection accordingly.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include a clear representation of the marks applied for and a list specifying the goods or services with which the mark is proposed to be associated. The Registrar may require an applicant to amend the description of goods or services if he considers it too wide or vague, ensuring clarity in identifying goods. Such amendments shall not alter the essence of the application. Where the trade mark includes non-distinctive elements, the applicant must demonstrate acquired distinctiveness through use, providing evidence of reputation and consumer recognition relating to the purposes identifying goods. The registered proprietor shall possess exclusive rights to use the trade mark in relation to the specified goods or services, subject to any limitations imposed during registration.

Subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, an application for the registration of a plant variety shall be deemed invalid if the proposed denomination is demonstrably confusingly similar to a previously assigned denomination under this Act, or infringes upon any existing trademark or other intellectual property right. The Registrar may require the applicant to provide evidence demonstrating that the denomination does not constitute an unfair appropriation of another’s creative work, particularly where such work involves a dramatic work used in promotional material relating to the variety. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the governing assignment denomination may file an appeal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order; provided that the Appellate Board shall consider whether the Registrar acted reasonably and fairly in reaching its determination.

For the purposes of this Act, a respect registered application shall mean an application filed under this Act seeking rectification of a registered trademark. Such application may seek to have a registered trademark expunged from the register or amended concerning its description of goods or services. A respect registered application is deemed to be without merit if it alleges solely that the mark has become non-distinctive due to use by another party, provided that such other party’s use was undertaken with consent from the registered proprietor. The Registrar may reject a respect registered application if it appears frivolous or vexatious as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if he considers that the proposed marks are likely to be confused with any registered trade marks under this Act. Upon such refusal, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Where an application is accepted and registered, the person whose name appears on the register as the proprietor of the trade mark shall be entitled to enforce the rights conferred by registration against all persons infringing or likely to infringe that trade mark. The Registrar may, upon receiving a request in writing from any interested party, require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark. Any alteration to details recorded concerning an application register proprietor must be notified to the Registrar within thirty days.

An application to register said geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes may be filed by any association of persons or producer group being residents of the Taluka of Devgad, Maharashtra, provided that such association or group demonstrates continuous and exclusive use of the name “Alphonso” in connection with mangoes originating from within the defined geographical boundaries for a period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. The Registrar shall require evidence establishing adherence to quality standards as prescribed by the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Packing) Order, and verification that any breeder registered variety utilized in cultivation maintains genetic purity consistent with traditional practices. Failure to comply with these conditions will render the application liable for rejection under this Act.

Any person claiming ownership of a services trade mark shall, prior to commencing provision of said services, apply for registration as provided herein, and failure to do so may attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a registered services trade mark is used by another person without the consent of the proprietor, a suit for infringement may be instituted in a District Court having jurisdiction. The Court, upon establishing infringement, shall grant an injunction restraining such use and may also award damages, assessed on the basis of lost profits or a reasonable royalty, to the aggrieved party. Any false application for a services trade mark, or any fraudulent misrepresentation in relation thereto, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, a registered proprietor failing to renew their services trade mark within the prescribed period shall be liable to a late fee, and the mark may be removed from the register if the delay exceeds six months.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against the registration of a proposed trade mark on the ground that it is likely to be confused with an earlier mark, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the proprietor use mark. The proprietor use mark may, within the time specified in such notice, file its response and evidence demonstrating the absence of likelihood of confusion. Such evidence may include data relating to actual consumer perception and sales figures for both marks. If the Registrar is satisfied, after considering the response and any counter-evidence filed by the objector, that there exists no reasonable possibility of confusion arising from the use of the proposed trade mark, registration shall proceed as provided herein. An appeal against this determination lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an application for registration of a geographical indication relates to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines, spirits, liqueurs, or beverages, compliance with established production practices shall be demonstrated to the Registrar through documented adherence to quality control measures. Such documentation must detail origin verification protocols and demonstrate consistent conformity to recognized standards applicable within the specified geographic area. Further, any association claiming collective ownership of a geographical indication shall provide evidence of widespread acceptance amongst producers operating within the defined territory; otherwise, registration may be denied. It is provided that impliedly registration shall occur where a mark incorporating a protected geographical indication is used in trade, and such use creates consumer confusion regarding origin, subject to an objection filed under this Act within six months.

Where any person alleges that the use of a sign or mark by another constitutes infringement under this Act, and such alleged infringer claims to be a bona fide user having adopted the sign or mark prior to the date of application for registration by the trade marks proprietor, the aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property forum. The defendant shall bear the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, both their prior use and that said use was genuinely continuous and not solely for the purpose of establishing rights against the proprietor. Further, if the alleged infringer is also a patentee holding valid patent protection relating to goods or services identical or closely related to those associated with the trade mark in question, this shall not automatically preclude them from claiming bona fide user status; however, such claim will be subject to heightened scrutiny as provided herein.

An applicant seeking protection through an application patent cooperation procedure shall furnish a declaration attesting to the best of their knowledge that the invention disclosed is novel and involves inventive step, failing which rectification proceedings may be initiated under this Act. Where an international search report indicates a lack of novelty or inventive character, the Controller may require the applicant to submit arguments rebutting such findings within a prescribed period; failure to do so shall render the application liable for rejection.
