Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to the grant or revocation of a patent arising from an application patent cooperation procedure may appeal to the Appellate Board. The burden of proving prior use or publication negating novelty lies upon the appellant, subject to procedural safeguards as provided herein regarding evidence and hearings.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee shall be entitled to grant exclusive licenses under the means patent granted, either for the whole duration of the patent or for such period as may be specified in the license agreement. Such license agreements may include conditions relating to royalty payments and sub-licensing rights, provided that these conditions do not unreasonably restrain trade or competition. Where a patentee desires to assign their interest in a means patent granted, including any pending application therefor, they shall execute an instrument of assignment in the prescribed form. This assignment shall be registrable under this Act and shall vest in the assignee all rights and privileges which the assignor possessed as patentee. The Controller may require such further information or undertakings from the assignee as are deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the provisions relating to working conditions.

An order appellate under this Act shall be made to a designated authority established by the Central Government, possessing requisite technical expertise in the relevant field of patenting. Such authority shall be empowered to review any decision of a Controller of Patents, including refusals of applications, revocations of patents, and determinations regarding infringement. Subject to the provisions contained herein, any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the order appellate within a period of sixty days from the date of the order sought to be appealed. The appellate authority may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend this period by a further thirty days. Provided that, the appellate authority shall not entertain any appeal unless the appellant has deposited the prescribed fee and furnished a certified copy of the order appealed against. Any decision of the order appellate shall be final and binding, except as otherwise provided for review to the High Court.

An application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which it is received by the Controller or his representative. For the purposes of this Act, an application relating to a process for producing a substance shall include an application relating to the use of that substance. An applicant may be required to furnish such particulars concerning the invention as the Controller deems necessary for the purpose of examination under this Act. Where an application is filed jointly by two or more applicants, they shall be deemed to have taken steps jointly for the prosecution of the application india and any communication relating thereto shall be sent to one of them.

Any person dealing in goods bearing a registered geographical indication that is falsely represented as originating from a region to which it does not belong shall be liable to a penalty as provided herein, and the goods so represented shall be deemed counterfeit goods for the purposes of seizure and destruction. The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall have the right to seek an injunction from a court of competent jurisdiction restraining such acts of misrepresentation, and may also claim damages for loss suffered due to such unlawful use. A collective body representing producers of the registered geographical indication may, with the leave of the court, institute legal proceedings on behalf of its members. Subject to due process, the court may order the destruction or disposal of goods bearing the false geographical indication, and may also impose a fine on the offender. Provided that, any action taken under this Act shall be without prejudice to any other remedies available under existing laws. The Registrar may maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications, accessible for inspection during office hours.

An application for registration disclosing an india disclosed application shall be filed with the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed, and shall contain a clear representation of the trade mark as to its essential features. The applicant shall state the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought, categorized according to the Nice Classification, and shall indicate the class or classes accordingly. Where the application claims priority under the Paris Convention, a statement to that effect, along with particulars of the prior application, must be furnished within the stipulated period. The applicant may, subject to the provisions of this Act, claim colour as a feature of the trade mark, provided that a clear and unambiguous representation of the colour is included in the application. Any misrepresentation in the india disclosed application shall render the registration liable to revocation. The Registrar may require the applicant to amend the application to remove any ambiguity or inconsistency.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (q) “package” includes any enclosure, wrapping, or container used for the containment, protection, transport, delivery or presentation of goods, whether such enclosure is of natural or artificial material, and whether it is a constituent part of the goods or separate therefrom. Provided that a label affixed to a package, bearing a trade mark, shall be deemed to be part of the package for the purposes of determining infringement under this Act. Furthermore, any device bearing a trade mark intended to be affixed to or displayed with goods, even if not physically part of a package, shall be construed as a package as provided herein, subject to the provisions relating to colour and get-up. A package shall not include any purely functional element devoid of any branding or trade mark application.

Where any interested party alleges that a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design has been infringed, they may file a complaint with the Registrar Semiconductor. The Registrar shall serve notice upon the alleged infringer, providing them an opportunity to submit their response within sixty days of such service. If the infringer fails to respond or their response is deemed insufficient under this Act, the Registrar may proceed ex parte and issue an interlocutory order restraining the infringing activity pending a full hearing. Any party aggrieved by an interlocutory order may appeal to the relevant High Court within thirty days. Compensation for damages resulting from infringement shall be determined based on the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had a license been granted, or in absence thereof, net profits attributable to the infringing layout-design, as provided herein.

Any person who is the owner of a registered trade mark under this Act may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, apply for international registration of that trade mark through the Trade Marks Registry. The application shall be in the manner specified by the Madrid Protocol and accompanied by a statement identifying the goods or services for which protection is sought in each designated country. Where an applicant seeks to limit the scope of protection in any designated country, such limitation must be clearly stated within the application itself. A licensee of a registered trade mark may, with the express written consent of the owner, apply for international registration as if they were the owner, provided that evidence of this licensing agreement is submitted alongside the application. Any assignment of an international registration or application for international registration shall be subject to the same requirements and procedures governing domestic assignments under this Act; failure to comply may render such transfer invalid. The Trade Marks Registry retains discretion to refuse processing where inconsistencies arise between the national registration and the details provided in the international application.

Any person being the proprietor of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to others for the use of such layout-design, either generally or subject to conditions, and such licenses may include the right to assign them to third parties. The registrar semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall maintain a record of all registered assignments and licenses, and any transfer of ownership without proper registration shall be considered null and void. An assignment may be absolute, transferring all rights, or partial, retaining certain rights with the assignor, provided that such partial assignment does not unduly restrict the licensee’s reasonable use of the layout-design. Where a license is granted for a definite period, the registrar may, upon application by either party and subject to just terms, determine the reasonableness of any renewal terms proposed. Any dispute concerning the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the appropriate court.

Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act relating to revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a claim in a patent, may file an appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such an appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The form petition for appeal shall contain a concise statement of the grounds on which the appeal is founded and must be verified by the appellant or their authorized representative. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements may result in dismissal of the appeal. Further, where an appeal concerns infringement proceedings, any party dissatisfied with the outcome may pursue remedies under this Act, subject to penalties for frivolous claims as provided herein.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention, and subsequent to its grant but prior to the expiration of three years from the date of grant, the Controller receives information indicating that the patented invention was not adequately described in the complete specification filed under this Act, he may direct the patentee to furnish such clarifications or amendments as are necessary to ensure compliance with the requirements for patentability. Such direction shall be accompanied by a reasoned order detailing the deficiencies identified and providing the patentee a period of ninety days to respond. Failure by the patentee to satisfactorily address these concerns within the stipulated timeframe will constitute a *patent consequence communication* triggering review proceedings, potentially leading to revocation or modification of the patent as provided herein.

A trade mark shall be registerable under this Act if it is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. An application for registration shall be made in the prescribed manner to the Trade Marks Registry, and shall include a clear representation of the mark and a statement of the goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, require the applicant to limit the goods or services specified in the application. Where a trade mark is register respect goods falling within Class 31, relating to agricultural, horticultural and forestry products, the Registrar shall, prior to acceptance of the application, satisfy himself as to the origin of such goods and compliance with relevant agricultural standards as provided herein. A mark shall not be registered if it is likely to cause confusion with an existing trade mark. The Registrar may, after considering any objections, either accept or refuse the application.

A layout design shall be deemed to infringe under this Act if, without authorization, a person directly or indirectly makes, uses, offers to sell, sells, distributes, imports, or otherwise deals with a layout design substantially similar to the registered layout design commercially. Such similarity shall be assessed considering the overall impression created on an informed user examining the two layout designs as a whole, taking into account all relevant features and characteristics. It is provided that unintentional reproduction of elements of a layout design, arising from common industry practice or publicly available information, shall not constitute infringement unless it demonstrates clear evidence of copying. Furthermore, any act undertaken solely for private use or research purposes may be exempted from the provisions relating to commercial exploitation as defined herein.

An aggrieved party, including but not limited to a person claiming ownership rights distinct from the registered owner, shall have standing to apply for cancellation justified registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design. Such an application must specify the grounds upon which the registration is challenged, demonstrating prima facie invalidity under this Act. The Registrar may, after affording the registrant and the applicant an opportunity for hearing, order cancellation if satisfied that the design does not meet the requirements for originality or other conditions precedent to registration. Any party dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the relevant appellate authority as provided herein; fees in any proceeding before the Registrar or the appellate authority shall be determined according to prescribed scales.

An application entitled breeder shall be deemed to have misrepresented facts if, at any time after the publication of an advertisement under this Act, it is established through verifiable documentation that the claimed novelty of the plant variety was not maintained during the entire period preceding the date of filing. Such misrepresentation shall render the applicant liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may result in the revocation of the certificate of registration granted, as provided herein. Further, any person demonstrating demonstrable financial loss due to reliance on false information presented by an application entitled breeder may pursue civil remedies against that individual or entity. Repeated instances of such misrepresentation shall attract enhanced penalties and potential prohibition from future applications under this Act.

Where an applicant for registration of a trade mark is refused registration under this Act, and subsequently seeks to assign the right to apply for registration to another party, the Registrar may require both the original applicant and the assignee to furnish such evidence as the Registrar deems necessary to establish the grounds for refusal. The assignment shall not be effective until the Registrar has acknowledged receipt of the required documentation and deemed it satisfactory. Further, if the initial application was refused due to a conflict with an earlier trade mark, the assignee’s right to proceed is subject to the existing rights holder's consent or a determination by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board that the refusal was unwarranted. The Registrar shall refuse register assignment where the grounds for original refusal remain unresolved.

Where any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration of a proposed mark for particular goods, or by the acceptance of a registered mark as identical or similar to an earlier mark used in relation to those goods, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. The Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them a reasonable opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. It is provided that registration of a mark for goods shall not be refused solely upon the basis of prior use unless such use demonstrably affects the distinctiveness of the mark registered goods.

Any assignment of copyright in a cinematograph film, whether made before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be subject to a requirement that the assignee secure the consent of the principal performer whose performance constituted an integral part of the film, and such consent shall be evidenced in writing and registered with the appropriate authority as prescribed. Where a copyright owner licenses the right to reproduce a work, and such reproduction constitutes an infringing copy, the copyright owner may, subject to the terms of the license, pursue remedies against the licensee. A legal practitioner acting on behalf of a copyright owner may, with leave of the court, serve notice on any person suspected of possessing or distributing an infringing copy, requiring them to disclose the source and extent of such possession or distribution. Provided that, any assignment or license failing to adhere to these provisions shall be deemed void *ab initio*, and the copyright owner shall remain entitled to all rights and remedies as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the validity of an assignment or license shall be subject to judicial determination.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be distinctive, as provided herein, if it is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another, and shall include shape, colour, or any combination thereof, where such shape or colour acquires distinctiveness through use. Any person claiming to be the owner of a determining trade mark, and alleging infringement by another, shall furnish to the adjudicating officer, within thirty days of notice served, a sworn statement detailing the extent and duration of such use establishing distinctiveness. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the claim inadmissible. Where a mark is not inherently distinctive, evidence of acquired distinctiveness through continuous and substantial use for a period of not less than five years shall be considered. Any false representation concerning the nature, manufacturing process, or characteristics of goods bearing a determining trade mark shall constitute an actionable offence, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine not exceeding two lakh rupees, or both.

Where any individual or entity engages in conduct that constitutes threatened infringement trade concerning a trademark registered under this Act, and such conduct includes representations, either express or implied, to restrain another from using a similar mark or engaging in activities likely to cause confusion amongst consumers, an aggrieved party may institute proceedings before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Such proceedings shall be initiated within six months of the date upon which the threatened infringement trade first occurred. The tribunal may, after affording all parties concerned an opportunity for hearing and presenting evidence, determine whether the conduct constitutes a threat of infringement as provided herein. If the tribunal finds that such threats exist, it may issue orders restraining the offending party from continuing with the threatening behaviour and directing them to retract any misleading representations made.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication relating to Alphonso mangoes shall include particulars demonstrating the qualitative and reputational characteristics attributable exclusively to the origin of the goods. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further evidence substantiating these claims, including historical records pertaining to cultivation practices and market presence. Where an objection is raised against the application based on a challenge to the asserted geographical boundaries, the applicant must submit documentation establishing the factual basis for those boundaries as a registration referred fact. This documentation shall be deemed sufficient if it comprises verifiable data from meteorological reports, soil surveys, or trade association records. The Registrar may conduct site visits to verify these details and consider expert opinions in assessing the validity of the application.

Any person claiming to be an exclusive licensee of a copyright in a work shall submit to the Registrar an application, in the prescribed form, seeking registration of such exclusive license, accompanied by certified copies of the licensing agreement and a no-objection certificate from the copyright owner. The Registrar shall, subject to verification of the submitted documents and satisfaction that the applicant is indeed an exclusive licensee as per the terms of the agreement, register the license and maintain a registrar index registered detailing the scope and duration of the exclusivity. An appeal against the refusal of the Registrar to register an exclusive license may be preferred to the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the date of the refusal. However, registration of an exclusive license shall not be conclusive evidence of its validity, and any dispute regarding the interpretation or enforceability of the licensing agreement shall be subject to the ordinary course of civil proceedings.

Where any person is found to have contravened any provision of this Act relating to the registration of patent applications or the maintenance of the register, an inquiry imposing penalty shall be initiated by the Controller. The Controller may direct the court registrar to serve notice upon such person detailing the alleged infraction and specifying the maximum amount of penalty that may be levied under this Act. Such inquiry shall proceed expeditiously, affording the concerned party a reasonable opportunity to present their defence and any relevant evidence. The Controller is empowered to determine whether a contravention has occurred and, if so, to impose a penalty as deemed appropriate, subject to principles of natural justice and proportionality. Appeals against such determinations may be made under the prescribed procedure.

The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, constitute a Registration Office for the purpose of receiving applications for registration of semiconductor integrated circuits layout-designs and maintaining a register thereof as provided herein. Every application for registration shall be accompanied by a layout-design drawing, a detailed description of the layout-design, and the prescribed fee. The Controller of the Registration Office shall, upon examination, satisfy themselves that the layout-design is novel and intrinsically capable of being realized. A function judicial member, possessing qualifications in law and experience in intellectual property matters, shall be appointed to assist the Controller in determining novelty and to adjudicate on any objections raised during the examination process. Subject to the provisions relating to priority, the Controller shall register the layout-design and enter the particulars in the register, and a certificate of registration shall be issued to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Controller may file an appeal.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be administered by a management committee constituted by the Central Government, and shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, and for the benefit of farmers and breeders alike. Any dispute regarding the equitable distribution of benefits derived from the utilization of the gene fund, particularly concerning contributions from commercially exploited plant varieties, may be raised before the designated authority. Provided that, any aggrieved party dissatisfied with the decision of the designated authority may prefer an appeal to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding limitation periods for such appeals. The management committee shall maintain detailed records of all contributions to, and disbursements from, the gene fund, and such records shall be open to inspection by any person upon reasonable request and payment of prescribed fees. Furthermore, the committee may establish a system of rewards for farmers who contribute unique germplasm to the fund, fostering innovation and biodiversity.

A trade mark shall be deemed infringed where any individual, firm, or company employs a sign, including words, logos, symbols, or combinations thereof, in connection with goods or services. This infringement occurs if said sign is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark, and the use takes place within the class of goods or services for which registration subsists. Provided that, such use must create a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or affiliation of those goods or services. Further, this shall not apply where the defendant demonstrates honest concurrent usage established prior to the date of application for the registered trade mark, subject to conditions as provided herein concerning territorial scope and consumer perception. The burden of proving a trade mark infringed rests upon the claimant.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against a patent specification alleging lack of clarity or insufficiency to enable a person skilled in the art to put the invention into practice, it shall be open to the applicant to demonstrate, through expert testimony and supplementary documentation submitted within thirty days of the notice of objection, that the specification does disclose the best method contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Such demonstration need not encompass every conceivable variation but must reasonably satisfy the Controller that a skilled professional could implement the claimed subject matter without undue experimentation beyond what is customary in the art. The Controller may allow the applicant to amend the specification to address such objections, provided that the amendment does not substantially alter the scope of protection sought and remains consistent with the original disclosure.

Where the copyright in any cinematograph film or sound recording has been assigned under this Act, the assignor may, subject to the terms of the assignment, apply for registration of such assignment. Upon receipt of the application and after satisfaction that the provisions herein relating to assignments have been complied with, the Registrar shall register the same and issue a certificate accordingly. Such certificate shall be prima facie evidence that the copyright has been validly assigned. An exclusive licence granted in respect of any work or sound recording shall be deemed to be an assignment for the purposes of registration under this Act, provided that the terms of such licence expressly state it is intended as an exclusive grant and specify the duration thereof.

The breeder of a new plant variety, desiring to avail of the benefits under the scheme established for commercial exploitation of the variety, shall submit a proposal to the Plant Variety Protection Authority outlining the terms of licensing proposed for third parties. Such proposals shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to, propagation, sale, and distribution of harvested material. The Authority may, subject to verification of the breeder’s rights and the novelty of the variety, approve the proposal, thereby initiating the section 41 scheme for that variety. Any person seeking a license to exploit the variety shall apply to the breeder, and the terms negotiated shall be consistent with the approved proposal. Where agreement cannot be reached, the Authority may, after due process and consideration of equitable principles, impose licensing terms. The breeder retains the right to assign their rights under any license granted, provided that the assignee adheres to the conditions stipulated herein and any subsequent modifications approved by the Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in revocation of the license and associated benefits.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person claiming rights over a registered variety may apply for registration of plant propagating material derived from such *variety registered* as a distinct variety. The application shall specify the characteristics of the derived material and demonstrate its traceability back to the original registered variety. Such registration is subject to an examination confirming that the derived material maintains essential traits consistent with the parent *variety registered*, without introducing substantial alterations affecting its identity or stability. An applicant seeking registration of propagating material may be required to submit samples for testing at a designated authority, as provided herein. The Central Government shall maintain a record of all registrations pertaining to derived plant propagating material.

For the purposes of this Act, “misleading indication” with respect to goods or services means any statement or representation which is likely to create confusion in the minds of the public as to the nature, quality, origin, characteristics, or suitability of such goods or services. Such misleading indications include, but are not limited to, representations concerning the geographical origin of goods where such origin has a reputation extending beyond the place of origin. Any person who makes any false representation under this Act shall be deemed guilty of an offence and shall cognizance offence by a court; provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify further categories of misleading indications.

Where an application for a patent has been rejected by the Controller under this Act, and the applicant desires to challenge said rejection, he may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall give notice to the Controller requiring him to submit his reasons for such rejection within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of service of the notice. Upon hearing the appellant and the Controller, and considering all relevant evidence presented, the Board may allow the appeal and direct that the patent be granted as originally applied for, or may modify the application and direct that a patent be granted according to such modification, or may dismiss the appeal. The court permits patent grant only after due consideration of the Board’s findings, subject to any legal challenge brought before it under established procedures as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a *dramatic work* shall be deemed to include any musical work which is incorporated therein and forms an integral part thereof. Any person claiming copyright in such a *dramatic work* shall furnish to the Registrar of Copyrights a detailed synopsis outlining the plot, characters, and setting, along with a list of all musical works integrated within it. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary materials deemed necessary for proper assessment under this Act. Where an adaptation of a dramatic work is registered, the copyright therein shall be subject to the prior rights of the original author as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of such registration must be filed with the relevant High Court within ninety days from the date of publication of the register and shall be adjudicated according to established procedures. The Registrar’s decision regarding the originality of a *dramatic work* is final, subject to judicial review.

Where any person has made a basic application relating to an invention, and subsequently files a further application under this Act, such subsequent application shall be deemed to relate back to the date of the initial basic application for the purposes of determining priority. Provided that if the applicant or their assignee fails to disclose all information known to them which could reasonably affect the patentability of the invention at the time of filing the subsequent application, the Controller may refuse the grant of a patent or impose such conditions as they deem fit. Any party aggrieved by a decision under this provision relating to priority or patentability may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The applicant shall be liable for costs incurred in any proceedings challenging the validity of the patent based on non-disclosure, subject to considerations of fairness and good faith.

A registration for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been cancelled if, following an inquiry as provided herein, the Registrar finds that the registered layout-design was obtained through fraud or misrepresentation. For the purposes of this Act, a “cancelled registrar layout” refers specifically to such a layout-design whose registration has ceased to have effect under these provisions. The notice applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments against the proposed cancellation. Further, any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar cancelling a layout may appeal to the relevant appellate authority within a prescribed time period, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Any person desiring to register a biological material as a new variety under this Act shall submit an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, accompanied by a detailed description of the characteristics of the said variety, demonstrating its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability. The application shall further include evidence of the origin and development of the variety, and a statement regarding the essential characteristics which are relevant for the purpose of assessment. Where the applicant claims a variety derived from another variety, full particulars of the parent variety shall be furnished, subject to the provisions relating to breeders’ rights as provided herein. The Plant Variety Protection Authority may, if satisfied that the application is complete and conforms to the requirements of this Act, proceed to examine the variety in the prescribed manner and grant a breeder’s certificate if the variety meets the criteria for registration. Any material submitted as part of the application shall be treated as confidential.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products or foodstuffs may be filed with the Registrar, specifying the name of the indication and the geographical area comprising the territory where such goods are produced. The application shall include particulars regarding the qualities, reputation or other characteristics which identify the goods as originating from that area, along with a map of the defined geographical boundary. Any person claiming to represent the interests of the producers of the indicated good may apply for registration, provided that they demonstrate adequate representation under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice inviting objections. The gene fund shall be utilized for supporting research and development activities related to the preservation and promotion of registered geographical indications. This act shall binding on all persons involved in the production, processing, or trade of goods bearing a registered geographical indication.

Where any individual or entity holds exclusive rights pertaining to a product’s distinctive character and utilizes a specific trade description in connection with its sale or offering, that right holder may grant a license permitting another party to employ said trade description for similar goods or services. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the scope of permitted use, including geographical limitations and duration. The licensor retains ownership of the underlying trade mark rights and may assign those rights, along with any associated licenses, to a successor entity subject to adherence to conditions stipulated under this Act concerning prior consent from licensees. Any assignment or license granted subsequent to the initial registration shall be recorded as per prescribed procedures. Furthermore, a licensee may, with written permission from the licensor, sub-license certain aspects of the permitted trade description usage, provided that such sub-licensing does not contravene the terms of the original agreement.

A person proposed for appointment as a Technical Member of the Trade Marks Registry shall possess a postgraduate degree in science or engineering from a recognized university, or be a person holding a degree in law with a postgraduate diploma in intellectual property rights from a recognized institution. The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks may, if satisfied that a candidate does not possess the aforementioned qualifications but has demonstrable experience in the field of trade marks, including practical knowledge of examination and registration procedures, consider such a person for appointment, provided that such experience shall not be less than ten years. Any appointment of a Technical Member shall be subject to a rigorous screening process conducted by a committee constituted by the Central Government, ensuring adherence to principles of transparency and merit. The Controller shall maintain a panel of eligible candidates for future vacancies, updated annually. A Technical Member shall exercise jurisdiction as provided herein, and their decisions are subject to review by the Appellate Board.

A certificate issued under this Act, when purporting to be signed by an authorized officer and bearing the official seal of the Trade Marks Registry, shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein, subject to the provisions for rectification as provided herein. Such a certificate may relate to the registration of a trade mark, the renewal thereof, or any alteration made to the register concerning a registered trade mark. The Registrar may issue certificates relating to assignments and licenses affecting registered trade marks, and these shall be deemed conclusive evidence of such transactions unless proven otherwise before an intellectual property tribunal. Any challenge to the validity of a certificate must be brought within the time limits prescribed under this Act.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be filed with the Controller in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The applicant shall furnish proof of ownership or right to apply, as determined satisfactory by the Controller. Where an objection is raised against the validity of a layout design under this Act, the concerned legal practitioner person representing the objector may submit written arguments and supporting documentation within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the objection. The Controller shall afford the applicant an opportunity for rebuttal and may conduct hearings as deemed necessary to ascertain the facts relevant to the objection. Any decision made by the Controller regarding the registration or rejection of a layout design government shall be communicated in writing to all parties involved, including the applicant and any objector. Appeals against such decisions lie with the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Any transmission of a registered trade mark, whether by assignment, transfer, or operation of law, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of the new proprietor, and failure to comply with such provisions may render the transmission voidable at the instance of any aggrieved party. However, a transmission occurring as a consequence of a corporate restructuring, where a director of the original entity demonstrably authorized the transfer prior to the restructuring’s completion, shall be viewed differently. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of such a transmission, an application may be made to the High Court, and the Court shall consider evidence of authorization and the bona fides of all parties involved. Provided that, the Court may stay the transmission pending resolution of the dispute, and any continued use of the mark during the stay shall not be construed as an admission of valid title. Any appeal from the decision of the High Court shall lie to the Supreme Court.

A practitioner person registered under this Act may grant a license to utilize a protected integrated circuit layout design subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in a written agreement executed by both parties. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is recorded with the Controller of Layout-Designs within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so renders the assignee liable for penalties as prescribed herein. Further, where a license granted includes rights relating to manufacture, the licensor shall retain the right to audit the licensee’s production records to ensure compliance with the licensed quantity and quality standards. A patent shall not be deemed to invalidate an existing layout design registration merely by virtue of similarity in functionality; however, any infringement proceedings arising from such patents will be adjudicated independently under relevant intellectual property laws.

Where an application for the registration of a trade mark is pending adjudication before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, any subsequent action taken by the trade mark proprietor concerning the subject matter of that application shall be deemed to be without prejudice to the outcome of the proceeding. The Registrar may, upon receiving notification from the Intellectual Property Appellate Board indicating that a dies pending proceeding has been initiated, suspend further processing of any related applications or oppositions until resolution of the original dispute. Further, a trade mark proprietor seeking to rely on prior use in support of an application shall provide documentary evidence demonstrating continuous and uninterrupted usage throughout the pendency period, as determined by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, a “6referred convention country” shall be deemed to include any nation that has acceded to the Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property and which is designated by the Central Government through notification in the Official Gazette. Applications filed in a 6referred convention country by persons residing or having domicile therein shall be treated as convention applications under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding priority claims. The determination of whether a nation qualifies as a 6referred convention country may be reviewed periodically by the Controller and reported to the Central Government annually. Any dispute arising concerning the status of a particular country as a 6referred convention country shall be resolved at the discretion of the Controller, whose decision is final and binding. Further, an application claiming priority from a convention application shall be examined in accordance with the established procedures outlined herein.

Where a cinematograph film infringes the copyright in any work, and such infringement is attributable to an act or omission by a director during the creation of the film, both the producer and the director shall be jointly and severally liable for damages. Any person demonstrating substantial involvement in the infringing activity may also be held accountable under this Act. Failure to adequately supervise directorial activities relating to copyrightable elements constitutes negligence actionable at law. The Court may order the seizure and destruction of any equipment used in facilitating such infringement, subject to due process. Repeated or willful violations shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not less than two years, and fines up to five hundred thousand rupees.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall furnish with their produced registrar application a detailed specification including all relevant technical data and diagrams. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in rejection of the application. Where an objection is raised regarding the novelty or originality of the layout-design, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written arguments and counter-evidence. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the acceptance or refusal of registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The remedies available under this Act include injunctions restraining infringement and damages for past infringements; however, such damages shall not exceed a sum determined by the Appellate Board. Mark regulations pertaining to layout-design identification are also subject to review upon application.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to a written instrument signed by or on behalf of the assignor and the assignee, and shall be in the prescribed form. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of the business carried on under that trade mark, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the trade mark in relation to those goods or services in respect of which the goodwill is assigned. However, assignment of a trade mark for the purpose of falsifying or deceptively imitating the mark, or for the purpose of gaining an unfair advantage, shall be void, and any rights acquired thereunder shall be extinguished. A license to use a trade mark may be granted, either generally or subject to limitations, and shall be in writing and signed by both parties. The proprietor of a trade mark may, as provided herein, assign or license the mark, or any right therein, subject to any conditions deemed necessary to protect the integrity of the mark and prevent its use for purpose falsifying used goods or services.

An application for rectification of register may be made by any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Designs Register. Such application shall be in Form D and accompanied by a statement specifying the grounds upon which the applicant relies, supported by all relevant documents and evidence. The application must be presented to the Controller within six months from the date of the publication of the design in the Designs Journal, subject to an extension granted by the Controller for reasons deemed sufficient.

The Controller shall serve notice of the application on the registered proprietor, affording them a reasonable opportunity to file a counter-statement. Proceedings relating to rectification shall be conducted as nearly as may be in accordance with the procedure followed in suits before ordinary courts of law. The Controller’s decision regarding the rectification register is final and binding, provided that an appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall include any representation, indication, or suggestion relating to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, quantity, or intended purpose of goods or services. Such a description is deemed misleading if it deceives or is likely to deceive the public regarding the identity of the source of the goods or services. A depiction employing fanciful imagery, provided that such imagery directly and unambiguously conveys information about the aforementioned attributes, shall also be considered within this definition. This understanding applies irrespective of whether the representation is expressed in words, symbols, marks, figures, shapes, colours, sounds, or any combination thereof, as provided herein.

Any person found guilty of contravening the provisions relating to benefit sharing under this Act, including unauthorized commercialization of plant varieties registered hereunder, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding five lakhs rupees for the first offence. Subsequent offences may attract penalties up to ten lakhs rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. The Authority established as provided herein may issue cease and desist orders directing any infringing party to immediately halt activities violating farmers’ rights or intellectual property protections. Further, damages equivalent to thrice the value of profits derived from such unauthorized use shall be recoverable. This applies particularly where infringement occurs in direct disregard of stipulations outlined under section 41 clause (b), concerning geographical indications.

A registration variety, to be considered for protection under this Act, shall demonstrate distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability, as evidenced by a detailed description of the plant characteristics submitted with the application for registration. The applicant shall furnish proof of the origin and development of the variety, including the date of first commercialization or availability to the public. Where a mark international registration relating to the variety exists, a certified copy of the international registration and details of the designated countries shall accompany the application. Provided that, the applicant is a person who has effectively contributed to the creation of the variety, or has acquired the right from such a person. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application, subject to an opportunity for rectification as provided herein. The Registrar may, at their discretion, require additional evidence to verify the veracity of the claims made in the application.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be subject to renewal upon expiry of the initial registration period of ten years, and such renewal may be effected by application to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. The applicant shall demonstrate continued bona fide use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, failing which the renewal request may be disallowed. Safeguards prescribed register relating to associated rights, including but not limited to licensing agreements and assignments, must accompany any application for renewal where such arrangements are extant. Provided that, if a valid objection is raised concerning potential conflict with prior rights, the Registry may suspend processing of the renewal until resolution of said dispute as provided herein. Any alteration to the registered trade mark during renewal shall be treated as a separate registration process and subject to examination anew. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in cancellation of the trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, "Darjeeling Tea" means tea produced exclusively in the Darjeeling district and having specific characteristics attributable to the terroir of that region, including but not limited to altitude, slope, rainfall, and soil composition; provided that such characteristics are demonstrably distinct from teas produced elsewhere. The central government shall determine, by notification in the Official Gazette, the precise geographical boundaries constituting the territory of production for Darjeeling Tea, subject to periodic review as may be necessary. Any use of the term "Darjeeling Tea" on goods not conforming to these criteria is prohibited under this Act and constitutes an infringement.

A person seeking registration of a certification trade mark shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Trade Marks Registry, demonstrating that the applicant is authorized by the owner of the certification trade mark. The application shall include a statement detailing the standards and procedures governing the use of the mark, ensuring consistent quality or characteristics of goods or services certified thereby. Where a collective trade mark has been registered, any association of applicants may apply for registration of a corresponding certification trade mark to certify that goods or services originate from members who meet certain criteria. The Registrar shall examine the application and, subject to satisfaction of all requirements as provided herein, register the certification trade mark. Registration shall confer upon the owner the exclusive right to use the mark in relation to certified goods or services, preventing unauthorized usage by any other entity; however, such right is limited to ensuring adherence to the stated standards and does not constitute ownership over the underlying goods themselves.

Any proprietor seeking rectification of a registered geographical indication may apply to the Geographical Indications Registry, and such application shall specify the particulars of the registration sought to be rectified and the grounds upon which it is claimed that rectification is necessary. The Registry shall give notice of the application to the applicant and any other interested parties as identified under this Act, affording them an opportunity to submit objections or counter-claims. Following consideration of all submissions, the Registrar may order such modifications to the register as are deemed appropriate, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Furthermore, the Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing instances where rectification orders have been issued and outlining any challenges encountered in their implementation, including assessments of impact on producers.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license or assign the rights pertaining to a patent granted under this Act, such license or assignment shall be in writing and executed by the patentee or their authorized representative. The Patent Office shall maintain a register of all licenses and assignments recorded as provided herein. Any person seeking to acquire an interest in a patent through license or assignment may apply to the Patent Office for registration, furnishing details including consideration paid, territorial extent, and duration. Subject to payment of prescribed fees, the Patent Office shall record such licenses and assignments, providing notice thereof in the Official Gazette. Provided that any license granted prior to the commencement of this provision which is not registered shall be deemed invalid unless it has been subsequently registered within a period of six months from the date of its execution. The patentee shall retain ownership until full registration occurs.

Any goods or produce a mark which is likely to be mistaken for a registered geographical indication, or falsely suggest an association with such indication, shall be liable for damages as determined by the relevant High Court. The authorised user of a geographical indication may institute proceedings against any person who falsifies that geographical indication and seek injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification. Provided that, in determining the amount of damages, due consideration shall be given to the extent of the loss suffered by the authorised user, including but not limited to lost profits and damage to reputation. Further, where an act of falsification is committed with fraudulent intent, the court may award punitive damages up to three times the actual damages proven. Nothing in this Act prevents a person from using their own trade name or trademark, subject to it not constituting a falsify geographical indication under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the assessment or recovery of registry fees may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Board shall, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity for being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which shall be binding on the Registrar. Failure to pay any prescribed registry fee within the time specified in a notice issued by the Registrar shall render the trade mark liable for removal from the register. In cases where an alleged offence has been committed involving fraudulent representation concerning the ownership of a registered trade mark and the subsequent evasion of applicable fees, the offender shall be subject to penalties as determined by the Board, without prejudice to any other action that may be taken under this Act.

A specification patent shall define the scope of protection granted under this Act with precision and clarity. For the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step, the term "specification" refers to the written description of the invention accompanying an application for grant of a patent, including any drawings or other diagrams incorporated therein. The specification must disclose the matter which the inventor claims as his invention in such manner as to enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the same. Provided that, where the claimed invention incorporates elements derived from previously known technologies, the specification shall clearly articulate the synergistic effect resulting from their combination.

An application for the cancellation registration of a layout-design may be presented to the Controller by any person claiming an interest adversely affected by the registration. Such application shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to instances where the layout-design was registered in contravention of section 7 or section 8 under this Act. The applicant must provide evidence substantiating the claims made within the application; failure to do so may result in its rejection. The Controller shall afford the registrant an opportunity to file a counter-statement responding to the allegations, and both parties shall be given reasonable time for such submissions. A decision regarding cancellation registration will only be rendered after due consideration of all relevant materials presented.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if the marks applied for includes any identifier that is identical or confusingly similar to an existing unregistered trade mark used by another person in relation to goods or services. Such refusal may be overridden where the applicant can demonstrate continuous use of the potentially infringing sign for a period exceeding five years prior to the date of application, and that such use has established amongst the relevant consuming public a clear association between the sign and the applicant’s goods or services. The Registrar shall consider evidence presented by both parties in determining whether confusion is likely, taking into account all surrounding circumstances as provided herein.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall maintain a true and accurate entry register document detailing all licenses granted under the mark, including the duration, territory, and terms of each license. This entry register document shall be open for inspection by the Registrar during the course of any examination or proceeding under this Act. Failure to maintain such a document, or to present it when requested, may be considered prima facie evidence of an intent to deceive or cause confusion. A certified copy of any entry within the entry register document may be admitted as evidence in any legal proceeding concerning the trade mark. The Registrar may, subject to reasonable cause, direct amendment of the entry register document to reflect accurate licensing information. Provided that any material misrepresentation in the entry register document shall render the registration liable to revocation as provided herein. All amendments to the entry register document shall be dated and initialed by the registered proprietor.

The registered owner of a trade mark shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring the right to use the name embodied within that trade mark, subject to the conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements may specify geographical limitations on usage, permitted goods or services associated with the name, and duration of the license. Further, the registered proprietor may assign the entire interest in a trade mark, including any existing licenses relating to its use as a name, to another party, provided that all licensees consent to such assignment unless the license agreement expressly prohibits it. Any subsequent owner acquiring the trade marks registered shall be bound by the terms of any pre-existing license agreements concerning the use of the name, and may not unilaterally alter those conditions without obtaining licensee approval.

Where an applicant seeks to amend a pending application permitted amended under this Act, such amendment shall not alter the fundamental character of the goods or services for which registration is sought. Any alteration intended to circumvent existing registrations or create confusion amongst consumers will be deemed a falsifying trade mark and shall be rejected outright. The Registrar may, at any time, require an applicant seeking amendment to submit evidence demonstrating the continued distinctiveness of the amended mark in relation to the specified goods or services. Failure to provide such evidence within the prescribed period shall result in rejection of the application and imposition of a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees; repeated offences will attract enhanced penalties and potential prosecution under relevant provisions relating to trade malpractices.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit may grant licenses granting rights to use, reproduce, or commercially exploit the said layout-design. Such license shall be assignable, either in whole or in part, by instrument in writing duly executed and registered with the Controller General. Where the terms of a license are not clearly defined, any dispute arising therefrom shall be resolved as per principles of equity and good faith. Further, cancellation of registration under this Act shall automatically render all existing licenses relating to that semiconductor integrated circuit null and void; however, rights accrued prior to such cancelling registration shall remain enforceable against those who have legitimately obtained them through the registered proprietor’s actions. The Controller General may issue guidelines regarding the form and content of assignment documents as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark for a pharmaceutical substance, or rejecting evidence submitted in support of such application, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order of the Registry. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the impugned order and a statement of the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, require the appellant to deposit a sum equivalent to the prescribed fee for registration of the trade mark as security for payment of costs. Provided that, if the Appellate Board is satisfied that the appeal is frivolous or vexatious, it may dismiss the appeal with costs and direct the Trade Marks Registry to restore the application to its original status, or to proceed with examination as if no appeal had been filed. Any order of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error.

Where an application for patent relating to a process or composition for any article or substance is accompanied by a provisional specification, the applicant shall file a complete specification within a period of twelve months from the date of the initial filing. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the application liable to be refused. Provided that, where the Controller considers it necessary for the understanding of the invention, he may allow an extension of time not exceeding six months for filing the complete specification, subject to such conditions as he deems fit. Any person aggrieved by a refusal under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The applicant shall be entitled to claim priority from the provisional application’s filing date only if the complete specification discloses the matter disclosed in the accompanied provisional specification.

Any person desiring registration of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design shall present an application to the Registrar in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee, and containing all particulars as required under this Act. The application, upon being deemed complete, shall be recorded as a produced registrar application and assigned a unique reference number. Subject to verification of the layout-design’s originality and compliance with the provisions herein, the Registrar may, after conducting a thorough examination, register the layout-design. Should the Registrar raise objections regarding the application, the applicant shall be afforded a period of thirty days to address such objections, failing which the application may be deemed abandoned. A registered proprietor shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in India, and any unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or commercial use thereof constitutes an infringement, giving rise to remedies as provided herein, including injunctions and damages. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision may appeal to the High Court.

Any person deriving benefit from the commercial exploitation of a registered layout-design shall be deemed to have infringed the exclusive right of the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. The proprietor of any layout-design registered under this Act shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, distribute, import, or otherwise deal with the layout-design. However, such exclusive right shall not extend to acts done for private personal use or for the purposes of research, provided that such research does not prejudice the legitimate commercial interests of the proprietor. A layout-design, if not registered, may still be protectable under other applicable laws, but the remedies available under this Act are contingent upon valid registration. Any unauthorized commercial exploitation, including the manufacture or sale of integrated circuits embodying the layout-design without the proprietor’s consent, constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act. The registered proprietor may seek injunctions and damages for any proven infringement.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, direct that the shape of specified goods be considered as part of the distinctive character of such trade mark. Such direction shall only be granted if the applicant demonstrates, through evidence presented during proceedings under this Act, that the shape in question signifies a substantial and unique association with the goods and has acquired distinctiveness through reputation or recognition earned by the proprietor’s use thereof. The application must include detailed technical specifications delineating the precise trade marks shape, including dimensions and material composition where relevant. Any party may object to the direction being granted, submitting counter-evidence demonstrating that the shape is primarily functional or descriptive of the goods, thereby precluding its registration as a trade mark shape.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be specified in the instrument of assignment and recorded with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a license is granted permitting a party other than the registered proprietor to use the trade mark, the licensor shall maintain control over the quality of goods or services associated with the application registration trade, failing which the rights conferred by such license may be revoked as provided herein. An exclusive licensee shall have the right to sue for infringement of the trade mark subject to the terms of the licensing agreement and notification to the registered proprietor. Assignment or transmission of a trade mark shall not affect the validity of any existing registrations unless expressly stated in the instrument, but all subsequent dealings with the trade mark must reflect the updated ownership as recorded with the Registry. Any assignment without proper recording is voidable at the option of the assignor.

Any person who, without obtaining a license from the owner of copyright, reproduces any work protected under this Act for commercial gain shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to a reasonable royalty that would have been payable had such license been obtained. The amount of said royalty shall be determined by the relevant High Court, taking into consideration factors including the extent of reproduction, the potential impact on the market value of the original work, and any demonstrable loss suffered by the copyright owner as a direct consequence of the unauthorized act. Further, where an infringement has been committed wilfully and for the purpose of undue gain, the court may award punitive damages not exceeding ten times the amount of compensation determined under this provision. The right to claim such remedies is subject to limitations regarding time, as provided herein.

Where the registered proprietor of a trademark desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights to use the trademark within a defined geographical territory or for specific goods and services, such proprietor shall submit a form petition to the Trade Marks Registry. This petition must detail the scope of the licensed rights, including any limitations on usage and duration of the license. The Registrar shall appear before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board if any party objects to the proposed licensing arrangement, citing concerns regarding dilution or unfair competition. Provided that the registered proprietor affirms their continued responsibility for ensuring compliance with trademark law by the licensee, the Trade Marks Registry may approve the assignment or sub-license of these rights subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all approved licenses and assignments on the public register.

Where a trade mark is registered, and subsequently an earlier right arises that would, but for the registration, preclude the use of the sign by the proprietor of the registered trade mark, the proprietor may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board seeking relief. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating the prior honest usage of the sign in relation to goods or services identical or similar to those for which registration is sought, and establishing that the public would be unduly confused if both marks were permitted to continue concurrently. The Board may grant such remedies as it deems fit, including but not limited to a declaration regarding the validity of the registration. Notably, an amendment antedating registration, arising from this prior right, shall take precedence over the registered mark’s exclusive rights, subject to equitable considerations and due regard for bona fide users.

Any person deriving commercial benefit from an integrated circuit which incorporates a layout-design registered under this Act shall be liable for such derivation unless duly licensed by the proprietor of said layout-design. A registered proprietor may institute civil proceedings in a competent court having jurisdiction over the matter to restrain any act constituting infringement of their rights, and may also claim damages sustained due to such infringement; however, no injunction shall be granted if the defendant proves they were unaware of the registration and exercised reasonable diligence in ascertaining whether a valid layout-design existed. Subject to provisions concerning national emergency or non-commercial research, compulsory licensing of a registered layout-design may be granted by the court upon application demonstrating sufficient cause and payment of adequate remuneration to the proprietor. Any person aggrieved by an order pertaining to such licensing shall have recourse to appeal as provided herein, and any falsification of information presented in support of either infringement claims or applications for compulsory license constitutes grounds for prosecution under relevant penal laws.

Any person found to be engaging in the unauthorized reproduction or application of registered designs relating to military equipment, critical infrastructure components, or systems vital to national defense shall be deemed guilty of an offense against this Act. Such offenses are particularly egregious when undertaken with the intent to compromise the security of India or undermine its strategic interests. Where it is established that a design infringement constitutes a threat to public order or involves a condition declared unlawful by the Central Government, the infringing party shall be liable to imprisonment for a term not less than five years and a fine exceeding fifty lakhs of rupees. Further, any assets derived from such illicit activities are subject to seizure under procedures as provided herein.

Where a patentee elects to utilize a standardized graphical representation, commonly referred to as a ‘form reference act,’ for depicting aspects of their invention within the patent documentation, such representations shall be considered integral components of the disclosed subject matter. The right to reproduce and distribute these form references acts is governed by this Act and may be assigned or licensed under terms agreed upon between the patentee and any third party. Provided that such assignment or license explicitly acknowledges the originating inventor’s intellectual property rights, it shall not prejudice the validity of the underlying patent. Any subsequent modification or adaptation of a form reference act requires express consent from the original patentee unless such alteration is demonstrably necessary for interoperability with existing technologies as determined by the Controller. The patentee retains ownership of all copyright associated with their created form references acts.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding rights in a new variety may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the commercial exploitation thereof, including but not limited to rights for propagation, sale, distribution, or research purposes. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area and duration for which they are valid, and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the grantor. Assignment of rights in a new variety is permissible with prior notification to the Authority, detailing the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the protected material. The Authority may impose conditions on such assignments to ensure continued benefit to farmers and preservation of genetic resources. Further, any license granted or assignment made shall be recorded within one month with the designated registering authority, as provided herein.

Where an owner of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings alleging that another person has used a sign identical or confusingly similar to their trade mark in relation to identical or similar goods or services, the Court shall determine whether such use constitutes a violation under this Act. The Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from any further acts of infringement, and may order the delivery up or destruction of all goods bearing the infringing sign. Further, where it is established that the defendant’s actions have resulted in damage to the reputation or goodwill associated with the registered trade mark, the owner shall be entitled to claim damages commensurate with such harm. The determination of trade mark accordance requires consideration of consumer perception and the likelihood of confusion arising from the use of the allegedly infringing sign.

Where an individual or entity utilizes a substantial portion of a copyrighted work without authorization, such action constitutes infringement under this Act. Provided that, where the reproduction is solely for private and non-commercial use, and does not prejudice the rights of the copyright owner as provided herein, it shall not be deemed to constitute infringement. Further, if the alleged infringing act involves fair dealing with a literary or artistic work for research, criticism, review, or reporting current events, such usage may be permissible subject to conditions relating to acknowledgement of the source and author. Any person found guilty of copyright infringement shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the copyright owner, considering factors including the extent of unauthorized reproduction and commercial gain derived therefrom.

Any person possessing a registered layout-design may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign or license the same, either wholly or partially, and either generally or subject to conditions, to any other person. Any assignment of a layout-design shall be in writing and shall specify the rights assigned, and a copy of such instrument shall be furnished to the Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry. Where an assignment is made without specifying any rights, it shall be deemed to be an assignment of all rights subsisting in the layout-design. A Bench of the Registry may, upon application, record any such assignment or license. Should a dispute arise concerning the validity of an assignment or the scope of a license, the aggrieved party may seek redressal as provided herein, and any decision rendered may be sought appealed to a higher authority. The assignor shall remain liable for any breach of conditions attached to the license by the assignee, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

A provisional specification, filed under this Act, shall be treated as a document establishing an early filing date for an invention, subject to the subsequent filing of a complete specification as provided herein. The provisional specification need not conform to the formal requirements prescribed for a complete specification, but must adequately describe the invention to allow a person skilled in the art to understand its nature. An applicant desiring to claim priority based on an earlier application in a convention country may, within the prescribed period, file a complete specification claiming priority, referencing the provisional specification as the basis for the claim. Failure to file a complete specification within twelve months from the filing of the provisional specification will result in the application being deemed abandoned, unless an extension of time is granted by the Controller of Patents, and any such extension shall be subject to applicable fees and conditions.
