The complete specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention, including the best method known to the applicant for carrying out the invention.

An invention shall be deemed to be non-obvious if it does not involve any element which is susceptible of being anticipated or derived from knowledge available to a person skilled in the art prior to the priority date. The determination of obviousness shall take into account, inter alia, the totality of the circumstances, including relevant publications and public use, both before and after the priority date. Where an application claims an invention far claimed beyond the scope of the disclosure in the specification, the Controller may require the applicant to amend the claim to bring it within that scope. Such amendment shall be permissible only if the amended claim is supported by the original disclosure and does not introduce any new matter. The Board constituted under this Act may entertain appeals against orders passed by the Controller relating to the assessment of obviousness or the requirement for amendments, subject to prescribed procedures.

A “Member” shall, for the purposes of this Act, denote a person who is registered as the proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuits layout-design, and includes their duly authorized agent or assignee, subject to the provisions contained herein. A ‘registered user’ is a natural or legal person who has lawfully accessed a layout-design for the limited purpose of manufacturing a semiconductor product, and such access does not confer membership as defined herein. Membership is contingent upon the filing of an application, accompanied by the prescribed fee, and subsequent verification of the layout-design’s originality. Provided that, a Member shall remain liable for any infringement arising from unauthorized use of the layout-design, even if such use occurs through a registered user. Any dispute regarding membership shall be adjudicated by the designated authority as provided herein.

Any person found to have made a false statement or representation in connection with an application india provisions relating to a patent, whether in the form of the specification, claims, or any accompanying documentation, shall be liable for penalties as determined by the Controller. Such penalties may include fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Furthermore, where it is established that such false representation was made with intent to deceive or defraud, the application shall stand rejected ab initio, and any patent granted based on said misrepresentation shall be deemed invalid and subject to revocation proceedings initiated by the Controller. The burden of proving the falsity of a statement rests upon the party alleging the same, subject to due process considerations.

Any person claiming a geographical indication, as provided herein, shall apply for registration in the manner prescribed, furnishing a statement of case including an indication of the goods, their geographical origin, and details of the inspection undertaken to ascertain authenticity. The application shall also include a statement of the conditions governing the production and processing of the goods, demonstrating a consistent character, quality, or reputation attributable to that geographical origin. Where a geographical indication is sought to be registered for agricultural goods, proof of adherence to established standards or certifications relating to organic farming or sustainable practices may be submitted to support the claim. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed necessary, require further evidence or clarification regarding the geographical indication complained of, or conduct independent verification to ensure compliance with the provisions of this Act. A registered geographical indication shall be valid for ten years, renewable upon application and payment of the prescribed fee.

Application for registration of a biological entity shall be accompanied by a detailed report specifying the method of isolation and characterization of said entity, including particulars regarding its genetic makeup and metabolic pathways. The Controller General may require submission of additional data demonstrating stability and reproducibility of the biological entity across multiple generations or experimental conditions. Further, an applicant seeking to secure a patent act relating to a genetically modified organism must provide evidence substantiating that the modification does not unduly prejudice public health or environmental safety, as determined by guidelines issued by the relevant regulatory authority. The application shall also include a declaration affirming adherence to bio-containment protocols and ethical considerations during experimentation.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Layout-Design Registry concerning the validity of a layout-design right, or the refusal of an application for registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board established under this Act. The Appellate Board shall, prior to commencing adjudication of any appeal, ascertain whether the appellant has deposited the prescribed fee and furnished such evidence as may be required to substantiate the grounds of the appeal. A crucial function judicial member of the Appellate Board shall be appointed from amongst persons who are, or have been, judges of a High Court, or are qualified to be so appointed, and shall preside over any bench hearing appeals relating to the interpretation of legal principles. Provided that, in cases involving complex technical issues, the Board may constitute a special bench with enhanced technical expertise, subject to the approval of the Chairperson. The decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for any recourse permissible under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

The Controller shall maintain a register of patents, and such register shall be open for inspection by any member of the public subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect the register shall submit an application in the prescribed form and pay the prescribed fee. The Controller may, if satisfied that the applicant has a legitimate interest, grant access to the register. Where an application for a patent is refused, the applicant may, within a period of one month from the date of the refusal, file an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. 

For the purposes of determining novelty, an invention originating in an invention convention country shall be treated as if it were part of the state of the art only if it was made available to the public before the date of filing of the complete specification in India. The means register shall be updated monthly with details of all applications received and patents granted. Any error in the register may be rectified by the Controller upon application and subject to verification of records.

An application for a patent shall be accompanied by a statement specifying the class or classes to which the invention relates and a full description of the invention, including all drawings necessary to understand it. The Controller General may require the applicant to furnish further particulars concerning the nature and scope of the claimed invention, provided that such requirements are reasonable and do not unduly delay the registration process. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall assign an official filing date and record the details in the prescribed register. Any person claiming inventorship under this Act must provide documentation substantiating their contribution to the conception of the act patent. The Controller may reject an application if it is found to be deficient in clarity or completeness as per guidelines issued by the Central Government.

An applicant seeking to respect filing application for a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit Form IC-LA along with a declaration verifying originality and freedom from prior publication. The Registrar may require further documentation, including detailed schematics and manufacturing process descriptions, if deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act regarding substantial similarity. Failure to provide requested information within thirty days of notification will result in suspension of processing until such time as complete data is furnished. An application shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee payable to the Government, and any subsequent amendments must adhere to prescribed formatting guidelines. The applicant’s identity and address details provided at the time of respect filing application are deemed accurate for all official correspondence under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "copy" with respect to any work shall mean and include any mere reproduction of the work in any medium whatsoever, including but not limited to, the making of copies of a work, by photocopying or similar processes. Such copy shall be deemed an infringing reproduction where it is made without authorization from the owner of copyright under this Act, provided that such authorization may be granted expressly or impliedly. A digital file containing identical data as the original work shall also constitute a copy for the purposes of determining infringement. The term "similar processes" includes any technological means resulting in a substantially similar reproduction of the protected elements of the work.

Any person holding copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical, or artistic work intended for broadcast, and subsequently incorporated into a broadcast work stating, may grant a license conferring the right to reproduce the work in any medium. Such licenses shall specify the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses of the reproduction rights granted. The grantor retains full ownership of copyright under this Act unless explicitly transferred by written assignment registered with the Copyright Office. Any assignee acquiring such rights shall be bound by the terms stipulated within the original license agreement. Further, a broadcaster may elect to secure exclusive performance rights for a broadcast work stating, provided that equitable remuneration is paid to the copyright holder as determined through negotiation or, failing that, arbitration under procedures established herein.

Where a denomination variety is registered, the Registrar shall issue a certificate specifying the registrant as the owner of the breeder’s rights in respect of that denomination. Subject to any conditions imposed during registration, the registrant shall be entitled to institute civil proceedings for infringement of those rights and may seek remedies including injunctions, damages, and account of profits derived from the infringing activities. Provided that, where an unauthorized person sells propagating material or harvest bearing a registered denomination variety, the owner may apply to the Authority for appropriate action under this Act. Further, any act of misrepresentation concerning the origin or characteristics of plant material involving a registered denomination variety shall be deemed an infringement and subject to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar may also issue warnings and directions to prevent unfair competition relating to such denominations.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor of a layout-design or a related layout-design, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or displays a product which infringes the said layout-design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the relevant adjudicating officer and may include compensation equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringing party obtained a license from the proprietor. Further, where an infringement is established under this Act, the Court may order the destruction of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The Central Government may, through notification, prescribe penalties for contravention of these provisions, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. This applies specifically to matters concerning the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act 2000.

For the purposes of this Act, “educational institution” means any establishment registered under law and primarily engaged in providing instruction or training in any field of knowledge, including but not limited to schools, colleges, universities, vocational training centres, and research institutions; provided that such establishments are recognized by a governmental authority or accredited by an established body. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, add to or remove from the list of educational institutions as it deems fit, subject to guidelines framed under this Act. Any decision regarding recognition or accreditation shall be final and binding.

Any person being the proprietor of a registered trade mark, desiring to grant a license to another party for the use of said mark in relation to specified goods or services, shall execute an instrument of licensing in writing, detailing the scope of permitted use, geographical territory, and duration of the license. Where a business india application is made seeking assignment of the trade mark, the transferor shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, clearly delineate all existing licenses granted prior to the proposed assignment, including particulars of the licensees, royalty rates, and any conditions attached thereto. The assignee shall be deemed to be bound by the terms of such pre-existing licenses unless expressly agreed otherwise in writing by all parties concerned. Assignment of a trade mark incorporating a license shall not automatically terminate said license; however, the assignee may, with reasonable cause, seek modification or termination of any license as provided herein, subject to dispute resolution mechanisms established under this Act. Failure to disclose existing licenses in a business india application may render the assignment invalid.

A breeder who has developed a new denomination variety shall be entitled to registration, subject to the provisions of this Act, if such variety conforms to the essential characteristics as prescribed and is duly registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Any farmer who has bred or developed a new denomination variety, or a descendant thereof, may, as provided herein, apply for registration, notwithstanding any rights accruing to the initial breeder, provided that such farmer can demonstrate substantial contribution to the development of the said variety. Where a registered variety is found to be essentially derived from an existing variety, the breeder of the existing variety shall have the right to equitable compensation from the breeder of the essentially derived variety. The Authority may, upon application and subject to verification, grant a license to a registered breeder to utilize a protected denomination variety for research purposes, and any commercialization arising from such research shall be subject to a royalty agreement negotiated between the parties. Any dispute regarding the entitlement to benefit sharing or compensation shall be adjudicated by the designated tribunal.

A proprietor of a trade mark aggrieved by any act or omission constituting infringement may institute suit for damages and an injunction as provided herein; however, where a defendant in such a suit claims that their use of the sign does not infringe the registered trade mark, they shall be entitled to demonstrate bona fide acquisition of a corresponding right under this Act. Further, notwithstanding any order made by a court or tribunal regarding interim relief or permanent restraint, a party proceeding notwithstanding an injunction may apply for modification or vacation thereof, demonstrating substantial compliance with the terms of the original order and proving that continued operation is essential for their livelihood. The proprietor shall be entitled to claim damages proportionate to the extent of actual loss suffered due to such continuing use; provided that contributory infringement shall be actionable only where the infringer knew, or had reasonable grounds to know, of the registered trade mark.

Where an invention has been patented under this Act, and the patentee demonstrates to the satisfaction of the Controller that the invention is being commercially used within India, a right of action shall accrue to the patentee for infringement. Any person who, without authorisation from the patentee, makes, constructs, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports into India any patented article, or attempts so to do, shall be deemed to have infringed the patent and is liable for damages. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint of infringement, issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, provided that such actions demonstrably impede the use invention by others. Penalties for wilful infringement as determined under this Act will apply.

A service, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall include any activity, benefit or facility offered or rendered to another, whether by electronic means or otherwise, and encompassing but not limited to the provision of intangible goods. An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark used in connection with a service shall clearly and accurately delineate the scope of said service in the application, adhering to the classification of services as prescribed by the Nice Classification, as adopted from time to time. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, require further clarification regarding the nature of the service if the initial description is found to be vague or ambiguous. Where a service is provided as an integral component of the sale of goods, the application shall specify both the goods and the service, and registration may be granted for either or both, as appropriate. Any dispute regarding the classification of a service shall be determined by the Registrar, whose decision shall be final and binding.

Any proprietor of a geographical indication comprised of Darjeeling tea shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement under this Act. Such infringement includes any use of a sign liable to cause confusion as to the origin of the goods, or where such use constitutes an unfair appropriation of the reputation associated with the registered geographical indication. Remedies available to the proprietor include injunctions restraining further infringing acts and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer. Provided that, in determining damages, due consideration shall be given to any bonafide use prior to registration. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the registered proprietor, direct any person found to be using the geographical indication deceptively to cease such use and pay compensation for losses incurred.

Where an applicant seeks to amend a filed patent application, such amendment shall only pertain to details concerning the description and claims; alterations impacting the substance of the invention as originally presented are prohibited. The amended specification must fully disclose the subject matter sought to be protected, adhering strictly to principles of clarity and enabling disclosure. Further, any addition or modification to the filing specification matter requires explicit written consent from the Controller, obtained prior to publication under this Act. Such consent shall only be granted if the Controller is satisfied that the amendment does not substantially alter the nature of the invention claimed and maintains compliance with all relevant provisions regarding novelty and inventive step as provided herein.

Where the proprietor of a patent has granted a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, relating to the patented invention, such license may be assigned by the proprietor subject to the provisions herein. The assignor shall provide written notice to the Controller within thirty days of any assignment affecting the rights conferred under the patent, detailing the assignee’s name and address, and specifying the extent of the assignment. Further, where a patent has been surrendered or revoked, any license granted prior thereto shall remain valid unless expressly terminated by agreement between the licensor and licensee. The patent office shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses affecting patents, which shall be open to public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees. Any person seeking to enforce rights under an assignment must provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller confirming the validity of said assignment.

The Controller, exercising the powers vested under this Act, shall maintain a public register of all patents granted and applications pending, ensuring accessibility subject to reasonable fees as may be prescribed. Any person desiring to inspect such register shall submit a written request to the Controller, detailing the scope of inspection and identifying the patent or application of interest. The India Registrar requires that all entries in the register be accurately maintained and indexed, facilitating efficient search and retrieval of information. Where an application is amended, the Controller shall ensure that the register reflects the most current version of the specification and claims. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, require a certified copy of any document to be furnished by the applicant before granting access to the register. Any objection to a decision of the Controller regarding access may be made to the designated appellate authority as provided herein, and the India Registrar shall forward such objection without delay.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved may petition the Controller for its restoration. Such petition shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable grounds for the failure to pay said fee. The Controller may, subject to just cause shown, grant leave for the patentee to apply for a continuation of the patent, effectively enabling renewal. This application shall include payment of all outstanding renewal fees together with any applicable late payment penalties as determined under this Act. Provided that the Controller may require an additional hearing if the restoration would prejudice the public interest or affect existing rights derived from the expired patent. The decision of the Controller regarding such petitions is final, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any application for registration of a trade mark which discloses a justified reason for its adoption, notwithstanding any prior use by another, shall be subject to a rigorous examination as provided herein to determine the bona fides of the applicant and the extent of potential confusion. Where the applicant demonstrates, to the satisfaction of the Registrar, that the disclosed justification outweighs the established rights of a prior user, registration may be permitted, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary to protect the interests of the prior user. However, any decision of the Registrar regarding such disclosed justified registration shall be appealable to the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order, and the Board may, after hearing both parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the Registrar’s decision. A finding of bad faith on the part of the applicant shall be conclusive against registration, even if a technical justification is initially presented.

An applicant desiring to secure an international registration for a trade mark, in addition to fulfilling the requirements as provided herein relating to domestic applications, shall file with the Trade Marks Registry a statement indicating the countries or territories beyond India where protection is sought. The application for international registration shall be accompanied by a certified copy of any basic application or registration relied upon and shall conform to the provisions of the Madrid Protocol on International Registration of Marks. Where an applicant seeks to designate a country which is not a member of the said Protocol, such designation shall have no effect unless reciprocal arrangements exist between India and that country as determined by notification in the Official Gazette. The Registry may require translation of any document submitted which is not in English or Hindi, subject to payment of prescribed fees. Any opposition to an international registration extending to India shall be governed by the provisions relating to domestic oppositions, with such modifications as the Central Government may deem necessary. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in refusal of the application for international registration or limitation of its effect.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a Plant Variety Protection Agreement, whether entered into prior to or subsequent to the registration of a plant variety, may stipulate conditions relating to the licensing and assignment of farmers’ rights pertaining to propagated material. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted uses, including but not limited to cultivation for self-consumption, sale, and exchange. The Agriculture Commissioner may, upon receiving a complaint regarding unfair or restrictive clauses within such an agreement, initiate inquiries and issue directives to rectify imbalances affecting farmer interests. Assignment of farmers’ rights under this Act requires prior written consent from the concerned farmer and registration with the appropriate authority. Any transfer shall be deemed invalid if it contravenes the principles of equity and fairness as determined by the Agriculture Commissioner.

An application trade mark shall be deemed to infringe this Act if, following its publication under section 59, any person knowingly uses a sign identical or confusingly similar to the applied-for mark in relation to goods or services for which the mark is registered, with the intent to gain an unfair commercial advantage or to exploit the reputation of the proprietor. Such infringement shall be actionable at the suit of the applicant and may result in damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the applicant, not exceeding five per cent of the infringer’s turnover attributable to the infringing use. The Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint, issue an injunction restraining the infringing activity and order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the mark, provided that due process is followed as prescribed herein.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark shall, as part of the application, furnish a clear and accurate trade description detailing the goods or services to which the mark relates, and specifying the class thereof according to the prescribed classification. The trade description shall not include any misleading indication as to the character, quality, or geographical origin of the goods or services. A trade description may, subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry, include a statement of colour, material, or other essential characteristics, provided that such statement is factual and does not create a false association with any other trade mark. Where the goods or services are manufactured or provided by a licensee, the application shall disclose the nature of the license and the conditions governing its use, and this shall form part of the registered trade description. Failure to accurately represent the trade description may render the application liable to be refused, or the registration subject to revocation as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised by any person under this Act against the acceptance of an application for registration of a trade mark, such objector may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of notice of the decision. The Appellate Tribunal shall hear arguments and consider evidence presented by both the applicant and the objector, and may allow or dismiss the appeal as it deems fit. It is provided that in cases where the objection relates to the similarity of the trade mark sought to be registered with an earlier trade mark used by a business india situate outside the territory of India, the Tribunal shall give due consideration to the reputation and goodwill attached to such foreign trade mark.

For the purposes of this Act, “description means trade” shall be interpreted liberally and with due regard to consumer perception; provided that, where an entity utilizes a visual representation purporting to indicate the origin, quality, or characteristics of goods, such representation constitutes a description within the meaning of this Act even if lacking explicit textual claims. An appeal against any order determining whether a particular depiction qualifies as a misleading trade description may be made to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal; however, such appeal shall only be entertained where it is demonstrated that the original determination was manifestly arbitrary or based on an erroneous interpretation of established legal principles concerning deceptive advertising practices and consumer detriment.

Any registered proprietor of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, grant licenses to use the mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, and such licenses may be granted on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon between the parties, including provisions as to quality control and duration. An assignment of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the same conditions and restrictions as apply to the assignment of goodwill of a business, and shall be in writing and registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Where a trade mark is assigned with the goodwill of a business, the assignee shall be deemed to be the proprietor of the mark, subject to any agreement to the contrary. Any agreement restricting mark use, whether by way of license or assignment, shall be construed as limiting the rights of the assignor or licensor only to the extent expressly stated therein, and shall not affect the rights of others. A transfer of ownership, even without formal assignment, resulting in continued mark use may be considered equitable assignment.

Where an infringement action is brought before a competent court, and the defendant alleges that the patent in question lacks novelty or involves an obvious invention, the patentee shall be entitled to present evidence demonstrating the inventive step. Should the court find, upon review of such evidence, that the alleged lack of novelty or obviousness substantially impacts the scope of the claims as initially granted, it may order a rectification of the patent. This rectification shall clarify the legitimate subject matter protected by the patent. Further, if the defendant demonstrates through credible testimony and documentary proof that attempts to secure a voluntary license from the patentee were made on reasonable terms and conditions, yet remained unsuccessful within a reasonable period, the court may consider this factor in determining damages for infringement. The assessment of what constitutes a reasonable period shall be guided by principles of fairness and equity.

Where an application for registration of copyright is rejected under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such rejection to the relevant High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of communication of the order of rejection. Such appeal may be made on grounds that the Registrar’s decision was erroneous in law or fact, including but not limited to misinterpretation of originality criteria or improper consideration of evidence presented. The applicant shall bear the burden of demonstrating such error; however, the Court may consider any reference use mark appearing on submitted materials as relevant context for assessing claimed authorship. It is provided that the High Court may require the Registrar to submit further documentation and reasoning supporting their decision prior to rendering judgment.

A cinematograph film shall be deemed to include any visual recording on celluloid or other medium, and the rights therein vest initially with the producer. However, where a cinematograph film is produced based upon a pre-existing literary or artistic work, the owner of copyright in such work retains their respective rights, subject to the terms of contract between them and the producer. Any dispute regarding ownership of copyright in a cinematograph film, or concerning infringement thereof, may be brought before the High Court having jurisdiction. Should any party feel aggrieved by an order of the High Court, they shall have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days from the date of the impugned order and demonstrating substantial questions of law requiring consideration on appeal; the manner applying appellate procedure will be as prescribed by the rules of said court. The producer’s rights are not absolute and remain subject to provisions relating to fair dealing as provided herein.

Where any patentee or licensee fails to comply with the conditions of a license granted under this Act, or otherwise acts in contravention of the provisions relating to assignment or transmission of patents, the Controller shall initiate an inquiry imposing penalty. Such inquiry may be conducted by the Controller or by an officer duly authorised for that purpose. The person against whom the inquiry is initiated shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present their case and adduce evidence in mitigation. Any agreement restricting the exploitation of the patented invention, entered into without complying with the requirements as provided herein, shall be deemed void and subject to such penalties as may be determined during the inquiry. Further, any assignment made contrary to the provisions regarding royalty payments shall be liable for rectification or revocation at the Controller’s discretion.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of registration of a geographical indication may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to file an appeal within the prescribed time shall be deemed a waiver of the right to challenge the order. Where a registered proprietor institutes proceedings against any party proceeding in contravention of the provisions relating to use or production, the Registrar may intervene as a party and assist the Court with relevant technical information pertaining to the geographical indication's characteristics. Any penalty imposed for infringement shall be recoverable from the defaulting party as an arrears of land revenue, subject to judicial review.

Where a person has made an infringing copy of a registered semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, that person shall be liable to damages. Such damages shall be assessed subject to the principles of fairness and equity, taking into account the benefit accruing to the infringer as a result of the infringement, and the loss suffered by the owner of the registered design. The owner may further seek an injunction restraining the infringing party from continuing such acts or engaging in conduct that is likely to cause damage to the reputation of the layout-design. Provided that, where the infringement was demonstrably unintentional, the Court may reduce the amount of damages awarded as it deems just and equitable. Any order for delivery up or destruction of the infringing semiconductor shall be made under this Act.

Where a person aggrieved by an order appellate relating to infringement of layout-design rights believes that the Appellate Tribunal has acted without due consideration of material facts presented during proceedings, that person may file an application seeking review. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order appellate and must specify the errors apparent on the face of the record which are alleged to have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. The applicant shall further demonstrate how the omission or misdirection impacted the ultimate determination of infringement. Failure to respect filing application requirements, including payment of prescribed fees, will render the review application inadmissible. Any counter-claim arising from such an application shall be dealt with expeditiously under this Act.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to the revocation or infringement of a patent believes such order to be manifestly unjust or without due regard to the evidence presented, that party may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board shall give notice to all other parties interested in the matter and afford them an opportunity to present their views. Upon hearing arguments and considering the record of proceedings before the Controller, the Appellate Board may confirm, vary or reverse the order appealed against. Any amount directed to be paid as damages or costs under this Act shall be recoverable from the defaulting party as if it were a decree of a civil court. The adjudicating officer appointed by the Controller for conducting inquiries relating to patent infringement shall act in accordance with principles of natural justice.

Where a proprietor of a registered trademark has established a reputation in relation to specified goods or services, no person shall use any sign or mark, or any mode of presentation thereof, that is identical or confusingly similar to the registered trade mark and which, when used in relation to goods or services not authorized by the proprietor, creates a false impression regarding the nature, quality, origin, or suitability for purpose of those goods or services. This prohibition extends where such use constitutes used falsifying trade, being an imitation intended to deceive consumers into believing that the goods or services originate from, or are approved by, the registered proprietor. Provided that this restriction shall not apply if the defendant demonstrates clear and conspicuous differentiation sufficient to preclude consumer confusion, as determined under this Act.

Any aggrieved party claiming infringement of copyright under this Act may appeal to the Copyrights Appellate Board against an order passed by the Registrar of Copyrights. The appellant shall deposit with the Board such sum as may be prescribed, failing which the appeal shall stand dismissed. Where a dispute arises concerning the determination of who is the true and first inventor of a work subject to copyright, the Board may conduct inquiries and hear evidence from all relevant parties before rendering its decision. Any person found guilty of wilful infringement by the Board shall be liable to pay damages not exceeding ten times the actual pecuniary loss suffered by the copyright owner or rupees one million, whichever is greater, and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

A broadcasting organisation intending to make any use of a copyrighted work under this Act shall first obtain a license from the owner or authorized agent thereof, provided that such organization demonstrates compliance with established industry standards for royalty distribution. The application for said license must include detailed particulars regarding the intended broadcast, including date, time, geographical area of transmission, and the specific works to be utilized. Further, where the copyrighted work incorporates elements subject to moral rights, the broadcasting organisation shall ensure adequate attribution is given as stipulated by law. Failure to secure prior authorization or demonstrable adherence to these conditions may render the broadcasting organization liable for infringement proceedings under this Act.

Any person dissatisfied with a decision made by an adjudicating officer concerning infringement proceedings relating to a registered trademark shall have recourse to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within ninety days of communication of that decision. Failure to file such an appeal within the prescribed period will render the aggrieved party estopped from further challenging the adjudicating officer’s determination, subject to just cause demonstrated to the satisfaction of the Tribunal. The adjudicating officer period for rendering a reasoned order following a hearing shall not exceed one hundred and twenty days from the date of service of notice; exceeding this timeframe may invite penalties as determined by the Tribunal.

Every application for the registration of a work under this Act shall be made in writing in the prescribed form and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in Schedule III. The applicant shall furnish all details relating to authorship, ownership, publication, and other particulars relevant to the determination of copyright subsisting in the work. Where an application is for the registration of a cinematograph film, proof of necessary censorship certification from the Central Board of Film Certification shall be submitted along with the application. An incomplete application may, at the discretion of the Registrar, be returned to the applicant requesting clarification or additional information; however, no such request shall extend the statutory processing time beyond ninety days. Subject to verification and satisfaction that all requirements are met as provided herein, the Registrar shall enter the particulars of the work in the Register of Copyrights and issue a certificate of registration. Any false representation made within an application will be subject to penalties under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “transmission” with respect to a registered trademark shall mean the voluntary transfer of all rights and privileges pertaining to the said trademark from the proprietor thereof to another person. Such transmission may occur by way of assignment, license, pledge, or any other instrument recognized under law as conveying ownership or control. Provided that, where such transmission is effected through a license agreement, the terms and conditions governing the use of the mark shall be clearly stipulated within the agreement itself. The proprietor shall provide notice of any such transmission to the Registrar, who may require supporting documentation demonstrating due execution and validity thereof, as provided herein.

Where a layout design owner desires to grant a license or assign rights in respect of a registered integrated circuit layout design, such license or assignment shall be documented through a formal instrument specifying the full particulars of the transaction. These particulars include, but are not limited to, the identity of the licensor and licensee or assignee, a precise description of the licensed or assigned elements of the layout design, the geographical scope of the grant, and the duration thereof. Any subsequent modification to the terms of such license or assignment must also be recorded in writing, adhering to similar form petition particulars as initially prescribed. Provided that, where the license is non-exclusive, the owner may grant further licenses without requiring consent from prior licensees; however, any royalty rates shall be disclosed under this Act.

A proprietor of a registered trade mark, or a person using a trade mark with his consent, may, where another person is using a deceptively similar trade mark, seek remedies as provided herein, notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act. However, such remedies shall not be available against a person who uses the trade mark solely to indicate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin or time of production of the goods or services in question, or to describe the characteristics of the goods or services. 

Specifically, a defendant shall not be liable if the use of the mark constitutes fair use, including descriptive fair use, and is reasonably necessary to indicate the connection between the defendant and the goods or services offered. Where a mark is established as a reference use mark, the proprietor of the registered trade mark shall bear the burden of proving that the defendant’s use is likely to cause confusion or deceptively indicate a connection. Any injunction granted under this Act shall be subject to such terms and conditions as the Court may deem fit.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark relating to services connected with proceedings within a house parliament session, conduct such examination as is provided herein. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar refusing registration on the grounds that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the said parliamentary services may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal shall hear appeals under this Act and may allow or dismiss the appeal, or make such other order as it deems fit. Further, where an objection is raised alleging likelihood of confusion with a prior registered trade mark used in connection with similar services, the Registrar shall provide both parties with an opportunity for cross-examination and submission of written arguments. The Registrar’s decision on any such matter shall be final subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark has, in relation to any goods or services, also registered one or more other trade marks as associated trade marks, no person shall, without the consent of the proprietor of the primary trade mark, use any representation that is identical or confusingly similar to such associated trade marks. Any infringement under this provision shall be deemed a willful violation and subject to damages assessed at not less than ten times the actual loss suffered by the registered proprietor, nor less than fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, upon finding of infringement, the Court may order the destruction of all goods bearing the infringing mark, as well as any materials used in their manufacture or packaging, provided that such order is consistent with principles of natural justice.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, whether relating to the grant of a patent, the rectification of a register, or the revocation of a patent, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s order, unless an application for a certified copy of the order has been made, in which case the appeal may be filed within ninety days from the date of receipt of the certified copy. The Appellate Board may, subject to sufficient cause being shown, extend the appeal period by a further thirty days. All appeals shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee and a statement of the grounds on which the appellant relies, and failure to comply with these requirements may render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for recourse to the High Court on grounds of error of law.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a patentee may grant exclusive licences relating to the production and sale of their invention within India. Such licences shall be assignable and transferable in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, and any such assignment or transfer shall be notified to the Controller for registration. Where a compulsory licence is granted permitting export of a patented product, the patentee shall be entitled to receive royalties calculated on a sliding scale based upon the quantity exported and the prevailing market price within India, as determined by the Central Government. The terms of such compulsory licence export agreements may include provisions regarding technology transfer, provided that these are consistent with national industrial policy objectives. Any sub-licensing undertaken pursuant to an exclusive license shall require prior approval from the patentee.

Any person being the owner of a registered trade mark, or a trade mark pending application for registration, relating to goods produced limits india, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, assign the trade mark, or any right therein, to any other person. An assignment shall be valid only if it is in writing and authenticated by the assignor. Where the assignment includes the goodwill of the business carried on under the trade mark, notice of the assignment shall be published in the Trade Marks Journal. The assignee may apply to the Registrar to register the assignment, and upon such application, the Registrar shall register the assignment subject to verification of title and payment of the prescribed fee. A license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, may also be granted in respect of such trade marks, and all terms and conditions of the license shall be subject to the overriding provisions of this Act. Failure to comply with these provisions relating to assignment or licensing shall render the transaction voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, provided that such option is exercised within two years from the date of knowledge of the non-compliance.

Where a proprietor establishes that use by another person is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication, the Board may grant an order injunction restraining such use. This restraint shall extend to acts which create a false association between the goods or services offered under the infringing mark and the genuine product originating from the geographically defined area. Provided that, in determining whether use constitutes dilution, the Board shall consider the extent to which the geographical indication has come to be recognized by the relevant public as identifying a particular quality, origin, or reputation of goods or services. Further, any person aggrieved by an order injunction may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order, subject to conditions regarding costs and interim relief pending disposal of the appeal.

Applications filed under this Act may, subject to compliance with the regulations prescribed by the Controller, be treated as international applications for the purposes of the Patent Cooperation Treaty. Where an applicant elects to pursue examination and grant in India following a stage under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the application shall be deemed to have been filed on the date it was initially received by the International Bureau. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating adherence to timelines stipulated within the Patent Cooperation Treaty for processing international applications. Further, any fees paid to the International Bureau relating to search or preliminary examination shall be taken into account when determining applicable Indian patent application fees, provided that a certificate of payment is submitted with the request for such consideration.

Any layout-design, to be registrable under this Act, shall demonstrate a manner issuing from an original creative skill and technical development in the creation of a semiconductor integrated circuit. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require a detailed specification of the article in which the layout-design is incorporated, and a statement of its functional purpose. Subject to the provisions herein, a layout-design primarily intended for cosmetic or ornamental application, analogous to those regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 concerning packaging or aesthetic presentation, may be registered provided it also possesses a demonstrable technical character distinct from mere visual appeal. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered layout-designs, detailing the applicant, proprietor, and duration of protection. Any alteration to a registered layout-design, affecting its essential characteristics, shall necessitate a fresh application for registration, and the existing registration shall be deemed to have lapsed upon grant of the new registration. The prescribed fees for all applications and registrations shall be as determined by the Central Government.

The assignment of copyright in cinematograph films produced under this Act shall be valid only if executed by an individual holding at least fifty percent equity shareholding in the production company and registered with the designated Copyright Office within thirty days of execution. Such assignments may include, but are not limited to, rights pertaining to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or public performance. Where a copyright owner desires to license any right under this Act, the terms of such licensing agreement shall be clearly defined, specifying duration, geographical scope, and royalty rates payable to the assignor. Any dispute arising from an assignment or license agreement may be referred for resolution to an instituted district court, whose decision shall be final and binding on all parties involved. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all assignments and licenses registered under this provision.

A registered user may grant a license to use the trade mark for which he is registered, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in such license being consistent with the protection afforded under this Act. Such licenses shall be assignable by the registered user, provided that any assignment requires prior notification to the proprietor of the trade mark and consent obtained where the license expressly stipulates it. The proprietor may object to an assignment on reasonable grounds relating to the potential dilution or impairment of the distinctive character of the trade mark; such objections must be communicated within thirty days of the notice. A registered user shall not, without express written authorization from the proprietor, use the trade mark in a manner that is deceptive or contrary to honest practices in industrial competition. Any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee shall remain subject to the original license terms and conditions as provided herein.

Where any party, other than the applicant for a patent, considers that the grant of a patent has been obtained contrary to this Act, or that the patented invention does not satisfy the requirements of novelty or inventive step as provided herein, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Opposition Board. The Opposition Board shall serve a copy of the notice on the patentee and afford both parties an opportunity to present their respective arguments and evidence in support of or against the validity of the patent. Any decision made by the Opposition Board regarding the use patent may be appealed to the relevant High Court within a period of three months from the date of such decision, subject to any applicable fees and procedural requirements as prescribed under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee or assignee may grant exclusive licences under the patent, and such licence shall be irrevocable without the consent in writing of the licensee. Where a patent has been assigned, the assignee shall have all rights which the patentee might have had under this Act. The power to assign or license a patent shall extend to include the right to grant licenses relating to inventions claimed in a corresponding application for patents filed in a 6referred convention country. Provided that any such assignment or licence granted prior to the publication of the patent, if it contains terms which restrict the exploitation of the patented invention within India, may be challenged under provisions pertaining to anti-competitive practices as determined by relevant regulatory authorities. The Controller may require evidence demonstrating compliance with these conditions before registering an assignment or license relating to a 6referred convention country.

Where an application for registration of a patent is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds upon which the applicant relies in challenging the decision. The Board shall afford the applicant and any other party interested an opportunity to present their respective cases, including oral arguments, and shall record its findings on each issue raised during the appeal proceedings.

The register references maintained by the Controller are deemed conclusive evidence of the status of patent applications and granted patents subject to any fraud or misrepresentation proven before the Board. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Appellate Board may further petition the Supreme Court under this Act, provided that such petition is filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed from.

A patent application shall not be deemed valid unless the claims defining the scope of the invention are clear and supported by the description provided herein. Claims so drafted must particularly define the matter for which protection is sought, distinguishing it from prior art and establishing a definite boundary for the exclusive right conferred upon grant of a patent. Where a mark use is asserted as integral to the functioning or identification of an invention claimed, such use shall be explicitly detailed within the specification and correspondingly reflected in the claims themselves. Any claim lacking sufficient clarity or support may be subject to objection during examination and require amendment before proceeding further. Provided that, amendments made to claims must not extend beyond the disclosure originally presented in the complete specification. The Controller of Patents may, notwithstanding any other provision, reject a claim deemed ambiguous or unsupported by adequate description, thereby affecting its validity under this Act. Failure to adhere to these requirements shall render the application liable for refusal.

An application for designation of India in an international application filed under the Madrid Agreement shall be examined as if it were an application for registration of a trade mark in India, subject to the provisions herein relating to relative grounds for refusal. The Trade Marks Registry may require the applicant to furnish such information or documents as are necessary to ascertain whether the marks indicated in the international application comply with Indian law and practice concerning clarity, distinctiveness, and acceptability of marks indications. Where an international registration extends to India, it shall be deemed to be registered in the Register of Trade Marks maintained under this Act, and the International Bureau shall be notified accordingly by the Registry. Any opposition proceedings relating to such extended registrations shall be conducted as provided herein, with the Registrar having jurisdiction over all matters arising during those proceedings.

Where any person offers or provides a service relating to telecommunications infrastructure, and uses a sign, whether descriptive or not, which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trademark used by another person for services identical or akin to their own, that first-mentioned person shall be deemed to have engaged in an act of detrimental imitation. Such acts are actionable under this Act as passing off, irrespective of any prior use or registration relating to the imitated mark. Any proprietor of a registered trademark may apply to the relevant adjudicating authority for relief, including injunctions preventing further infringing conduct and damages commensurate with the loss suffered due to such infringement. The adjudicating authority shall have power to impose penalties not exceeding ten lakhs rupees for each instance of proven violation.

Where any person applies a false trade description to any goods or services offered for sale, or makes use of any false representation in connection with the sale thereof, such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. For the purposes of this provision, “description means trade” and includes any indication which is likely to mislead as to the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, suitability or other aspect of the goods or services. Any infringement of this section shall attract a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, and in the case of a second or subsequent offence, not less than one million rupees. Furthermore, where an offence occurs repeatedly, the court may order the seizure and destruction of the infringing goods.

Any person committing an alleged offence under this Act, involving the falsification of a registered trade mark or the fraudulent application thereof, shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where the alleged offence relates to goods of a significant value, exceeding five lakh rupees, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years. The court, however, may, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, impose a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. A subsequent commission of an alleged offence within three years of a prior conviction shall be deemed an aggravated offence, attracting a minimum imprisonment of one year, irrespective of the value of goods involved. Any evidence obtained through lawful means, including digital records, shall be admissible in proceedings relating to such an offence, provided that the authenticity of said evidence is duly established. The Registrar may, with the approval of the Central Government, initiate investigations into suspected instances of such offences.

A claim to an invention shall not be allowed unless the applicant establishes a priority date, and such date shall be the filing date of the complete specification, subject to the provisions herein. Where an applicant claims priority from an application made in a convention country, proof of such earlier application, duly attested, shall be furnished within the prescribed period, failing which the priority date shall be the date of filing in India. However, any intervening publication, whether by the applicant or a third party, relating to the invention, may invalidate the claim to the asserted priority date, unless such publication was unavoidable and disclosed only information strictly necessary for the purpose of scientific advancement. An objection to the claimed priority date, raised by the Controller, may be appealed to the Appellate Board, and the Board’s decision shall be final, save for any recourse to writ jurisdiction as provided by law. The burden of proving the validity of the priority date rests with the applicant.

Any applicant seeking application registration shall furnish a detailed representation of the geographical area constituting the origin of the goods, accompanied by a special trust or association of producers, demonstrably representing the majority interest within that area. Should the Registrar deem the application incomplete or lacking sufficient evidence of origin, a notice specifying the deficiencies shall be issued, allowing the applicant sixty days to rectify the same. Failure to comply within this period may result in rejection of the application, subject to appeal before the Appellate Board. However, a concurrent objection filed by a party claiming prior and continuous use of a similar mark, even if unregistered, may suspend the registration process pending resolution of the conflicting claims. The Appellate Board’s decision regarding such objections shall be final and binding, provided that the objection is demonstrably bona fide and not merely to delay legitimate application registration. Any appeal to the Board requires a prescribed fee and adherence to procedural rules as provided herein.

Applications for grant of Plant Variety Rights shall be accompanied by a detailed statement specifying the denomination proposed for the variety and a justification demonstrating its distinctiveness relative to existing varieties. The Examining Authority may require further clarification or experimental data regarding claimed characteristics, provided that such requests are made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the application. Objections relating to novelty or distinctiveness must be filed by any interested party within ninety days from the publication of an advertisement under this Act inviting objections. Claims purposes section 18(2) dictates that all objections shall state the grounds upon which they are based and provide supporting evidence, failing which they shall be deemed inadmissible. The Authority shall afford both the applicant and the objector a reasonable opportunity to present their case during hearings. Decisions regarding the acceptance or rejection of claims shall be recorded in writing and communicated to all parties involved.

Any person desiring a licence of a patent, being a patent granted for a process for the manufacture of a substance intended for use in any industry, shall submit an application to the Controller in the prescribed manner, demonstrating sufficient grounds for the grant of such a licence. The application shall include a statement of the applicant’s intended use of the patented invention and the scope of the proposed manufacture. The patentee shall be notified of the application and afforded an opportunity to submit objections, subject to confidentiality provisions as provided herein. A licence granted under this Act shall be non-exclusive, and royalty rates shall be determined by the Controller, considering the applicant’s manufacturing capacity and the patentee’s legitimate interests. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, refuse the application if the applicant fails to demonstrate a genuine intent to work the invention for the benefit of the public. Any dispute regarding the terms of the licence patent shall be subject to appeal to the High Court.

Applications for registration shall be examined by the Registrar to ascertain whether the mark is distinctive and not deceptive. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information relating to the use of the trade mark or any other relevant matter. Where an application relates to a composite mark consisting of words, devices, or three-dimensional features, the representation of each element shall be clearly delineated in the application. Matters included register are subject to periodic review by the Registrar and may be amended or removed if they no longer comply with the provisions of this Act or any rules made thereunder. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to matters included register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an examiner discovers that a patent has been granted in contravention of any provision of this Act, or any rule made thereunder, he shall forthwith report such discovery to the Controller. The Controller, upon receiving such report, may direct the Registrar to issue a notice to the patentee concerned, affording him an opportunity of being heard in the matter. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of that decision. Failure on the part of any officer or authority to comply with directions issued by the Controller shall be deemed as contempt of the Controller and such person shall liable penalty which may extend to fifty thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. The Controller may, in his discretion, impose a further penalty not exceeding ten thousand rupees for every day during which the default continues.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark may apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner for the registration of the trade mark under this Act. The registrar application shall contain a statement of particulars of the trade mark, including a representation thereof in the manner directed by the regulations. An applicant may, subject to the provisions herein, apply for registration of a trade mark for goods or services falling in more than one class. Where an application for registration is filed for services, the applicant shall indicate the description of the services in clear and unambiguous terms. The Registrar may, prior to accepting the application, require the applicant to amend the specification of goods or services to ensure clarity and compliance with the classification of goods and services as adopted under this Act. Provided that, no amendment shall be permitted which alters the essential character of the trade mark.

Where an application for registration of a mark is filed under this Act, the determination of priority between competing applications shall be predicated upon the respective application dates. For the purposes of establishing prior use and subsequent claim to ownership, it is provided that the *application date shall* be conclusively deemed to be the date on which the formal request for examination is received by the Registry, subject to any evidence presented demonstrating a clear error in recording such receipt. Any party disputing the recorded application date may petition the Intellectual Property Appellate Board with supporting documentation; however, such petitions must be filed within three months of notification of acceptance and are subject to costs as determined by the Board. The Registrar’s decision on priority is appealable to the Appellate Board.

Where an applicant has filed an application in India for a patent relating to a process or composition for the manufacture of a substance and subsequently discovers that the invention disclosed is not novel, the Controller may, subject to due notice being given to the applicant, grant a certificate of postponement. This certificate shall remain valid until the expiration of a period of six months from the date of publication of an advertisement in a trade journal specifying the particulars of the application india filed and the reasons for the postponement. During this period, the applicant may submit arguments or evidence demonstrating the novelty of the invention. Failure to do so within that timeframe will result in the application being deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by such a decision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order.

Where an application for patents is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal. The Appellate Board shall hear such appeals and may allow the appeal, dismiss it, or make such other disposition as it considers appropriate, subject to just consideration of the evidence presented by both parties. Any person aggrieved by an order made by the Appellate Board may further appeal to the Supreme Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The effect India patent granted shall be void if it is found, upon review under this Act or subsequent judicial proceedings, to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation.

Where a patentee elects to receive royalties in lieu of damages for infringement under this Act, the amount of such royalties shall be determined by agreement between the patentee and the infringer; provided that where no such agreement is reached within ninety days from the date of written notice served by either party, the matter may be referred to an Arbitral Tribunal constituted as per sub-section (2) of section 40. The Tribunal’s award shall be final and binding subject to appeal to the High Court only on grounds limited to jurisdiction or a demonstrable error apparent on the face of the record relating to the assessment of patentee consideration royalties. Any challenge to the reasonableness of royalty rates determined by the Arbitral Tribunal outside these specified grounds shall be deemed inadmissible.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, any person alleging infringement of a registered Integrated Circuit layout-design may file a complaint before the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act was committed, or where the cause of action arose. The complainant shall specify in the complaint the particulars of the registration certificate of the Integrated Circuit layout-design and details of the alleged infringing activity. Upon receipt of such complaint, the Commercial Court may issue interim orders restraining the defendant from continuing the infringing activity pending disposal of the suit, provided that it is satisfied that irreparable injury would be caused to the complainant if the order is not made. The court shall also have power to direct the defendant to provide an account of sales and profits derived from the alleged infringement. Any party aggrieved by any order passed under this Act may appeal to the appellate forum as provided herein.

An application for registration of a mark shall be deemed refused if the proposed mark, when used in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, conflicts with existing prior rights under this Act. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application provided that the applicant demonstrates clear and sufficient evidence of acquired distinctiveness through extensive use of the mark following its initial adoption. Such evidence must include verifiable data relating to consumer recognition and association between the mark and the applicant’s goods or services. Further, the acceptance is subject to a condition requiring the applicant to file an affidavit confirming their continued intention to utilize the registered mark in commerce within the territory of India.

Where a patent has been granted to a government undertaking engaged in the manufacture or production of essential goods, and an objection was duly raised against the grant of such patent under this Act based on grounds of anticipation or lack of novelty, the Central Government may, after affording the patentee an opportunity for being heard, direct that the invention be available for use freely to any person. Such direction shall not prejudice the right of the government undertaking to utilize the patented process or manufacture the patented product; provided that the aggrieved patentee may appeal against such direction before a High Court within thirty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate jurisdiction conferred under this Act shall extend to all questions involving the legality or validity of any direction issued by the Central Government.

Where any person proposes to use a trade mark in contravention of the rights of the registered proprietor, that person shall be required to notify the Registrar of their intention at least sixty days prior to commencement of such use. The Registrar may, after affording opportunity of being heard to both the proposer and the registered proprietor, determine whether the proposed use constitutes an infringement under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the notification process may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within a period of ninety days from the date of such determination. Provided that, if the proposed use is demonstrably for fair dealing purposes, the Registrar may waive the requirement to notify, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

Where an application for registration of a plant variety is deemed to be refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is contested. The Registrar case shall then proceed with due consideration given to the points of law and fact raised in the memorandum of appeal, and all relevant documents submitted by the appellant. Further, the Registrar may require the appellant to provide additional information or clarification regarding the claimed novelty or distinctiveness of the plant variety. Provided that the Appellate Board finds merit in the appeal, it shall direct the Registrar to reconsider the application in accordance with its directions.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the proposed marks consist exclusively of geographical indications defining places of origin of goods, unless proof satisfactory to the Trade Marks Registry is furnished demonstrating that the applicant has used the trade mark genuinely in relation to those goods for a continuous period not less than five years immediately preceding the date of application. Furthermore, any alteration made to an accepted trade mark shall require prior approval from the Trade Marks Registry and such approval may be withheld if the alteration misrepresents the nature or quality of the goods or services with which it is associated. The Registrar may also direct rectification of a registered trade mark where use thereof constitutes unfair competition as provided herein.

A compulsory license shall be granted where an application is made to the High Court demonstrating reasonable grounds for belief that works protected under this Act are unavailable to the public at large despite diligent efforts. Any such application relating to a sound recording, cinematograph film or literary work subject to an India application must demonstrate prior negotiation with the copyright holder in good faith and a clear indication of proposed remuneration consistent with prevailing market rates. The Court may, if satisfied that the conditions for grant are met, direct the Registrar of Copyrights to issue a license upon such terms as it deems fit, including royalty payments and duration. Provided that no compulsory licence shall be granted unless the applicant undertakes to make the work available to persons with disabilities at no additional cost beyond standard access fees. The copyright holder may appeal any decision regarding the grant of a compulsory license before the designated appellate authority within sixty days of the order’s issuance, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if the applicant fails to comply with all prescribed requirements relating to the submission of documentary evidence substantiating the claimed user date.
