Provided that, where an applicant demonstrates reasonable cause for non-compliance, such as unforeseen technical difficulties in procuring requisite records, the Registrar may, at his discretion and after due consideration of representations made by the applicant, reinstate the application. The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall maintain accurate and readily accessible records detailing all instances of use of the mark within India. Failure to do so may render the proprietor liable for penalties as provided herein. Any challenge to the validity of an application registered proprieto must be brought before the relevant intellectual property tribunal within six months of publication in the Trade Marks Journal.

The Registrar may require an applicant for registration of a proposed trade mark to furnish evidence demonstrating the extent and nature of the *mark use* undertaken prior to the date of application. Such evidence shall include, but not be limited to, invoices relating to sales, advertising materials distributed, and specimens illustrating the manner in which the mark is affixed to goods or packaging thereof. Where the applicant claims user as a potential trade mark, the period of such use shall be calculated from the earliest date of any such *mark use*. The Registrar may consider evidence submitted by third parties challenging the genuineness or extent of claimed *mark use*, provided that such challenges are filed within the prescribed timeframe and accompanied by supporting documentation. Any determination regarding the validity of *mark use* evidence is subject to appeal under this Act.

Any person alleging infringement of copyright in a sound recording shall, prior to initiating proceedings before a competent court, furnish proof of registration with the Central Government as evidence of ownership; however, failure to provide such proof shall not *ipso facto* bar consideration of their claim but may be considered by the Court when assessing credibility. Where a request for a compulsory licence pertaining to a musical work or sound recording is made under this Act, and the copyright owner fails to respond within sixty days from receipt of said request with reasonable terms, an application may be filed with the designated authority seeking adjudication on appropriate royalty rates. Any determination rendered by that authority shall be binding on all parties subject to appeal before the High Court; provided that such appeal must commence within ninety days of the order’s issuance and demonstrate substantial grounds for review regarding either procedural fairness or quantum of remuneration. The aggrieved party may seek interim relief pending final adjudication, but only upon demonstrating irreparable harm.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of layout-design rights or concerning rectification proceedings may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal shall be duly constituted with a Chairperson and at least two other members, including a *functions judicial member* possessing expertise in intellectual property law. Appeals shall be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. Failure to file an appeal within this period shall ordinarily preclude further recourse under this Act. Where the aggrieved party is located in a *Contracting Party*, as defined under Article 1(1) of the Paris Convention, the Appellate Tribunal may consider relevant jurisprudence and administrative practices of that Contracting Party when determining the merits of the appeal. Penalties for non-compliance with orders of the Appellate Tribunal shall be determined as provided herein.

Where an appeal is brought under this Act against a decision of the Registrar refusing to accept an application for registration of a trade mark, the Appellate Board may, subject to any conditions it deems fit to impose, direct that the matter be remitted to the Registrar for reconsideration. Such direction shall specify the grounds upon which the original decision was deemed erroneous. The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the right to institute proceedings in the High Court against any person infringing their rights under this Act, notwithstanding any prior communication or warning given. Provided that, if the infringement is alleged to be unintentional, the Court may, as provided herein, order rectification of the error rather than award damages.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services other than those specified in the registration, and such use is likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or nature of those goods or services, any person aggrieved may apply to the Court for an injunction. Such application shall be accompanied by evidence demonstrating both the similarity between the registered trade mark and the impugned sign, and a reasonable prospect that consumer detriment will result from continued unauthorized use. The Court may grant such injunction subject to conditions regarding the scope of prohibited activities, provided that it is satisfied that the applicant has made sufficient effort to mitigate any potential harm to other interested parties. Further, the Court may require undertakings as to future conduct before granting an injunction.

Any person who falsely represents a trade mark as registered, or as being in the process of being registered, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a person applies to register a trade mark proposing use by another, and such proposed use is contingent upon conditions not fully disclosed at the time of application, the Registrar may, subject to such terms as deemed appropriate, refuse registration until satisfactory evidence of compliance with said conditions is furnished. Any assignment of the right to register proposed under this Act, without the prior written consent of the original applicant, shall be void ab initio and attract a penalty equivalent to twice the official fee applicable for registration. Failure to provide accurate particulars regarding the proposed registered user, or any misrepresentation thereof, shall render the application liable to be rejected, and the applicant may be barred from submitting a similar application for a period of one year.

An ex parte injunction may be granted by a court competent to hear matters under this Act, restraining the defendant from the manufacture, sale, import, export, or other disposition of goods, including those embodying a semiconductor integrated circuit, that are alleged to infringe a registered trade mark or are deceptively similar thereto. Such injunction shall be issued pending the actual notice to the defendant and the opportunity for them to be heard, provided that the plaintiff demonstrates a prima facie case, the balance of convenience lies in their favour, and irreparable harm will result if the injunction is not granted. The court may require the plaintiff to provide security, as it deems fit, to cover potential damages to the defendant should the injunction ultimately be discharged. Any person aggrieved by an ex parte injunction may apply to the court for its variation or discharge.

Any party possessing prior mercantile use of a sign or trade mark, or any registered user thereof, may institute an opposition registration against an application for registration under this Act, provided that such use occurred honestly and in the course of trade. The notice of opposition shall clearly specify the grounds upon which it is founded, including but not limited to similarity between the applied-for mark and a previously used sign, or likelihood of confusion arising from the proposed registration. Further, the opponent must demonstrate evidence substantiating their claim of prior use, failing which the Registrar may summarily dismiss the opposition. The applicant for registration shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition within the prescribed timeframe as provided herein and present counter-evidence where applicable.

Where an aggrieved party alleges that a patent has been granted in contravention of this Act and seeks to challenge its validity, it shall be incumbent upon the Controller to determine whether the specification does disclose the invention claimed. Such determination will consider whether the description enables a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention without undue experimentation, taking into account the state of knowledge at the date of filing. Failure to adequately disclose essential elements, or where the disclosure is deceptive regarding the operational principles, shall constitute grounds for revocation under this Act. Any party demonstrating such deficiency may petition the Controller for a rectification order, subject to penalties as provided herein for frivolous claims and vexatious litigation.

An application constituting a convention application shall be deemed to be filed on the date on which the corresponding application was first made in the Convention Country, subject to the provisions regarding priority under this Act. Where an applicant has filed more than one convention application relating to the same invention, he shall indicate in each such application the date of filing and particulars of any other convention application earlier filed in respect of the said invention. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the first application made in the Convention Country as evidence of the priority claim. Failure to comply with this requirement within the time specified by the Controller shall render the convention application liable to be deemed withdrawn. An official fee, as prescribed, shall be payable for the furnishing and examination of such certified copies.

For the purposes of this Act, registration of a cinematograph film shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership of copyright therein, subject to the provisions relating to joint authorship. An application for such registration may be made by the producer who is recognized as the owner of the film under this Act, or by any person claiming ownership through assignment or license. The application shall include particulars regarding the title of the cinematograph film, the name and address of the applicant, details concerning the principal director and author of the script, and a synopsis of the work. Provided that, where the copyright in musical works incorporated within the cinematograph film is separately owned, such ownership shall be clearly indicated on the application form.

An applicant seeking registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design under this Act shall furnish to the Layout Design Registrar such particulars relating to the layout design as are prescribed, including but not limited to, a complete description of the circuitry and its intended function. The registrar may require the submission of additional documentation deemed necessary for verification of originality and novelty, provided that any request for further information must be accompanied by a reasoned explanation. Upon receipt of an application, the Layout Design Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Any alteration to the layout design after the initial filing requires notification to the registrar prior to proceeding with registration.

For the purposes of this Act, an “injunction subject” is defined as a mark which, at the time of application for registration, is identical or confusingly similar to a prior registered trade mark used in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the applicant seeks registration. Such similarity shall be assessed considering not only the visual appearance of the marks but also their phonetic and conceptual elements, as provided herein. An injunction subject mark may still proceed towards registration if the applicant demonstrates honest concurrent use prior to the date of application, or that no confusion is likely to arise due to differences in the goods or services indicated.

Where a patent claimant person alleges infringement of their patent, they may institute proceedings for remedy before the appropriate commercial court, subject to the provisions regarding jurisdiction as provided herein. The court shall have power to grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including but not limited to injunctions restraining further acts of infringement, damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the claimant person, and costs incurred in bringing the action. Provided that, where the alleged infringing act was committed unknowingly and without intent to infringe, the court may reduce the amount of damages awarded. Further, a patent claimant person shall be entitled to seek discovery from the defendant relating to their manufacturing processes and sales records, as deemed necessary by the court to ascertain the extent of infringement. The right to appeal any judgment rendered under this Act is preserved.

Where an objection is raised by a party against the acceptance of a trade mark application on grounds specified in this Act, the Trade Marks Registry shall afford that party an opportunity to present its case and be heard. The Registrar may, after considering the evidence submitted, either uphold the objection or direct acceptance of the application, providing reasons for the decision recorded in writing. Any party aggrieved by such order of the Registrar may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. Further, the Appellate Board’s determination shall be final and binding, subject only to an appeal under the provisions relating to appeals from orders of appellate tribunals. The manner informing international authorities concerning any rectification proceedings shall adhere strictly to regulations prescribed herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark may be refused by the Registrar if it contains any disclaimers required under this Act; provided that such refusal shall not prejudice any subsequent application filed by the applicant incorporating the same mark but omitting the disclaimer. Where an application register proprietor seeks to alter the particulars relating to ownership or address appearing in the Register, they shall submit a request in the prescribed form and along with the requisite fee. The Registrar may require verification of the information provided, subject to satisfying themselves that the proposed alteration does not contravene any provisions of this Act or the Marks Act 1999. Any such alteration shall be recorded in the Register and notified as per regulations framed by the Government.

The Registrar shall, upon examination of an application for registration and finding it meets the requirements as provided herein, cause the trade mark to be advertised in the Trade Marks Journal as a condition precedent to registration. Such advertisement shall specify the trade mark, the goods or services for which registration is sought, the applicant’s name and address, and a statement of any conditions subject to which the application is accepted. Any person may, within the prescribed period, file a notice of opposition to the registration, detailing the grounds upon which the application is contested. The Registrar may, after considering any opposition and subject to such further evidence as may be required, either accept or refuse the application, or accept it subject to modifications or limitations. Gazette subject conditions shall be clearly stated in the certificate of registration if the mark is ultimately registered.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is opposed under this Act, service of that opposition shall constitute payable notice to the applicant. Such service must be effected by way of registered post with acknowledgement due or through electronic means as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. The applicant shall be deemed to have received such payable notice within seven days of the date of posting or transmission, whichever is earlier. Provided that, if the address for service specified in the application changes after its filing, it shall be the responsibility of the applicant to promptly notify the Registrar of the updated details; failure to do so will not invalidate the operation of payable notice. The opposition period shall run from the date of such service and remain subject to any extensions granted as provided herein.

In determining whether an application for trademark registration should proceed, the Registrar shall consider any evidence submitted by the applicant demonstrating acquired distinctiveness relating to the goods or services specified in the application. This assessment will take into account the period during which the mark has been used in India and the extent of recognition amongst the relevant consumer base. The Registrar may require further clarification or supporting documentation from the applicant if the initial submission is deemed insufficient to establish acquired distinctiveness, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay the processing of the application. Further, the Registrar shall consider any opposition filed under this Act in relation to the mark’s similarity to existing trademarks.

For the purposes of this Act, "description means trade" shall be interpreted to encompass all representations made concerning the nature, quality, characteristics, origin, and suitability for a particular purpose of goods or services offered for sale. Such representations, whether expressed verbally, graphically, or through any other medium, are deemed descriptions within the meaning of this Act if they create an impression in the mind of the consumer regarding the identity or attributes of those goods or services. Provided that, a representation shall not be considered a description unless it is likely to induce purchasers to believe them concerning the origin or production process of the goods. Any alteration made to such representations with intent to deceive consumers shall also be subject to penalties as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “necessary security india” shall be deemed to include protection of critical infrastructure relating to national power grids, transportation networks, and communication systems. Any design incorporating representations or configurations directly replicating elements essential for the functionality or identification of such infrastructure shall be ineligible for registration under this Act. The Registrar may refuse registration if satisfied that a proposed design’s similarity to existing designs poses a threat to necessary security india, provided that such determination is based on objective criteria and documented reasoning. Information pertaining to applications and registrations deemed relevant to necessary security india shall be treated as confidential.

Impliedly registration shall, for the purposes of determining the authenticity and origin of goods bearing a geographical indication, extend to the reasonable and consistent application of a sign or symbol denoting such indication, even absent explicit textual reference to formal registration under this Act. However, such implied registration is subject to the condition that the sign or symbol must be demonstrably linked to a defined geographical area and consistently associated with goods originating from that area, as evidenced by established usage and consumer perception. Provided that, the Registrar may, upon sufficient evidence of consumer deception or misrepresentation, require formal registration to clarify the status of the geographical indication. Any claim of rights arising from implied registration may be challenged before the Appellate Board.

A person desiring to obtain a patent shall present an application in the prescribed form to the Controller, accompanied by a provisional or complete specification and the necessary fee as provided herein. The specification shall fully and particularly describe the invention and manner in which it is to be performed; and where diagrams or drawings are referred to in the specification, they shall conform to the requirements of the rules made under this Act. Any amendment to the specification may be permitted by the Controller, subject to such conditions as he may deem fit, provided that no amendment shall introduce matter extending beyond the content of the original application. 

Where an applicant claims a patent for a process, he shall disclose the best method known to him for carrying out the invention; and failure to do so may be grounds for rejection of the application. A patent granted under this Act shall confer upon the patentee exclusive rights in relation to the invention, subject to limitations as are prescribed. The term of every patent granted under this Act shall be twenty years from the date of filing the application.

For the purposes of this Act, the registered proprietor shall be deemed to include a person who, although not formally recorded as such in the register, possesses and exercises dominion over the trade mark, subject to proof of ownership satisfactory to the Controller. A finding of register sufficient cause for non-registration despite actual use may be made where the applicant fails to demonstrate bona fide adoption or continuous user prior to opposition. However, assignment or transmission of rights shall not be valid without appropriate notation in the register, and any subsequent claim by a transferee will be assessed from the date of such registration. The registered proprietor retains exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered as provided herein.

Any breeder, hereinafter defined, who registers a plant variety shall be liable to pay annual fees proportionate to the extent of commercial exploitation undertaken, as determined by the Board established under this Act. Failure to remit such fees within the prescribed period will result in suspension of registration and forfeiture of rights accrued under this Act. Any person found infringing upon the registered rights of another, including unauthorized propagation or sale of a variety belonging to a protected genera species specified during registration, shall be deemed guilty of an offense punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and a fine not exceeding ten lakh rupees. Repeated offenses may attract enhanced penalties as provided herein.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute proceedings in the relevant High Court for relief against an act of indication falsified occurring within its territorial jurisdiction. Such proceedings shall include claims for damages sustained by the proprietor as a direct result of the deceptive use, and injunctive relief preventing further acts of falsification. Where it is established that a registered geographical indication has been used in a manner constituting indication falsified, the Registrar may, following due notice to the registrant and opportunity for comment, initiate revocation proceedings under this Act. The revocation shall be effective from the date of the order unless the Registrar determines otherwise, considering factors such as the duration and extent of the deceptive use.

Any party alleging infringement who fails to establish register sufficient cause for initiating proceedings under this Act shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed appropriate, require the complainant to furnish security for the due prosecution of the complaint. Where a registered proprietor grants a licence to another party, such licence shall be in writing and shall specify the conditions governing its use, including territorial limitations and quality control measures. Failure to adhere to the terms of a duly registered licence shall constitute grounds for revocation of the licence, and the licensee may be subject to injunction and damages. Any false representation regarding a licensed trade mark shall be punishable with imprisonment not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar shall have the power to impose these penalties following a summary inquiry.

For the purposes of this Act, a copyright case shall be deemed to exist where an aggrieved party alleges infringement of rights vested under this Act and seeks redress through legal proceedings. Such a case may involve claims relating to reproduction, distribution, adaptation, or public performance of copyrighted works. The determination of whether a copyright case has arisen is subject to considerations of originality as defined herein; a work lacking sufficient originality shall not be eligible for copyright protection, thereby precluding the possibility of an actionable infringement claim. Further, any assertion of fair dealing under this Act shall constitute a defense in a copyright case.

For the purposes of this Act, "photograph" means a fixation of an image on light-sensitive material produced through a process involving optics and chemical or electronic means. A photograph shall be deemed to include any positive or negative representation derived therefrom, whether such derivation involves alteration or manipulation of the original image. The term “photograph” does not extend to representations that are primarily artistic in nature, even if created using photographic techniques; however, where a photograph incorporates substantial elements of originality beyond mere mechanical reproduction, it may be considered an artistic work subject to protection under this Act. As provided herein, ownership of copyright in a photograph shall vest initially in the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the photograph’s creation have been undertaken.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registration variety” shall mean a plant variety that has been formally recorded in the Register of Plant Varieties and granted protection under this Act, subject to the conditions stipulated therein. The grant of such registration confers upon the registrant exclusive rights relating to the production, sale, distribution, and importation of propagating material of the registration variety. Any person who, knowingly or fraudulently, uses a false trade description in relation to any plant material offered or exposed for sale as being a registration variety shall be liable to penalty, as provided herein. This prohibition extends to misrepresenting the origin or characteristics of such material.

An application for registration of a layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a representation of the integrated circuit in a form suitable for reproduction and verification. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or clarification regarding the layout design, provided that any such request must specify the deficiencies perceived. The manner issuing certificates of registration shall conform strictly to the format detailed in Schedule A, appended hereto. Any alteration to this prescribed manner requires prior notification published in the Official Gazette. Furthermore, an appeal against a refusal of registration may be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, detailing the grounds for challenge and submitting supporting documentation as stipulated under this Act.

An application for registration of a proposed trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if the Registrar considers that the mark, or any element thereof, is likely to cause confusion with an earlier registered act. The applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating a lack of likelihood of confusion; such submissions shall be considered by the Registrar in accordance with principles of natural justice. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered which includes a representation of a geographical indication as defined under another Act, the Registrar shall require proof that the applicant has authorization from the proprietor of the geographical indication or is otherwise entitled to use it. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to registration may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of the order.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design, or imposing conditions on registration, may, within ninety days of the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be in such form and be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed, and shall set forth the grounds upon which the order is sought to be reversed or modified. The Appellate Board, upon consideration of the appeal and subject to such evidence as it may require, shall pass such orders as it deems fit, confirming, varying, or setting aside the order of the Registrar. The manner applying appellate procedure shall be determined by rules made under this Act, and shall ensure a reasonable opportunity for all parties to be heard. Any further appeal from the decision of the Appellate Board shall lie to the High Court, provided that such appeal is instituted within sixty days of the Appellate Board’s order, and only on a substantial question of law. The Registrar may, at any time, call for the record of any proceeding before the Appellate Board for the purpose of satisfying itself as to the legality or propriety of any order made therein.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, wines and spirits, natural remedies, handicrafts, and manufactured goods shall be filed with the Registrar in such form as may be prescribed. The application must specify the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the agricultural product or good to which it relates, the area of its production or association, and particulars of prior usage, if any. Any person claiming an interest in a geographical indication may file representations against the registration, stating the grounds on which such opposition is based. The Registrar shall give notice of such representation to the applicant and afford both parties an opportunity of being heard under this Act. Decisions regarding oppositions shall be recorded and made available for public inspection. The Registrar may require further information or clarification from any party involved in proceedings concerning houses parliament, ensuring due process as provided herein.

An applicant intending to apply patent shall furnish with the prescribed fee a statement of priority claiming benefit from any earlier filing, provided that such earlier filing was made by the applicant or a legal representative. The particulars of the practitioner, being a practise patent agent, who assists in the preparation and filing of the application shall be clearly indicated on the form. Failure to disclose this information may result in delays in processing. Any modification to the statement of priority after the initial filing requires prior written consent from the Controller. Further, any subsequent assignment or alteration of ownership relating to the invention must also be registered with the patent office and accompanied by a duly executed instrument as provided herein.

An applicant seeking to avail of the benefits of the Madrid Protocol shall file with the Registrar a certified copy of an international application, accompanied by a declaration specifying the Contracting Parties in respect of which protection is sought. The Registrar may require such further particulars or documents as are necessary for determining compliance with the requirements under this Act and the Regulations implementing the Madrid Protocol. Where an international registration extends to India, the mark shall be deemed to be registered in the Register of Trade Marks maintained by the Registrar subject to any limitations specified in the international registration. Any opposition that may arise concerning such extension shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein for oppositions to applications for registration under this Act. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all extensions of protection resulting from an international registration, accessible for public inspection.

Registration of musical works shall be deemed conclusive evidence of ownership, subject to proof demonstrating fraudulent intent at the time of registration. An applicant seeking registration of a sound recording may also register any underlying musical work incorporated therein, provided that such application specifies the nature and extent of the claimed copyright. Where disputes arise concerning the authenticity of a registered work or the validity of an asserted claim under this Act, proceedings shall be initiated in a district court having jurisdiction over the place where the applicant’s principal place of business is situated. The Court may order inspection of original manuscripts, recordings, or other relevant materials to determine rightful ownership and resolve any ambiguities as provided herein.

Any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark is a proprietor registered trade, uses such trade mark in connection with goods or services without the consent of the proprietor shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Where any infringing use occurs after the proprietor has given notice specifying the nature of the infringement, the offender shall also be liable to pay damages to the proprietor. Further, where goods are knowingly offered for sale or exposed for hire or otherwise made available for use bearing a false trade mark identical or deceptively similar to a proprietor registered trade, such goods shall be deemed forfeited and may be destroyed under this Act.

A trade mark shall be registerable under this Act if it is distinctive and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of another. Register respect goods shall be determined in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe. A mark shall not be registerable if it is descriptive of the goods or services concerned, or if its use would be likely to deceive the public as to the quality, nature or origin of those goods or services. Provided that a mark which has acquired distinctiveness through use may be registered notwithstanding its initial descriptiveness, subject to proof of such acquired distinctiveness. Any application for registration may be opposed on grounds specified herein.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the district court under this Act relating to the revocation of a patent, or concerning the validity of a design registered under the Designs Act, may appeal from such order to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the district court originally exercised its authority. Such appeals shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate High Court may, after hearing all parties involved and considering the evidence presented, confirm, reverse, or modify the decision of the district court, as it deems just and equitable. Costs in such appeal shall be determined by the High Court. Further, any party dissatisfied with the judgment of the High Court may petition to the Supreme Court of India on a point of law, subject to the provisions regarding special leave petitions.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark used in India may apply for registration of the trade mark under this Act in the prescribed manner. The application for registration shall contain a representation of the trade mark and a list of goods or services in respect of which registration is sought. Upon receipt of an application duly complying with the requirements as provided herein, the Trade Marks Registry shall examine it and, subject to such conditions as it may deem fit, accept it for proceeding to advertisement. 

Registration shall confer upon the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. However, such registration may be subject to limitations or conditions as may be specified in the register. Where a mark is deemed similar to an existing registered mark, the Registrar may require evidence of distinctiveness, and shall consider the likelihood of confusion among consumers. A certificate of registration shall be issued upon completion of all necessary procedures.

Any person desiring to obtain a license under this Act, or seeking assignment of rights in a registered layout-design, shall submit a petition particulars to the appropriate authority, detailing the scope of the proposed license or assignment, including the territory, duration, and field of use. The petition shall clearly identify the registered layout-design in question, referencing the application number and registration date. All petitions for assignment must specify the consideration offered for the transfer of rights, and demonstrate that the proposed assignee possesses the technical capacity to exploit the layout-design commercially. An appeal fee accompanied, as prescribed by rules made under this Act, shall be submitted with the petition, and failure to do so may render the petition inadmissible. The authority may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant the license or approve the assignment, provided that the applicant demonstrates a legitimate interest and the proposed arrangement does not unduly restrict competition. Any modification to the petition particulars requires prior written consent of the authority.

Any person who publishes or causes to be published any information relating to an invention, whether patentable or not, with intent to prejudice the grant of a patent to another person, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a person, not being the inventor or the assignee of an invention, applies for a patent under this Act, knowing that such invention is not his own, such application shall be void and the applicant shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine, or with both. Provided that, if the applicant proves that he reasonably believed himself to be the inventor, the court may impose a lesser penalty. Any false representation concerning the inventive step of an invention, made to obtain a patent, constitutes an offence punishable as provided herein. The Controller may, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed, revoke a patent obtained through fraudulent means.

An application for registration of a registered layout shall contain particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, the title of the layout-design, and a representation of the layout in the form of a mask or other suitable medium, conforming to standards as may be prescribed. The Registrar may reject an application if he is satisfied that the layout-design does not substantially consist of a three-dimensional representation of any work protected under copyright law, or if it contains matter which is wholly devoid of originality. Provided that, where a registered layout incorporates elements derived from prior art, the applicant shall demonstrate sufficient inventive step to warrant registration under this Act. The Registrar shall notify the applicant and any other interested party before proceeding with examination.

The application for grant of a patent, once received by the Controller, shall be examined to ascertain compliance with all requirements under this Act and rules made thereunder. Provided that, if the applicant has failed to comply with the prescribed formalities relating to the making of the complete specification or claims, the Controller may direct the applicant to amend such deficiencies within a period not exceeding six months from the date of the direction. Further, where an objection is raised concerning the novelty or inventive step of the claimed invention, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasoned statement detailing the grounds for said objection. The applicant shall then have opportunity to respond and present arguments rebutting the objection; such response must be filed within three months from the date of notification.

Where an act is done without obtaining the requisite license under this Act, and that act involves the reproduction of a substantial portion of a copyrighted work, such act shall constitute infringement. The owner of copyright may, subject to provisions regarding fair use and transformative works as provided herein, institute legal proceedings seeking injunctive relief against any person found to be engaged in acts infringing upon their exclusive rights. Damages recoverable in an action for copyright infringement shall include reasonable compensation to the copyright owner for any detriment suffered by him by reason of such infringement, not less than a sum determined by the Court and not exceeding five times the amount of damages assessed. Further, where wilful infringement is established, enhanced damages may be awarded as deemed just by the court.

Any person manufacturing, selling, importing or distributing cosmetics shall ensure adherence to the standards of quality and safety as prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards, in consultation with the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation. A cosmetic product, for the purposes of this Act, includes any substance intended for rubbing, pouring, sprinkling or spraying on, into, or otherwise applying to the human skin or hair for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance. No cosmetic shall contain any substance prohibited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, or any other enactment for the time being in force relating to public health. 

The Trade Marks Officer, upon receiving a complaint regarding misbranded or spurious cosmetics, may direct the manufacturer or distributor to submit samples for analysis to a recognised laboratory. Provided that, such analysis shall be conducted within thirty days from the date of receipt of the samples. Failure to comply with this provision shall attract a penalty as provided herein, and may result in the suspension of the registration of the trade mark associated with the offending cosmetic.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is rejected under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall only be entertained if the requisite fee has been paid and the grounds of appeal are clearly specified, demonstrating a substantial error in the interpretation or application of the provisions relating to novelty or originality as provided herein. The Tribunal may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to both parties, confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed against. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal may further appeal to the Supreme Court on a question of law, subject to the conditions and limitations prescribed under this Act; it is provided that the design registry shall not be bound by any prior determination made in respect of a similar layout-design.

Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered geographical indication shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, be entitled to institute a civil suit in a District Court not inferior to that of a Principal Civil Court, having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs. The plaintiff forthwith, upon reasonable cause to believe that an infringement has occurred, may apply ex parte to a Magistrate for an order restraining the defendant from the further unlawful use of the geographical indication. Such application shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of the grounds for the claim and a verified copy of the registration certificate. The court, if satisfied of the prima facie case and the likelihood of irreparable harm, may grant an interim injunction. Provided that no such injunction shall be granted unless the plaintiff undertakes to provide security, as the court deems fit, to compensate the defendant for any loss that may be suffered by reason of such injunction being granted and subsequently found to be erroneous. Any person dealing with goods bearing an infringing geographical indication in good faith shall not be liable for damages.

An amendment to an application for registration of a trade mark is deemed permitted under this Act where such amendment relates only to the representation of the mark and does not alter the identity of goods or services for which the mark is sought. The Registrar shall consider any proposed amendment permissible if it conforms with the provisions regarding clarity and distinctiveness as provided herein. Further, an application permitted amended may be subject to objection from any interested party within a period specified by the Registrar; such objections shall be considered before proceeding further with registration. Any alteration affecting the scope of protection sought requires fresh filing.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no person shall register a trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered trade mark relating to any drug unless such use has been continuous for at least five years immediately preceding the date of application and demonstrably indicates consumer recognition of the applicant’s goods as distinct from those of the proprietor of the earlier trade mark. Where an application for registration includes a representation of a drug, it shall be accompanied by a certificate from a recognized pharmacopoeia confirming compliance with established standards regarding efficacy and safety. The Registrar may require further evidence to ascertain whether the proposed use of the trade mark is likely to deceive or cause confusion among consumers concerning the origin or quality of the drug.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall be submitted to the Central Government in the prescribed form and accompanied by such documents and materials as may be specified therein. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the genetic composition of the variety, its distinctiveness, uniformity and stability, along with details regarding its expression potential and resistance to pests or diseases. Upon receipt of an application, the Central Government shall publish a notice indicating the nature of the plant variety sought to be registered and inviting objections from any person having knowledge of the matter. Objections received shall be considered by the Central Government, which may require further information from the applicant or objector as deemed necessary for proper evaluation.

An application for registration of a plant variety may be made by any person claiming rights in the variety, subject to compliance with the requirements as provided herein. Such application shall include particulars concerning the designation of the variety, its source, and the method of its derivation, along with detailed phenotypic data conforming to the guidelines published by the Authority. The Registrar shall register a plant variety only if it is deemed distinct, uniform, and stable, following established procedures for conducting necessary trials and observations. Further, registration may be refused if the applicant fails to disclose information relevant to assessing the novelty of the registration variety or if the claimed rights are demonstrably invalid. An application seeking registration make international shall be processed in accordance with reciprocal agreements entered into by the Central Government.

A person shall not engage in the business of representing applicants before the Controller for the purposes of applying for, obtaining, revoking, or defending patents, nor perform any act relating to such representation, unless that person is a registered practitioner. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe qualifications and conditions for registration as a practitioner, including requirements concerning educational background and experience within the field of patent law. An application for registration as a practise patent agent shall be made in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee. Upon receiving an application, the Controller may require such further information or documentation as deemed necessary to assess eligibility. Registration shall remain valid subject to compliance with continuing professional development requirements as specified under this Act. Any person found to violate these provisions is liable for penalties as provided herein.

Where, upon review of a patent granted under this Act, it appears to the Controller that there has been an error apparent from the record relating to the scope or validity of the invention, or concerning the identity of the patentee, the Controller shall provide notice to all interested parties and may initiate proceedings for court section rectifying such error. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this Act regarding rectification may appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures during rectification proceedings will render any subsequent appeals inadmissible, subject to just cause shown. The Controller shall ensure that all orders issued are enforced diligently and without undue delay, imposing penalties as provided herein for non-compliance.

Where an objection is raised before the Controller regarding the originality of any work claimed to be subject matter for copyright under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the designated Appellate Board. The appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of the Controller. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum of grounds specifying the errors apparent on the face of the record and setting out the points of law or fact which the appellant desires the Appellate Board to consider.

The Appellate Board shall give notice to the Controller, who may file its written submissions within thirty days from the date of receipt of such appeal. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, hear oral arguments from both parties. Any order made by the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to further appeal to the High Court under provisions as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, the term “patent controller” shall mean the officer appointed by the Central Government and designated as such, who is responsible for exercising powers and performing duties relating to the examination of patent applications, determining whether an invention meets the criteria for patentability under this Act, and granting or refusing patents in accordance with prescribed procedures. The patent controller may delegate any of their functions to other officers working under their direction, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government. Decisions made by the patent controller are appealable as provided herein, and such decisions shall be binding until modified or reversed by an appellate authority.

An application register proprietor desiring to grant a license concerning their registered trademark may execute an agreement specifying the scope of use permitted under such license. Such agreements shall be filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, providing details of the licensee’s identity and the geographical territory covered by the license. The Registrar shall record these licenses in a supplementary register maintained for that purpose. Further, where the application register proprietor fails to utilize the trademark continuously for a period exceeding five years following the grant of such a license, any interested party may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for a compulsory licence under this Act, subject to demonstrating substantial prejudice resulting from the non-use. The Registrar shall provide notice to the applicant register proprietor prior to any determination by the Board.

An application for a certificate of registration shall be deemed to satisfy the requirements for an *applicant variety registrable* where the applicant provides documentary evidence demonstrating stability and uniformity consistent with established agricultural practices. However, any person aggrieved by a decision granting such a certificate may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of publication of the notification under this Act. The appellate board shall consider whether the grounds for registration were adequately substantiated, particularly concerning distinctiveness relative to existing varieties. Provided that an opposition is filed demonstrating prior use or knowledge of the variety by another party, the Board may direct a fresh examination of the application and its compliance with the provisions herein.

Where a registered trade mark is used in relation to goods providing services without the consent of the proprietor, any person claiming an interest may apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. Such relief shall include an injunction restraining the infringing party from further use of the mark and an order requiring delivery up or destruction of all materials bearing the infringing mark. The tribunal may also award damages reflecting the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringement, taking into account the extent to which the infringing use has damaged the reputation associated with the trade mark. Provided that, where the infringement is demonstrably malicious, punitive damages may be awarded subject to principles of fairness and proportionality as determined by the tribunal.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person claiming rights in an artistic work may grant a license permitting the reproduction and distribution of that work, specifying the duration, geographical scope, and permitted uses. Such licenses shall be assignable in writing, either wholly or partially, and the assignee shall possess all rights granted under the original license agreement. Where a licensed copy is made without authorization, constituting an infringing copy of the original artistic work, the licensor may pursue remedies available under this Act against both the unauthorized reproducer and any distributor of such infringing copies. Provided that, where the reproduction is incidental to the lawful use of the original work as permitted by another license or exemption, it shall not be deemed an infringement unless explicitly prohibited within the terms of that other license. The terms of assignment shall govern the relationship between assignor and assignee regarding enforcement actions.

For the purposes of this Act, a “patent outside India” means a patent granted by any competent authority in a country other than India, relating to an invention for which an application for patents has been filed in India, provided that such foreign patent was not obtained in violation of any provision under this Act or any rule made thereunder. The term "competent authority" shall include any governmental body or agency authorized to grant patents within the jurisdiction of the relevant country. An applicant seeking to rely on a patent outside India as prior art shall furnish an authenticated copy thereof, duly translated into English if originally in another language, subject to verification by the Controller.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may grant a license to use the mark subject to terms and conditions recorded in writing. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The licensee under a granted license shall hold only such rights as are expressly conferred upon them by the written agreement; no implied right to challenge the validity of the mark or claim ownership thereof shall arise from the licensing arrangement. Further, where a trade mark has been assigned, the assignee may, with the consent of the assignor and subject to any restrictions contained in the assignment deed, grant sub-licenses relating to the mark’s use within the scope of the original license agreement. These mark regulations are intended to facilitate commercial exploitation while safeguarding the integrity of registered trademarks.

A geographical indication shall be deemed to be a geographically defined area under this Act if the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of goods originates from that place. For the purposes of registration as a geographical indication authorised, the name of the geographical indication must accurately identify the originating area and not contain any descriptive terms which are misleading regarding such characteristics. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating the link between the goods and the originating area; this evidence may include documentation relating to traditional production methods or integrated circuits layout designs employed in their manufacture. Goods bearing a registered geographical indication shall be identifiable as such, subject to provisions concerning fair use.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be refused if, following an examination under this Act and after providing the applicant with an opportunity of being heard, the Registrar is satisfied that use of the name in connection with goods or services is continuous and widespread, notwithstanding that such use does not constitute a deceptive practice. Any party aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or requiring amendment thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Board shall consider whether the applicant has adequately demonstrated distinctiveness arising from qualities associated with the considered geographical indication and determine if the impugned use genuinely misleads consumers regarding origin.

Any person desiring to initiate a dispute regarding the validity of a registered layout-design, or alleging infringement thereof, shall submit a zm form petition to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, duly completed in all respects as prescribed by rules made under this Act. The petition shall clearly identify the registered layout-design in question, the alleged infringer, and the specific grounds upon which the dispute is based, supported by verifiable technical documentation. Should the petition lack sufficient detail or fail to meet the procedural requirements, the Board may, at its discretion, request further clarification or reject the petition outright. It is further provided that any amendment to the petition, affecting the scope of the claim or the identity of the parties, requires prior approval of the Board. The Parliament may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe additional forms or modify existing ones to facilitate efficient adjudication of disputes arising under this Act, ensuring consistent application of the prescribed procedures. Compliance with these provisions is mandatory for the valid commencement of any legal proceedings.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce a registered trade mark shall, upon proof of prior use consistent with the class designation appearing in the alphabetical index classification, be entitled to injunctive relief against any party employing a sign confusingly similar to their mark within that designated class. Provided that such prior use must have been continuous and uninterrupted for a period not less than three years immediately preceding the date of infringement. Further, where an applicant demonstrates bad faith adoption of a trade mark by another, relying on the alphabetical index classification as a deceptive tactic, damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered due to dilution or misrepresentation. The Registrar shall maintain a publicly accessible record detailing all classifications and any subsequent amendments made under this Act, ensuring transparency in the application of these remedies.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, file a notice of opposition within six months from the date of publication of the grant. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step as defined under this Act. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during the opposition proceedings may render the notice inadmissible and result in penalties for frivolous filings. The Controller shall provide an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to present evidence and arguments; any attempt at obstruction or misleading testimony will be subject to fines and potential criminal prosecution. Decisions of the Controller regarding opposition are final, but appeal lies to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is deemed to be deficient, the Registrar shall issue notice to the applicant specifying the deficiencies and requiring them to rectify such deficiencies within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of the notice. The manner issuing notice shall conform to Form D as prescribed in the First Schedule. Failure to comply with the requirements of the notice within the stipulated time may result in the application being deemed withdrawn, subject to an opportunity for reconsideration if the applicant can demonstrate that the delay was caused by circumstances beyond their reasonable control and establishes a clear priority date for the layout-design. Any such demonstration shall be accompanied by supporting documentation as determined by the Registrar.

The gene fund established under this Act shall be utilized for the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources, and for the welfare of farmers and plant breeders, subject to the provisions herein. Any performer of traditional knowledge associated with registered plant varieties, demonstrably contributing to the development of said variety, may apply to the Plant Variety Protection Authority for equitable sharing in the benefits accruing from the gene fund. The Authority shall, following due process and verification of such contribution, determine the extent of benefit sharing. Contributions to the gene fund shall also include royalties received from the commercial exploitation of varieties incorporating indigenous knowledge, and any penalties levied for infringement of breeder’s rights as provided herein. The Authority may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate guidelines for transparent and equitable distribution of funds, prioritizing initiatives that enhance farmer livelihoods and promote biodiversity.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall be entitled to inspect the computer inspection register maintained under this Act relating to their application. Such inspection may be conducted during normal business hours at a location designated by the Registrar, and access shall be provided subject to reasonable restrictions necessary to prevent disruption or damage to the system. The Registrar may prescribe fees for such inspections, which shall be remitted to the Consolidated Fund of India. Any person found tampering with the register or extracting data in violation of these provisions is liable to prosecution under the Information Technology Act. Further, any unauthorized reproduction or dissemination of information obtained through inspection will constitute an offense and render the offender subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any person who manufactures, imports, distributes, sells, or offers for sale any cosmetic which is deleterious to health or contains an ingredient prohibited under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, shall be deemed guilty of an offence. Such offender shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding two thousand rupees for the first offence and five thousand rupees for each subsequent offence. Further, where a misbranding or adulteration of any cosmetic is proven, the proprietor or manager responsible for such act may face imprisonment extending to six months, or both. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe standards for cosmetics as provided herein. Any contravention of these standards shall attract additional penalties and be subject to prosecution under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, "performance" shall mean any recitation, delivery, declamation, address, presentation, enactment, or musical rendering given live before an audience. Such performance may include dramatic works, literary works, and musical compositions as incorporated therein. A performance is deemed to be a derivative work only if it substantially alters the original work’s character or expression; provided that incidental elements necessary for the delivery of the performance itself shall not constitute such alteration. The right of a performer in respect of their performance shall subsist independently of, and subject to any rights existing under this Act relating to copyright in the underlying work.

Where an objection is raised against the registration of a trade mark under this Act, the Registrar shall afford the applicant and the objector an opportunity to be heard. The objector shall serve upon the applicant, by registered post or article delivered personally, a copy of the notice of opposition not less than thirty days prior to the date fixed for hearing; such service constituting payable notice. Failure to provide this payable notice shall render the objection unenforceable in proceedings before the Appellate Board. Provided that, if the objector demonstrates reasonable cause for failing to comply with the prescribed timeframe, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, entertain the appeal notwithstanding the deficiency in notice, subject to just terms and conditions.

The owner of a mark registered respect of goods or services may grant licenses conferring the right to use the mark exclusively within a defined geographical territory, provided that such license agreement specifies the duration and scope of permitted usage. Any assignment of the mark shall include all rights and obligations pertaining to prior licenses granted under this Act; furthermore, the assignor remains liable for any breach of those licensing agreements occurring before the date of assignment. Where a licensee uses the mark in a manner inconsistent with the terms of the license, the owner may pursue remedies available under contract law, without prejudice to their right to initiate proceedings concerning trademark infringement. The Registrar shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses relating to marks registered respect of goods or services, accessible for public inspection upon payment of prescribed fees.

Where any registered trade mark is used exclusively for the export of goods, the proprietor shall not be deemed to have used such trade mark in India unless and until the goods are imported into India; provided that this condition does not apply where the use occurs outside India by a licensee authorized under this Act. The provisions act relating to importation shall be interpreted strictly according to prevailing customs regulations. Furthermore, any entity claiming entitlement to use a registered trade mark based on prior assignment must provide documented evidence of such transfer, conforming to standards prescribed by the Trade Marks Registry. Failure to comply with these evidentiary requirements will render the claim invalid and subject to cancellation proceedings as provided herein.

Where a proprietor certification trade mark is registered, the proprietor shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement against any person using a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to the certified trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered. Such remedies may include an injunction restraining the infringing use and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement, subject to considerations of fair use. Furthermore, any layout design registered under the Designs Act that incorporates elements of the proprietor certification trade mark shall be deemed protected against unauthorized reproduction or application in connection with goods or services covered by the certification. Provided that, nothing herein shall prevent the use of such designs where they are incidental and do not create a likelihood of confusion among consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods.

An opposition to registration under this Act is deemed to exist when a registered proprietor or any other person interested in the reputation of a trade mark applied for, or of a similar mark used in relation to identical or similar goods or services, notifies the Registrar that they oppose the application. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to prior use and acquired distinctiveness. The Registrar may require further particulars supporting the opposition within a prescribed timeframe. Failure to provide such particulars as provided herein may result in the rejection of the opposition. Any party affected by an opposition registration may appeal under this Act.

Where any party believes that the registration of a design is detrimental to the interests of proprietors, designers, or the public, such party may file a notice of opposition with the Controller within four months from the date of publication under this Act. The opposition shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, including but not limited to allegations of prior use, lack of novelty, and insufficiency of disclosure. Upon receipt of such notice, the Controller shall direct the proprietor of the design to file a counter-statement. The matter shall then be referred to an Opposition Board for hearing and determination as provided herein. Decisions of the Opposition Board are appealable to the Appellate Board.

The right to use a registered trade mark is, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, deemed to be transmissible by way of operation of law or by agreement in writing. Provided that any such transmission shall only be effective upon registration thereof with the Trade Marks Registry, and such registration may be refused if the proposed assignee does not meet the eligibility criteria as determined under this Act. Further, where a trade mark is registered jointly, the consent of all co-owners shall be required for its transmission unless otherwise stipulated in the agreement establishing joint ownership. The High Court may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review any registration of transmission deemed to have been obtained through fraudulent means or misrepresentation.

An application for the registration of a Geographical Indication shall be filed with the Registrar in such form and containing such particulars as may be prescribed. The applicant shall furnish evidence, satisfactory to the Registrar, establishing the origin of the goods and their association with a particular geographical area. Where the name of the Geographical Indication includes an expression indicating quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods, the application shall specify the characteristics which give rise to that quality, reputation or other characteristic. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents as deemed necessary for assessing the distinctiveness and protectability of the proposed Geographical Indication. Any person claiming to be an interested party may, within sixty days from the date of publication of a notice under this Act, file objections relating to the registration of the Geographical Indication.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the proposed design is not new or does not involve an aesthetic feature; provided that information which has been disclosed to the public by any means before the date of filing of the application, subject to certain conditions as provided herein, shall not preclude registration. The Controller may require the applicant to amend the design drawings and specifications to clearly define the features claimed as original. A registered design confers upon the proprietor exclusive right to apply or import the design in relation to articles falling within the class specification indicated in the register. Any person infringing a registered design shall be liable for damages, subject to limitations regarding proportionality of compensation awarded under this Act.

Where, upon examination under this Act, it appears that the invention claimed in a patent application is anticipated by prior art existing in a 6referred convention country, the Controller may grant the patent only if the applicant demonstrates that the said prior art was not reasonably discoverable by a person skilled in the relevant field within India at the time of the application’s filing. The burden of proving such reasonable non-discoverability shall rest entirely upon the applicant. Failure to satisfy this requirement will result in the rejection of the patent claim or, if already granted, may be grounds for revocation under procedures as provided herein. This provision is without prejudice to any remedies available to aggrieved parties, including the right to appeal decisions before houses parliament. The Controller’s decision on discoverability shall be final subject to judicial review.

A trade mark, whether registered or unregistered, shall be subject to assignment and transmission as provided herein, and such assignment or transmission may occur with or without any associated goodwill of the business undertaking. Any assignment or transmission of a trade mark shall be evidenced in writing and shall be subject to verification by the Trade Marks Registry to ensure lawful transfer of ownership. Where a trade mark constitutes a transmissible case, meaning it is assigned with the goodwill of the business, the assignee shall acquire the right to use the mark in connection with the same goods or services as the assignor. However, assignment without goodwill does not automatically confer such rights, and the assignee’s use may be restricted to the scope explicitly outlined in the assignment agreement. The Registrar may, subject to due process and examination of relevant documentation, record the assignment or transmission in the Register of Trade Marks, thereby establishing a clear record of title. Failure to register the assignment may impact the enforceability of the trade mark against third parties.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right in it, including a license, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding registration of such transfer. The proprietor of a trade mark, upon any such assignment or licensing, shall forthwith enter a memorandum of the particulars thereof in the inspection register maintained by the Trade Marks Registry. Such memorandum shall include the date of the assignment or license, the names and addresses of the assignor and assignee or licensor and licensee, and a clear description of the rights transferred or licensed, including any geographical limitations. 

The Registrar may, if satisfied that reasonable cause exists, permit inspection of the inspection register, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and adherence to conditions ensuring confidentiality. Failure to maintain an accurate inspection register, or providing false information therein, shall be deemed a material misrepresentation and may invalidate any subsequent assignment or licensing agreement, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the accuracy of entries may be referred to the Registrar for adjudication.

Where a person alleging infringement of a registered layout design demonstrates, subject to verification by the Controller, that another has reproduced the said layout design for commercial purposes without due authorisation, and it is established that such reproduction creates a substantial similarity with the original layout design, then the infringing party shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the owner. Such damages may include not only lost profits but also reasonable royalties which the owner would have received had the license been granted. Further, any person found guilty of contravention under this Act relating to a layout design relation is subject to penalties as provided herein and may be ordered to deliver up for destruction all infringing articles.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may institute a suit in the competent court against a defendant geographical indication for relief from acts of manufacture, processing, packaging, sale, hire, exhibition, or use which constitute an infringement of their exclusive right under this Act. Such infringement includes any representation, mark, label, notice, sign, or symbol falsely suggesting association with the registered geographical indication, or likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of goods. The court shall grant such remedies as it deems appropriate, including injunctions restraining further infringing acts and an order for the delivery up or destruction of infringing goods. Damages may be awarded to compensate for losses suffered by the proprietor, provided that wilful infringement is established. Costs of litigation shall be determined according to prevailing rules.

The owner of a trade mark registered in India may, subject to fulfilling all conditions as provided herein, extend the protection afforded by such registration through an international application under the Madrid Agreement concerning the International Registration of Marks. Such extension shall be deemed a license granted to the applicant’s designated representative for the purpose of managing and prosecuting the international registration within specified territories. Any assignment of the underlying Indian trade mark registration prior to the completion of the international registration process shall require notification to the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by evidence demonstrating continued consent from the assignor regarding the extension application. Further, any subsequent transfer or licensing agreement concerning the internationally registered mark must explicitly address the rights and obligations pertaining to the original Indian registration, ensuring compliance with provisions relating to territorial scope and duration as determined under this Act.
