The Controller of Designs may, if the disclosure of any design registration information is likely to be prejudicial to national security, refuse to permit inspection of the design register or copies of registered designs as provided herein. Any application for registration which, in the opinion of the Controller, relates to a design the publication of which would be detrimental to necessary security india, shall be treated as confidential. Provided that such confidentiality shall not extend beyond a period of ten years from the date of application, unless the Central Government, upon review, determines a continuing threat to national security warrants extended restriction. The Controller shall maintain a separate confidential register for such designs and may require applicants to execute a non-disclosure agreement as a condition of filing. Any breach of confidentiality shall be subject to penalties under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and the regulations framed thereunder, any person claiming patent rights in a biotechnological application involving biological material shall disclose the origin and source of said material in a manner consistent with prevailing international norms and the protection of traditional knowledge. A patent applicant shall, prior to grant, furnish a detailed description of the biological material, including its characteristics and any modifications made thereto, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements shall render the patent application liable to be rejected, and any patent granted based on incomplete or inaccurate disclosure may be revoked. Provided that, where the biological material is freely available to the public or has been lawfully acquired, such disclosure requirements shall be subject to reasonable limitations. The patentee shall also be responsible for demonstrating that the claimed invention possesses novelty and involves an inventive step, considering the prior art relating to the disclosed biological material.

Any assignment of rights in a registered trade mark to a person resident in a non-contracting state shall be subject to the prior approval of the Registrar, provided that such assignment does not contravene any provisions of this Act or any other law for the time being in force. Where the assignee is a nominee of a contracting state, the requirement for prior approval may be waived at the discretion of the Registrar, subject to satisfactory evidence of the nominee’s bona fide connection with that contracting state being furnished. A license to use a registered trade mark may be granted to a person resident in any state, but such license shall be subject to the conditions as may be prescribed. The rights and obligations of the licensor and licensee shall be governed by the terms of the license agreement, and any dispute arising therefrom shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the courts as provided herein. Any transfer of ownership to a person not ordinarily resident in a means contracting state requires a formal undertaking regarding continued use of the mark within India.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall be empowered to grant licences conferring the right to use the trade mark for specific goods or services, provided that such licence is documented in writing and filed with the Registrar. Any assignment of a trade mark, whether partial or complete, including assignments of rights granted by way of licence, requires prior notification and registration under this Act to be deemed valid against third parties. The registrar shall power to scrutinize any proposed licensing agreement for compliance with equitable terms and conditions, particularly concerning royalty rates and duration of the grant. Further, a proprietor may assign the benefit of any registered trade mark to another party, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to stipulated procedures as provided herein. Such assignments are irrevocable except by consent of the assignee and registration with the Registrar.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, a “registered act” shall mean any transaction concerning a registered trade mark, including assignment, transmission, mortgage, license, or any other disposition thereof, which is duly recorded in the Trade Marks Registry. Such registration constitutes *prima facie* evidence of the rights of the proprietor, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any instrument creating or transferring a registered act shall be in writing and shall identify the trade mark with reasonable particularity. A registered act, if not duly recorded, shall not be binding on any subsequent purchaser or assignee of the trade mark acting in good faith. The Registrar may require such further evidence as may be necessary to satisfy themselves as to the validity of any registered act, and shall maintain a public record of all such transactions.

Any application for a patent claiming a biotechnological invention shall be examined in the prescribed manner, and the Patent Office may require the applicant to furnish additional information or data relating to the biological material deposited with a recognized depositary institution, subject to the provisions of this Act. The applicant shall demonstrate that the deposited material is viable and capable of replication, and that access to such material will be provided to the Patent Office for the purposes of examination, in accordance with internationally accepted protocols. Provided that, failure to comply with the requirements regarding biological material, as detailed in the guidelines issued by the Patent Office, may result in the rejection of the application. Any challenge to the examination process shall be subject to review as provided herein, and the decision of the Patent Office shall be final, unless overturned by a competent court. The prescribed manner of claiming such inventions must also clearly delineate the scope of the claimed subject matter.

Where any interested party opposes the registration of a proposed geographical indication, the Registrar shall serve notice upon both the applicant and the opponent, specifying the grounds of opposition. The Registrar may require the submission of further documentation from either party to clarify the nature of the claim or objection. Following such service, the registrar shall hearing be convened within ninety days, unless circumstances demonstrably preclude adherence to this timeline; a reasoned order detailing any deviation must then be recorded. During the hearing, both parties shall present arguments and evidence relevant to the opposition. The Registrar’s decision, provided that it is in writing and accompanied by reasons, shall be final subject to appeal under this Act.

Applications for registration of copyright shall be submitted in the prescribed form to the Copyright Office, accompanied by the requisite fee as determined by notification issued from time to time. The applicant shall furnish such particulars relating to the work and its author as may be required under this Act. Upon receipt of an application, the Copyright Office shall assign it a serial number and intimate the same to the applicant. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Copyright Office regarding the acceptance or rejection of an application may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. The Registrar of Copyrights may require the applicant to submit certified copies of any document relevant to the claim of copyright. Information submitted to the Copyright Office shall be treated as confidential, subject to disclosure for the purposes of processing applications and conducting inquiries.

An application for registration of a *registration variety* shall be made to the Authority in Form A, accompanied by such documentation as the Authority may prescribe, including detailed phenotypic data demonstrating distinctness and stability across multiple generations. The applicant shall furnish evidence substantiating the genetic uniformity of the variety, where applicable, and indicating its resistance or susceptibility to prevalent pests and diseases within relevant agro-climatic zones. Provided that an application relating to a farmers' variety need only include information pertaining to its traditional cultivation practices and geographical distribution. The Authority may require further clarification or additional data from the applicant at any stage of the examination process. Any technical report submitted by the Examining Officer shall be considered confidential until publication under this Act, subject to review by the Appellate Board upon request.

An appeal lies from any order passed by the Controller relating to the acceptance or rejection of a basic application, or concerning any matter arising during the examination thereof, to the relevant High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Provided that where an order is made against which an appeal would lie under this Act, and the order relates also to some other matter in respect of which no appeal lies, the applicant may appeal only on the ground(s) relating to the matters as to which an appeal does lie. The High Court shall have power to entertain such appeals notwithstanding any technical objection concerning the maintainability thereof, subject to just cause shown. Further, the decision of the High Court shall be final, save for further appeal to the Supreme Court under provisions governing appeals from High Courts.

Where an objection is raised under this Act against the registration of a proposed geographical indication on the ground that it conflicts with an earlier registered trademark, or any right in a patented article, the Registrar may direct the applicant to amend the proposed indication so as not to cause such conflict, provided that the Trademark Registry or patent holder demonstrates demonstrable and ongoing commercial confusion arising directly from the similarity. The applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to present its case against such direction. Any party aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision under this provision may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees; the Appellate Board's determination shall be final. A reference geographical indication is deemed to conflict where it creates a likelihood of association with an existing trademark or patented article.

The registration of a trademark, as provided herein, may be subject to cancellation upon application by any interested person demonstrating that, subsequent to the date of registration, the mark has not been genuinely used in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. For the purposes of this Act, “interested person” shall include any party having a reasonable interest in the prevention of unfair competition or deception. The Registrar shall afford the proprietor of the trademark an opportunity to be heard and present evidence of genuine use before determining whether cancellation should proceed under this procedure cancelling registration.

Any person intending to rely on copyright registration as evidence of ownership under this Act shall submit an application, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a true copy of the work claimed. Registration of a work does not *ipso facto* confer validity upon it; however, in any proceeding concerning infringement of copyright, a certificate of registration serves as prima facie evidence of facts stated therein. Should a substantial similarity between a registered work and another work be demonstrated, the burden shifts to the alleged infringer to prove independent creation or lawful use, subject to permissible fair dealing as provided herein. Failure to register does not preclude a claim of copyright, but may affect evidentiary weight in cases of infringement. A registration shall remain valid for a period of seven years from the date of issuance and may be renewed upon payment of a renewal fee. Any false entry made during the registration process will attract penalties as prescribed under this Act.

Any person claiming that a geographical indication comprised in a registered geographical indication has been infringed may, notwithstanding any other remedy available under law, apply to the Registrar for an interim injunction restraining the defendant from the infringing acts. The application shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the registration certificate and a statement detailing the nature of the infringement, including particulars of the goods sold or manufactured by the defendant bearing the deceptively similar geographical indication. Provided that, the Registrar may, before granting such interim injunction, require the applicant to furnish security, as deemed fit, to compensate the defendant in case the injunction is subsequently found to have been wrongly granted. Any order passed by the Registrar under this provision shall be subject to appeal to the High Court, and such appeal shall be filed within a period of thirty days from the date of the order. The High Court’s decision on such appeal shall be final and binding.

An application for a trade mark relating to goods or services connected with an existing business carried on by another person shall be deemed to include an implied assignment of any right, title, or interest the applicant possesses in respect of similar marks previously used or applied for, but not registered under this Act. Such assignment shall extend to all territories where the other person conducts such business, provided that a written agreement detailing the scope and duration of the license is filed with the Registrar at the time of the trade mark application. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the applicant’s claim to ownership or usage rights prior to acceptance of the application. This provision shall not apply where the applicant demonstrates good faith reliance on advice from a registered trade mark attorney, and the assignment is executed in accordance with prescribed forms.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar under this Act relating to rectification of a registered layout-design, or concerning infringement proceedings, appeals to the Appellate Board, such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, subject to provisions regarding natural justice, entertain and determine such appeal, and for that purpose shall have all powers of a civil court trying a suit under Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Any order passed by the Appellate Board shall be final, provided that an appeal lies from such order to the High Court within ninety days from the date thereof on grounds specified in law relating to errors apparent on the face of the record. The composition and functioning of the *member appellate board* will adhere to guidelines prescribed by the Central Government.

The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Registry of Plant Varieties, which shall be a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal. The central government shall appoint a Registrar of Plant Varieties who shall be the chief executive officer of the Registry. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the central government may, by regulations, provide for the procedures relating to the application for registration of new, distinct, uniform and stable varieties of plants. Any person claiming to be the breeder of a new variety may apply for registration, provided that the variety conforms to the criteria as laid down in the regulations. The central government shall maintain a database of all registered plant varieties and make it accessible to the public. The Registrar may, with the approval of the central government, prescribe fees for all applications, registrations, and other services provided by the Registry.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a prescribed fee, and no application will be entertained unless such fee has been duly remitted. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or documentation relevant to establishing distinctiveness and origin as provided herein, and any additional requests will necessitate payment of an ancillary processing fee. Failure to submit all required information alongside the initial paid fee payable shall result in rejection of the application without further notice. Any alteration or amendment proposed by the registrant after registration is subject to a separate assessment and requires remittance of a revised fee before consideration. The Registrar may, at his discretion, waive fees for applications from recognized producers' cooperatives operating within the claimed geographical area.

Where the proprietor of a patent desires to permit another person or entity to exercise rights pertaining to the invention claimed in the patent, such permission may be conveyed through a license agreement executed as provided herein. Such license shall specify the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to manufacture, use, sale, and importation, and the geographical territory within which these actions are authorized. The proprietor retains full ownership of the patent unless explicitly transferred by assignment in writing, duly registered under this Act. Any unauthorized making, using, or selling of the patented invention without a valid license agreement or assignment constitutes infringement patent, entitling the proprietor to seek remedies as prescribed. Further, any licensee may assign their rights and obligations under the license subject to the prior consent of the original patentee, which shall not be unreasonably withheld.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association, cooperative society, producer group, or individual engaged in the production, processing, and/or supply of goods claiming such protection. The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application, issue a public notice inviting objections from interested parties within three months from the date of publication. Any objection received shall be communicated to the applicant, who may submit their response within one month thereafter. Following consideration of all submissions, if the Registrar is satisfied that the indication is distinctive and conforms to the requirements as provided herein, he or she shall proceed with registration. Upon registration, the Register of Geographical Indications shall record particulars including the registered proprietor, which may be an assignee where ownership has been transferred in accordance with applicable law. The geographical indicati registered shall then be deemed protected under this Act.

A person who adopts a deceptive trade name or falsely represents a trade mark as being registered under this Act shall be liable to penalties as prescribed. Any aggrieved party may institute a suit for infringement of their trade mark, subject to providing proof of ownership and prior use relating to the goods or services specified in the registration certificate. Where a trade mark registered is used by a person not duly authorized, the owner thereof may seek an injunction restraining such unauthorized use, along with damages sustained due to said infringement. Provided that, no suit for rectification of the register shall be entertained unless filed within three years from the date of registration of the trade mark in question. The Court may, at its discretion, order delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark and award costs as deemed appropriate. A registered proprietor may assign their trade mark rights subject to any conditions specified in the instrument of assignment.

Where a patent is assigned or licensed under this Act by a sole proprietor, partnership, or individual, the assignee or licensee shall be subject to the same obligations and liabilities as would have been borne by the assignor or licensor had they continued to hold the patent. In relation to a firm, any assignment or license granted by the partners acting for the firm shall be deemed valid only if it is executed by all such partners or their duly authorized representatives. Provided that, where a license is granted exclusively to one party, the firm shall not subsequently grant a conflicting license without obtaining the express written consent of the original licensee. Further, any agreement concerning royalty payments arising from such assignment or license shall be binding on the firm and its successors in title. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board may entertain appeals against orders pertaining to disputes regarding these assignments and licenses as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, “storage” with reference to any work includes any material record of the work in any physical form, and shall be deemed to include transient incidental storage. Transient incidental storage is defined as the temporary recording of a work or performance on a computer system or other electronic device solely for the purpose of enabling communication between that device and another device, or facilitating access to such work or performance through an online service, provided that such storage does not constitute reproduction under this Act. Such storage shall be considered incidental where it is neither intended nor reasonably foreseeable by the user as a primary function of the device or service.

Where a patentee grants a licence relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted under this Act, the terms of such licence shall be governed by the provisions herein. The Controller may, upon receiving a complaint from any aggrieved party alleging unfair or restrictive conditions within a licence patent terms agreement, initiate inquiries and direct the parties involved to submit relevant documentation pertaining to the grant, operation, and termination of the licence. Such directions shall include but not be limited to copies of the licence agreement itself, correspondence relating to its negotiation, and records demonstrating compliance with any stipulated performance metrics. The Controller may also require the patentee or licensee to provide evidence substantiating claims regarding royalty rates or other financial considerations as part of the licensing arrangement. Failure to comply with these directions shall render a party liable to penalties as provided herein.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use that trade mark throughout India in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered, and may grant licences permitting such use by third parties. Any licence granted under this Act shall be in writing and specify the territory within which, and the time during which, the licensee is authorized to make use of the registered trade mark. The proprietor may assign any right arising under this Act relating to the use registered trade mark, including any licence agreement, subject to prior approval from the Controller if such assignment involves a foreign entity or concerns goods deemed critical to the security of India. Such approvals shall be granted only after due consideration of national interests and potential economic impact. The proprietor is responsible for ensuring that all licensees adhere to conditions stipulated in their agreements.

An application for registration of a patented invention shall be deemed to include a declaration by the applicant specifying the claims defining the scope of protection sought; such declaration being binding upon the applicant and forming an integral part of the registered patent. Where it is found that any process or article falls within the scope of a claim in a granted patent, then such act constitutes infringement patent under this Act. The Controller may, subject to due process and affording opportunity for hearing, issue directions regarding the interpretation of claims where ambiguity arises during proceedings relating to validity or infringement. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised by the Controller regarding the clarity or sufficiency of the filing specification matter contained within a patent application, the applicant shall have the opportunity to amend said specification and/or claims subject to the proviso that such amendments do not substantially alter the invention originally claimed. The Controller may require a written explanation accompanying any amendment, detailing the basis for its introduction and demonstrating compliance with the requirements under this Act concerning novelty and inventive step. An appeal against an order rejecting an application based on insufficiency of disclosure within the filing specification matter lies to the Appellate Board, provided that the applicant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Controller’s interpretation.

“Semiconductor” with reference to this Act means any material or device embodying circuitry originating from a semiconductor substrate; "layout-design" means a three-dimensional representation of the arrangement of elements, accurately depicting their relative positions and connections on an integrated circuit. The term “means registrar semiconductor” shall refer to the officer appointed by the Central Government under this Act, who is responsible for receiving applications for registration of layout-designs, conducting examinations as provided herein, and maintaining the Register of Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Designs. An application filed with the means registrar semiconductor shall include detailed technical specifications subject to guidelines issued from time to time.

The right to utilize a registered trademark, including any associated domain name registrations directly related thereto, is an assignable transmissible case subject to the conditions prescribed herein. Any such assignment shall require registration with the Registrar within thirty days of execution, and failure to register will render the assignee’s claim against the proprietor unenforceable. The proprietor may grant licenses relating to the use of the trademark, provided that any such license does not extend to the entire geographical area in which the trademark is registered, unless explicitly stated otherwise in the licensing agreement. Further, an assignment or transmission shall be void if it prejudices the interests of the consumers or unfairly exploits a reputation acquired by the prior proprietor. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint, investigate and determine whether such prejudice exists, and may refuse registration accordingly.

Any party aggrieved by a grant of patent may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step under this Act, and shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as prescribed. The Controller shall serve a copy of the notice on the patentee, who may then file a counter-statement within two months defending the validity of the patent. Failure to file a timely counter-statement shall render the patent vulnerable to revocation. Where an opposition is filed, the Controller may direct the parties to submit written arguments and evidence; any wilful suppression of material facts will attract penalties as provided herein.

Any person desiring to obtain a patent shall submit an application for registration to the Controller of Patents in accordance with the regulations established under this Act. The particulars required for such registration shall include a complete specification of the invention, any drawings necessary for its understanding, and a declaration of inventorship as provided herein. A request for registration must be accompanied by the prescribed fee, failing which it shall not be processed. 

The Controller may require an applicant to amend their application or provide further information before proceeding with the examination for registration. Upon satisfactory completion of the examination and subject to fulfilling all statutory requirements, the invention shall be entered in the register, and a patent will be granted. The register maintained by the Controller is open to public inspection during office hours. Any alteration to details recorded in the register requires notification to, and subsequent registration with, the Controller.

Where any person makes a false statement or representation with intent to deceive, or suppresses material facts relating to the invention for which patent is sought, or otherwise acts contrary to honesty and good faith in relation to the grant of a patent, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Any party aggrieved by such action may institute civil proceedings seeking damages proportionate to the loss suffered as a direct consequence of the false representation or suppression of facts. The Controller, upon receiving credible evidence of such deceptive conduct, may issue a notice requiring the individual or entity to rectify the misrepresentation within a specified period. Failure to comply with this notice shall render the party liable for further penalties and potential revocation of any patent granted based on the fraudulent information. A commission offence shall be cognizable under the relevant criminal procedure code.

Any person possessing the right to a layout-design through assignment, transmission, or operation of law, may apply to the Controller for the assignment of the registered layout-design in the design register, subject to the payment of the prescribed fee. The application for assignment shall be in such form as may be prescribed and shall include a statement of the title under which the applicant claims the right to the layout-design. Where a layout-design is jointly held, the assignment requires the consent of all registered proprietors, unless otherwise provided in a written agreement amongst them. 

A license to work a registered layout-design may be granted by the registered proprietor to any other person, and such license shall be in writing and shall specify the scope of the license, including the duration, geographical area, and any royalties payable. The Controller shall maintain a record of all assignments and licenses registered under this Act, and any person may inspect such record upon payment of the prescribed fee. Failure to register an assignment or license does not invalidate it, but such unregistered transfer shall not be enforceable against any person other than the parties thereto.

The right accruing to the proprietor of a registered trade mark shall be subject to transmissibility under this Act, whether by way of absolute transfer, license, pledge or any other means. Where an artistic work incorporates a registrable trade mark and such work is assigned or transmitted alongside the trade mark, the assignee or transferee shall acquire rights pertaining solely to the trade mark, provided that the assignment or transmission does not prejudice existing rights in the underlying artistic work held by another party. A transmissible case arises when a registered trade mark, used in connection with goods or services, is transferred and the subsequent proprietor continues use of said mark without demonstrable dilution of reputation. Any person aggrieved by an unauthorized transfer may seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein. The Registrar may require proof of consent from prior proprietors before registering any such transmission.

For the purposes of facilitating efficient examination and adjudication under this Act, the Controller may, at his discretion and subject to guidelines framed by the Central Government, appoint independent scientific advisors. Such appointment shall be made where complex technical aspects of an invention are involved, or when clarification is required regarding prior art references cited in opposition proceedings. The Controller shall maintain a panel of qualified individuals possessing relevant expertise for this purpose. Any party aggrieved by the appointment or conduct of such advisor may file representations with the Controller, who shall consider them and take appropriate action as provided herein. Further, the costs associated with the services of any appointed independent scientific advisor shall be borne equally by the parties unless otherwise determined by the Controller.

Where an exclusive licensee is granted rights under this Act relating to copyright in any work, such licensee shall be entitled to institute proceedings for infringement as if they were the owner of the copyright. Any act of reproduction, distribution, or adaptation of a work done without the authorization of the exclusive licensee, where such authorization would have been necessary had the copyright owner themselves acted, shall constitute an actionable infringement. The Court may, in determining damages for such infringement, consider the extent to which the licensee has exercised their rights and mitigated any losses suffered as a consequence of the infringing act. Failure by the grantor of the license to provide reasonable assistance to the exclusive licensee in enforcing these rights may render them liable to penalties as provided herein.

Any person claiming ownership of copyright shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply for registration with the Registrar of Copyrights in the prescribed manner. The application for registration shall be accompanied by the requisite fee as specified in Schedule I and include particulars relating to authorship, publication, and other details necessary to establish a prima facie case for copyright. Registration is not compulsory; however, it creates a rebuttable presumption of valid copyright ownership and date of creation, facilitating legal proceedings. Provided that failure to register does not invalidate the copyright itself, but may affect evidentiary weight in disputes concerning infringement or assignment. The Registrar may require further evidence or clarification before granting registration, and shall maintain a public Register of Copyrights accessible for inspection as provided herein. Any alteration to particulars registered shall be duly notified to the Registrar within thirty days of such change occurring.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been duly produced before the Registrar when it is presented at his office and accompanied by the prescribed fee. For the purposes of this Act, "produced registrar application" signifies an application that has undergone initial verification regarding its formal requirements under this Act and which remains pending for substantive examination. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further particulars or modifications to the layout-design as provided herein, subject to the applicant’s right to submit a written representation against such requirement. Any alteration made pursuant to such direction shall be recorded in the register.

Any person possessing copyright in a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work may assign all or part of their copyright by instrument in writing. Such an assignment shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding duration, termination, and permissible scope. Where the owner of copyright assigns the right to receive royalties, such assignment must clearly delineate the basis for calculating said royalties, including but not limited to a percentage of gross sales or a fixed sum per unit sold. 

Provided that an assignment intended to be effective only in relation to specific modes of exploitation—such as digital reproduction or public performance—shall explicitly state those limitations within the instrument. An assignee acquiring rights under this Act shall hold them subject to any prior existing licenses granted by the copyright owner, unless otherwise expressly agreed upon and documented in writing. Failure to adequately specify the nature of the assignment may render it voidable at the option of either party.

Any person claiming ownership of a collective mark shall furnish to the Registrar a statement of membership rules governing the use of such mark, and any subsequent amendment thereto shall be duly notified. Failure to maintain accurate records of members authorized to use the collective mark, or misuse by an unauthorized party despite reasonable efforts to prevent it, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, or with fine, or with both. Where a dispute arises regarding membership or the right to use the collective mark, any aggrieved party may apply to the High Court for redressal, subject to exhaustion of internal grievance mechanisms as outlined in the stated rules. The Registrar may initiate *suo motu* inquiry into allegations of fraudulent registration or improper usage and impose penalties including suspension of rights under this Act. Any profits derived from unlawful use shall be recoverable by way of damages.

For the purposes of this Act, a “claim” in a patent application shall define the scope of protection sought for the invention. Each claim must be clear, concise and supported by the specification; it shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the applicant considers as his invention. A dependent claim incorporates all limitations of the claim to which it refers, and also includes any additional features specifically recited in the dependent claim. Claims may be independent or dependent, and where a claim is ambiguous or lacks clarity, such ambiguity shall be resolved against the patentee.

Any suit for infringement of a patent, under this Act, shall be instituted in the district court within the local limits of which the cause of action arises, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. Where multiple defendants reside or carry on business in different districts, the plaintiff may institute a suit in any one of those districts, provided that such plaintiff satisfies the Court that it is necessary for the ends of justice to do so. The district court, upon receiving a plaint alleging infringement, shall issue a summons to the defendant requiring them to appear and defend the claim. Any evidence submitted in support of a claim of infringement shall be subject to the rules of evidence as applicable in civil proceedings. The Court may, at any stage of the proceedings, direct the parties to produce any document or thing necessary for the purpose of the suit, and may impose reasonable costs for non-compliance. A temporary injunction may be granted pending the final determination of the suit, subject to such terms and conditions as the Court deems fit.

The Board shall, upon receiving an objection under this Act from any person asserting a right or interest in relation to a proposed trade mark, afford such objector an opportunity for a hearing. The applicant for registration shall be notified of the objection and the time, date, and place fixed for the hearing at least thirty days prior to the appointed date, by registered post acknowledgement due. If, following such hearing, the Board is satisfied that the grounds raised by the objector are substantiated and that the proposed trade mark would infringe any right or interest possessed by the objector, registration may be refused. However, if the Board finds that the applicant has demonstrated a genuine use of the mark in accordance with the provisions herein, or otherwise provides compelling justification for registration notwithstanding the objection, justified registration may nonetheless be granted subject to such conditions as the Board deems appropriate to protect the interests of both parties.

An applicant seeking to register patents shall furnish with the application a statement indicating the claimed priority, if any, based on an earlier publication or application for the same invention. The Controller General may require further documentation substantiating this claim and verifying its authenticity under this Act. Where an international preliminary examination is requested, the details of such request shall be recorded in the register. Any modification to the particulars relating to the inventor or assignee after registration must be notified to the patent office, and these alterations shall then be entered into the register as provided herein. The applicant’s declaration regarding the novelty and non-obviousness of the invention remains crucial for successful registration.

The Chairperson shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor integrated circuits, or a person possessing expertise in law, engineering, or management, and appointed by the Central Government. The Chairperson shall exercise such powers as are necessary to ensure the effective administration of this Act, including the constitution of Benches and the regulation of proceedings. Any person appointed as Chairperson shall be eligible for a monthly remuneration, the amount of which shall be determined by the Central Government. An applicant seeking registration of a layout-design shall remit the prescribed registry fee, the schedule of which shall be determined by notification in the Official Gazette, and such fee shall be a condition precedent to the processing of the application by the Registry. The Chairperson may, subject to the provisions of this Act, delegate any of their powers to an officer of the Registry.

A certification trade mark denoting conformity to specific standards may be registered under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained. An application for such registration shall clearly state the nature of the certification and the persons or classes of persons authorized to use the mark upon compliance with specified requirements. The Registrar shall, before accepting any application for a certification trade mark, satisfy himself as to the existence of an institution or body capable of effectively performing the functions of ensuring that goods or services conform to the certified standards. 

Where the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant meets all criteria and the proposed use will not be deceptive, registration may proceed. The owner of a registered certification trade mark shall maintain records demonstrating compliance by licensees with established quality control measures. Any aggrieved person may apply to the Appellate Board for redressal if they believe the standards are not being consistently upheld or that misuse is occurring; such application shall be made within ninety days of becoming aware of the alleged violation, and subject to payment of prescribed fees.

An applicant seeking registration of a design affidavit registered relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall submit Form D along with the requisite fee as prescribed. The application must contain a true and complete representation of the layout-design, including all relevant technical specifications and supporting documentation demonstrating originality. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any deficiencies or provide further clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Failure to comply with such directions within the stipulated period shall render the application liable for rejection. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained by the Office. Objections, if any, may be filed within two months from the date of publication as provided herein. The applicant shall have an opportunity to respond to such objections before the Registrar proceeds with examination.

An application for a patent shall be deemed invalid where it is established, through civil suit in the appropriate jurisdictional court, that the invention was previously known or used within India, notwithstanding the applicant’s good faith belief in its novelty. Any party aggrieved by the grant of an allow application patent may petition the High Court seeking revocation, presenting evidence demonstrating prior public knowledge undermining the inventive step. Failure to provide verifiable documentary proof substantiating claims of prior use shall render the petitioner liable for costs incurred by the patentee in defending the action. The Controller may issue interim injunctions preventing exploitation of a patent pending judicial determination under this Act, subject to conditions as deemed just and equitable.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed abandoned if, after publication under this Act, the applicant fails to proceed with the matter within six months, unless such failure is satisfactorily explained. Where an objection is raised by any person against the acceptance of an application, or where the Registrar directs amendment or alteration of the proposed trade marks, the notice applicant shall have a period of three months from the date of receipt of such direction or objection to file his response and take necessary steps as provided herein. The Registrar may, upon receiving a satisfactory explanation for the delay, extend this time limit by a further period not exceeding three months. Failure to comply with these timelines will result in automatic abandonment without further notice.

The Authority shall establish and maintain a Gene Fund sub-account specifically designated for supporting research into traditional crop varieties and farmer-led breeding initiatives. Contributions to this sub-account shall include a portion of benefit-sharing fees received from commercial breeders, as determined by regulations framed under this Act. Any dispute concerning the allocation or disbursement of funds from the Gene Fund sub-account may be referred to an appellate forum constituted for that purpose. The Authority’s decision regarding such allocations is final, subject to review on grounds of legal error demonstrable through documentary evidence presented within sixty days of notification. Further, any farmer aggrieved by a determination impacting their eligibility for accessing resources derived from this sub-account may appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein.

Where an investigation into a suspected infringement of registered trademarks is initiated by the Registrar, any Government undertaking involved in the production or distribution of goods bearing the allegedly infringing mark shall be notified forthwith. The notification shall detail the nature of the alleged offence and provide copies of all relevant documentation pertaining to the trademark registration and the evidence supporting the claim of infringement. Upon receipt of such notification, the Government undertaking is obliged to furnish a report within thirty days outlining its assessment of the matter and detailing any remedial actions taken or proposed. Failure to submit this report may result in penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall have the power to conduct on-site inspections of premises belonging to the Government undertaking if deemed necessary for the purpose of ascertaining compliance with the provisions under this Act.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a detailed specification, clearly and concisely describing the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. Any application patent found to be lacking such a specification, or containing a specification deemed insufficient by the Controller, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Provided that, the Controller may, at their discretion, allow a period of sixty days for rectification of the deficiency, subject to payment of a late submission fee as prescribed. Failure to rectify within this period shall result in the application being deemed abandoned. Furthermore, any person found to have knowingly submitted a false or misleading specification in an application patent, with intent to deceive, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or with a fine, or with both. All fees levied under this Act shall be non-refundable, except as otherwise provided herein.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, any registered breeder who fails to comply with the provisions relating to benefit sharing with farmers, or the maintenance of a seed stock of a protected variety as stipulated under this Act, shall be liable to a penalty as may be prescribed. However, such non-compliance shall not, *per se*, invalidate the breeder’s rights, provided that the Authority, upon receiving credible evidence of such failure, initiates an inquiry and affords the breeder a reasonable opportunity to be heard. Should the inquiry establish a prima facie case of non-compliance, the Authority may impose a financial penalty, and direct remedial action. Any determination of the Authority regarding breeder complied provisions may be appealed to the Appellate Board, subject to the conditions outlined herein. A claim of a new variety, even if demonstrably so, does not absolve the breeder from obligations under this Act. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act against any infringement shall be entitled to seek remedy for damages sustained by reason of such infringement, provided that the amount of damages shall not exceed three times the value of the goods or services sold bearing the geographical indication. Further, where a notice of opposition is filed and subsequently withdrawn, the applicant shall be entitled to recover from the opponent a paid fee payable representing costs incurred in defending the application during the period of opposition. The Registrar may, upon receiving proof of such costs, issue an order directing the opponent to pay the sum so determined. Any variety registered as a geographical indication shall enjoy protection against use by any person who is not authorized to do so, and unauthorized use will be deemed unfair competition.

An application for registration as a trade mark shall be deemed refused if, upon examination, it is found that the proposed marks are substantially identical or confusingly similar to an earlier registered trade mark in relation to goods or services identical to those for which the application is filed. Where such refusal is based on grounds relating to section 36e ixd of this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a further opportunity to amend the application to distinguish it from the prior mark. This amendment may include alterations to the representation of the trade mark or limitations upon the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registrar shall provide written reasons for any such refusal and the applicant may submit counter-arguments within sixty days of receipt of the notice of refusal. Furthermore, an application patent relating to a similar invention may be considered in determining similarity under this provision.

Any person aggrieved by the grant of a patent for a patented process may, subject to conditions prescribed herein, institute rectification proceedings before the Controller within one year from the date of publication of the grant. Such proceedings shall be limited to demonstrating that the claimed patented process does not involve an inventive step or is obvious in view of prior art available to the public prior to the filing date of the patent application. Failure to demonstrate such lack of novelty or inventiveness shall render the aggrieved party liable for costs, including reasonable attorney’s fees as determined by the Controller. Furthermore, any infringement of a patented process established through rectification proceedings will be deemed null and void ab initio.

An applicant seeking registration of a layout design shall furnish with the application, a detailed technical description outlining the functionality and intended purpose of the integrated circuit. The Registrar may require further clarification or supplementary documentation deemed necessary for assessing novelty and originality under this Act. Where an applicant has previously published the layout design prior to filing the application, such publication shall not preclude registration provided that the applicant demonstrates due diligence in safeguarding confidentiality before the disclosure. Any subsequent modification to a registered layout design which substantially alters its characteristics may necessitate a fresh application for registration as a new layout design. The right of layout design providing is conferred upon the registered proprietor for the duration specified herein.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license for an invention in respect of which a compulsory license has been granted under this Act, they shall notify the Controller and all licensees previously identified. The terms of any subsequent license agreement must not conflict with the conditions stipulated in the original compulsory license, provided that the patentee may apply to the order appellate authority for modification or revocation of such conflicting clauses. Any assignment of a patent, whether partial or complete, including rights pertaining to a compulsory license, shall require prior notification and approval from the Controller. The order appellate authority may, upon application by an aggrieved party, review any decision made by the Controller concerning the validity or terms of such assignments. Further, the authority shall consider representations regarding equitable compensation to the patentee for licenses granted post-compulsory licensing.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a layout-design registered under this Act as their own, or uses such a layout-design without the authorization of the registered owner, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees. The court, as provided herein, may also order the seizure and destruction of all infringing articles and materials used in the manufacture thereof. A means member appellate, constituted for the expeditious hearing of disputes relating to infringement, shall have the power to impose such fines and direct such remedies. Any appeal against the decision of a means member appellate shall lie before the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act, and such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order. Failure to comply with an order of the court shall constitute a separate offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

Where the registered proprietor of a trade mark desires to grant a license conferring the right to use the trade mark exclusively or non-exclusively, he shall execute an assignment agreement detailing the scope and duration of such permission. This agreement must specify the goods or services in relation to which the licensee is authorized to employ the trade mark, subject to conditions as may be prescribed by the Registrar. Any subsequent transfer of ownership of the licensed business shall not automatically invalidate the license, provided that the assignee notifies the registered proprietor within thirty days and consents to a review of the licensing terms under this Act. The registered proprietor retains the right to terminate the license if material breaches occur, referencing the specific clauses violated in written notice. Further provisions act reference regarding royalty payments and audit rights are detailed in Schedule B annexed hereto.

A legal practitioner engaged by an owner of integrated circuit layout designs shall be deemed to hold such engagement subject to compliance with the stipulations outlined herein. Such practitioners must maintain records detailing all consultations undertaken concerning the protection and enforcement of layout-design rights, accessible for inspection upon reasonable notice from an authorized officer. A practitioner person providing advisory services relating to infringement proceedings shall file a declaration annually confirming adherence to professional standards as prescribed by the relevant Bar Council regulations. Further, any legal practitioner representing a claimant in respect of alleged infringement must disclose all prior engagements concerning the same or related integrated circuit layout designs, provided that such disclosure does not compromise client confidentiality under this Act.

Any party aggrieved by a decision relating to the revocation of a patent granted under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision. Such appeal shall be finally determinable by the Board, subject to review by the High Court only on a point of law. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during an application patent act proceeding renders any subsequent enforcement action vulnerable to challenge and dismissal. The Controller may, upon receiving evidence of wilful infringement, initiate proceedings for recovery of damages sustained by the patentee, including lost profits demonstrably attributable to the infringing activity. Penalties for false statements made in support of a patent application shall be imposed as provided herein.

All applications for registration of new plant varieties of crop sciences indian origin shall be accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its lineage, characteristics, stability, and uniformity, as demonstrated through multi-location field trials conducted over a period of not less than three growing seasons. The applicant shall, subject to verification by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, submit evidence of the variety’s distinctiveness from any commonly known variety or existing registered variety. Provided that, in cases where the applicant claims a substantially derived variety, full details of the initial variety and the process of derivation shall be disclosed. Any farmer or group of farmers who have bred or developed a new variety, and who seek registration under this Act, may submit a farmer’s variety, subject to compliance with the prescribed procedural requirements and payment of applicable fees. The Authority may, at its discretion, require additional data or clarification from the applicant to ensure full compliance with the provisions herein.

Where a trade mark consists entirely or substantially of a sign which is identical or confusingly similar to an earlier trade mark lawfully used in relation to goods or services identical or closely related to those for which the registration is sought, and it is demonstrated that such use has resulted in demonstrable detriment to the proprietor of the earlier trade mark, the Registrar may entertain a petition for revocation. Such petition shall be accompanied by evidence establishing the extent and nature of said detriment. The petitioner shall bear the burden of proving both similarity and harm. Any party aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the relevant High Court within sixty days of such order, subject to any prescribed fee.

Where a patentee elects to manufacture the patented invention within India following grant of the patent, such manufacturing shall be deemed an act of infringement only if it is carried out otherwise than in accordance with the terms and conditions stipulated under this Act or any rules made thereunder. Provided that, where the patentee has previously imported the patented article into India prior to commencement of manufacture within India, subsequent manufacture shall not constitute infringement unless it exceeds quantities reasonably required for demonstration, testing, or analysis purposes as determined by the Controller. Furthermore, a patentee seeking to enforce their rights under this Act must demonstrate continuous and active exploitation of the invention in India, failing which, such rights may be subject to limitation as provided herein.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall be accompanied by a declaration verifying the originality of the design and confirming that the applicant is either a legal practitioner, or a person registered in the prescribed manner as a layout-design agent, or a person in the sole and regular employment of the principal. The Registrar may require further documentation to establish the applicant’s entitlement under this Act, including proof of prior use or publication, provided that such requirements shall be reasonable and proportionate to the complexity of the design involved. A practitioner person registered as an agent shall adhere to a code of conduct prescribed by the Controller, failure to do so rendering them liable for disciplinary action and potential revocation of registration.

A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion among consumers, considering the overall impression created and the class of persons likely to deal with the goods or services concerned. However, the Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct that two trade marks, though deceptively similar, may be registered in respect of different descriptions of goods or services, provided that such goods or services are not ordinarily likely to be confused as being the same or of the same kind. Where a trade mark incorporates a geographical indication prescribed under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, the assessment of deceptive similarity shall also consider the reputation and distinctiveness of the geographical indication itself, and whether its use in relation to the disputed mark would mislead consumers as to the origin of the goods. Any decision of the Registrar regarding deceptive similarity shall be subject to appeal to the High Court.

The owner of a registered geographical indication may, subject to any conditions specified therein, grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable by the licensor, provided that prior written consent of the registering proprietor is obtained from the licensee. Upon the expiration registration of a geographical indication, any license granted prior thereto shall continue in force for a period not exceeding five years from the date of such expiration, unless earlier terminated by mutual agreement between the licensor and licensee or by order of the Geographical Indications Registry. Further, an assignment of a license under this Act requires notification to be filed with the Registry within thirty days of its execution; failure to do so shall render the assignment void. The registering proprietor may revoke any license granted if the licensee acts in contradiction to the conditions specified therein.

Where any patentee, assignee or other person claiming under this Act fails to comply with the requirements of sub-section (1) of section eighty-two, the Controller may, after giving opportunity for hearing, issue an order directing such person to rectify the particulars relating to the invention within a specified time. Failure to do so shall render the patent liable to be revoked under this Act. In instances where the patentee is deceased or has become insolvent, action against the estate or insolvency representative shall proceed as if such individual were living and capable of acting. Any legal representative appointed by due process of law may, subject to any order made by a competent court, exercise all rights and powers vested in the deceased or bankrupt party concerning enforcement of patent validity and infringement remedies as provided herein.

Where an applicant has filed an international application claiming priority from an Indian patent application, and a request for preliminary examination is received under this Act, the Controller shall proceed with the examination as if the international application were a domestic application. However, any communication relating to maintainability or novelty raised during the preliminary examination stage of the international application shall be deemed to be in response to the said application only, and not to the underlying Indian patent application. The applicant may appeal against such communications before a Bench constituted under sub-section (1) of section 105. Provided that any decision rendered by the Bench concerning an international application shall not prejudice the rights or remedies available to any party in relation to the corresponding Indian patent application, should it proceed independently.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent under this Act based on a convention application shall provide evidence satisfactory to the Controller demonstrating compliance with all applicable laws pertaining to inventorship within the convention country. The Controller may, after affording the applicant an opportunity of being heard, reject the application if he is not convinced that the claimed invention was indeed conceived by the inventor(s) as represented in the documentation submitted. Any such rejection shall be accompanied by reasoned findings and a statement of the grounds upon which it is based; and the applicant shall have recourse to appeal under this Act against such determination, presenting arguments supported by documentary evidence refuting the Controller’s assessment.

Where any proprietor of a registered trade mark seeks to alter the representation of that trade mark, such alteration shall not be permissible without prior approval obtained under this Act. The application for such approval must specify the nature and extent of the proposed modification, accompanied by representations demonstrating its continued distinctiveness following the change. Provided that an alteration does not affect the essential characteristics or connotations associated with the registered trade mark, it may be approved. Furthermore, any proprietor seeking to amend their trade mark shall provide evidence confirming that consumers are likely to recognise the altered representation as denoting the same goods or services previously indicated under this Act. The provisions act shall govern all applications for alteration and subsequent registration thereof.

Any person aggrieved by an order relating to the revocation of a patent, or the rectification of a specification claim, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall have power to entertain appeals under this Act and shall pass such orders as it deems fit, subject to the provisions herein. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines for filing an appeal shall render the appellant liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable by way of fine. Further, any party seeking enforcement of a patent granted under this Act may apply to the relevant High Court for appropriate remedies in cases of infringement, provided that such application is made within three years from the date of the order appealed against.

An application for registration of a design shall be refused if the design incorporates or comprises any coat of arms, public seal, flag, emblem, name or initials of any sovereign nation or foreign state; provided that the Registrar may entertain an application containing such elements if the applicant demonstrates to his satisfaction that use is authorized by the appropriate government authority. The Controller General shall furnish a certified copy of the design registration to any person applying for it, upon payment of the prescribed fee and subject to verification of identity as per rules framed under this Act. Any individual found to be infringing a registered design may be required to submit detailed documentation pertaining to their manufacturing processes. Designs deemed essential for national security, particularly those relating to defense or critical infrastructure, are considered necessary security india and shall receive heightened protection.

Where any proprietor institutes proceedings under this Act alleging infringement of layout-design rights, and such proceedings result in a judgment finding the defendant guilty of said infringement, the court may order the recovery of damages as determined by prevailing schedules. Further, where the defendant has been found to have acted with intent to deceive or wilfully disregard the proprietary rights vested in the registered layout-design, the court shall be empowered to direct the forfeiture to the Government of any equipment, materials, and intermediate products utilized directly in the infringing activity. This order for forfeiture is without prejudice to any other penalties prescribed under this Act. The proprietor may petition for restoration of such forfeited assets subject to a demonstration that they are not readily identifiable as having been used in the commission of the offence. A convicted order forfeited shall be deemed final and binding, barring appeal solely on grounds of procedural irregularity.

Where any party aggrieved by the grant of a patent may, within six months from the date of publication of the grant under this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. Such notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to lack of novelty or inventive step, and the person opposing shall provide particulars supporting their claim. The Controller shall afford an opportunity for both the patentee and the opponent to be heard, and may direct the presentation of evidence as deemed necessary. If, following such hearing, the Controller finds merit in the opposition, a register effect order suspending the effects of the patent may be issued pending further inquiry or revocation proceedings. The patentee shall have the right to appeal any such register effect order under this Act.

The owner of a distinguishable registered layout may grant licenses to third parties enabling the manufacture, import, sale and offer for sale of integrated circuits incorporating such layout. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive, as determined by the licensor, and shall specify the geographical territory within which the licensee’s rights are exercisable. Assignment of ownership of a registered layout is permissible subject to registration with the Controller General, and any subsequent dealings in the assigned layout shall be deemed valid only upon such registration. Where an assignment includes pre-existing licenses, the assignor warrants that it possesses full power and authority to grant those licenses under this Act. Furthermore, any license or assignment granted prior to registration of the layout is void unless specifically endorsed by the Controller General following application for registration.

Any person who, without due cause or consent from the proprietor of a registered trademark, uses any mark which is identical or deceptively similar to such proprietor’s trademark, shall be liable for damages. The amount of damages recoverable shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss suffered by the proprietor as a result of the infringing use and the profits made by the infringer. Further, where an infringement has occurred, the Court may order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark or packaging thereof. It is provided that any registered proprietor trade marks shall be afforded protection against dilution even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services associated with those marks.

Any proprietor seeking remedies against a defendant geographical indication user found to have engaged in activities constituting unfair competition or misrepresentation under this Act may institute proceedings in the High Court. Such action shall be predicated upon demonstrable evidence of consumer confusion reasonably attributable to the defendant’s use of a sign identical or deceptively similar to the registered Geographical Indication. The court, upon finding infringement, may grant such relief as it deems appropriate, including but not limited to injunctions preventing further infringing acts and orders for accounts of profits derived from the unauthorized use. Where an international application has been filed in respect of a geographical indication, the provisions relating to remedies shall apply with due regard to any conflicting rights or obligations arising under treaties or conventions ratified by India. The court may also order the defendant to undertake corrective advertising to mitigate consumer deception.

Any person who, having knowledge that a denomination is likely to be confused with an existing denomination variety sub for any plant variety, uses such denomination in connection with the marketing or sale of propagating material or seed of any kind shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of the infringing material. Further, under this Act, any officer empowered by the Central Government may seize and detain any propagating material bearing an unauthorized denomination variety sub pending investigation. Where a contravention of these provisions is established, the offender shall also be subject to a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees, recoverable as civil debt. The Authority may issue orders restraining further use of the infringing denomination.

An application india filed relating to a process for producing a novel pharmaceutical intermediate shall be deemed invalid if the applicant has previously published or publicly disclosed the invention outside India unless such publication or disclosure was made under conditions preventing exploitation of the patented subject matter. The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from any interested party regarding prior publication, require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating that the publication did not compromise the novelty and inventive step requirements as provided herein. Further, if the application incorporates subject matter derived from a previously filed application india filed by another person, the applicant must provide written consent from the original applicant confirming the transfer of rights and acknowledging compliance with all relevant provisions concerning divisional applications.

The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall retain exclusive rights pertaining to its use; however, permission for specific trade mark uses may be granted through licensing agreements executed in writing. Such licenses shall clearly define the scope of permitted activities, including but not limited to, manufacturing, distribution, and advertising relating to goods or services specified within the license. Assignment of a registered trade mark, or any right pertaining thereto, requires registration with the relevant Trade Marks Registry and is only valid upon such registration. A licensee may further sub-license rights granted under this Act, provided that such sub-licensing does not exceed the scope of the original agreement and is subject to approval by the proprietor. Any unauthorized trade mark uses shall be actionable as infringement, irrespective of any prior consent or purported assignment.

The Appellate Board shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a copyright register, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the procedural requirements as provided herein. Where an application is found to be incomplete or deficient, the Appellate Board shall notify the applicant, specifying the deficiencies and granting a period of thirty days to remedy them. Any application not remedied within the stipulated period shall be deemed to be withdrawn, and no further consideration shall be given to it. However, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, extend this period if sufficient cause is demonstrated. Respect registered application, the Board shall ensure that all submissions relating to the rectification request are duly documented and maintained as part of the official record. The Appellate Board shall issue its reasoned order within one hundred and eighty days of the completion of the evidentiary proceedings. Failure to do so shall require a written explanation to the Registrar.

Where a trade mark owner desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights relating to specific goods or services associated with a registered trade mark, such license shall be recorded with the Registrar prior to its operation. The recording shall include details of the licensed territory and the duration of the license. Further, any assignment of a registered trade mark, or of the benefit of any application for registration, including assignments incorporating licenses, must also be formally documented with the Registrar. The India registrar require that such documentation clearly identifies both the assignor and assignee, along with a precise description of the rights being transferred. Provided that, where an assignment includes a continuing security interest, this shall be explicitly stated in the recorded document. Failure to record these transactions as provided herein will render them unenforceable against third parties.

Any assignment of rights relating to a patented process used in the manufacture of goods bearing a distinctive trade mark shall be subject to the provisions concerning passing off as detailed herein. A licensee of such patented process may, provided that reasonable royalties are paid and the terms of the license agreement are adhered to, continue use of said process even after assignment of the trade mark itself, unless it can be demonstrated that such continued use is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. However, where an assignee of a trade mark also acquires rights in the associated patented process, they shall not engage in any activity calculated to mislead the public into believing that goods manufactured using a different process are equivalent to those previously produced under the assigned mark and process combination. Any claim of passing off arising from such circumstances may be adjudicated upon by the appropriate court as provided herein, considering both trade mark rights and patent entitlements. The burden of proving lack of deceptive intent shall lie with the assignee.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, represents a layout-design which is not an original layout-design as provided herein, or who falsely states that a layout-design is his own, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to five lakh rupees.
