Where an offence under this Act involves commercial scale reproduction, distribution, or sale of integrated circuits embodying such falsely represented layout-design, the term of imprisonment may extend to five years and the fine may extend to ten lakh rupees. The Controller, upon receiving credible information of such an offence, may initiate an inquiry and, subject to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, direct a police officer to investigate. Furthermore, any evidence obtained during such investigation shall be admissible in any proceedings under this Act, and the Controller’s findings shall be considered persuasive by any court of competent jurisdiction concerning section 53 zn.

Where an application for patent includes drawings depicting objects or processes, such drawings shall be construed as representations intended solely to illustrate aspects of the invention claimed. The Controller may, at any stage of examination, direct the applicant to provide further clarification regarding any element depicted within said drawings, provided that such direction is accompanied by a reasoned explanation outlining the ambiguity necessitating additional detail. Any reference made under this Act to “the drawing” shall encompass all sheets submitted as part of the application’s technical documentation, irrespective of their sequential order or labeling. The interpretation of claims referencing specific features shown in the drawings shall be governed by principles of form references act, ensuring consistency between textual descriptions and visual representations. Failure to comply with a direction under this provision may result in rejection of the patent application.

Where any person alleges that another has contravened any provision relating to the specification of a patent, such allegation shall be made within three years from the date of grant of the patent and shall specify with particularity the nature of the alleged non-compliance. Failure to adequately disclose the best method known to the inventor for carrying out the invention, as detailed in the specification, renders the patent liable to revocation under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision regarding the validity of a patent based on deficiencies within its specification may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Controller shall impose a penalty not exceeding one million rupees upon any applicant found to have knowingly misrepresented facts pertaining to their invention's specification.

Any application for the registration of a copyright, or for the rectification of any entry in the Register of Copyrights, shall be presented to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the applicant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, if the applicant is not a legal person, the application may be presented to the High Court within whose jurisdiction the principal place of business of the applicant is situated. Where any dispute arises regarding the determination of the appropriate court having jurisdiction, the matter shall be referred to the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned, whose decision shall be final and binding. Subject to the provisions of this Act, the High Court shall, upon being satisfied that the application is duly completed and accompanied by the prescribed fee, proceed to examine the same. Any objection to the registration shall be filed within sixty days of the publication of the application.

The proprietor of a use certification trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the application of the mark, provided that such license expressly defines the scope and limitations of permitted usage. Any assignment of the registration of a use certification trade mark shall include all associated licensing agreements then in force unless otherwise stipulated within the instrument of transfer. Further, where a licensee sub-licenses the certified goods or services, the proprietor retains the right to audit records pertaining to such sub-licensing activities and ensure adherence to quality standards as defined under this Act. The proprietor may revoke any license agreement if the licensee engages in practices detrimental to the reputation or integrity of the certification trade mark. Such revocation shall not affect existing assignments made by the licensee, subject to their continued compliance with the original terms.

Where an invention relates to a process for producing a substance, any person claiming title to the patent or possessing a license to exercise the patented process shall be deemed to hold an implied license to use such process for the manufacture of that substance, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the assignment agreement or licensing contract. This provision applies irrespective of whether the substance is itself claimed as part of the invention. Any proceedings act undertaken by a licensee relating to infringement of the patent by another party shall be considered an exercise of rights granted under this implied license, provided that such proceedings do not contradict any restrictions outlined within the original contractual agreement. The Controller may issue directions regarding the scope and validity of these implied licenses in cases where disputes arise concerning their interpretation or application, ensuring equitable access to patented technologies while respecting legitimate commercial interests.

Any person being the proprietor of a registered layout shall have the right to assign, or otherwise transfer, all or any of the rights vested in such registered layout to any other person, whether such transfer is by way of sale, gift, or otherwise, and such assignment or transfer shall be subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon between the parties. Provided that, any assignment or transfer of a registered layout shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly registered with the Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Registry as provided herein. The Registry shall, upon application and payment of the prescribed fee, register the assignment or transfer and issue a certificate of registration to the assignee or transferee. A commercial license relating to a registered layout may be granted by the proprietor, and such license shall define the scope of permitted use, including territorial limitations and the duration of the license. Any dispute arising from the interpretation or enforcement of such licensing agreements shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the competent court.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout design shall be accompanied by such particulars and documents as the Registrar may require, including certified copies of any relevant prior publications or disclosures. The applicant shall furnish an execution specifying the layout design claimed to be registered and identifying its salient features. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall issue an acknowledgment containing a date of filing. Subsequently, the Registrar may serve notice on the applicant requiring further particulars within a prescribed period; failure to comply will result in rejection of the application. The register sub section pertaining to rectification proceedings allows for applications to be made by any person aggrieved by an entry or omission in the Register. Such applications must specify the nature of the grievance and provide supporting evidence as provided herein.

A trademark shall be deemed to infringe if, subject to the provisions regarding use in describing the character or quality of certain goods, it is identical to the registered trademark or so nearly resembling it as to likely cause confusion among the public. The determination of such likelihood shall consider all relevant circumstances, including but not limited to the nature of the goods or services, the distinctiveness of the earlier mark, and any prior use by the defendant. Where an application for registration is refused on the ground of similarity to a previously registered trademark, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The Board shall consider whether the marks in question possess trade mark identity sufficient to warrant protection under this Act. Evidence presented before the Board shall be admissible as provided herein and subject to established rules of evidence.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to a Bench constituted for that purpose. The appellate Bench shall be presided over by a judicial member and two technical members, one of whom shall be experienced in semiconductor integrated circuit layout design. Failure to comply with the provisions relating to notice as provided herein before filing an appeal shall render the appeal inadmissible. Where any person is found to have made a false statement or suppressed material facts in relation to any proceedings before a Bench, that person shall be liable to pay such penalty as may be determined by the Board, not exceeding five lakhs of rupees. The appellate Bench’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to revision by the High Court only on a point of law.

An application made to the Registrar shall be deemed complete only upon submission of all prescribed forms and requisite fees, and compliance with the requirements detailed under this Act regarding representation of the trademark. The Registrar may require further clarification from the applicant concerning the classification of goods or services associated with the proposed mark, provided that such request is made within thirty days of receipt of the application. Failure to respond adequately to a query issued by the Registrar shall result in the application being held in abeyance until satisfactory information is furnished. Any alteration to the details initially presented in the registrar application after its deemed completion will necessitate a fresh filing and associated fees, subject to conditions regarding minor clerical errors as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Trade Marks Registry refusing to register a trade mark, or requiring the rectification or cancellation of a registered trade mark, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Trade Marks Registry. Provided that, an appeal shall not be entertained unless the appellant deposits with the Appellate Board such sum as the Board may determine, not exceeding five thousand rupees, to meet the costs of the proceedings. Where a dispute arises concerning the use of trade marks registered under this Act, and the parties fail to reach a mutually acceptable resolution through mediation, the Appellate Board may appoint an arbitrator to adjudicate the matter, and the decision of the arbitrator shall be final and binding.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a “person interested” shall be deemed to include any individual or body corporate who has directly funded research and development leading to the claimed invention, provided that such funding was material to the conception or reduction to practice thereof. Further, a person interested includes an assignee of the right to apply for a patent, where assignment is duly registered with the Controller. Any entity claiming status as a “person interested” shall file a declaration along with the application for registration, specifying the nature and extent of their interest in the invention. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating such claim under this Act. This determination rests solely within the discretion of the Controller, subject to appeal before an appellate tribunal.

Where an application for registration of a mark is advertised under this Act and subsequently accepted by the Registrar, such acceptance shall constitute conclusive evidence against all persons claiming through the applicant until the expiry of the opposition period. Any party aggrieved by an acceptance may institute proceedings to challenge the validity of the acceptance before the relevant intellectual property tribunal. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines for filing objections following application advertised acceptance will render any subsequent claim invalid and subject the claimant to penalties as provided herein. The Registrar shall be empowered to impose a monetary fine not exceeding one hundred thousand rupees upon any party found to have wilfully obstructed or hindered the advertisement process.

An application for registration of a trade mark, once examined and refused by the Registry, may be subject to an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The appellant shall, within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal order, file a written petition particulars contained therein detailing the grounds upon which the sought appealed is based. Such petition must clearly articulate how the trade mark satisfies the requirements for registration as provided herein and addresses any objections raised by the examining officer. Failure to adequately address these objections in the appeal may result in its dismissal. The Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented, including prior use of the mark, consumer perception, and potential confusion with existing marks.

Any computer programme created for the purpose of assisting in pharmaceutical research, specifically relating to the identification of novel drug candidates or optimisation of existing formulations, shall be deemed a literary work under this Act and is subject to copyright protection from the moment of its creation. Assignment of all rights in such a computer programme, including but not limited to source code, object code, and accompanying documentation, may be effected by written instrument duly executed by the author or their authorised agent. Where a pharmaceutical company commissions the development of a bespoke computer programme for drug discovery, it shall have the right to negotiate an exclusive license to utilise said programme for a defined period, subject to equitable remuneration being agreed upon with the programmer. Provided that, any modifications or derivative works created utilising the original computer programme remain subject to the terms of the initial assignment or licensing agreement unless otherwise stipulated in writing. The rights conferred herein are not diminished by the incidental use of publicly available algorithms within the said computer programme.

Any assignment or license granted relating to a patent, or any right conferred thereunder, shall remain valid notwithstanding that an appeal has been filed against a decision concerning the validity of the patent itself; provided that such assignment or license was executed prior to the expiry of the sixty-day period for preferring an appeal under this Act. Where a patent holder assigns their interest in a patent, and subsequently receives notice of an order questioning the patent’s validity, the assignee shall be deemed to have inherited the right to exercise the appeal period as if they were the original patentee. Further, any sub-licensee deriving rights from such assignment may also pursue this appeal within the prescribed timeframe, subject to fulfilling conditions stipulated by the Controller. The Central Government may issue guidelines regarding procedural aspects of these appeals relating to assignments and licenses.

A person interested, for the purposes of opposition to a patent granted under this Act, shall demonstrate a sufficient proprietary interest, being either a holder of a valid patent relating to the same invention or a party demonstrably likely to be materially injured by the grant of the patent in question. However, mere commercial rivalry, absent evidence of specific and foreseeable damage to existing proprietary rights, shall not constitute sufficient interest to maintain an opposition. Any decision regarding the locus standi of a person interested may be appealed to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the Controller’s decision. The Appellate Board, in considering such appeals, shall have the power to require the applicant to furnish further evidence substantiating their claim of being a person interested and to determine whether the alleged injury is speculative or substantial. Failure to comply with the timelines as provided herein shall render the appeal inadmissible.

The Registrar may, upon application by any person claiming rights in a trade mark, investigate whether a particular trade mark is a well known trade mark in India. Such investigation shall proceed according to principles of natural justice, affording all interested parties an opportunity to present evidence and arguments. The applicant shall furnish such documentation as the Registrar deems necessary to substantiate the claim, including but not limited to market share data, consumer surveys, and advertising expenditure records relating to the use of the trade mark. Evidence demonstrating widespread recognition and association of the mark with its proprietor is essential for establishing well known status under this Act. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision.

For the purposes of this Act, an “alleged offence” shall mean any act or omission constituting a violation of provisions relating to registered trademarks, including but not limited to passing off, dilution, or use as a trademark without due cause. An alleged offence may be predicated on actions taken by any person, whether acting alone or in concert with others, and subject to the principles of vicarious liability as provided herein. Where an individual is charged with an alleged offence, it shall be presumed that such individual had knowledge of the facts constituting the violation unless proven otherwise. The determination of whether a particular act constitutes an alleged offence shall be made considering the totality of circumstances.

Permitted use of a registered trade mark shall be subject to the conditions as provided herein, and any deviation therefrom may constitute grounds for revocation of such permission. A registered proprietor may, under this Act, grant licenses authorizing the use of their trade mark by another party, specifying the scope, duration, and territorial limits of such permitted use. Any permitted use extending beyond the terms of the license, or involving a material alteration of the registered trade mark, shall be deemed unauthorized. Furthermore, the quality of goods or services offered under permitted use must consistently meet the standards associated with the registered trade mark, failing which the proprietor may initiate action for passing off. The registered proprietor shall maintain a register of all permitted users and licenses granted, and shall furnish a copy thereof to the Registrar upon demand. Any transfer of a license for permitted use requires prior written consent of the trade mark owner.

Any person who owns a registered trade mark and alleges an infringement involving associated trade marks may apply to the High Court for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from making further use of the offending mark. An application for such injunction shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the ownership of the trade mark and the likelihood of irreparable harm resulting from continued infringement. The Court, while considering such application, shall also assess whether the marks in question are indeed associated trade marks as determined under this Act, and whether the defendant’s use is likely to cause confusion or deception amongst consumers. Provided that, the plaintiff shall demonstrate a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and the likelihood of success in the ultimate adjudication of the dispute. The Court may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant the injunction pending the final determination of the suit, and may also direct the defendant to provide an account of profits. Any order made under this provision may be modified or vacated upon sufficient cause being shown.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; provided that the Appellate Board may, if it is satisfied that there was reasonable cause for the delay, entertain an appeal lodged after the expiry of the said period. Where a party proceeding shall seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against any order passed by the Appellate Board, such application must be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order of the Appellate Board. Further, where an appeal is preferred under this Act, all parties concerned shall be served with notice of the proceedings and given a reasonable opportunity to present their case as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license in respect of a patented pharmaceutical product, or assign the rights pertaining thereto, shall provide a detailed inventory of all relevant documentation submitted during the prosecution of the patent, including but not limited to the provisional specification complete and subsequent amendments. This disclosure is mandatory irrespective of whether the license agreement concerns domestic manufacture or export patented pharmaceutical products for sale in foreign territories. The Controller may require further clarification regarding the scope of such licenses or assignments, particularly concerning royalties and sub-licensing arrangements. Any party receiving a license or assignment shall be bound by the terms stipulated within the patent grant itself, as well as any additional conditions imposed by the patentee relating to quality control measures for exported goods. Failure to comply with these disclosure requirements may render the license or assignment voidable under this Act.

A party proceeding before the Geographical Indications Registry concerning the validity of registration for “Kanthaloor Pepper” shall furnish, within thirty days of notification under this Act, a detailed affidavit verifying their standing as a producer or trader directly involved in the production, processing, and packaging of pepper originating from Kanthaloor village. Such an affidavit must specify the geographical area from which the applicant sources its raw materials, and demonstrate adherence to quality control measures prescribed by the Spice Board. Provided that any party proceeding who fails to submit this affidavit within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed to have abandoned their challenge unless a request for extension is made with adequate justification and approved by the Registry. Further, the Registry may require submission of additional documentation to ascertain compliance with relevant regulations.

An application for registration as a plant variety shall be accompanied by detailed documentation establishing distinctiveness and stability across successive generations. The Registrar may require submission of data pertaining to morphological characteristics, genetic uniformity, and disease resistance relevant to assessing the traits of the applied-for new variety. Such data must demonstrate that the variety maintains its essential features under specified environmental conditions as prescribed by regulations framed under this Act. Further, an applicant shall provide a comprehensive pedigree chart tracing lineage and demonstrating derivation from known parentage where applicable. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the claimed new variety does not meet the criteria for novelty, or if the documentation submitted fails to adequately substantiate its stability.

An application for the registration of a geographical indication may include particulars relating to the agricultural area, specified quality or other characteristic attributable geographical to the goods. Such an area shall be defined with precision and clarity, delineating its boundaries in terms readily ascertainable by reference to established physical features or administrative divisions. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further details concerning the production techniques employed within the identified geographical region, demonstrating a direct link between those methods and the unique qualities of the goods. Provided that the applicant demonstrates exclusive use of the indication by authorized producers, as verified through supporting documentation, registration shall be granted subject to such conditions as the Registrar deems appropriate under this Act.

Where an application for registration of a layout-design is granted and a certificate of registration issued, the applicant shall become the registered proprietor layout in respect of that design. The registered proprietor layout shall have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design commercially, subject to any conditions specified in the certificate of registration or imposed under this Act. Any person desiring to exploit a registered layout-design must obtain prior authorization from the registered proprietor layout, provided that such authorization may be granted on terms and conditions as determined by the Controller. Failure to comply with the prescribed procedures for obtaining authorization constitutes an infringement actionable under this Act. The registered proprietor layout shall maintain records of all licenses granted and make them available for inspection upon request by the Controller.

For the purposes of determining similarity and likelihood of confusion under this Act, the Registrar shall, when examining applications for registration, consider whether trade marks are associated trade marks. A finding of association shall be made where one trade mark is identical with, or closely resembles, another trade mark, and both are used by the same person or by persons connected financially. However, association may also be established where one trade mark is a well-known trade mark and the other is not, subject to a demonstration of a clear link between the marks that would lead the public to believe in an association. 

Where a proprietor seeks to register associated trade marks, an application specifying the nature of the association shall be filed with the Registrar, and notice of such application shall be open to opposition as provided herein. The Registrar may, if satisfied that a genuine association exists, register the marks as associated, even if they would otherwise be considered conflicting. Failure to disclose a relevant association may be considered grounds for refusal or revocation.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration protection” shall mean the benefit derived from an international registration made under the Madrid Protocol, wherein a trade mark registered in India is extended to designated contracting states. Such extension is subject to any limitations or conditions prescribed by the laws of those states and as provided herein. Producers intending to avail themselves of such international registration protection must demonstrate that their goods or services conform to relevant quality standards applicable within each designated territory. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating this conformity prior to granting extensions, provided that the trade mark remains eligible for renewal under this Act.

Applications for registration as a geographical indication shall be accompanied by certified copies of relevant documents establishing, subject to verification by the Registrar, the origin and characteristics of the goods. The applicant shall specify the territorial extent of the geographical area from which the goods originate, clearly delineating its boundaries on an accompanying map. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to submit further information or clarification deemed necessary for assessment under this Act. Any opposition to a proposed registration must be filed within three months from the date of publication in the Geographical Indications Journal. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and provide each party with an opportunity for hearing. If, after due consideration, the Registrar is satisfied that the geographical indication meets the criteria as provided herein, it shall be entered into the included register geographical.

Any person found to have knowingly reproduced or distributed any work in violation of the provisions of this Act shall be liable for damages equivalent to a sum not less than fifty thousand rupees and not exceeding two hundred thousand rupees, determined at the discretion of the civil court before which the suit is brought. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved copyright owner, direct law enforcement agencies to seize any infringing copies or materials found in possession of the offender. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed a contempt of the said court and subject the defaulting party to penalties as provided herein. Further, the Central Government reserves the right to impose additional pecuniary sanctions on repeat offenders determined through judicial review.

The Copyright Act provides that any society registered under this Act shall, within three months of the close of each financial year, remit to the Office prescribed fees as determined by the Central Government. Failure to remit such fees in full and on time constitutes a breach of the terms of registration and renders the society liable for penalties as may be specified through notification. Any aggrieved party, including but not limited to authors or beneficiaries entitled to royalties, may file an appeal against any assessment of copyright society fee deemed excessive or improperly levied. Such appeals shall be heard by a designated officer appointed by the Central Government, whose decision is final subject to judicial review under established principles of law.

Any aggrieved person may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board against any order passed by the Registrar, concerning the refusal of registration, revocation of a layout-design right, or any other decision impacting rights as provided herein. Such appeal shall be heard by a member appointed bench, constituted specifically for the purpose of expeditiously resolving the dispute, and comprising at least one member possessing legal expertise and one member with significant technical knowledge in the field of semiconductor integrated circuits. The composition of the bench may be altered by the Appellate Board Chairperson, subject to ensuring a balanced representation of expertise. Should the member appointed bench be unable to reach a unanimous decision, the matter shall be referred to a larger bench, including the Chairperson, for a final determination. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the larger bench may seek clarification from the Board within thirty days of the order.

Where any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Controller relating to revocation of a patent or rectification of the register, and failing satisfaction with the decision, seeks redressal before the Order Appellate Authority, such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The appellate authority may, after affording opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed against. Failure by any party to comply with a direction issued by the appellate authority regarding production of documents or attendance at hearings shall render them liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees, recoverable as arrears of land revenue. Any willful disregard of an order made under this Act may be deemed contempt of the Order Appellate Authority.

Any person to whom copyright has been assigned, whether wholly or partially, may, subject to the provisions of this Act, further assign such rights to any other person. However, an assignment of copyright in a work shall be revocable at the option of the assignor, provided that reasonable notice of such revocation is given to the assignee and that the assignee has materially failed to exploit the rights assigned. Material failure shall include, but not be limited to, a consistent inability to commercially benefit from the work within a period of two years from the date of assignment, absent demonstrable efforts to secure such benefit. Notwithstanding this, an assignee may petition for continued assignment if they can prove substantial investment in the work, even without immediate commercial returns, and demonstrate a clear plan for future exploitation. The assignor’s right of revocation shall not prejudice any existing licenses granted by the assignee prior to the notice of revocation, unless otherwise agreed.

Applications filed under this Act for compulsory licensing shall be examined by the Authority constituted as provided herein. The applicant shall furnish with the application a statement detailing the reasons which compel the grant of such license, including particulars regarding non-availability of the plant variety and its essential characteristics. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that the proposed use is primarily for domestic consumption and addresses unmet needs within India.

The Authority may require the applicant to provide additional information or clarification concerning the claims purposes articulated in the application. Any interested party, including the registered holder of the plant variety concerned, shall be afforded an opportunity to present their objections or counter-arguments during the inquiry process. The decision of the Authority regarding the grant or refusal of a compulsory license shall be final and binding, subject to appeal under this Act.

Where an entity seeks to register a trademark relating to financial services, it must demonstrate that its business india situate is actively engaged in the provision of such services at the time of application. The Registrar may require submission of audited accounts and relevant documentation substantiating this engagement, as provided herein. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable for rejection. Furthermore, any individual found to be knowingly submitting false or misleading information regarding the location or operational status of a business india situate in support of a trademark registration application is punishable imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and also liable to fine. This obligation applies irrespective of whether the entity is incorporated within India or operates as a foreign company.

Any person who exploits a patented invention without the authorization of the patent holder, or a licensee duly authorized under this Act, shall be liable to an action for infringement in a District Court having jurisdiction. Where an infringement involves a plant variety protected by a patent and subject to breeder complied provisions, the patent holder may, in addition to injunctive relief and damages, seek an accounting of profits derived from the sale of the unapproved variety. Provided that, the accounting shall exclude any costs legitimately incurred in independently developing the infringing variety, subject to proof satisfactory to the Court. A patent holder may elect to pursue either damages or an accounting of profits, but not both, as provided herein. The Court may, at its discretion, award enhanced damages in cases of willful infringement. Any order granting relief under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court.

An applicant seeking registration of an invention under this Act shall file a formal application specifying the particulars of the invention and claiming protection thereof. The application shall include a statement outlining the technical field to which the invention relates, along with detailed descriptions enabling persons skilled in the art to reproduce the same. Upon successful completion of examination and grant, the applicant is entitled to an application patent period of twenty years from the date of filing the application. Renewal fees for maintaining the application patent period shall be payable as per prescribed rates and timelines. Failure to remit such renewal fees may result in the application being deemed abandoned, subject to provisions regarding revival under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by a refusal to register an application for a mark, or by the acceptance of another’s application, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall be finally determined under this Act, and the Board's decision is binding on all parties involved. Where a registration has been improperly granted, any person claiming an interest in the mark may petition the High Court for relief, including but not limited to seeking rectification of the register. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such a petition, provide copies to all interested parties as provided herein. Failure to comply with procedural requirements during proceedings relating to an application registration mark may render submissions inadmissible. Remedies available include injunctions and damages against those infringing on registered marks.

The trade mark proprietor shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall be subject to an instrument in writing and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry as provided herein. Where a trade mark proprietor fails to exercise their rights for a continuous period of five years, and there is no justifiable reason for such non-use, a petition for revocation may be presented to the Registrar. 

A registered proprietor may, at any time, apply to the Registrar for an order restraining any person from infringing their trade mark, and the Registrar shall, after such inquiry as may be deemed necessary, issue such order. The rights conferred by registration shall be subject to the rights of prior users, and no registration shall prejudice the rights of any person who, before the date of registration, was lawfully using the trade mark. Any dispute regarding the ownership of a trade mark shall be determined by the appropriate court.

Where a person, by falsely representing that goods or services are affiliated with, connected to, or endorsed by another person, induces, or has induced, any member of the public to believe such representation, and thereby gains an unfair advantage or causes detriment to the claimant, then the Registrar may, upon receiving a complaint duly verified before him, issue directions for rectification. Such directions shall include, but not be limited to, orders restraining the continuance of the false representation and mandating corrective advertising measures as deemed appropriate by the Registrar. The complainant shall bear the burden of proving the falsity of the representation and its detrimental effect. Provided that any order issued under this provision is subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order. Further, the claimant may seek interim relief pending determination of the matter.

Where a person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar refusing registration or revoking registration under this Act appeals to the Appellate Board, the appeal shall lie within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against, subject to just considerations. Any party dissatisfied with the decision of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within a period of ninety days from the date of that decision. The registration proprietor shall be deemed to hold title to the design only upon successful completion of the registration process and payment of prescribed fees; any challenge to this title is subject to judicial review as provided herein.

Where an application for a patent relates to a method or process applicable to agriculture or horticulture, the Controller may, subject to compliance with prescribed conditions, grant registration if satisfied that the invention is novel and involves an inventive step. Such registration shall not confer upon the patentee any right to prevent others from using the said method or process unless it is shown that such use would involve exploitation of the patented invention directly or indirectly. Further, where a justified registration has been granted under this Act, the patentee shall be obliged to disclose all relevant information pertaining to the application and subsequent modifications thereof, as provided herein. The Controller may require further documentation demonstrating adherence to ethical guidelines concerning genetically modified organisms if applicable to the registered process.

Where an infringing copy of a work has been made and offered for sale or distributed without authorization under this Act, any person aggrieved may institute civil proceedings seeking injunctive relief. Such proceedings shall be brought before a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurred or where the cause of action arose. The court may, upon being satisfied that an infringing copy exists and has been made in violation of the provisions herein, grant temporary injunctions restraining the defendant from further acts of reproduction, distribution, or sale. It is provided that any party seeking such relief shall furnish security to compensate the other party for losses incurred as a result of the injunction. The court may also order the destruction of infringing copies and materials used in their creation, subject to due process considerations. Further, evidence presented demonstrating commercial exploitation of the infringing copy will be given significant weight during proceedings.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely applies a geographical indication registered under this Act to goods not originating in the region to which such indication relates, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months, but which may extend to three years, and with a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Provided that the court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of the goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Registration shall not be granted if the geographical indication is likely to cause confusion with a previously registered trade mark or geographical indication, and the Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed fit, require the applicant to obtain a no-objection certificate from the owner of such trade mark or geographical indication. Any appeal under this Act shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against.

Any person making an application for registration of a layout-design, or for any matter ancillary thereto, shall pay such fee as may be prescribed. Failure to remit the requisite application fee accompanied by proof of payment within thirty days from the date of presentation of the application shall render the application void ab initio. The Controller may, subject to conditions specified in the regulations, entertain an application where the fee is deficient, provided that a request for rectification and full remittance is received within fifteen days of notification of deficiency. Repeated failure to comply with this provision, or providing false information regarding payment status, constitutes an offence punishable with monetary penalties as determined under this Act. The Controller shall maintain records of all fees paid and may conduct audits to ensure compliance.

An applicant intending to seek protection for a trade mark in any designated contracting country under the Madrid Protocol shall file an international application form with the Trade Marks Registry, accompanied by the prescribed fee and a copy of the basic trade mark registration certificate. The international application form must accurately reflect the details contained within the original Indian trade mark registration, including but not limited to the representation of the mark, any claims of colour or three-dimensional features, and the list of goods or services for which protection is sought. It shall be the duty of the applicant to ensure that the information provided on the international application form corresponds precisely with the particulars recorded in the Register of Trade Marks. Any discrepancies discovered during examination may result in rejection of the international registration.

For the purposes of this Act, a ‘protected characteristic’ in relation to a geographical indication means any quality, reputation, or other attribute directly attributable to the origin of goods and which is perceived by consumers as an essential factor in their purchase decision. A geographical indication relates to agricultural products where the qualities, characteristics, or attributes of such product are essentially linked to its geographical origin, including factors such as soil composition, climate, farming practices specific to that location, and traditional processing methods employed therein. Provided that, a geographical indication shall not relate to goods which are non-agricultural in nature unless specifically provided for under this Act.

Where a proprietor claims infringement of a registered trade mark under this Act, and the defendant asserts that use of the impugned sign does not create confusion amongst the relevant public, the Tribunal shall consider all surrounding circumstances including, but not limited to, the similarity of the goods or services, the degree of recognition enjoyed by the plaintiff’s trade mark, and any evidence demonstrating dilution of distinctiveness. The proprietor seeking relief for registration respect shall bear the onus of proving such infringement. However, if the defendant demonstrates that the alleged infringing use is in honest descriptive employment relating to the characteristics of their own goods, or constitutes permissible comparative advertising, the Tribunal may allow such use subject to conditions designed to mitigate any potential confusion. Appeals against decisions of the Tribunal under this provision lie to the High Court.

Any person may file a written opposition to the grant of a patent at any time within four months from the date of publication of the application for a patent, as provided herein. Such opposition shall be based on grounds specified under this Act and shall clearly articulate the alleged deficiencies in the claimed invention. Failure to submit a complete and reasoned opposition may render it inadmissible. The Controller, upon receiving an opposition, shall furnish a copy thereof to the applicant, who shall have three months to file a counter-statement. Evidence supporting both the opposition and the counter-statement shall be filed within a further period stipulated by the Controller. Any false or misleading representation made in connection with an opposition shall attract a penalty of imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. The decision of the Controller on the opposition is subject to appeal before the High Court.

The owner of a registered indication certification trade mark may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to the use of the mark, subject to conditions stipulated within the license agreement. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any such assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution and accompanied by the prescribed fee. Further, where a proprietor seeks to transfer ownership of their registered indication certification trade mark, including all associated licensing agreements, they must provide detailed documentation outlining the terms and conditions applicable to each existing license. The assignee shall be bound by any restrictions or limitations previously imposed on licensees under this Act. Any alteration to these conditions requires prior consent from the Registrar, ensuring continued adherence to standards of quality and origin as originally defined for the certification mark.

An applicant aggrieved by a decision of the Controller regarding the assessment or refund of filing application fees may, within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision, prefer an appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The appeal shall be accompanied by a memorandum stating the grounds of appeal and the relief sought, and subject to payment of such additional fee as may be prescribed. Provided that if the applicant demonstrates undue hardship due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, the Tribunal may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the delay in its presentation, after hearing arguments from both parties. The Controller shall furnish a copy of all relevant records pertaining to the assessment of filing application fees to the Tribunal within thirty days of receipt of notice of the appeal.

Any person seeking to prevent use of an indication which misrepresents the geographical origin of goods, and who has suffered damage as a consequence thereof, may institute legal proceedings against such user for damages, subject to demonstrating that the public is likely to be misled regarding the true origin of the goods in question. Where a registered Geographical Indication is contravened, the aggrieved party shall be entitled to seek an injunction restraining further infringing activity and recovering compensation proportionate to the extent of the detriment suffered. The Central Government may, upon receiving complaints concerning unauthorized use of geographical indications relating to placed houses parliament, direct any local authority or other appropriate agency to investigate such allegations. Any order made under this Act shall be enforceable as if it were a decree of a civil court.

Where copyright subsists in any work, the author or owner of copyright shall be entitled to control the inclusion of Right Management Information pertaining to that work. Such information includes, but is not limited to, the title of the work, the name of its author, and details regarding the terms and conditions under which it may be used. Any person who knowingly distributes a copy of a work containing altered or removed Right Management Information shall be deemed to have infringed upon the copyright therein. The Registrar of the Patent Office may, at the request of any aggrieved party, investigate allegations of such infringement and issue directives for compliance with this provision. Further, failure to comply with these directives may result in penalties as provided herein. This right is subject to reasonable limitations necessary to enable lawful research or analysis undertaken by accredited institutions.

For the purposes of this Act, a "performer" includes an actor, musician, dancer, singer, acrobat, juggler, stunt performer or other person who performs in public. A performer shall be deemed to have performed publicly where the performance, although not transmitted by any means of visual representation, is attended by an audience. The rights conferred upon a performer under this Act are without prejudice to rights which may exist under any contract made with the producer of the work in which such performance is incorporated. Provided that, nothing contained herein shall affect the right of a performer to receive royalties as determined by agreement or custom.

Where the Registrar has reason to believe that any person is engaged in the manufacture, importation, sale or offer for sale of goods bearing a mark used in relation to goods or services for which a trade mark is registered under this Act, and that such use constitutes a falsifies trade mark, he may direct such person to appear before him at a time and place specified in the direction. The direction shall specify the grounds upon which the belief is based and provide the party concerned with an opportunity of being heard. If, after affording such opportunity, the Registrar finds that the mark does indeed falsify the registered trade mark, he may issue an order prohibiting further use of the infringing mark, subject to any conditions he deems fit to protect the interests of the proprietor of the registered trade mark and ensure fair competition.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark has used the mark continuously in India as the proprietor use mark for at least five years from the date of registration, any alteration to the notified goods or services shall not prejudice his right to enforce that trade mark against all persons. Provided that such alteration does not involve a fundamental change in the character or reputation of the registered trade mark. The proprietor may institute legal proceedings for infringement notwithstanding any subsequent modification of the description of goods or services appearing on the register, subject to demonstrating continued use consistent with the original registration. Any party seeking to challenge the validity of this right shall bear the burden of proving that the alteration constitutes a fundamental change and has materially impacted consumer perception. The remedies available under this Act for infringement remain applicable irrespective of such alterations.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate a clear distinction from any commonly known or publicly available variety, assessed through characteristics including morphology, physiology, and, where relevant, DNA profiling as determined by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Provided that, a farmer who has bred or developed a new variety may apply for registration, subject to demonstrating that the variety possesses substantial characteristics differing from existing registered varieties and that it has been commercially exploited for a period of not less than three years. Any person alleging infringement of a breeder’s right in a new variety shall have recourse to an appropriate tribunal, and may seek an injunction restraining further exploitation, as well as damages for loss suffered. The tribunal may, at its discretion, order the seizure and destruction of any propagating material of the infringing variety, and shall consider the legitimate interests of farmers in exercising their rights to save, use, sow, re-sow, and sell farm-saved seed, subject to the conditions prescribed herein.

Where a patent has been granted in respect of any invention, and it is shown that the invention was not at the time of the grant obvious to a person skilled in the art, but that the claims in the patent are subsequently found to be invalid due to lack of novelty or inventive step, the Controller may order the revocation of the patent. Such an order shall only be made after affording the patentee an opportunity of being heard and presenting evidence under this Act. The remedies available to a party aggrieved by a patent’s validity extend to seeking damages for infringement occurring before the date of revocation, provided that such infringement was demonstrably based on information disclosed in the patent itself. Any appeal against an order revoking claims shall lie to the appellate authority as provided herein.

Where an objection is taken under this Act against a claim in respect of novelty or inventive step, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish such documentary evidence as he deems necessary to substantiate the claims made in the patent application. Such requirement shall be accompanied by a reasoned statement outlining the specific deficiencies identified and the information sought. The applicant shall have thirty days from the date of receipt of said requirement to comply; failure to do so will render the application liable for abandonment, subject to an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days thereafter. In cases involving an invention convention, the burden of proving adherence to timelines stipulated under this Act rests entirely upon the applicant, and any discrepancy shall be construed strictly against them.

Any person infringing a patent in respect of an invention, or inducing infringement thereof, shall be liable to pay damages which are commensurate with the loss suffered by the patentee as a consequence of such infringement; provided that where the infringer was cognizant of the existence of the patent and continued the infringing activity thereafter, enhanced damages may be awarded not exceeding six times the amount of damage assessed. The term of patent granted under this Act shall extend for twenty years from the date of filing of the application unless the invention relates to a process for producing a substance applied as or contained in an article, in which case the term shall be five years from the date of grant. Failure to comply with these provisions renders the offender liable for prosecution and penalties as provided herein.

Any person who, not being a registered proprietor or a duly licensed assignee, represents themselves to be a Member, or uses any business identifier or mark suggesting association with a registered Member, shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a Member knowingly permits or facilitates any such misrepresentation, that Member shall be jointly and severally liable for the imposed penalty. Any act of falsely claiming membership, undertaken with intent to deceive and obtain undue benefit, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or with fine, or with both. The Controller, upon receiving credible information of such an offence, may initiate an investigation and, subject to the provisions of this Act, direct the relevant authority to commence prosecution. Evidence obtained through legitimate means shall be admissible in any proceedings under this Act, and the burden of proof regarding lawful use shall lie with the accused.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be refused if it contains exclusively such descriptive characters relating to the goods providing services which are commonly used by traders in that field, provided that such refusal may be withheld if subsequent use has acquired distinctiveness through consumer recognition. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating established usage and widespread familiarity with the proposed mark within the relevant trade sector. Further, a mark shall not be registered if it is deemed likely to cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the identity of the provider of goods or services, considering the inherent similarity between the applied-for mark and existing registrations for identical or similar goods providing services.

A breeder seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable denomination to the said variety, conforming to the requirements prescribed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The assigned denomination, constituting the ‘assignment denomination’, shall be clearly marked on all propagative material commercially sold, offered for sale, or otherwise distributed by the breeder or their authorized agents. Any transfer of rights, whether by way of assignment, license, or other means, in respect of a registered variety shall necessitate the formal notification of the change in ownership to the Authority, along with confirmation of continued adherence to the denomination requirements. Provided that, where a variety is commonly known by a designated common name, the breeder may, subject to the Authority’s approval, utilize such common name in conjunction with the assignment denomination for marketing purposes. Failure to comply with these provisions may render the registration liable to revocation, as provided herein.

For the purposes of determining entitlement to equitable remedies relating to acts of plagiarism or unauthorized adaptation of literary works, the term "court having jurisdiction" shall mean a High Court exercising original civil jurisdiction where the cause of action arose wholly or in part, or a District Court within the local limits of whose territorial jurisdiction the defendant resides or carries on business. Subject to any reciprocal arrangements between States as provided herein, no suit for damages may be entertained by a court lacking such jurisdiction. The determination of whether a particular court possesses jurisdiction shall be governed by principles of ordinary civil procedure and precedence established under this Act.

Where any person considers that another person has infringed his patent, he may institute proceedings for relief against such infringement subject to the provisions of this Act. The remedies available to the patentee include injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement and damages sustained by the patentee as a consequence of the infringement. In determining the amount of damages, due consideration shall be given to the extent of the use made of the patented invention by the infringer and any profits which he has derived therefrom. The Controller may, upon application by the defendant in an action for infringement, order discovery of information relating to the patent or the alleged infringing act. A party seeking to apply patent must demonstrate reasonable grounds for believing that the claimed invention is novel and non-obvious.

The Registrar, upon receiving an application for registration of a trade mark incorporating marks indications, shall examine it for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. If the Registrar determines that the mark, while not directly prohibited, presents a likelihood of confusion with an earlier mark already registered or applied for, notice of such objection shall be served upon the applicant, affording them an opportunity to submit representations within a period not exceeding thirty days. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the objections, or if the Registrar remains unconvinced, the application may be refused. Any aggrieved party, dissatisfied with the Registrar’s decision, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the procedural requirements as laid down. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition before the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice.

Any person who, having applied for registration of a trade mark and having paid the prescribed act fee, subsequently fails to comply with any requirement under this Act or makes default in providing information as directed by the Registrar, shall be deemed to have abandoned the application. The Registrar may, upon receiving written complaint from any aggrieved party alleging such abandonment, issue notice to the applicant affording an opportunity of being heard. Failure to satisfy the Registrar that the application has not been abandoned within the stipulated period will result in automatic rejection and forfeiture of the act fee paid. Any attempt to circumvent this provision through fraudulent means shall be punishable with a fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees.

For the purposes of determining deceptively similar trade marks under this Act, regard shall be given to all relevant circumstances including, but not limited to, the class of goods or services to which the trade marks relate, the manner of use of the marks, and the channels of trade through which the goods or services are likely to be offered to the public. A trade mark shall be deemed deceptively similar if it is likely to cause confusion or deception as to the origin, character or quality of the goods or services, even if the marks are not identical. However, a mere visual resemblance shall not, by itself, be sufficient to establish deceptive similarity; phonetic similarity and conceptual similarity, considered in their totality, must also be demonstrated. Provided that, in cases involving well-known marks, a lesser degree of similarity may be sufficient to establish deception.

The register court shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of the register under this Act, conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain whether the application meets the procedural requirements as prescribed and is accompanied by the requisite fee. Should the application satisfy these initial criteria, the register court may direct the proprietor of the trade mark in question to file a counter-statement within a period not exceeding sixty days from the date of such direction. Failure to file a counter-statement within the stipulated timeframe shall be deemed an admission of the grounds for rectification, subject to further scrutiny by the register court. Any evidence submitted by either party shall be admissible, provided that it is relevant and obtained in accordance with the principles of natural justice. The register court shall, after considering all evidence and submissions, issue a reasoned order either allowing or dismissing the application for rectification, and such order shall be final and binding, unless appealed to a higher court as provided herein.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the relevant document establishing collective ownership or control over the quality and reputation of the goods associated with the indicated geographical origin. Where an objection is raised concerning the distinctiveness of the proposed geographical indication, the applicant may submit counter-evidence demonstrating acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition. The Registrar shall consider such evidence in accordance with established principles of trademark law. Furthermore, any person claiming rights adversely affected by the registration of a geographical indication applied to goods may petition for invalidation under this Act within six months from the date of publication of the registered geographical indication. Such petitions must specify grounds relating to lack of distinctiveness or misrepresentation. The validity of such registration shall be subject to periodic review, and an addition validity patent may be sought after ten years.

Access to the computer inspection register shall be permitted to any person upon payment of such fee as may be prescribed, provided that access is subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential commercial information. Any party aggrieved by a denial of access or by conditions placed on such access may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of communication of the order denying or restricting access. The Tribunal shall consider any submissions made by the applicant and the Registrar, and may direct the Registrar to grant access subject to reasonable safeguards designed to protect legitimate business interests. Further, the Registrar may require a bond to be executed by an applicant seeking access if there is reason to believe that information obtained will be misused.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute proceedings for relief against any contravention of the rights afforded under this Act. Such proceedings may include claims for damages sustained by reason of the unauthorized use of the geographical indication, including but not limited to loss of profits and damage to reputation. Where an authorized user has been granted a license to make use of a registered geographical indication, the proprietor shall be entitled to enforce the terms of that license as if it were a contract. Further, impliedly registration shall extend to prevent the application of confusingly similar signs or indications in relation to goods with which the registered geographical indication is associated, even where such use does not directly incorporate the protected name. This protection applies irrespective of whether the user had knowledge of the existence of the registration.

Any registered proprietor of a geographical indication, upon establishing a prima facie case of infringement, may apply to the High Court having jurisdiction for an interim injunction restraining the defendant from the unlawful use of said geographical indication. The Court, considering the potential harm to the reputation of the goods and the likelihood of consumer deception, shall, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, grant such injunction. Where a plaintiff demonstrates irreparable harm and a strong probability of success, the Court may, as provided herein, direct the defendant to forthwith account for all profits derived from the infringing use. However, such accounting shall not be ordered unless the defendant fails to demonstrate a legitimate independent source for those profits. Any order relating plaintiff forthwith shall include a clear specification of the prohibited acts and the geographical area to which the injunction applies. The Court may also direct the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing geographical indication, ensuring due process and opportunity for representation to the defendant.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark or concerning damages awarded pursuant to infringement proceedings may prefer an *112a order appellate* to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such appeals must be filed within three months from the date on which the order was received, subject to extension not exceeding ninety days if sufficient cause is shown and recorded in writing. The Tribunal shall hear parties de novo and may affirm, reverse or modify the order appealed against. Failure to comply with procedural requirements relating to service of notice under this Act will render an appeal inadmissible. Any costs associated with the appeal shall be determined by the Tribunal as it deems just, considering the conduct of the parties involved.

Where a patentee, in relation to an invention, desires to grant a license conferring exclusive rights within India, such license shall be recorded with the Controller. The application for recording shall specify the scope of exclusivity granted, the territory covered by the license, and the royalty rate payable under the terms thereof. Any subsequent assignment or transfer of such license, whether in whole or in part, shall also require recording as provided herein. Failure to amend register shall render the licensee’s rights unenforceable against third parties claiming prior use based on publicly available information. The Controller may, upon application by any interested party and after due notice to the patentee and licensee, inquire into the reasonableness of royalty rates stipulated within a recorded license agreement.

For the purposes of registration under this Act, a sound recording shall be deemed to comprise all sounds fixed on any medium of expression. An application for registration of a sound recording may be filed by the owner of the copyright in such sound recording, or by an authorized agent acting on their behalf. The Registrar shall require particulars relating to the date of first publication, if any, and details of the producer responsible for the creation of the sound recording. Where a sound recording incorporates elements previously existing, the applicant shall provide evidence demonstrating ownership of rights pertaining to those incorporated elements, subject to provisions regarding fair dealing under this Act. Any alteration or modification to a registered sound recording requires notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

Any proprietor of a registered geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the use of such indication on goods conforming to the standards as defined in the registration certificate. Such license may specify the territory within which and the duration for which the licensee is authorized to utilize the geographical indication, subject to conditions ensuring continued compliance with those standards. The proprietor may also assign the right to use a registered geographical indication to any person, provided that such assignment does not prejudice the rights of other proprietors or licensees. Any transfer or license granted shall be recorded in the Register and shall be binding on all subsequent dealings concerning the geographical indication. Further, under this Act, the proprietor retains the power to revoke licenses for breach of conditions or misuse detrimental to the reputation of the registered geographical indication.

Any person being the applicant for registration of a geographical indication prescribed under this Act, may, subject to the provisions herein, assign, transfer or license the rights to the said geographical indication, or any part thereof, to any other person or entity, whether incorporated or not. Any such assignment, transfer or license shall be in writing and shall be registered with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registry shall maintain a public register of all registered assignments, transfers and licenses, accessible for inspection upon payment of the prescribed fee. Where a geographical indication is subject to international registration protection under any treaty or convention to which India is a party, any assignment or license affecting the rights in that geographical indication shall also be notified to the International Bureau of the World Intellectual Property Organization, in accordance with the relevant regulations. Failure to register an assignment, transfer or license shall not invalidate the transaction, but may affect its enforceability against third parties. The registered proprietor shall remain responsible for ensuring the quality and standards of the goods bearing the geographical indication, even after assignment or licensing.

Subject to compliance with prescribed guidelines, a person claiming ownership of copyright in any cinematograph film shall furnish a statutory declaration, in the form specified by the Registrar, detailing the extent of their *india rights* and identifying all persons entitled to share in those rights. This declaration must be submitted within thirty days of the first publication of the work. Provided that, where such publication occurs outside India, the declaration may be filed within ninety days thereafter. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the copyright holder liable for a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees and may preclude enforcement of certain exclusive rights under this Act against any person demonstrably unaware of the claimant’s entitlement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made in such declarations.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark which constitutes a business basic application shall be subject to the provisions of this Act relating to assignment and transmission. Where the assignment is made as part of a larger transfer of a business, goodwill, or concern, notice of such assignment shall be furnished to the Trade Marks Registry in the manner as prescribed. The assignee, upon satisfying the Registrar that the transfer represents a genuine transfer of business, may apply to have the trade mark registered in their name. However, an assignment intended to create a false or misleading impression regarding the source or character of goods or services, or to unfairly take advantage of the reputation of the registered trade mark, shall be deemed invalid as provided herein. Any assignment made in contravention of this provision, or where the purpose falsifying used is evident, may be subject to rectification of the register. The Registrar may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be deemed fit, require evidence of the bona fides of the assignment.

Where an action is brought alleging unauthorized reproduction or adaptation of a copyright design, and the defendant’s place of business or residence is situated within the territorial limits of multiple districts, the plaintiff may elect to initiate proceedings in any district court having jurisdiction over such defendant. Provided that, if the defendant contests the jurisdictional basis for venue under this Act, the court shall determine whether it possesses subject matter and personal jurisdiction as provided herein. Further, an appeal from any order or decree made by a district court having jurisdiction concerning copyright design infringement may be made to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the district court is situated, subject to such conditions regarding costs as the High Court may prescribe.

Any person deriving a commercially viable crop variety through the application of protected plant variety information, as provided herein, shall be obligated to obtain a license from the registered breeder or the successor in title, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The licensing agreement shall clearly delineate the scope of permitted propagation, sale, and distribution of the essentially derived variety, and shall include provisions for royalty payments calculated as a percentage of net profit derived from such commercial exploitation. Assignment of such licensing rights requires prior written consent of the original breeder, and notification to the Authority within thirty days of the effective date of assignment. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the commercial activity unlawful and subject to penalties as prescribed under this Act. Furthermore, any dispute regarding the terms of the license or the validity of the assignment shall be adjudicated by the designated appellate tribunal, considering the principles of equitable benefit sharing and the advancement of crop sciences.

Every application patent shall be examined by the Controller in accordance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and the Controller may require the applicant to amend the application or to furnish further information as may be necessary for the purpose of examination.
