Where a form filed patent is found to be incomplete or does not meet the requirements as prescribed, the Controller shall issue a statement of objections to the applicant, allowing a period of one month to remedy the deficiencies, subject to extension granted at the Controller’s discretion. Should the applicant fail to adequately address the objections within the stipulated timeframe, the application patent shall be deemed abandoned. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller relating to an application patent may, within the prescribed period, file an appeal to the Appellate Board, and the Board’s decision shall be final and binding, provided that such appeal does not contravene principles of natural justice. The Controller may, as provided herein, revoke a patent if it is proven that a prior claim exists.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration of a geographical indication, shall examine it for conformity with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Where the application relates to goods geographical, the examination shall specifically ascertain whether the claimed geographical indication accurately represents the origin of the goods, and whether a demonstrable link exists between the qualities or reputation of the goods and their geographical origin. Any evidence submitted regarding traditional methods of production, or unique environmental factors contributing to the characteristics of the goods, shall be considered during this examination. 

Provided that, if the application seeks to register a geographical indication already registered for identical or similar goods, the Registrar may require the applicant to demonstrate material differences justifying a separate registration. The Registrar may, at any stage, require further information or clarification from the applicant, and failure to provide such information within a specified timeframe may lead to rejection of the application, subject to appeal as provided herein. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications.

Where any proprietor of a registered mark becomes aware that any other person, without his consent, is using an identical or deceptively similar mark in relation to goods or services for which the registration is effective, he shall be entitled to apply to the relevant intellectual property tribunal for relief. Such application may seek an injunction restraining the infringing use and damages commensurate with the loss suffered by the proprietor as a consequence of the infringement. The tribunal shall consider whether the defendant’s mark causes confusion amongst consumers or dilutes the distinctiveness of the registered mark, and if so, shall grant appropriate remedies. Failure to comply with any order made under this Act may result in penalties including fines not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years.

Applications filed under this Act, claiming priority from an application filed outside India, shall be processed in conformity with the Patent Cooperation Treaty. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish copies of correspondence relating to the international search report and written opinion, as well as any subsequent examination reports received under the aforementioned treaty. Further, where an invention is deemed non-obvious by the Controller, but fails to meet requirements for patentability as provided herein, a request for reconsideration shall be entertained only if the applicant demonstrates substantial novelty arising after the initial filing date, subject to section 36e ixd regarding post-grant opposition based on prior publications. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all applications processed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, accessible for public inspection.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, applies for registration of a trade mark identical with or resembling a trade mark registered in a Convention country, and concerning goods or services identical with or similar to those for which the existing trade mark is registered, shall be deemed to have committed an offence under this Act. Provided that the applicant proves, on the balance of probabilities, that they acted in good faith and had no knowledge of the prior registration, no penalty shall be levied. The Trade Marks Officer may, following due process and subject to the provisions herein, direct the applicant to cease and desist from pursuing the application. Failure to comply with such direction shall attract a monetary penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees. The manner informing international organizations of such fraudulent applications, and the associated evidence, shall be determined by the Central Government through public notice. Any funds collected through penalties shall be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India.

The applicant shall remit the prescribed registry fee for each class of goods or services in respect of which a trademark is sought to be registered, and such fee shall be non-refundable, save as otherwise provided herein. Any application not accompanied by the full and correct registry fee shall be deemed incomplete and may be rejected without further notice to the applicant. A reduced registry fee may be applicable for natural persons and small enterprises, subject to the submission of supporting documentation establishing their eligibility as determined by the Registrar. Where an application is amended to include additional classes of goods or services, a supplementary registry fee corresponding to those additional classes shall become due and payable within one month of the amendment request. Failure to remit such supplementary fee may result in the amendment being disallowed. The Registrar may, at their discretion, waive a portion of the registry fee in cases of demonstrable financial hardship, provided that a detailed justification is submitted with the application.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a india trade mark register may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which it is based. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the decision appealed against. Further, where a trade mark is used in contravention of the rights conferred by registration, the registered proprietor shall be entitled to seek remedies including injunctions and damages as provided herein. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to all relevant factors, including but not limited to lost profits and reputation.

An application for registration of a collective mark shall be made to the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall include a representation of the mark and a statement of all goods or services in connection with which the applicant desires to register the said mark. The applicant must demonstrate that it represents an association of users, and that such users are engaged in the production, manufacture, processing, or supply of goods or services as specified in the application. Further, the regulations governing use of the collective mark shall be submitted alongside, detailing procedures for ensuring uniformity of quality and adherence to standards. Where a publication translation of promotional material relating to the goods or services is included, it must be certified accurate by an authorised translator.

Any aggrieved party seeking redressal concerning an order passed under this Act relating to infringement of copyright, or regarding rectification of entries in the Register of Copyright, may appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Appellate Board may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them a reasonable opportunity for being heard, confirm, vary, or reverse any such order. Failure to comply with the prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible, subject to an application for condonation of delay which may be entertained only in exceptional circumstances. An assignment of copyright does not preclude recourse to the Appellate Board concerning pre-assignment disputes. Penalties for non-compliance with orders issued by the Appellate Board shall be as determined under this Act.

Any individual seeking registration of a geographical indication relating to agricultural products, foodstuffs, or beverages shall submit an application in the prescribed form to the Registrar, detailing the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services to which it relates, and the area of its origin. The applicant must also furnish particulars regarding the history, traditions, and characteristics of the indicated product, demonstrating a clear link between the product’s qualities and its specified geographical origin. Further, the application shall include a map of the relevant territory as determined by the Registrar. Any false or misleading statement in the application renders the applicant liable for prosecution under the Indian Penal Code. The Registrar may require further documentation to verify authenticity and prevent fraudulent claims, subject to guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation or modification of a plant variety protection, or concerning any infringement of farmers’ rights regarding regard plant varieties, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented by the appellant and the respondent, including expert testimony pertaining to genetic stability and distinctiveness. Subject to just considerations, the Board may affirm, reverse, or modify the original order. Failure to comply with a cease-and-desist order issued by the Board concerning unauthorized propagation of protected plant varieties shall render the offender liable to pay damages as determined by the Board, provided that such damages shall not exceed five times the value of the infringing material.

An application for protection granted breeder rights shall be made to the Plant Varieties Registration Board in the prescribed form and accompanied by a detailed description of the variety, including its essential characteristics, distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity. The application must also specify the origin of the variety and, where applicable, the name and address of the initial developer. Evidence demonstrating that the variety is new and possesses one or more traits substantially differentiating it from existing varieties shall be submitted with the application. Any person claiming to have a right over the variety may file an objection under this Act within the period specified, stating reasons for opposing registration. The Board may require further information or clarification from the applicant during processing of the application.

Where any question arises concerning the validity of a Plant Variety Registration or the enforceability of any right conferred under this Act, such question shall be determined by a decree civil court having jurisdiction over the territory within which the cause of action arose. The Authority may, at its discretion, refer any dispute relating to infringement of Farmers’ Rights to a decree civil court for adjudication, provided that the Authority has first attempted conciliation between the parties as per the procedures outlined herein. Any order made by a decree civil court in relation to matters falling under this Act shall be final and binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal to the High Court within ninety days of such order. The Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify the jurisdiction of particular courts for certain types of disputes as provided herein.

Where any person infringes upon the copyright in a work, the owner of the copyright shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief restraining that infringement, subject to demonstrating reasonable prospects of success and irreparable harm resulting from the continued violation. Furthermore, such owner may also claim damages proportionate to the loss suffered by reason of the infringement, taking into consideration the benefit accruing to the infringer, provided that the amount claimed does not exceed an aggregate sum as determined by the court. The right to seek remedies under this Act is without prejudice to any other rights or remedies available to the copyright owner in law or equity. It shall be the duty of every judicial officer exercising jurisdiction in a matter relating to infringement to ensure fair representation for all parties involved, recognizing the significant role of parliament in safeguarding artistic expression and intellectual creation.

Where any dispute arises concerning whether a territory constitutes a Contracting State for the purposes of this Act, such determination shall be subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. The Registrar’s initial assessment regarding the territorial extent of trademark protection granted under this Act is deemed prima facie correct; however, this presumption may be challenged by any aggrieved party demonstrating demonstrable evidence to the contrary. Further, a challenge predicated on the assertion that a territory's legal framework fundamentally diverges from principles recognized as essential for maintaining reciprocal trade relations shall be entertained. The burden of proof regarding such divergence rests entirely upon the appellant and must be substantiated with documentary evidence admissible under the Evidence Act.

For the purposes of this Act, goods shall be understood as movable property, and shall include all materials, substances, articles, and things, whether raw, processed, or manufactured. Services, however, shall denote the performance of any action, undertaking, or labour for the benefit of another, and may encompass intangible benefits conferred. A transmissible case arises where rights in a registered trade mark, relating to specific goods providing services, are legitimately assigned, transferred, or otherwise devolved to a successor in title, subject to the provisions herein. Any such transmission shall not prejudice the validity of the registration, provided that the transferor has duly extinguished their own rights and the transferee meets all requirements as stipulated under this Act. The Registrar may, upon application, record such transmission.

Any person who, having benefited financially from the commercial exploitation of a plant variety, fails to make contributions as provided herein to the Gene Fund shall be liable for penalties determined by the Authority. The amount of such contribution shall be proportionate to the gross revenue derived from the sale or other commercial use of the protected plant variety and may be adjusted periodically based on prevailing economic conditions. Failure to remit contributions within the timeframe specified under this Act will attract a daily compounding penalty, not exceeding five percent of the outstanding amount. Furthermore, any entity found guilty of repeated non-compliance shall face revocation of its Plant Variety Registration and potential prohibition from applying for further registrations under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order granting or refusing protection for an entitled produce variety, or by any condition attached thereto, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed against and may confirm, reverse, or modify the order appealed from, subject to just considerations of fairness and equity. Where a farmer alleges infringement of his right to save, reuse, exchange or share farm saved seed of an entitled produce variety, he may institute civil proceedings for damages and injunctive relief as provided herein. The burden of proving such infringement shall lie upon the claimant, and any award of damages shall be proportionate to the loss suffered by the farmer.

Where a trade mark has acquired substantial recognition of the public as being distinctive and representative of particular goods or services, it shall be deemed a well-known trade mark for the purposes of this Act. Any use of an identical or confusingly similar indicator in relation to goods or services not identical with those associated with the well-known trade mark shall constitute infringement, subject to limitations imposed by equitable considerations. The owner of a well-known trade mark may apply to restrain any such infringing use even if there is no direct competition between the goods or services involved, provided that the infringing indicator creates a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public or otherwise dilutes the distinctiveness of the well-known trade mark. Damages shall be awarded as provided herein, taking into account the extent of the dilution and any resulting loss of reputation.

Any person who, with intent to deceive, falsely represents a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design as being the original layout-design of another, or issues or publishes such false representation, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The manner issuing of such false representation, whether through digital means, printed materials, or any other form of dissemination, constitutes an offence under this Act. Any layout-design determined to be a fraudulent imitation, and any semiconductor device embodying such imitation, shall be liable to seizure and destruction, subject to an order of a designated court. Furthermore, any profits derived from the sale or exploitation of such falsely represented layout-design shall be forfeited to the Government, and the offender may be barred from applying for registration of any layout-design for a period of five years from the date of conviction, as provided herein.

Where a complaint alleging an offence under this Act is filed before the Registrar, such complaint shall specify the particulars of the alleged offence, including the date, place, and manner in which it is claimed to have been committed. The respondent may, within thirty days from the date of service of notice of the complaint, file with the Registrar a written statement denying or explaining the commission alleged offence, supported by affidavits where necessary. Provided that the Registrar shall afford the complainant an opportunity to rebut such defence. Any party aggrieved by any order made by the Registrar under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Appellate Board’s decision shall be final.

Any party failing to comply with the requirements for international applications filed under this Act, particularly those relating to the designation of States under the Budapest Treaty, shall be deemed to have committed a violation subject to penalties as provided herein. Such violations may include, but are not limited to, omissions in prescribed forms, incorrect translations, or failure to remit requisite fees within stipulated timelines. The Controller General shall issue notices requiring rectification of deficiencies; persistent non-compliance will result in the application being rejected and any associated filing fees forfeited to the government. Further, wilful attempts to circumvent the provisions regarding designated States under the Budapest Treaty may attract fines not exceeding five lakhs of rupees and imprisonment for a term up to three years.

Where any party institutes proceedings alleging infringement of a trade mark registered under this Act, and such proceedings are found by the relevant adjudicating authority to be manifestly frivolous or vexatious, or brought with the primary intent to harass or delay the defendant, the court may order that party to pay compensatory damages to the defendant. Such damages shall include, but not be limited to, reimbursement for reasonable legal costs incurred in defending against the unfounded claim, and any demonstrable loss of business opportunity directly attributable to the unwarranted proceeding infringement. Further, the adjudicating authority may impose a punitive element on such damages, subject to judicial review, to deter similar abusive litigation tactics. The court shall also have the power to award costs against the claimant in respect of such frivolous proceedings.

A permitted register trade mark is defined as a trade mark that has been entered upon the Register under this Act and remains so until removed therefrom or subject to an order for rectification. For the purposes of determining entitlement to relief in proceedings concerning a permitted register trade mark, such registration shall be deemed to confer upon the registered proprietor exclusive rights within India relating to the goods or services specified in the register. A trade mark may be considered for inclusion on the permitted register if it is distinctive in its nature and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, "associated trade marks" shall mean two or more trade marks owned by different persons but used in relation to goods or services that are essentially the same, closely related, or complementary. A trade mark may be designated as an associated trade mark through a formal declaration filed with the Registrar, provided that such designation is accompanied by evidence demonstrating the commercial relationship between the owners of the respective marks. Further, where any index registered trade mark is part of a series of identical signs used to identify goods or services, the Registrar may direct their registration as associated trade marks under this Act.

Any invention arising from research undertaken by a government undertaking, and funded wholly from public revenues, shall be the exclusive property of that government undertaking, notwithstanding any novelty or inventive step demonstrated by said invention. However, a compulsory license may be granted by the Controller, subject to the payment of adequate remuneration, if a reasonable time, not exceeding five years from the date of patent application, has elapsed since the filing of the application and the invention is not being worked to address a national emergency or public health crisis. Any dispute regarding the determination of ‘adequate remuneration’ or the existence of a national emergency shall be appealable to the High Court, with the government undertaking retaining the right to present evidence of ongoing research and development costs. Provided that, the Controller’s decision regarding the grant of a compulsory license is final and not subject to appeal, except on grounds of procedural irregularity.

An appeal lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal from any order passed by the Registrar refusing registration of an application for a permitted register trade mark, or directing its removal from the register. Such appeals shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Where the refusal relates to a similarity assessment with a prior patent process application, the Tribunal shall consider evidence pertaining to inventive step and non-obviousness as relevant to the distinctiveness argument. The decision of the Tribunal is final subject to further appeal under this Act.

For the purposes of this Act, “compulsory license” means a license granted by the Controller under this Act authorizing manufacture, use or sale of a patented invention without the consent of the patentee; and where a compulsory license is granted, any person holding such license shall be deemed to be an exclusive licensee with respect only to the acts specifically authorized therein. An exclusive licensee shall have standing to enforce the rights conferred by the patent against infringers not parties to the licensing agreement, subject to conditions as provided herein relating to reasonable terms and conditions of use. The Controller may specify these conditions in the grant of a compulsory license.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a registered user layout, or imposing conditions on such registration, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order. Such appeal shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the order appealed against, and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may, if satisfied that sufficient cause exists, extend the time for filing an appeal, but not beyond a further period of thirty days. Where the appeal concerns the validity of a registered user layout, the Board may direct the respondent to produce evidence supporting the claim of originality and independent creation, as provided herein. A decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, subject to any remedies available under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concerning errors apparent on the face of the record. Failure to exhaust this appellate remedy shall preclude any subsequent judicial review of the Registrar’s decision.

Where an application for patent relating to a process for producing a substance is filed, and it is subsequently alleged by a third party that the claimed invention incorporates elements derived from prior art not publicly available in India at the time of the initial filing, the Controller may, upon review of evidence submitted by both parties, determine whether such incorporation invalidates the patent. For purposes of assessing novelty and inventive step under this Act, shall date filing is to be construed strictly; any reliance on publications or public disclosures occurring after the aforementioned date will not be entertained unless it can be definitively established that such subsequent disclosure was a direct consequence of an unauthorized act by the applicant or their agents. The decision regarding validity may be appealed to the Appellate Board.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any registered Geographical Indication owner may grant exclusive licenses relating to the use of the indication in connection with goods for which it is registered, provided that such license shall be documented in writing and specify the territory and duration of the granted rights. Any assignment of a registered Geographical Indication, including by way of mortgage or pledge, shall also be recorded as per the prescribed manner. Further, any licensee or assignee may sub-license or assign their respective rights subject to the terms stipulated in the original license or assignment agreement. The Central Government shall cause to be placed before both Houses of Parliament once a year a parliament year report detailing all licenses and assignments granted relating to registered Geographical Indications, including particulars of the parties involved and the scope of such authorizations; patent means patent as defined under the Patents Act, 1970, will be considered in assessing potential conflicts.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar of Trade Marks refusing to register a trade mark, or varying the terms of registration, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the parties an opportunity of being heard, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and may direct any necessary corrections to be made in the Register of Trade Marks. An appeal under this Act shall not operate as a stay of the Registrar’s order unless specifically directed by the Appellate Board. Furthermore, any claim of passing off, alleging that a registered trade mark deceives or causes confusion, shall be adjudicated upon considering the overall similarities in the marks and the goods or services offered, and the likelihood of association in the mind of the average consumer. Provided that, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, remit the matter back to the Registrar for fresh consideration.

Any farmer aggrieved by any action taken by a plant variety registration authority or the farmers rights authority may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board constituted under this Act. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date on which such action is communicated to the appellant, and the Board shall have the power to entertain appeals against orders relating to revocation of registration, imposition of penalties, or any other matter where the farmer’s rights are concerned. The Authority may, subject to regulations framed under this Act, provide for alternative dispute resolution mechanisms to address grievances concerning benefit sharing agreements between farmers and breeders. Provided that decisions of the Appellate Board shall be binding on all parties involved, and remedies including compensation for losses sustained due to wrongful actions may be awarded as deemed appropriate by the Board.

An application for entry on the register shall be accompanied by a declaration specifying the right to priority under this Act, provided that such declaration complies with the prescribed form and contains a statement verifying the accuracy of the particulars relating to the earlier application. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further documentation substantiating the claim to priority, including certified copies of official records from the jurisdiction where the initial application was filed. Failure to submit satisfactory evidence as directed by the Controller shall render the application liable for rejection under this Act. Any alteration to the details recorded on the register relating to a registered invention requires prior approval from the Controller and must be made in accordance with prescribed procedures.

The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for rectification of a registered layout-design, constitute a Bench to hear and determine the matter. Such Bench shall consist of not less than three members, appointed by notification in the Official Gazette, possessing expertise in intellectual property law and engineering disciplines relevant to semiconductor technology. The presiding member of the Bench shall be designated as its Chairperson. Parties seeking to present evidence or arguments before the Bench may do so through duly authorized representatives holding a certificate of practice under the Advocates Act. Decisions rendered by the Bench are subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, provided that appeals must be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The Registrar shall provide all necessary documentation and administrative support to facilitate the efficient functioning of the Bench as provided herein.

Where a plant variety is deemed eligible for registration subject to conditions relating to farmers’ rights and benefit sharing, the Authority shall establish a dedicated account within the National Gene Fund. Any compensation deposited into this account, hereinafter referred to as a ‘compensation deposited gene’, shall be held in trust for the exclusive benefit of affected farmer communities demonstrably impacted by the commercial exploitation of the registered variety. Such funds may only be disbursed upon verification by an independent committee constituted under these rules and regulations, confirming adherence to pre-determined criteria regarding equitable distribution amongst eligible beneficiaries. Provided that any disbursement from a compensation deposited gene shall not exceed the initially assessed impact value as determined during registration proceedings, and subject to annual auditing procedures as provided herein.

A geographical indication comprised of a name, word, phrase, logo, or any combination thereof shall be registrable under this Act if it relates to goods originating from a specified territory and that territory’s extension, boundary, or location is precisely defined in the application. The applicant must demonstrate that such indication identifies those goods by reason of specific qualities, characteristics, or reputation attributable to the geographical origin. Provided that, the use of the geographical indication shall not be susceptible to prevent others from using similar indications for goods not having any relation with the territory specified, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Any infringement of copyright established before a competent High Court shall be actionable by the owner of copyright, and remedies available as provided herein include injunctions restraining further acts of infringement. Where a plaintiff demonstrates actual damages sustained due to said infringement, recovery of such damages, not exceeding a sum equivalent to the retail price of legitimately produced copies reasonably estimated, may be awarded. However, should the defendant prove that the infringement was unintentional and they exercised due diligence in preventing its occurrence, the court may reduce the recoverable amount. Any person found knowingly facilitating or aiding an act of copyright infringement shall also be liable for damages as determined by the High Court. Furthermore, repeated violations despite injunctive relief will constitute aggravated circumstances subject to enhanced penalties, including imprisonment not exceeding three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees. All appeals concerning orders relating to interim injunctions issued under this Act lie before the designated bench of the relevant High Court.

Where an application relates to a patented process, the Controller may, prior to grant, require the applicant to disclose any biological material required for the implementation of the invention, provided that such disclosure does not compromise trade secrets or confidential information. The applicant shall furnish this disclosure in a manner prescribed by the regulations framed under this Act and may be subject to a confidentiality agreement as determined by the Controller. Any party aggrieved by the requirement to disclose biological material may file an appeal before the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Further, if the disclosed material is not readily available or accessible, the Controller shall provide reasonable opportunity for the applicant to demonstrate alternative means of implementation. The provisions relating to examination and sealing of applications shall apply mutatis mutandis to applications involving patented processes.

The Central Government shall, within one year from the date of enactment of this Act, constitute an appellate board for the purpose of hearing and determining appeals arising under this Act. The appellate board shall consist of a Chairperson who is or has been a Judge of a High Court, and such other members as the Central Government may deem fit, having special knowledge and experience in copyright law, literary, artistic or musical works, or related matters. Decisions of the appellate board shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court only on questions of law. The Board’s jurisdiction extends to disputes concerning ownership of copyrights and infringement claims as provided herein.

A ‘trade mark’ as defined under this Act, shall include any word, symbol, device, name, monogram, signature, or amalgam thereof, used to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of others. For the purposes of determining deceptiveness, a trade mark shall be considered in relation to not only the goods or services with which it is directly associated but also those that are similar or related thereto. Where infringement of a registered india trade mark is established, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board may grant an order injunction restraining the defendant from any further acts of infringement and directing him to deliver up for destruction the infringing materials.

Any person who obtains a registration for a trade mark shall be entitled to use such registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for which it is registered, subject to any conditions or limitations specified in the certificate of registration. Where a registered trade mark has been used by an unauthorised party, the registered proprietor may institute legal proceedings for infringement as provided herein, seeking remedies including but not limited to injunctions restraining further use and damages for loss suffered. A court considering such claims shall have full power to grant relief on equitable grounds. Provided that, if the defendant proves legitimate prior use of a similar mark, or establishes that their use is descriptive only, then no infringement shall be deemed to have occurred. The register maintained under this Act shall be prima facie evidence of ownership and validity of registration; however, such evidence may be rebutted by proof of fraud or other vitiating factors. Any assignment of a registered trade mark must be recorded in the Register to be effective against third parties.

Where any person reproduces the entirety or a substantial portion of a *broadcast work*, being a work which has been communicated to the public by way of a broadcast, without obtaining requisite permission from the owner of copyright therein, such person shall be deemed to have infringed copyright under this Act. Provided that, where the reproduction is undertaken for private and non-commercial use, it shall not constitute an infringement if such reproduction does not exceed reasonable limits and does not cause undue prejudice to the rights holder. The owner of copyright in a *broadcast work stating* may pursue civil remedies including damages proportionate to the loss suffered by them as a consequence of the unauthorized reproduction. Further, any intermediary facilitating or enabling such infringing activity shall be liable to assist in preventing further infringements and providing information relating thereto.

A proprietor registered layout may grant licenses conferring specific rights relating to acts restricted under this Act, subject to the terms and conditions stipulated in the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly define the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to reproduction, adaptation, and commercial exploitation of the registered layout-design. The proprietor retains full ownership of the intellectual property unless explicitly transferred through a written assignment executed as per prescribed procedures. Any assignment of a proprietor registered layout must disclose all prior licenses granted and their material terms. Further, any licensee may sub-license rights within the scope permitted by the original license agreement, provided that such sub-licensing is expressly authorized therein. The proprietor shall maintain records of all licenses and assignments and make them available for inspection upon request by the Controller.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Trade Marks relating to the registration of a trade mark for cosmetics, and alleging that such cosmetics do not conform to the standards prescribed under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board. Provided that such appeal shall be filed within ninety days from the date of the Controller’s decision, and shall be accompanied by a certified copy of the said decision and a statement of the grounds on which it is based. Notwithstanding any other provision contained in this Act, the Appellate Board may, if satisfied that the trade mark registration poses a demonstrable risk to public health, order immediate suspension of the mark pending a full hearing. Any party proceeding notwithstanding, the Board shall ensure a reasonable opportunity for all concerned to present evidence and arguments, and its decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review by the High Court. The burden of proof regarding conformity with the Drugs and Cosmetics Act shall lie with the applicant for registration.

Any person who is the registered proprietor of a trade mark and desires to license or assign the said trade mark in favour of a party located outside of India shall, prior to effecting such licensing or assignment, inform the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. Such intimation shall include details of the proposed licensee or assignee, including their country of domicile and principal place of business. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to verification of the particulars furnished, record the details of the foreign party against the relevant trade mark in the Register. Failure to comply with the provisions herein regarding informing international parties shall not invalidate the licensing or assignment agreement itself, but may render the proprietor liable to a penalty as prescribed under this Act. A register trade mark, properly licensed or assigned as provided herein, shall continue to enjoy the protections afforded under this Act, subject to the terms of the agreement and any applicable international conventions. The Trade Marks Registry reserves the right to request further documentation to ensure compliance.

Any proprietor seeking to enforce the rights conferred under this Act may institute legal proceedings for relief against acts constituting infringement or any use likely to be confused with, or detrimental to the distinctiveness or reputation of, the registered geographical indication. Such remedies shall include an injunction restraining further infringing activity and damages proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor, subject to limitations prescribed regarding contributory infringement. Where a notice of demand is served upon an infringer failing to comply with such a notice, the proprietor may recover from the infringer reasonable compensation representing the unpaid fee payable for the use of the geographical indication. The Central Government may, on application by any aggrieved party, order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing false indications or marks.

Where an applicant seeks registration of a printed copies translation of a work, such application shall include a certified copy of the original work and a complete transcript of the translated version. The Registrar may require the submission of additional materials demonstrating the fidelity of the translation to the underlying work, particularly where the original work is technical or literary in nature. Registration of a printed copies translation does not confer upon the applicant any rights with respect to the copyright in the original work; such rights remain vested as provided under this Act. The application shall state whether the translated version has been previously published anywhere in the world and, if so, provide full details including dates and locations. Failure to disclose prior publication may render the registration voidable.

A patent application shall be examined with particularity regarding the claims presented therein, and such examination shall ascertain whether said claims define a manner of new manufacture. Claims so drafted must clearly and concisely delineate the scope of the invention, avoiding ambiguity and encompassing only matter which is fully supported by the description provided within the complete specification. Where a claim depends upon or refers to an earlier claim, that dependency shall be explicitly stated and such dependent claim shall further limit the subject-matter defined in the prior claim. 

Any attempt to broaden the scope of the invention beyond what is disclosed in the specification, through expansive claims, shall render those claims invalid as lacking sufficient basis. Provided that, where a claim includes an alternative or disjunctive feature, each distinct element of said alternative shall be separately assessed for novelty and inventive step. The Controller of Patents may require amendment of claims to ensure clarity and compliance with provisions under this Act; however, such amendments shall not introduce new matter beyond the scope originally disclosed.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a pharmaceutical substance, the Controller may direct that particulars of such patent be withheld from publication for a period not exceeding six months from the date of grant. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of notice thereof. Upon expiry of the directed period, or upon revocation of the order by the Appellate Board, the patent shall published expiry and become accessible in the public domain. Failure to comply with this provision, including unauthorized dissemination prior to publication, constitutes an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, and with a fine which may extend to fifty thousand rupees.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by a competent authority under this Act may appeal to a Bench constituted for that purpose. Such appeal shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged. Failure to comply with this time limit shall ordinarily preclude the appellate Bench from entertaining the appeal, subject to just cause being shown. The appellate Bench may, after affording an opportunity for hearing to all concerned parties, confirm, modify, or reverse the order appealed against. Any decision made by a Bench regarding transmission operation law disputes is final and binding on all parties involved, and enforcement shall be pursued through civil courts as provided herein.

Where an objection is taken by the Registrar under this Act against an application for registration of a trademark, the applicant shall be afforded an opportunity to submit written representations addressing the grounds of said objection. Such representations must be filed within sixty days from the date of dispatch of the notice containing the objection. The registrar statement shall then be considered in conjunction with the original application and any prior art documents presented. If, following review of these submissions, the Registrar remains unconvinced that the trademark is registrable, a reasoned decision will be recorded. This decision may consider whether the applicant can demonstrate they are the true and first inventor of the mark’s distinctive elements, provided that such demonstration satisfies the requirements as provided herein.

The specification accompanying any application for a patent shall be drafted with absolute clarity and precision, detailing the invention in a manner sufficient to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it into effect. Failure to adequately disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention within the specification shall render the patent voidable at the suit of any person aggrieved. Any deliberate omission or misrepresentation concerning prior art known to the applicant, and not disclosed within the specification as required under this Act, will be deemed an act of fraud. Such fraudulent behaviour shall attract a penalty not exceeding five lakh rupees, and may further result in forfeiture of all rights pertaining to the patent. The Controller may, subject to due process, order rectification of the specification if it is found deficient or misleading, and any costs associated with such rectification shall be borne by the applicant.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, the holder of a registration variety may grant licenses conferring rights to exploit the registered variety for specific purposes, including but not limited to propagation, sale, and distribution. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and may be exclusive or non-exclusive as determined by the licensor. Assignment of ownership of a registration variety is permissible, provided that prior consent of the Controller General is obtained, demonstrating adherence to principles of benefit sharing with any affected farmers’ varieties. Any assignment agreement must clearly delineate the scope of rights transferred and include provisions for royalty payments where applicable. Further, sub-licensing may be granted by the initial licensee with the approval of the registration holder, ensuring continued compliance with conditions stipulated under this Act regarding protection of plant variety rights.

An application for the registration of a trade mark shall be deemed refused if the Registrar considers that any registered trade mark or trade mark applied for by another person in respect of identical or similar goods or services creates an unreasonable likelihood of confusion, subject to the provisions regarding honest concurrent use. The applicant may submit counter-arguments and evidence demonstrating that no such likelihood exists; this submission must be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the refusal notice. Where a trade mark is registered under this Act, any subsequent application for registration containing a similar representation shall be examined with particular regard to the existing registration’s *registration mentioned clause*, ensuring that the public interest in maintaining distinctiveness and preventing unfair competition is adequately protected. The Registrar may require further clarification from either party during these proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, “association with goods” in relation to a trade mark means the use of a sign, whether registered or unregistered, in connection with goods or services in such a manner as to indicate, directly or indirectly, sponsorship or approval by the owner of the trade mark. A trade mark relation shall be deemed to exist where there is an intentional representation that the proprietor of the trade mark has approved of, or is connected with, the goods or services; provided that such representation may be inferred from the manner in which the sign is used and the impressions created in the mind of the public. Nothing herein shall prevent the use of a trade mark for descriptive purposes only, as provided herein.

The Registrar shall register a trade mark if the application submitted therewith satisfies the requirements as provided herein and is accompanied by the requisite filing application fees as prescribed in the First Schedule. An application deemed incomplete due to insufficient fees or lacking necessary documentation shall be subject to a notice of deficiency issued to the applicant, allowing a period of thirty days for rectification. Should the applicant fail to remedy the deficiencies within the stipulated timeframe, the application shall be deemed abandoned. The Registrar may, however, extend this period in exceptional circumstances, recorded in writing, subject to the payment of a late filing fee. Registration shall confer upon the applicant exclusive rights in respect of the trade mark for the goods or services specified in the application, subject to any limitations imposed by this Act. Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision regarding registration may file a review petition within sixty days of the decision, supported by relevant evidence and a prescribed fee.

Where a translated printed copy of a literary or dramatic work is registered under this Act, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration specifying the particulars of the original work, the language into which it has been translated, and the name and address of the translator. Such certificate shall be prima facie evidence of the facts stated therein and conclusive as to the validity of the translation for all purposes under this Act. An application for registration of a translated printed copy may be made by the translator or any person duly authorised by him in writing. Provided that, if the copyright in the original work is vested in any other person than the applicant, consent from such owner shall be obtained and submitted as evidence with the application. The Registrar may require such further information to be furnished as he deems necessary for verification of the claim. Any appeal against a decision of the Registrar relating to registration of translated printed copies shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal.

Any individual seeking to assert ownership claims regarding artistic works, including but not limited to musical compositions and cinematograph films, shall be required to obtain prior registration as provided herein. Failure to secure such registration before initiating legal proceedings alleging infringement will render the claimant ineligible for remedies relating to damages or injunctive relief under this Act. Any application for registration may be rejected if it contains false statements materially affecting the validity of the claim, in which case a subsequent application concerning the same work shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny and potential penalties. The Registrar may impose a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees upon any applicant found to have wilfully misrepresented facts during the registration process.

Where any right or interest in a patent shall arise by virtue of inheritance, death, insolvency, or otherwise, such right or interest may be assigned by transmission in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act. The Controller General shall maintain a register of assignments and transmissions relating to patents, and particulars of every such assignment or transmission shall be recorded therein within thirty days of registration. Any person claiming an interest in a patent as assignee or transmittee shall furnish proof of such claim, duly authenticated, for recording purposes. A notice of the proposed assignment or transmission shall be published in the Official Gazette, providing opportunity for objections under this Act. Further, a patent shall assigned only with the consent of the Controller General, provided that such consent may be withheld if deemed contrary to public interest.

Where an invention is granted patent protection under this Act and a condition imposed as part of the terms of grant relates to the utilization of the patented invention for purposes deemed beneficial to public health or national security, such condition shall be considered a condition declared unlawful if it demonstrably restricts competition within the relevant market. This determination may be challenged by any aggrieved party through appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Provided that, the appellant must demonstrate with clear and convincing evidence that the imposed condition operates as an unreasonable restraint of trade or creates a monopolistic advantage contrary to the principles enshrined in this Act. The burden of proof regarding such unlawfulness shall rest upon the appellant.

A patent of addition may be obtained for any invention which is a modification or improvement relating to an invention for which a patent has been granted, subject to the provisions of this Act. An application for a patent of addition shall be made in Form 24, and shall include a declaration stating that the invention for which the patent of addition is sought is a modification or improvement of the invention patented, and that the subject matter of the patent of addition is not separately patentable. The application shall be examined as if it were an application for a separate patent, but the examination shall be limited to determining whether the claimed invention constitutes a sufficient modification or improvement of the patented invention. Where a patent of addition is granted, it shall be subject to the same terms and conditions as the original patent, and the expiry date shall be the same as that of the original patent. A revocation of the original patent shall also extend to the patent of addition, unless the patentee of the addition proves to the satisfaction of the Controller that the addition is independently patentable.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Registrar to register a denomination variety sub, or by any decision concerning the scope of the breeder’s or farmer’s rights relating to such variety, may file an appeal before the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be presented within ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, accompanied by a certified copy of the order and a statement of the grounds on which the appeal is based. The Appellate Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to deposit a sum sufficient to cover the costs of the respondent, and may dismiss the appeal if such deposit is not made within the time specified. Provided that, where the appeal relates to a claim of essentially derived variety, the Board shall consider evidence of phenotypic and genotypic characteristics demonstrating substantial derivation. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to the right of appeal to the Supreme Court as provided herein. Any delay in filing an appeal may be condoned if sufficient cause is shown.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall vest in the proprietor thereof the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services in respect of which it is registered, and to institute legal proceedings for infringement thereof. The term ‘well-known trade mark’ shall, for the purposes of this Act, mean a mark which has become recognised by the relevant public by reason of the proprietor’s use of the mark. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered trade mark shall be assignable and may be transmitted by operation of law, including by way of amalgamation, transfer of undertakings, or insolvency. However, such assignment or transmission shall be subject to any conditions or restrictions as may be recorded in the register of trade marks. Any person aggrieved by a decision relating to trade marks registered may seek redressal as provided herein.

Any person claiming to be the proprietor of a geographical indication, and alleging infringement of their rights as provided herein, may lodge a complaint with the Geographical Indications Registry. Such complaint shall be accompanied by a detailed statement geographical indication, specifying the goods to which the indication applies, the territory of origin, and the qualities or reputation linked to that origin. The Registry shall, subject to verification of the complaint and evidence presented, issue notice to the alleged infringer. An alleged infringer may file a counter-statement contesting the validity of the geographical indication or denying the act of infringement. Should the Registry find merit in the complaint, it may order provisional measures, including injunctions against the continued use of the infringing indication. Any party aggrieved by the order of the Registry may appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction, within a period of ninety days from the date of the order, seeking a review of the decision and appropriate relief.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller of Patents relating to an application for a patent, revocation of a patent, or any other matter arising under this Act, may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s order, subject to the provisions for condonation of delay as determined by the Board. The Appellate Board, upon receipt of a duly filed appeal and payment of the prescribed fee, shall issue notice to the Controller and any other necessary parties. The Board may, at any stage of the proceedings, require the appellant to furnish evidence or documents to substantiate the grounds of appeal. Any decision of the Appellate Board constitutes an order appellate and shall be final and binding, save for any recourse available through writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error or violation of principles of natural justice. Provided that the Board may, with reasons recorded, stay the execution of the Controller’s order pending disposal of the appeal.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the revocation of a Plant Variety Protection, or concerning the imposition of any penalty for infringement of Farmers’ Rights, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. The Appellate Board shall consider all materials placed before it and may affirm, modify, or reverse the original order. Where an infringement of Farmers' Rights has occurred, the aggrieved farmer shall be entitled to compensation commensurate with the loss suffered, determined by the Board based on prevailing market rates and agricultural practices. Further, the india department agriculture shall provide assistance in assessing damages and facilitating mediation between parties. The Appellate Board’s decision is final, subject to challenge only under writ jurisdiction before a High Court.

For the purposes of this Act, a “service mark” shall be deemed a type of trade mark. A *provisions act mark* is defined as any identifying sign, whether or not registered under this Act, used to distinguish the supply of services by one undertaking from those of others. Such marks may include names, symbols, slogans, numerals, letters, and combinations thereof. The Registrar shall have the power to require evidence of actual use of a *provisions act mark* in connection with specified services before registration is granted, provided that such requirement does not apply to collective marks or certification marks as defined herein. Any representation of a *provisions act mark* used in advertising materials shall be considered part of its public display.

An application for registration of a geographical indication alleging prior use and continued association with traditional artisans residing within the designated area, if opposed by any person claiming rights prejudicial to the interests of such artisans, shall be referred to an Adjudicating Officer appointed under this Act. The Adjudicating Officer may hear all parties involved, including representatives of the applicant and the opponent, and consider documentary evidence pertaining to the historical connection between the geographical indication and the goods in question, as well as any demonstrable impact on the livelihoods of those engaged in production within the specified territory. Any party aggrieved by an order passed by the Adjudicating Officer may appeal to the Appellate Board, subject to demonstrating that the decision was manifestly erroneous or based on a misapprehension of facts relating to the houses parliament’s oversight role.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design may be rejected by the Registrar Semiconductor Integrated if reasonable grounds exist to believe that the design incorporates an element substantially copied from an existing layout-design. Such rejection shall be accompanied by written reasons detailing the alleged infringement and specifying the prior layout-design in question. The applicant shall then have a period of sixty days from the date of notification of such rejection to submit a reasoned response, including counter-evidence, disputing the Registrar’s findings. Upon receipt of this response, the Registrar may either uphold the initial rejection or, if satisfied that the concerns are unfounded, proceed with registration as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within three months from the date of communication of the order.

Any person who suffers loss or damage as a consequence of any fraudulent application for registration of a trade mark, or of the registration of a trade mark in violation of the provisions of this Act, shall be entitled to recover from the applicant or registered proprietor, as the case may be, such loss or damage, together with an appropriate accounting for profits. Where a trade mark is registered and the registration is subsequently expunged from the register, any rights acquired in good faith by any person under such registration, prior to the date of expungement, shall not be affected. However, such rights shall be subject to proof of legitimate use and reliance on the register as means registered. Any action for infringement based on a means registered trade mark shall be maintainable only if the plaintiff demonstrates genuine and continuous use of the mark prior to the date of the alleged infringement, and that such use was not merely token. The Court may, at its discretion, award exemplary damages in cases of flagrant or wilful infringement.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, an application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout may be refused if the Registrar is satisfied that the layout incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered layout without due authorization. The applicant aggrieved by such refusal shall have thirty days from the date of receipt of notice thereof to file an appeal under this Act. Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may, upon examination of evidence presented by both parties, direct the Registrar to reconsider the application and register said layout if it finds that the elements in question do not constitute a substantial derivation or that due authorization was indeed obtained. The decision of the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to further appeal to the Supreme Court on grounds specified herein.

Any person claiming to be aggrieved by a proposed registration of a trade mark may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a notice of opposition with the Trade Marks Registry. Such notice shall be in writing and shall clearly articulate the grounds upon which the opposition is based, including but not limited to, similarity to existing marks, lack of distinctiveness, or deceptive character. The applicant for registration, upon receipt of the notice of opposition, shall be entitled to file a counter-statement, addressing each ground raised by the opponent, within a period stipulated by the Registrar. Failure to file a counter-statement within the prescribed time may result in the abandonment of the application. Evidence may be submitted by both parties, and the Registrar shall consider such evidence before rendering a decision on the opposition registration.

The registered proprietor of a Geographical Indication may grant exclusive licenses to third parties for specific uses relating to goods or services authorized under this Act, provided that such license agreements are documented and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of execution. Any assignment of rights in a registered Geographical Indication shall require prior consent from the Central Government, obtainable upon submission of a detailed proposal outlining the proposed assignee’s capabilities and intended use. The fee payable for registration of an assignment is determined according to the prescribed scale, as amended from time to time. Further, any sub-licensing undertaken by a licensee must be explicitly stated in the original license agreement and shall attract a further paid fee payable to the Registrar, calculated as a percentage of the sub-licensee’s turnover derived from the licensed goods or services.

For the purposes of this Act, “tea” with reference to the geographical indication ‘Darjeeling’ shall mean tea produced exclusively in the defined geographical area comprising villages within Darjeeling district, excluding areas beyond its specified boundaries as delineated under notification issued by the Tea Board. Registration shall apply only to producers and processors who adhere strictly to cultivation and processing methods prescribed by the competent authority. Any alteration of such methods, or use of teas not originating from the defined geographical area, will render the registration liable for revocation. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating adherence to these standards as a condition for maintaining registration.

A denomination variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall demonstrate substantial novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability in accordance with the prescribed guidelines. Any applicant seeking registration of a denomination variety must submit a detailed description of the variety’s characteristics, including its genealogy, physiological traits, and performance data, as evidenced by field trials conducted over a period not less than three successive generations. Provided that, where the denomination variety is a hybrid or a clone, the requirement of three generations may be waived subject to the competent authority being satisfied with the demonstrated stability of the variety. The variety shall be designated by a denomination that is clearly distinguishable from all other registered varieties, and the proposed denomination must not mislead or cause confusion. Any transfer of rights relating to a denomination variety shall be subject to notification to the Plant Variety Protection Authority and compliance with the conditions stipulated herein. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of registration.

Where any person applies a mark used in relation to goods or services, or uses such mark in connection with the offer for sale or supply of goods or services, and makes therein a false trade description, he shall be deemed guilty of an offence under this Act. A false trade description includes statements regarding the geographical origin of goods, the manufacturing process employed, or the quality characteristics possessed by those goods or services. Any consumer who believes they have been misled by such a false trade description may file a complaint with the Registrar for Trade Marks, detailing the particulars of the misleading representation and any resulting loss suffered. The Registrar shall investigate the complaint and may require the person alleged to have made the false trade description to submit evidence refuting the claim. If found substantiated, penalties as provided herein shall apply, including fines and potential injunctions preventing further use of the offending mark.

Where an application for patent relating to a process for producing a substance is filed, and such process involves one or more steps previously known in the art, the date claim shall be determined with reference to the earliest prior publication disclosing each step involved, provided that the applicant demonstrates, under this Act, that the combination of said steps results in an unexpected technical effect not predictable by a person skilled in the art. Further, if the invention relates to a method of treatment of human disease, the date claim shall be subject to verification regarding compliance with regulations pertaining to clinical trials as prescribed by the Drugs and Cosmetics Act. The Controller may require submission of relevant data substantiating such unexpected technical effect or regulatory adherence before proceeding with examination.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive registrar index, accessible to the public during normal office hours, detailing all patents granted under this Act. This registrar index shall include, for each patent, its registration number, the title of the invention, the name and address of the patentee, the date of grant, and a concise abstract summarizing the subject matter claimed. Further, the registrar index shall indicate any subsequent modifications to the patent, such as assignments or licenses, as recorded under this Act. Any person may inspect the registrar index and obtain certified copies thereof, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Any person seeking registration of a new plant variety shall, as a condition precedent to such registration, assign a unique and readily distinguishable assignment denomination to said variety, conforming to the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. The assignment denomination shall not cause confusion with any existing registered variety, nor shall it be deceptive or misleading to the public regarding the characteristics of the plant. Provided that, if a variety is commonly known by a particular name in local parlance, the Authority may, subject to verification of such usage and absence of conflict with existing registrations, permit its continued use as the assignment denomination. Any false representation concerning the assignment denomination, or any attempt to pass off a variety under a denomination already assigned to another, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both. The Authority shall maintain a public register of all assigned denominations.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, reproduction by means of reprography shall be permissible only where such reproduction is undertaken for private and non-commercial use. Provided that, where the work reproduced comprises literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, a reasonable number of copies may be made for educational purposes within institutions recognized by the Central Government, provided further that prior written permission from the copyright holder is not required in such instances. However, any commercial distribution or public display of materials obtained through reprography shall constitute an infringement under this Act and render the distributor liable to prosecution. The right to control reprography extends to all forms of works fixed in a tangible medium, as provided herein.

An application for rectification of the register may be made to the Appellate Intellectual Property Tribunal by any person aggrieved by an entry in the register relating to a trade mark. Such application shall specify the grounds on which the applicant relies and shall be accompanied by such documents or other evidence as the applicant deems necessary to substantiate their claim. The Tribunal shall serve notice of the application upon the Registrar and the proprietor of the trade mark concerned, affording them reasonable opportunity to file counter-statements. Upon consideration of the pleadings and any oral arguments presented, the Tribunal may order rectification of the register by deletion of an entry, amendment of an entry, or otherwise as it deems just and equitable. Decisions regarding rectification shall be final subject to appeal under this Act to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of such decision. The Registrar shall promptly give effect to any order made by the Tribunal concerning the court rectification register.

Where an adaptation of a work is made without authorization from the copyright owner, and such adaptation substantially reproduces the original work’s protected elements, including but not limited to its plot, characters, dialogue, and overall structure, it shall constitute infringement of copyright under this Act. Provided that, where the adaptation incorporates sufficient originality in its expression or treatment so as to create a demonstrably new aesthetic impact distinct from the underlying work, such use may be permissible subject to consideration of whether the adaptation unfairly prejudices or detracts from any potential market for the original work. Further, if the alleged infringing activity is undertaken solely for non-commercial educational purposes and involves minimal reproduction, it shall not automatically constitute infringement copyright, provided that proper acknowledgement is given to the author and owner of the original work.

Any design, the publication of which would be prejudicial to the security of India, shall not be registrable under this Act, notwithstanding any other provision contained herein. An application for registration disclosing such a design may be refused, and the applicant shall be informed of the reasons for such refusal. However, the Controller of Designs may, subject to the direction of the Central Government, permit the registration of a design relating to an article primarily intended for the defense forces, provided that such design does not reveal critical technological information impacting national security. The Controller shall, prior to any such permission, conduct a thorough examination to ascertain the potential implications for security india and submit a detailed report to the Central Government. Any disclosure made during the registration process relating to such designs shall be treated as confidential and shall not be accessible to the public without explicit authorization. The Central Government may, at any time, revoke the registration of a design if it deems it necessary in the interests of security india.

For the purposes of this Act, "makes performance photograph" means a photographic work that is created during the course of a live performance and which captures elements substantially representing such performance. Such a photograph shall be deemed an artistic work and subject to copyright under this Act. The creation of a makes performance photograph does not, however, grant any right to the performer in respect of their performance itself; provided that the photographer’s rights are derived solely from the photographic work created. This definition applies irrespective of whether the performance is recorded for broadcast or other purposes as provided herein.

An application for registration as a proprietor of a use certification trade mark shall be accompanied by a detailed scheme outlining the standards and procedures governing the certification process, including provisions for inspection, testing, and ongoing compliance verification. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish further documentation demonstrating adherence to these prescribed standards and establishing the impartiality of the certifying body. Such a scheme must specify the categories of goods or services eligible for certification under the mark.

The application shall also include evidence confirming that the proposed certification trade mark is distinctive in its character and capable of distinguishing certified products from those not so certified, as provided herein. The Registrar may reject an application if it determines that the certifying body lacks sufficient expertise or resources to effectively administer the scheme or if the standards are deemed arbitrary or discriminatory. Any alteration to the approved scheme requires prior notification and approval by the Registrar.
