The owner of copyright in any work shall have the exclusive right to control the incorporation and communication of Right Management Information, including but not limited to identifying information pertaining to the author, creator, and initial proprietor. Such Right Management Information may be embedded within digital works or attached thereto as metadata. Assignment of copyright under this Act shall include assignment of all rights relating to the management and protection of such information; provided that any subsequent licensee acquiring rights through transfer shall be bound by conditions precedent concerning the maintenance and accurate representation of said Right Management Information. Failure to adhere to these requirements may render a party liable for damages, subject to judicial determination as to reasonable compensation. The owner is empowered to license third parties to manage this information on their behalf, with terms agreed upon in writing.

Any person found guilty of making or publishing false statements concerning the subsistence of a patent, or the extent of its claims, shall be liable for damages to the patentee, recoverable by suit in a District Court. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from an aggrieved party alleging infringement of patent rights, direct the Registrar to initiate inquiries into the matter and issue notices to all concerned parties. Failure to comply with such directions issued by the Central Government shall constitute contempt of court and render the defaulting party liable for penalties as determined by the Court. Further, any entity found to be wilfully violating provisions relating to post-grant opposition may face suspension of its registration under this Act, subject to judicial review.

An application for a patent shall be deemed to relate to an invention if it is not contrary to law and involves a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. The determination of whether an invention falls within this definition is subject to examination by the Controller, who may require further clarification regarding the nature and scope of the claimed invention. For the purposes of assessing patentability, the invention territory India extends exclusively to the territory of India, including its land territory, territorial waters, and airspace over it. Any prior use or publication relating to an invention occurring outside this defined geographical area shall not be considered in determining novelty or inventive step under this Act. The applicant shall furnish such documentary evidence as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate claims regarding the originality and non-obviousness of the invention within the specified territory.

Where an applicant or patentee is deceased, or is otherwise incapable of conducting legal proceedings, any proceeding under this Act may be continued by their legal representative, subject to the provisions herein. For the purposes of this provision, the term ‘legal representative’ shall include a person appointed as executor or administrator of the estate of the deceased applicant or patentee, or any person authorised by a court of competent jurisdiction to act on their behalf. Should a patent application be filed jointly, the death or incapacity of one joint applicant shall not affect the rights of the surviving applicant or applicants to pursue the application, provided that such surviving applicant or applicants demonstrate to the Controller a clear intention to continue prosecution. Any assignment or transfer of rights relating to a patent, or an application for a patent, shall be valid and enforceable against the legal representative, insofar as those rights vest in the estate of the deceased or the assets of the incapacitated applicant or patentee.

The right to use a registered trade mark is deemed personal to the proprietor unless explicitly provided otherwise under this Act. Such rights are, however, freely *transmissible* by way of absolute assignment, pledge, or operation of law, subject to registration of such transfer with the Trade Marks Registry. Any governing assignment denomination shall be clearly stated in the instrument of transfer and must specify the exact trade mark(s) being assigned, along with any associated goods or services as defined in the original registration. The assignee becomes vested with all rights, privileges, and obligations that were held by the assignor immediately prior to the assignment. Provided that, where a pledge is made, the pledgor retains ultimate ownership until default occurs under the terms of the pledge agreement. Further, any subsequent dealing with the pledged trade mark shall require consent from both pledgor and pledgee.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before a competent court, furnish the alleged infringer with a notice of such infringement, detailing the specific layout-design relating registered to the claim and the nature of the alleged act of infringement. Should the alleged infringer, within thirty days of receipt of such notice, submit a statement demonstrating a valid defense, including but not limited to prior art or independent development, the aggrieved party may apply to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board for a determination of the validity of the defense. The Board shall, after affording both parties an opportunity to be heard, issue a reasoned order either upholding or rejecting the defense, and such order shall be binding on the parties subject to further appeal to the High Court. Failure to comply with the notice requirement as provided herein shall render the infringement claim inadmissible, unless the court is satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed justifying such non-compliance.

The central government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, establish a National Intellectual Property Fund for the purpose of promoting innovation and facilitating the commercialization of patented inventions. Contributions to the Fund shall be accepted from government sources, private entities, and international organizations, subject to such terms and conditions as the central government deems appropriate. Any expenditure incurred from the Fund shall be audited annually by a chartered accountant appointed by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India. Provided that, the central government shall ensure that the Fund is utilized primarily for supporting research and development activities in areas of national importance, and for providing financial assistance to small and medium enterprises engaged in the exploitation of patented technologies. The central government may also formulate guidelines regarding the prioritization of applications for financial assistance, considering factors such as the potential for import substitution and employment generation, as provided herein. All records pertaining to the Fund shall be open to inspection by authorized officers.

The proprietor of a registered trademark shall retain exclusive rights regarding its use within India, subject to any permitted uses granted under this Act. Any party desiring to utilize a mark registered manner that differs from the proprietor’s established practices must obtain prior written consent. Such consent may be granted on terms and conditions as determined by the grantor, including but not limited to royalty payments and restrictions on geographical scope of use. The grant of such license shall be recorded in the Register of Trade Marks, noting the duration and extent of permitted usage. Further, a proprietor may assign the right to utilize their registered mark, or any part thereof, to another party, provided that such assignment is also duly recorded. Any unauthorized use of a registered trademark, irrespective of intent, constitutes infringement and renders the user liable for damages as provided herein.

In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (b) “authorised user” means a person, firm, society, trust, or company registered as such under this Act in respect of a geographical indication and shall include any assignee or licensee of the registered geographical indication, subject to the terms and conditions of the registration and any agreement governing such assignment or license. An authorised user, upon establishing a prima facie case of infringement of a registered geographical indication, may apply to the appropriate Court for a temporary injunction restraining the defendant from manufacturing or selling goods bearing a deceptively similar geographical indication. The Court, if satisfied that irreparable harm will be caused to the reputation of the geographical indication or to the business of the authorised user, may grant such order injunction, pending final determination of the matter, and may require the defendant to provide security as deemed fit. Any person aggrieved by the grant or refusal of such an injunction may appeal to the appellate authority as provided herein.

The assignment of copyright, and any subsequent transfer thereof, shall vest in the assignee subject to the provisions contained herein. Any person desiring to record an assignment with the Registrar shall submit an application in the prescribed form accompanied by the requisite fee. The Registrar may, prior to registration, require further evidence or clarification regarding the validity or scope of the purported assignment. Where a copyright is assigned for a term, and that term expires, the assignee shall promptly notify the Registrar of such expiration, failing which continued recordation may be deemed an offence under this Act. 

Provided that, where an assignment involves multiple copyrights, a consolidated application detailing each work’s particulars must accompany the submission. The Registrar shall maintain a public register of assignments and licenses, accessible for inspection subject to reasonable conditions. Any dispute regarding ownership arising from registration with the Registrar shall be adjudicated by the competent court having jurisdiction over copyright matters as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed to be refused if, upon examination, it appears that the proposed trade mark is descriptive of the goods or services with which it seeks association. The Registrar may, however, accept such an application if the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use and consumer recognition prior to the date of the application. Evidence presented in support of this demonstration shall include market research data, sales figures, and advertising expenditure relating directly to the trade mark's usage. Any person aggrieved by a refusal order may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of that order. The Board’s decision is final subject to further appeal under this Act. Consideration shall be given to whether the use has created an appreciable association in the minds of consumers.

Where a registered layout design contains an inadvertent technical inaccuracy discovered subsequent to registration, the Register may, upon application by the registrant and subject to verification that such inaccuracy does not substantially alter the character of the layout design, permit an error amendment. Such amendment shall be recorded in the register with effect from the date of the original registration, provided that any party demonstrably prejudiced by reliance on the erroneous record prior to the error amendment may pursue remedies under civil law. The Register shall provide notice of such amendment and its effective date. Transient incidental storage of data during processing related to an error amendment does not constitute infringement under this Act. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures for seeking an error amendment will render any subsequent claim void.

For the purposes of this Act, “international registration keeping” means the process by which a trade mark proprietor maintains the effect of an international registration designating India, subject to compliance with prescribed procedures and payment of requisite fees. An international registration shall be deemed kept in force only when the Registrar confirms its continued validity following examination under this Act. Failure to respond to an official action within the stipulated time may result in partial or complete cancellation of the designation for India. The proprietor shall furnish such information as the Registrar deems necessary regarding changes affecting the ownership or status of the trade mark internationally.

Where the owner of copyright in an artistic work desires to grant a license or assign their rights therein, they shall submit a formal application to the designated Copyright Office, detailing the scope and duration of the proposed arrangement. Such application must specify the territory covered by the license or assignment and identify all parties involved, including the licensor, licensee, or assignee. The owner may reserve certain exclusive rights under this Act, provided that such reservation is clearly stated within the application and does not unduly restrict the reasonable use of the work. Any subsequent modification to a granted license requires another application, subject to approval by the Copyright Office. An assignment shall be deemed valid only upon registration with the office, and failure to register will render the assignee unable to enforce their rights under this Act against third parties.

Where any proprietor registers index names relating to goods or services under this Act, such registration shall not preclude the use of an identical or similar index name by another person where such use is solely for descriptive purposes and does not create confusion among consumers regarding the origin or quality of those goods or services. Common Regulations pertaining to the display and arrangement of goods in retail establishments shall apply equally to proprietors of registered trade marks as they do to all other vendors, provided that any signage employed complies with guidelines issued by the Controller General under this Act. The Registrar may require submission of detailed inventories listing index names registered alongside corresponding product categories prior to renewal of registration.

An application for registration of a layout-design relating to a semiconductor integrated circuit shall include particulars in Form A, as may be prescribed by the registrar, detailing the applicant’s entitlement to protection under this Act and specifying the geographical extent of such protection sought. The registrar may require submission of certified copies of relevant prior agreements or assignments pertaining to the right to apply for registration, provided that such requirement shall not unduly delay the processing of applications from small-scale enterprises as defined by the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises. Further, an applicant intending to claim priority under Article 1(3) of the Berne Convention must submit a certified copy of the original application within ninety days of its filing date. The registrar prescribed requirement for verification of these documents shall be strictly adhered to, and failure to comply may result in rejection of the application or subsequent amendment proceedings.

Notwithstanding anything contained herein, an appeal lies to the Appellate Board under this Act if any person aggrieved by an order determining the term of a patent alleges that the Controller has failed to adequately consider evidence pertaining to the date of first working of the patented invention. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order and may seek review of whether the claimed date demonstrably establishes commercial exploitation as required under this Act. The Appellate Board, in entertaining such an appeal, shall give due regard to any expert testimony submitted by either party regarding industry practices relevant to establishing first working. It is provided that the term of patent remains twenty years from the filing date unless altered by a finding of the Appellate Board.

Applications for registration of geographical indications relating to traditional dwellings, including but not limited to structures commonly known as placed houses parliament, shall require submission of detailed architectural plans demonstrating adherence to established regional construction techniques and materials. Such applications must further include documented evidence confirming continuous use of the indicated methods within the defined geographical area for a minimum period of thirty years preceding the date of application. The Registrar may reject an application if it is determined that the proposed geographical indication lacks distinctiveness or falsely suggests a connection with the identified traditional dwelling practices. Any alteration to the architectural design or construction methodology, subsequent to registration, shall be subject to approval by the Geographical Indications Registry and may invalidate the registered status as provided herein.

Any person authorized under this Act to inspect a trade mark register, or any document relating thereto, shall maintain a computer inspection register detailing the date, time, and specific entries accessed. Failure to accurately complete and preserve the computer inspection register shall be deemed a contravention of this Act, attracting a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees for each instance of non-compliance. The Registrar may, subject to reasonable cause being shown, authorize access to the computer inspection register for the purposes of audit or investigation. Any falsification of entries within the computer inspection register, with intent to conceal unauthorized access or modification of trade mark data, shall constitute an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or with fine, or with both. Provided that, the Registrar may, in cases of minor discrepancies, issue a warning instead of imposing a monetary penalty. All records pertaining to the computer inspection register shall be retained for a minimum period of three years.

An applicant seeking registration as an authorised user of a geographical indication registered under this Act shall submit evidence demonstrating lawful production of goods conforming to the standards prescribed in relation to such geographical indication, and a no-objection certificate from the producers’ association, where one exists. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted documentation, register such applicant as an authorised user for a period not exceeding ten years, renewable upon reapplication and satisfactory compliance with ongoing quality control measures. An authorised user shall conspicuously display the registered geographical indication on all packaged goods, and maintain accurate records relating to production volume and origin, available for inspection by officers duly appointed under this Act. Failure to adhere to prescribed standards or misrepresentation regarding geographical origin may result in suspension or revocation of authorisation, provided that a reasonable opportunity for rectification is afforded. Any person aggrieved by the actions of an authorised user may lodge a complaint with the Registrar as provided herein.

A patent for addition may be obtained for any improvement or modification of an existing patented invention, subject to the provisions of this Act and provided that such improvement or modification is itself new and involves a substantial inventive step. The claims in a patent of addition shall define the scope of the improvement or modification only, and not extend to the original invention; however, where the improvement or modification is of such nature that it could independently constitute an invention, the claims may be drafted accordingly but must clearly delineate the novel contribution. An applicant seeking a patent of addition shall file a declaration stating the basis for claiming priority from the earlier patented invention and demonstrating how the claimed subject matter differs sufficiently to warrant separate protection. Failure to comply with these requirements shall render the application liable to be refused, or the patent invalid upon challenge. The controller may require amendment of claims to ensure compliance as provided herein.

An applicant patent, if contested under this Act, shall be subject to a notice of opposition filed by any person alleging prior art or lack of inventive step, provided that such notice is served within four months from the date of publication of the application. The Controller, upon receipt of a valid opposition, shall communicate it to the applicant, who may file a counter-statement within three months. Failure to submit a counter-statement may result in the applicant patent being deemed withdrawn. Where the Controller, after examining the evidence presented by both parties, is satisfied that the applicant patent does not meet the requirements of novelty or involves an obvious variation of existing knowledge, it may reject the application. Any aggrieved party may appeal such rejection to the Appellate Board established for the purposes of this Act, subject to the payment of prescribed fees and adherence to the procedural timelines as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, unless a substantial question of law is involved, warranting review by a higher court.

A person entitled to a patent by way of assignment or transmission shall, upon becoming aware of such entitlement, provide written notification to the Controller within ninety days of the date of acquisition. Such notification shall detail the originating patentee and the terms of transfer as agreed between parties. The Controller may require further documentation substantiating the claim of ownership or interest, including but not limited to deeds of assignment and testamentary records. Where a license is granted under this Act, the licensee may assign such license subject to the consent of the patentee unless the original agreement expressly prohibits it. Any subsequent assignee shall be bound by the terms of the initial license agreement. A person entitled patent arising from an operation of law shall also adhere to these notification requirements and provide supporting legal documentation.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the grant or refusal of registration of a plant variety shall be required to remit a non-refundable fee, calculated as per the prevailing schedule annexed to this Act, prior to filing an appeal before the Appellate Board. Provided that, in cases where the appellant is demonstrably unable to pay such fees due to circumstances beyond their reasonable control, duly substantiated by certified documentation from a recognized authority, the Appellate Board may, at its discretion, waive or reduce the applicable fee. Further, any application for review of an order concerning revocation of registration shall also necessitate payment of prescribed fees in any proceeding; failure to remit said fees will render the application ineligible for consideration as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, an “application patent period” is defined as the duration commencing from the date of filing of a patent application and terminating twenty years from that same date, or such lesser period as claimed in the patent specification, whichever is shorter. This period shall be subject to extensions granted under this Act for delays in examination due to pending objections or requests for further information. An applicant may request an extension of the application patent period where unforeseen circumstances impede the completion of invention work prior to expiry. The extended period shall not exceed three years beyond the original expiration date, provided that adequate justification is furnished as per regulations framed under this Act.

An applicant seeking to grant of a patent may enter into agreements whereby rights pertaining to the invention disclosed in the application are licensed or assigned to another party; provided that such agreements explicitly state the terms and conditions governing the exploitation of the patented technology. Where an assignment or license is executed during the application patent period, the assignee or licensee shall be deemed to step into the shoes of the original applicant for all purposes under this Act, including the right to pay prescribed fees and extend the term of the application. The Controller may require submission of documentation demonstrating the validity of any such agreement before proceeding with examination. Further, where an invention is jointly developed by multiple parties, agreements concerning licensing or assignment must clearly delineate each party’s respective rights and obligations during the application patent period, as provided herein.

Any person deriving title to a registered semiconductor layout-design through assignment, or by operation of law, shall, within such period as may be prescribed, file an application with the Intellectual Property Office detailing the particulars of such derivation of title. The application shall include a certified copy of the instrument of assignment, or evidence establishing the operation of law, and shall be subject to verification in such manner as may be determined. Where a layout-design is subject to a license, the licensee may, with the consent of the registered proprietor, apply for registration of any modification thereof, provided that such modification is not substantial and does not prejudice the rights of the proprietor. Failure to respect filing application requirements as provided herein may render the subsequent assertion of rights in respect of the layout-design invalid, and the Intellectual Property Office may initiate proceedings for rectification of the register. All fees associated with such filings shall be payable as per the prescribed schedule.

Applications for registration of marks incorporating geographical indications shall be examined in accordance with the procedures prescribed under this Act, provided that the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating use of the mark within the territory associated with the indication. Such evidence must satisfy the Registrar as to the continued and authentic connection between the goods or services and the specified geographical origin. The provisions act relating to opposition proceedings shall apply mutatis mutandis to applications for registration involving geographical indications, allowing interested parties to challenge the validity of such registrations based on grounds including misrepresentation of origin or likelihood of confusion. Further, any alteration to a registered mark incorporating a geographical indication requires prior approval from the Registrar, ensuring preservation of its distinctive character and integrity as a designation of origin.

An application for patent shall be deemed to be published upon its entry into the Publication Application Section, subject to compliance with regulations as provided herein. The Controller may direct that an application not be entered into the Publication Application Section if it contains matter which is contrary to law or morality; however, such direction shall only be given after due opportunity has been afforded to the applicant for representation and revision of the offending material. Further, publication shall be withheld where the applicant requests confidentiality under this Act and provides a duly executed request form along with requisite fees, provided that such withholding may not exceed thirty-six months from the date of filing. Any person aggrieved by a decision regarding entry into or non-entry into the Publication Application Section may appeal to an appellate authority as prescribed.

Where an appeal lies from any order passed by the Registrar relating to the subsistence of copyright, or to any question of fact arising under this Act, the aggrieved party may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Tribunal shall follow such procedure as the Central Government may prescribe in this behalf and shall have the same powers as it possesses in relation to appeals under other provisions of this Act. Any order passed by the Appellate Tribunal shall be final, subject to an appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The determination of ownership in a copyright case shall be governed by principles of natural justice and fair hearing, ensuring all parties are afforded reasonable opportunity to present evidence and arguments.

Any assignment of a registered mark shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing, duly executed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall be registered with the Trade Marks Registry. The instrument of assignment shall clearly identify the mark, specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made, and state the consideration for the assignment, if any. Where an assignment is made without adequate consideration, the assignee may, as provided herein, be subject to claims from creditors of the assignor. Should the assignee fail to register the assignment within six months of its execution, the Registrar may, relating plaintiff forthwith, issue a notice requiring rectification of the register. A partial assignment of a mark, affecting only certain goods or services, is permissible, provided that it does not diminish the essential character of the mark as a whole. The assignor warrants to the assignee that they have full right and authority to assign the mark and that the mark is free from any encumbrances.

A variety shall be considered a new variety for the purposes of registration under this Act, provided that it satisfies the criteria of novelty, distinctiveness, uniformity and stability as prescribed. Novelty shall be determined by reference to all publicly available knowledge relating to plant varieties, including documented evidence of cultivation or sale, at the date of filing of the application. A variety exhibiting substantial similarity to a known, commonly cultivated variety, or a variety derived from a parent line widely grown in the country, shall not be deemed novel. However, a variety may still qualify as new if it possesses a unique combination of traits not previously observed, subject to demonstration of its distinctiveness through comparative trials. The applicant shall furnish evidence of the origin and development of the variety, including the date of the first exploitation of the propagating material, to substantiate a claim of novelty. Any variety essentially derived from another variety, where the essentially derived variety is not itself a new variety, shall not be eligible for independent registration.

A geographical indication prescribed under this Act shall identify goods originating from a specific geographical area, where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to that geographical origin. The term ‘geographical indication’ includes indications in the form of names, signs, or symbols, and may denote agricultural, natural, or manufactured goods. However, a geographical indication shall not be registered if it is likely to mislead the public or is contrary to public order or morality. Any association of producers, artisans, or persons engaged in the production of such goods may apply for the registration of a geographical indication, subject to the conditions as provided herein, and shall demonstrate a clear link between the goods and their geographical origin. The Registrar may, after examination, accept or reject the application.

Where any question arises as to the priority date of an application for patent revocation, the Controller shall determine such date based on evidence presented by both the petitioner and the patentee, subject to the provisions relating to grace periods under this Act. The burden of proving a prior publication or disclosure affecting the priority date shall lie upon the party asserting it; provided that the Controller may, at his discretion, direct either party to produce further documentation relevant to establishing the veracity of claims concerning an earlier invention. Any order made by the Controller determining the priority date may be appealed before the Appellate Board within a period of sixty days from the date of such order, and the appeal shall be finally determined as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order of the Registrar refusing to register a layout-design, or varying the terms of registration, or revoking a registration, may, within ninety days from the date of such order, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board. The Appellate Board shall, prior to the disposal of any appeal, require the appellant to deposit with it such sum as it deems fit, not exceeding the amount of the registration fee and any costs awarded by the Registrar. Failure to comply with this requirement shall render the appeal non-maintainable. The Appellate Board, in hearing any appeal, shall have the power to confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar, and may, subject to such conditions as it thinks fit, restore the registration. The manner applying appellate procedures as provided herein shall be in accordance with regulations prescribed by the Central Government, and any decision of the Appellate Board shall be final and binding, save for a writ petition to the High Court on grounds of jurisdictional error. Any wilful misrepresentation made to the Appellate Board shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both.

A person shall be entitled to register a certification trade mark if the sign distinguishes goods of a particular geographical origin or manufactured by a specific production method, provided that the applicant demonstrates control over the conditions under which those goods are produced and certified. The Registrar may require evidence establishing adherence to defined standards relating to quality, characteristics, or other relevant attributes of the certified goods. Such standards shall be documented and made publicly available, ensuring transparency in the certification process. Further, the applicant must demonstrate that the certification trade mark is used honestly and without misleading consumers regarding the origin or nature of the goods. Any alteration to the registered sign affecting its distinctive character will require prior approval from the Registrar.

The Registrar shall maintain a relevant entry register pertaining to each class of goods or services for which an application for registration has been filed under this Act. This register shall accurately reflect the status of applications, including those opposed, accepted with modifications, and finally registered trade marks. The information recorded within the relevant entry register is deemed public record and may be inspected by any person subject to payment of a prescribed fee. Any alteration or addition to an entry in the relevant entry register must be certified by the Registrar as correct and shall include the date and reason for such modification. Furthermore, copies extracted from the relevant entry register are admissible as evidence under this Act without proof of the original, provided they are duly authenticated.

Where a person aggrieved by any order made under this Act relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent has suffered loss or damage as a consequence thereof, that person may petition the High Court for redress. Such petition shall be maintainable only if it is presented within ninety days from the date of communication of the order concerned. The relief sought in such petition shall be limited to compensation commensurate with the demonstrable financial detriment incurred, excluding claims for exemplary or punitive damages. It is provided that in determining the amount of compensation, due consideration shall be given to the patent filed date and any intervening period during which the aggrieved party reasonably relied upon the validity of the patent. Further, the Court may order costs against either party as it deems just.

Any assignment of the right to use a means register trade shall be in writing and signed by or on behalf of the assignor, and shall specify the goods or services in respect of which the assignment is made. Where the assignment is made subject to conditions, those conditions shall be clearly stated in the instrument of assignment. The assignee of a means register trade may, subject to the provisions of this Act, apply to the Trade Marks Registry to have their name registered as the proprietor of the trade mark. 

An exclusive license granted in respect of a means register trade shall be equivalent to an assignment of the right to use the trade mark for the purposes of maintaining proceedings for infringement. However, a non-exclusive license does not confer such a right. Any transfer of a registered trade mark, whether by assignment, license, or otherwise, shall not affect the validity of the registration, provided that the transfer is duly recorded with the Registry. Failure to record such transfer may, however, impact the enforceability of rights against third parties.

A person claiming a foreign priority date in respect of a convention application shall, within the prescribed period, furnish a certified copy of the foreign application with a verified translation if not in an official language, as provided herein. Should the Controller raise an objection regarding the validity of the priority claim, or the authenticity of the supporting documentation, the applicant may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, request a hearing to present evidence substantiating the claim. In instances where the applicant fails to adequately address the Controller’s concerns, or where evidence of deliberate misrepresentation is established, the Controller may initiate security india action, requiring a deposit to cover potential damages. Any decision of the Controller regarding the acceptance or rejection of a convention application, or the imposition of security measures, shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that such appeal is filed within the time limits prescribed. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding, except on grounds of legal error.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Controller of Patents, or by any decision concerning the rectification of the register of patents, may present an appeal to the appropriate district court. Such appeal shall be presented within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, provided that the district court may, for sufficient cause, extend this period by a further thirty days. The district court exercising jurisdiction under this Act shall maintain a register of all appeals received and the status thereof, updated monthly. All evidence submitted before the district court shall be certified as true copies of the original documents. Subject to the provisions herein, the district court shall follow the principles of natural justice and may, at its discretion, require further evidence or expert testimony to arrive at a just determination. The decision of the district court shall be final and binding, except where an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.

Where an application for rectification of a registered trademark is filed under this Act, and the applicant alleges non-use of the mark by the proprietor, proceedings prosecution shall be stayed pending determination of the issue of use. Provided that the Registrar may, upon review of the circumstances, direct the continuation of such proceedings if it appears that undue delay or prejudice to other interested parties would result from a stay. The application for rectification must specify the period during which the mark has not been used and provide evidence supporting this claim. Further, the proprietor shall be afforded an opportunity to demonstrate continued use of the trademark through advertising, sales, or licensing agreements. Failure to adequately respond may impact the outcome as provided herein.

Where a person aggrieved by any order passed under this Act, including an order relating to rectification or invalidation of a registered layout-design, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, he may prefer an application for review before the Controller. Such application shall be made within ninety days from the date of communication of the order and shall specify the grounds on which the applicant seeks review. The Controller may, after affording opportunity to all parties concerned, pass such orders as he deems fit, confirming, modifying, or reversing the original order. An application under section 26 procedure is subject to a fee prescribed by regulations framed by the Central Government. Any party dissatisfied with an order passed by the Controller in review may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of that order’s communication.

Any person who, with intent to deceive or cause confusion, falsely applies a geographical indication to goods, or sells, offers for sale, or distributes goods bearing such falsely applied geographical indication, shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than six months but which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees but which may extend to two lakh rupees. Where a contravention involves goods of a value exceeding five lakh rupees, the court may, in addition to the aforementioned penalties, order the seizure and destruction of the offending goods. Any person aggrieved by the false application of a geographical indication may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a civil suit for injunction and damages. The Registrar, upon receiving a complaint of a geographical indication complained of, may initiate an inquiry and, if satisfied, direct the relevant authorities to take necessary action.

The right to utilize a registered trademark is subject to transfer by way of assignment or transmission, provided that such transfer does not prejudice existing rights under this Act. An application for registration of a trade mark shall be deemed a transmissible case upon notification to the Registrar, specifying the proposed assignee or transferee and detailing the extent of the rights being conveyed. The Registrar may require verification of consent from any registered proprietor whose interests might be affected by such transmission. Any objection to the transfer must be filed within thirty days of publication of the notice in the Trade Marks Journal. Failure to file an objection within this period shall preclude further challenge to the validity of the assignment or transmission. The Registrar, after considering all objections and relevant documentation, may approve or reject the proposed transfer.

Any dispute relating to the registration or validity of a trade mark, or any infringement thereof, arising within the territories of India, shall be subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the High Court having local jurisdiction over the place where the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business. Provided that, in cases where the defendant has no place of business within India but actively targets the Indian market through commercial activity, the High Court in Delhi shall, notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere, have jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate upon such disputes. 

Where a plaintiff seeks to enforce rights in a registered trade mark against a party located outside India, evidence of substantial connection between such party and India, including but not limited to, sales, advertising, or the maintenance of a website accessible within India, shall be presented to establish jurisdiction. The Registrar, as provided herein, may direct service of process on such foreign party through established diplomatic channels or in accordance with international treaties to which India is a party. Any order issued by a court regarding jurisdiction india trade shall be enforceable as if made by a court within its ordinary territorial limits.

An *index registered* in relation to integrated circuits shall comprise particulars of each circuit design registered under this Act, including but not limited to the name and address of the claimant, the date of registration, a representation of the circuit layout, and any associated marks or symbols affixed thereto. The Registrar may require that such representations be presented in both physical and digital formats as deemed necessary for efficient record-keeping. This *index registered* shall be maintained with due diligence and made accessible to the public subject to restrictions imposed under this Act concerning confidential information relating to national security or trade secrets, provided that access may be granted upon application and payment of a prescribed fee.

Where a patent has been granted to a government undertaking engaged in the manufacture or production of essential goods, the Central Government may, subject to such terms and conditions as it deems fit, direct that the patentee shall grant a non-exclusive licence to any other person for the utilization of the patented invention. Such direction shall be given if, in the opinion of the Central Government, the working of the patent is not satisfactory or adequate. The government undertaking may also assign its rights under this Act relating to such patents to another entity with prior approval from the Controller. Provided that any assignment made without such approval shall be deemed invalid. Any licensee granted under this provision shall be entitled to manufacture and sell the patented article, provided they comply with all conditions stipulated in the licence agreement.

Applications for registration of a Plant Variety shall include particulars relating to its designation, denomination if any, repository details where propagating material is available, and the name and address of the applicant. Where an application relates to a variety developed by or for a farmer, the application may be filed jointly by such farmer and any other person seeking commercial advantage from the variety. The Central Government may require submission of additional data concerning distinctness, uniformity, stability, and resistance to pests and diseases as deemed necessary for evaluation under this Act. All applications shall be processed in accordance with procedures established by the indian council agricultural, which will assess conformity with registration criteria.

The registered owner of a layout design shall be entitled to grant licenses conferring rights to utilize, reproduce, or commercially exploit the said layout design, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon in writing between the parties. Any assignment of ownership of a layout design, whether absolute or conditional, must be executed by way of a deed registered with the Controller General under this Act. A licensee may further assign their rights relating to the licensed use provided that prior written consent is obtained from the original owner and such assignment is also duly recorded. Where disputes arise concerning the validity of a license agreement or an assignment, parties aggrieved may appeal to the Layout Design Appellate Board for redressal, as provided herein. The filing application for registration shall not preclude the registered owner’s ability to enter into licensing agreements prior to grant.

Any person who, without due cause and in contravention of the provisions herein, applies for registration of a geographical indication which falsely suggests an association with any goods originating from a place different than the one claimed, shall be liable to pay a pecuniary penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees. Further, where a registered proprietor of a geographical indication discovers that another person is using the said indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed under this Act, they may apply to the relevant authority for an order restraining such use and recovering damages sustained. A geographical indication shall be deemed infringed if it is used in a manner which misrepresents the origin of the goods or services.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall include manufactured articles, raw materials, and any substance whether natural or processed, offered for sale or hire. The Registrar may, upon application by a registered proprietor seeking to extend the protection of their trade mark, investigate whether such goods fall within a class already designated in the registration. This investigation shall consider the essential character and intended use of the goods. An objection to the extension of protection may be filed by any person claiming a proprietary right or interest in similar goods under this Act. Such an objection must be supported by evidence demonstrating likelihood of confusion amongst consumers, provided that the Registrar shall give due weight to established trade channels and marketing practices. The applicant shall have opportunity to respond to such objections within the time prescribed.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, sells, distributes, or displays for sale any product containing a layout design commercially exploited in violation of this Act, shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to the reasonable royalty that would have been payable had the infringer obtained a license from the proprietor. Further, such infringing acts are deemed civil offenses and may attract penalties as determined by the adjudicating officer. The adjudicating officer shall also order the seizure and destruction of goods embodying the infringing layout design. Repeated contravention of these provisions will subject the offender to enhanced monetary penalties and potential criminal prosecution under relevant sections pertaining to fraud and misrepresentation.

Where an application for registration of a literary work, musical work, dramatic work, cinematograph film, or sound recording has been refused under this Act, the applicant may, within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal, appeal to an *instituted district court*. Such appeal shall be made in accordance with the procedure as provided herein and shall not suspend the operation of the order unless the district court directs otherwise. The appellate authority may, after affording the Registrar an opportunity of being heard, confirm the order of refusal, modify it, or direct registration subject to such conditions as it deems fit. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the *instituted district court* may further appeal to the High Court within a period of sixty days from the date of that decision.

Any person who suffers loss or damage as a consequence of another party's deceptive trading practices, constituting passing off, shall have recourse to remedies as provided herein. A claimant must demonstrate goodwill existing in the jurisdiction and misrepresentation likely to deceive a substantial number of consumers, leading to potential damage. Where a defendant attempts to pass off their goods or services as those of the plaintiff, by employing a name, sign, symbol, or other distinguishing feature deceptively similar to a trade mark owned by the claimant—whether registered or unregistered—an injunction may be granted restraining such acts. Monetary damages shall be assessed based on actual losses suffered by the claimant, including loss of profits and damage to reputation; an account of profits earned by the defendant through the wrongful conduct may also be ordered. Relief under this Act is not exclusive, and a claimant may pursue other remedies available at law, subject to principles of equity and fairness. The court may consider factors such as the extent of confusion created and any attempts made by the defendant to mitigate harm.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered layout-design right shall, prior to initiating proceedings before the High Court, furnish to the Controller a statement detailing the nature of the infringement and the relief sought, as provided herein. The Controller, upon receipt of such statement, may, if satisfied that a prima facie case exists, direct the alleged infringer to furnish a statement of their defense within thirty days. Failure to comply with such direction shall be deemed an obstruction of justice and subject to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. A function judicial member, appointed by the Central Government, shall preside over any hearing conducted by the Controller relating to such statements and shall have the power to summon witnesses and documents. Any knowingly false statement made to the Controller shall attract a fine of up to one lakh rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. The Controller’s decision on prima facie assessment shall be final and binding.

An international application filed under this Act shall be deemed to comply with the requirements of novelty and inventive step only if it meets all conditions prescribed herein relating to disclosure. The Controller may require submission of translations of any documents not originally in English or Hindi, subject to payment of such fees as are determined by notification issued by the Central Government. Where an international application claims priority from an earlier application filed outside India, documentation establishing said priority shall be furnished within six months of the date of filing the international application. Failure to provide adequate documentary proof may result in rejection of the application under this Act, provided that the Controller considers any extenuating circumstances presented by the applicant.

Where a person alleges infringement of a registered layout design, such person shall file a complaint before the Commercial Court having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged infringing act was committed, or where the cause of action arose. The complaint shall specify the particulars of the registered layout design, the nature of the alleged infringement, and the relief sought. Upon receipt of such complaint, the Commercial Court may issue interim injunctions restraining the defendant from further infringing activities pending final determination. Evidence pertaining to establishing ownership as the creator layout design shall be presented before the court, including but not limited to documentation demonstrating conception, reduction to practice, and publication. The court shall consider whether the defendant’s integrated circuit layout-design is substantially similar to the registered layout design, taking into account the overall impression created upon an observer skilled in the art.

Where, upon revocation of a patent under this Act, any person claiming title to the invention has suffered damage by reason of acts done during the term of the patent which but for the existence of the patent would have infringed a right vested in that person, such person may sue for damages against the patentee. The measure of damages shall be determined having regard to the benefit accruing to the claimant from the use of the invention as if the patent had never been granted. It is provided that an objection to the validity of the specification claimed claim may be raised by any interested party in proceedings before the Controller, and such objection shall be deemed to be a ground for revocation. The burden of proving the existence of such damage rests upon the claimant, subject to provisions regarding estoppel as provided herein.

Any person claiming ownership of a subject registration trade, and alleging infringement by another, shall first submit a notice of intent to the Registrar, detailing the grounds of the claim and the nature of the alleged infringement. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the claim’s prima facie validity, direct the alleged infringer to file a response within thirty days. Should the response fail to adequately address the concerns raised, or if no response is received, the claimant may then initiate proceedings before the appellate authority. However, where the alleged infringement incorporates elements protected by copyright, the claimant must demonstrate that the trade mark registration predates the copyright claim, or that the copyright work is wholly derivative of the registered trade mark, and does not independently possess artistic merit. An appeal against the appellate authority’s decision shall lie with the High Court, provided that such appeal is filed within ninety days of the appellate authority’s order. The Registrar retains the power to revoke a registration if fraudulent misrepresentation is established during any stage of these proceedings.

A registered trade mark shall confer upon the proprietor exclusive right to the use of the said trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered and shall include the right to sue for infringement. However, such right shall be subject to the provisions contained herein and any other applicable law for the time being in force. Where a patent shall relate to an article capable of being sold under different trade marks, the proprietor of the registered trade mark may, notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, obtain an injunction restraining the sale of such articles by any person other than a licensee authorized by him. Provided that nothing herein contained shall prejudice the rights and remedies available to the patentee under the Patents Act, 1970. Any assignment or transmission of a registered trade mark shall be governed by rules as prescribed.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication shall be entitled to institute civil suit for infringement under this Act and may seek injunctive relief restraining any person from making use of the geographical indication or any confusingly similar indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as prescribed. Provided that, where an alleged infringer has honestly used the geographical indication prior to the date of registration, but without intent to deceive consumers regarding the origin of the goods uses geographical indications, a court may grant such relief as it deems just and equitable, including a direction for the payment of damages. Any person found to have infringed a registered geographical indication shall be liable to pay compensation equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor or a sum not exceeding five per cent of the turnover attributable to the infringing activity, whichever is higher.

Any application for a patent claiming a biotechnological invention shall be examined in the prescribed manner, with due regard to the potential for commercial exploitation within the territory of India and consistent with public interest. Where an application relates to a micro-organism, the deposit of said micro-organism with a recognised depositary institution shall be a condition precedent to the grant of a patent, and the details of such deposit shall form part of the complete specification. A transmissible case, containing all relevant documentation pertaining to the deposited micro-organism, shall be maintained by the depositary institution and made available to the Controller of Patents as provided herein. Failure to maintain such a case, or to provide access thereto upon request, may be grounds for rejection of the application. The Controller may, subject to the provisions of this Act, require the applicant to furnish additional information or evidence regarding the deposited micro-organism to ensure compliance with the prescribed manner of examination. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the deposited material shall be adjudicated in accordance with established scientific principles.

Any person alleging infringement of a registered design shall, prior to initiating proceedings before any court, notify the alleged infringer of the particulars of the infringement and require them to cease the infringing act, subject to the provisions contained herein. Should the alleged infringer, upon receipt of such notice, fail to cease the infringing act within thirty days, the aggrieved party may apply to the High Court having jurisdiction. The High Court, upon being satisfied of the prima facie case of infringement and considering the interests of security India explanation, may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing the design. 

Provided that, in cases where the design is integral to a product essential for national security, the Court shall, before issuing any injunction, consult with the Central Government to ascertain whether the injunction would be detrimental to the security of India. Any damages awarded shall reflect the actual loss suffered by the plaintiff, or a reasonable royalty, whichever is higher, and may include costs as determined by the Court.

Where an applicant obtains registration of a trade mark under this Act as a certification trade mark, the Registrar shall issue a certificate of registration in the prescribed form. The holder of such registration shall be entitled to use the distinctive device specified therein and may institute proceedings for infringement against any person using or authorizing the use of a sign identical or deceptively similar to the certified trade mark in connection with goods or services covered by the certification. Any proprietor whose rights are adversely affected by the grant of registration as a certification trade mark may apply to the Registrar for rectification, subject to demonstrating material prejudice resulting from the registration. The Registrar shall consider such applications and may order cancellation or modification of the register certification if it is found to be obtained through misrepresentation or contrary to the provisions herein.

An application for an order concerning the rectification or cancellation of registration may be made by any person alleging that the registered layout-design does not satisfy the requirements of section 13. Such applications shall specify the grounds upon which it is based, and must include relevant documentary evidence supporting the claim. Where an order cancellation sub has been issued under this Act, the Central Government may, subject to just cause and after affording the registrant a reasonable opportunity for being heard, review such order. Any party aggrieved by any decision made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal as provided herein.

Any person found, upon investigation conducted pursuant to an inspection authorized under this Act, to have made use of any registered geographical indication in contravention of the provisions herein, shall be liable for damages equivalent to three times the value of the goods or services sold bearing the infringing mark, or where such value cannot be ascertained, one million rupees. Furthermore, proceedings initiated by the Register may result in a conviction and imprisonment term shall extend up to five years, subject to judicial discretion considering the severity and repetition of the offense. The Parliament year report detailing instances of infringement and enforcement actions undertaken will include particulars of each prosecution and any penalties imposed.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall include particulars verifying its originality and novelty, alongside a representation of the integrated circuit layout. The Registrar may reject an application if he is satisfied that the claimed layout-design lacks sufficient distinctive character to be considered a distinguishable registered layout from existing designs already recorded on the Register of Layout Designs. Further, registration shall not be granted where the applicant fails to demonstrate due diligence in preventing prior public disclosure of the layout-design’s essential features before the date of application. The Registrar may also refuse registration if it appears that the layout-design incorporates elements substantially derived from a previously registered design, subject to permissible modifications as provided herein.

Where a registered layout design owner desires to grant a license or assign their rights relating to a protected integrated circuit layout design, such license or assignment shall be in writing and executed by an authorized representative of the owner. The terms of any license granted under this Act may specify the field of use, duration, and geographical extent of the permitted exploitation. Further, where a license is assigned along with the underlying layout design rights, the assignee shall become the exclusive proprietor subject to any continuing obligations stipulated in the original licensing agreement. Any dispute arising concerning the validity or interpretation of such licenses or assignments may be referred to the Appellate Board sub for adjudication and binding determination, as provided herein. The Board’s decision shall be final and conclusive.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a registered trade mark and alleging an infringement thereof may, subject to the provisions of this Act, institute a suit for recovery of damages or an injunction, or both, in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the infringement occurs. The proprietor of a registered trade mark shall, notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, have the right to institute civil proceedings for infringement of such trade mark. Where a plaintiff, being the proprietor of a registered trade mark, succeeds in an infringement suit, the Court may grant an account of profits and also award damages not exceeding rupees two lakh for each such infringement. 

Provided that, in cases where the infringement is shown to be a result of a deliberate and willful act on the part of the defendant, the Court may also award enhanced damages, not exceeding rupees five lakh per infringement. Any order made under this Act relating to registered trade marks shall be enforceable by the same Court as if it were a decree in a suit in that Court.

Notwithstanding anything contained in this Act, a registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions herein, grant a license or assign the right to use the trade mark to another party, constituting a permitted use, provided that such license or assignment is in writing and specifies the scope of permitted use, including but not limited to the goods, services, geographical area, and duration. Any dispute arising from the interpretation of the scope of permitted use shall be subject to mediation facilitated by a mutually agreed upon mediator; however, if mediation fails, the aggrieved party may appeal to the High Court having jurisdiction. Where a registered user exceeds the scope of permitted use, the registered proprietor may seek an injunction restraining such unauthorized use and claim damages for any loss suffered. A bona fide user prior to registration, as established through evidence presented to the Registrar, shall not be affected by such permitted use.

For the purposes of this Act, “pharmaceutical composition” means a combination of two or more active ingredients intended for use in the treatment, mitigation, or prevention of disease, or for improving health conditions; and where such pharmaceutical composition is claimed in an application for patent, it shall be examined with particular regard to novelty and inventive step. The term "objectionable matter" includes any information disclosed in the description or drawings which relates to a process for producing a substance but does not necessarily involve the use of that substance for a novel purpose. The Controller may, at any time during the examination of an application, require the applicant to furnish further particulars relating to such objectionable matter.

Any person aggrieved by the misrepresentation or improper use of a registered geographical indication shall be entitled to institute a civil suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a court of competent jurisdiction. The proprietor of a geographical indication, or those authorized by them, may seek an order restraining the defendant from manufacturing or trading goods bearing the falsely applied geographical indication. Damages awarded shall be commensurate with the injury suffered, and may include loss of profits, brand reputation, and costs associated with corrective advertising, subject to proof of actual loss. 

Provided that, where the defendant proves they were unaware and had no reasonable grounds to believe the use constituted an infringement of the geographical indication complained of, the court may award only nominal damages. A court may, as an alternative to damages, grant an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unlawful use, and order its delivery to the proprietor. Any order of injunction issued under this Act shall be enforceable by the court.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered layout-design, or to assign or otherwise transfer rights therein, shall submit a statement of proposed registered assignment to the authority appellate board for its review and record. The statement shall clearly identify the parties involved, detail the scope of the assignment including territorial limitations, and specify any associated royalty or licensing terms. The authority appellate board may, subject to such conditions as it deems necessary to safeguard the interests of the original creator and ensure continued innovation, approve the proposed assignment. Approval shall be recorded in the register proposed registered layouts-designs maintained by the authority. Where the assignment involves a license, the terms of the license, including duration and field of use, shall be explicitly stated. Failure to obtain approval from the authority appellate board prior to any commercial exploitation, assignment or transfer may render such acts void and subject the offender to penalties as provided herein. The authority appellate board’s decision shall be final and binding, subject to judicial review.

Where an application for a patent is granted, and subsequently challenged under this Act on grounds of prior publication or lack of novelty, the patent office shall conduct a review in accordance with prescribed procedures. Such review will consider all documentary evidence submitted by both the patent holder and the challenger. The Controller may, after affording both parties an opportunity to be heard, determine whether the grant was justified. Provided that, if the Controller finds that the challenged invention infringes upon existing intellectual property rights, including but not limited to design registrations or trade secrets, an injunction subject terms relating to the scope of the patent shall be considered. The patent office is obligated to maintain records pertaining to all such reviews for a period of ten years from the date of determination.

Any person who makes use of a registered trade mark in relation to goods or services for the purpose of any trade or business, shall be deemed to have engaged in mark use as provided herein. However, such mark use shall not be construed as an infringement of the rights of the proprietor if it is demonstrably necessary to indicate the intended purpose of the goods or services, or if it is descriptive of the character or quality of the goods or services. A registered proprietor may, subject to the provisions of this Act, initiate civil proceedings for recovery of damages and an injunction against any party committing an act of unlawful mark use. Where a defendant proves that the use was bona fide and for the purpose of fair comment or criticism, the court may reduce the damages awarded. Any order for damages may also include an account of profits derived by the defendant from the unlawful mark use. The court shall have the power to grant relief as it deems fit, considering all circumstances of the case.

Where a person is charged with an offence under this Act relating to the use of a trade mark and accused pleads registration, the Court may direct that the validity of the said registration be determined as part of the proceedings. Such direction shall be given only if the accused demonstrates a reasonable basis for challenging the registration’s validity, supported by documentary evidence filed prior to commencement of trial. The Court shall provide the registered proprietor with an opportunity to file its response within thirty days from the date of such direction. Any determination made regarding the validity of the trade mark registration shall be final and binding only for the purposes of that particular prosecution. Further, this determination shall not prejudice any other proceedings concerning the same or similar matters under this Act or otherwise. The Court may, at any stage, set aside its earlier direction if it finds that the challenge to registration is frivolous or vexatious.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be filed by any association of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collective bodies representing such producers. The Registrar shall consider an application only if it is accompanied by evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods originates from the specified geographical area and that the applicant has the interest of the registered proprietor to protect the indication use geographical. Where multiple applications are received for the same geographical indication, the Registrar shall give preference to the applicant who can demonstrate a longer history of continuous use within the defined territory. Any company seeking registration must provide its certificate of incorporation and details of its governing body as part of the application process. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating claims made in the application before proceeding with examination.

For the purposes of this Act, a “registered proprietor proposed” is deemed to include any individual or entity seeking to obtain registration of a trade mark identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered trade mark, subject to demonstrating a demonstrable and lawful interest in such application. The Registrar shall consider all relevant factors pertaining to reputation and goodwill associated with the prior registered trade mark. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar concerning the acceptance or rejection of an application under this definition may appeal to the Authority Appellate Board as provided herein. Such appeals shall be conducted according to prescribed procedures.

The gene fund sub-account for the preservation of indigenous plant genetic resources shall be maintained by the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources, and contributions thereto may be made by any person, institution, or organization, subject to guidelines established by the Central Government. Any benefit derived from the commercial exploitation of varieties incorporating traits originating from registered geographical indications, particularly those associated with traditional knowledge, shall be preferentially allocated to this sub-account. The Bureau may, with the approval of the Central Government, license the use of genetic material held within the gene fund sub-account to registered plant breeders, provided that a royalty agreement is executed ensuring equitable benefit sharing with the communities from whom the genetic resource originated. Assignment of rights relating to such licensed material shall be subject to the prior consent of the originating community and the Bureau, as provided herein, and any transfer must be recorded with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Failure to comply with these provisions shall render the license voidable.

Any application for registration of a design shall be subject to a rigorous examination to ascertain its novelty and originality, and compliance with all provisions of this Act. The Controller of Designs may, at any time during the examination process, require the applicant to furnish further information or evidence to substantiate the claims made in the application. Where the Controller has reasonable grounds to believe that the publication of a design, even if registered, would be prejudicial to the security of India, the Controller shall not register the design. 

Furthermore, the Controller may initiate a security India action, requiring the applicant to demonstrate that the design does not compromise national security interests. Provided that, any such action shall be accompanied by a detailed statement of reasons and an opportunity for the applicant to respond. Failure to adequately address concerns raised during a security India action may result in the rejection of the application, even if the design otherwise meets all requirements for registration.

A patent, once granted and sealed under this Act, shall have effect India patent throughout the territory of India, subject to any modifications or limitations prescribed herein. The validity of such a patent may be challenged under this Act based on grounds specified in the First Schedule; however, no challenge shall be entertained regarding matters not explicitly addressed within the patent specification. For the purposes of determining novelty and inventive step, the patent specification constitutes the sole authoritative record of the invention claimed. Any alteration to the recorded details after grant is prohibited unless expressly permitted by regulations framed under this Act.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act concerning a plant variety registration, including but not limited to orders relating to revocation or modification, may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of such order. Failure to comply with prescribed timelines shall render the appeal inadmissible. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by all parties and may impose costs on any party found to have acted frivolously or vexatiously. Where a plant variety is determined to be a breeder entry relating to an extant registered variety, the original breeder shall be afforded priority in subsequent claims, subject to penalties for wilful infringement as provided herein. The Board’s decision is final and binding, enforceable through civil courts.
