An application for the registration of a geographical indication may be filed with the Registrar in such form and manner as may be prescribed, providing particulars relating to the name of the geographical indication sought to be registered, the goods or services for which it is used, and the area of its origin. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the quality, reputation, or other characteristic of the goods or services originates from the specified geographical territory. Consideration will be given to whether the sign functions in the eyes of the public as a badge of originality. Any person claiming an interest may oppose the registration; such opposition must be filed within the time prescribed and shall state the grounds for objection. A geographical indication, once registered, is considered geographical indication and enjoys protection as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trademark shall include a representation of the mark and a statement indicating the goods or services in relation to which the mark is sought to be registered. Where the Registrar considers that any action proceeding infringement may arise from the use of a proposed trade mark, he may require the applicant to amend the description of such goods or services to avoid conflict with existing registrations. The Registrar shall give notice of such requirement to the applicant and an opportunity for them to submit representations against it. Subject to these representations, the Registrar’s decision is final. An appeal from this decision lies to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Provided that any alteration made under this provision does not substantially affect the identity of the mark, the registration shall proceed as if the original application had been filed with the amended description.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, no trade mark shall be registered for food unless it is clearly distinguishable from those used for similar goods. The Registrar may require evidence demonstrating that the proposed trade mark does not indicate the nutritional composition, qualities, or properties of the food beyond what is generally known about such foods. Furthermore, any representation employed as a trade mark relating to food must comply with standards prescribed under the Food Safety and Standards Act concerning permitted colours, additives, and labelling requirements. Provided that the applicant satisfies the Registrar regarding adherence to these regulations, registration may proceed. Any alteration to the formulation or processing of the food after registration shall necessitate notification to the Registrar within thirty days.

For the purposes of this Act, a “new invention” shall mean an invention which is not previously known to the public, either by written or oral description or by use or in any other way. An invention shall be deemed new if, at the date of filing of the patent application, it does not involve any element disclosed in the prior art. Prior art includes information that has been made available to the public anywhere in the world, by any means, before the date of filing of the patent application as provided herein. Subject to this, a “new invention” may also include an improvement of an existing process or machine, so long as such improvement results in a technical effect and is not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

Any person who, without authorization from the registered proprietor, makes, imports, distributes, sells, hires or displays a layout design connected with any other layout design shall be deemed to have infringed upon the said registered layout design. Such infringement includes the reproduction of the protected elements of the layout design in another layout design, irrespective of alterations made thereto. The Court may, subject to appeal, impose a penalty not exceeding five times the cost of infringing activities or imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or both, as deemed appropriate. Further, damages shall be awarded to the registered proprietor to compensate for loss sustained due to the infringement, calculated based on prevailing market rates and demonstrable financial detriment.

An applicant seeking registration of a design shall furnish with the application such particulars as are prescribed, including detailed representations demonstrating the novelty and industrial applicability of the proposed design. The Controller may require the applicant to submit additional documentation or specimens to ascertain compliance with the provisions relating to distinctiveness and freedom from prior publication. Where the design incorporates elements indicative of national security, particularly those pertaining to infrastructure protection or critical systems, the application shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny under this Act. Such designs may necessitate a security india clearance certificate issued by the designated authority before proceeding towards registration. The grant of registration mark certification will only follow verification that the design does not compromise national interests as determined by the Central Government.

Any person claiming to be an indication plaintiff, alleging wrongful use of a registered geographical indication, may institute a suit for injunction, damages, or both, in a District Court having jurisdiction over the place where the wrongful act occurred, or where the defendant resides or carries on business. The Court, upon satisfactory evidence of such wrongful use, shall grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the geographical indication. Damages awarded shall not be less than five thousand rupees per contravention, and may extend to three lakh rupees, subject to proof of actual loss or potential loss suffered by the indication plaintiff. A false designation of origin or presentation, even if not identical to the registered geographical indication, but likely to cause confusion, shall be deemed a contravention as provided herein. Any order of the Court may be executed directly by the Registrar, upon request by the indication plaintiff, and the costs thereof shall be borne by the defendant. Failure to comply with an injunction shall constitute contempt of court, punishable with imprisonment not exceeding two years, or a fine, or both.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a registered plant breeder may grant a license conferring rights relating to the commercialization of their protected variety. Such licenses shall specify the geographical area within which the licensee is permitted to conduct activities such as propagation, sale, or distribution. The terms of any license granted under this Act may include royalty payments payable by the licensee to the grantor, and the frequency with which such payments are made. Furthermore, a breeder entry relating to an assignment of rights in a protected variety shall be recorded with the Registrar within thirty days of the execution of the assignment agreement. Any subsequent transfer of rights by the assignee shall also require notification to the Registrar as provided herein.

Any work involving the industrial application of a design shall not be considered to infringe copyright as provided herein, provided that such application is demonstrably distinct from the original artistic work and does not constitute a substantial reproduction thereof. However, this exemption shall not extend to works where the industrial application is merely a slavish copy, lacking any significant modification or adaptation. Appeals regarding determinations of ‘significant modification’ may be made to the High Court, subject to the provisions relating to limitation periods under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Where a plaintiff alleges that an industrial application, though modified, unfairly exploits the aesthetic qualities of their copyrighted work, the burden of proof shall lie upon the defendant to demonstrate sufficient originality in the applied design. Any dispute concerning the scope of ‘industrial application’ itself shall be adjudicated based on prevailing technical standards and market practices.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, a patentee shall have the exclusive right to exploit the patented invention throughout India, but such right shall be granted upon adherence to stipulated terms within the licence agreement. Any licensee operating under a patent license shall comply with all conditions expressly stated in the grant documentation regarding royalty payments, duration of exploitation, and territorial limitations. Further, the patentee may stipulate, as a condition precedent to granting a further sub-licence, that the sublicensee maintains quality control standards equivalent to those employed by the primary licensee, ensuring consistent product specifications. Failure to comply with any term specified within the licence patent terms shall render the license voidable at the discretion of the patentee.

Where an application for registration of a new variety of seed potato is opposed under this Act, the Registrar shall give notice thereof to the applicant and the opponent. The applicant may, within such time as may be specified therein, file with the Registrar a counter-statement replying to the grounds of opposition. Upon receiving the counter-statement, the Registrar shall afford the opponent an opportunity to file a rejoinder thereto. Any party aggrieved by any decision of the required registrar person relating to the acceptance or rejection of a new variety application may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such decision; provided that the Board may entertain appeals filed after the said period if satisfactory reasons are tendered for the delay.

Any person aggrieved by the refusal of the Controller to register a patent, or any amendment to a patent following examination, may file an appeal with the Appellate Board within ninety days of the order appealed against, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. The Appellant shall furnish security for costs as determined by the Appellate Board and failure to do so will render the appeal non-maintainable. Where a request for registration is refused on grounds relating to novelty or inventive step, the Controller’s decision shall include detailed reasoning referencing prior art considered during examination. Should the Appellate Board uphold the Controller's refusal to register, no further appeal under this Act shall be permissible; however, a petition may lie before the High Court on points of law only. The register maintained by the Controller shall be prima facie evidence of all matters entered therein and is open for inspection subject to payment of prescribed fees.

Where a patentee desires to assign or license rights pertaining to an invention disclosed in the patent specification, and such assignment or license involves claims extending beyond the scope explicitly defined within the specification itself, the assignee or licensee shall provide a written declaration to the Controller detailing the basis for said extension. This declaration must specifically identify any modifications to the originally claimed subject matter and justify their inclusion under principles of inventive step as provided herein. Failure to submit such a declaration, or submission of a declaration containing materially false statements, constitutes a commission offence punishable with imprisonment and fine. The patentee retains responsibility for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of this declaration, irrespective of whether the assignment or license was negotiated at arm's length.

Where an applicant has failed to comply with any requirement of this Act or the Regulations framed thereunder, the Controller may issue a communication specifying the nature of such failure and requiring compliance within a time specified therein. Failure to comply with such communication will render the application liable for rejection. However, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to make representations against the proposed rejection, and the Controller shall consider any submissions made before proceeding further. A patent shall examined only after the applicant has fulfilled all procedural requirements as provided herein. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Controller relating to examination may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of such order.

For the purposes of this Act, “goods” shall mean any kind of movable property including stock and all manufactures. The classification of goods for the registration of trade marks shall be in accordance with the Nice Classification, subject to such modifications as may be prescribed. An application claiming priority under Article 8 of the Paris Convention, or a 73 convention application asserting earlier filing dates in a contracting state, shall specify the country and date of the prior application within the stipulated timeframe as provided herein. Where goods fall into more than one class, separate fees shall be payable for each such class. The Registrar may require an applicant to indicate specifically the goods for which registration is sought, clarifying broad descriptions where necessary.

A denomination variety sub shall be deemed to be essentially derived if it is not substantially different from the parent variety in terms of characteristics relevant to the plant’s utility and is clearly demonstrable through objective, scientific methods. Compliance with the provisions relating to essentially derived varieties is subject to the establishment of a clear lineage tracing back to the initial variety, as recorded with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a breeder develops or commercially exploits an essentially derived variety without the authorization of the breeder of the parent variety, such activity shall constitute an infringement under this Act. Provided that, a farmer exercising the right to save, sell, share or distribute seeds of a protected variety, and who subsequently develops a variety meeting the criteria of an essentially derived variety, may do so without prior authorization, subject to the payment of royalties as determined by the Authority. Any dispute regarding the determination of ‘essentially derived’ status may be referred to the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Tribunal for adjudication.

An applicant desiring to obtain a patent shall file an application with the Patent Office in the prescribed form, accompanied by the requisite fee. The application must disclose the invention clearly and completely for enabling any person skilled in the art to put the same into practice. Where the application relates to more than one invention, each of which is separately patentable, the applicant may include them in a single application, provided that they relate to a common subject matter. However, the examination process under this Act shall consider each such invention individually for novelty and inventive step. The particulars required in an application sub section (1) must be meticulously adhered to, failing which the application is liable to rejection. Any alteration made after the date of filing requires notification to the Controller.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar may require the applicant to furnish, along with the application or at any subsequent stage prior to acceptance, a detailed manufactured notification specifying the precise geographical location and production methods employed in relation to the goods or services associated with the proposed trade mark. Such manufactured notification shall be deemed an integral part of the registration process and failure to comply with this requirement may result in rejection of the application. The Registrar shall maintain a public record of all such notifications, accessible for inspection by any interested party. Provided that, where the applicant demonstrates reasonable cause preventing full compliance, the Registrar may grant a temporary extension, subject to conditions as deemed appropriate.

Where a trade mark is registered internationally under the Madrid Protocol and such international registration incorporates a designation of India, the proprietor shall maintain the validity of that registration for so long as the underlying Indian registration remains in force. However, where an article patented incorporating the trade mark is subsequently withdrawn from sale within India or ceases to be manufactured therein, the proprietor may apply to the Registrar for a modification of the international registration’s scope relating to those specific goods. Failure to do so within six months of such cessation shall constitute grounds for revocation under this Act. The period of protection afforded by an international registration remains subject to the same renewal requirements as would apply to a domestic Indian trade mark, and any lapse in renewal will impact years international registration status accordingly.

For the purpose of determining entitlement to compensation or remedies under this Act, the “date accorded patent” in relation to an invention shall mean the date on which a communication is issued by the Controller accepting the grant of a patent and specifying the terms thereof. This date shall be conclusive evidence for all purposes, subject to any order made by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board following an appeal as provided herein. Where such communication is delivered electronically, the date accorded patent shall be deemed to be the date on which the electronic record is received by or accessible to the applicant. The Controller may, under this Act, extend the period for filing appeals relating to the date accorded patent.

Where an application for a patent is filed claiming priority from an application made under the Patent Cooperation Treaty, the Controller may require the applicant to furnish a certified copy of the international search report and written opinion. Failure to comply with such requirement within the time specified shall render the application liable to be refused. An appeal against this decision lies to the Appellate Board. The determination of whether the priority claim is valid, considering discrepancies between the original application and the subsequently filed Indian patent application, remains subject to judicial review. Further, if the mark 'Bharat Chemicals' is found to be a reference trade mark used in connection with similar goods or services as those claimed in the patent, this shall not automatically invalidate the patent but may be considered during any infringement proceedings.

The application registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct a thorough examination as provided herein to ascertain its registrability in accordance with the criteria outlined within this Act. Where the application relates to a mark used in connection with layout-designs of integrated circuits, the registrar shall, subject to the provisions concerning semiconductor integrated circuits, also verify compliance with the relevant regulations pertaining to the protection of layout designs manufacturers and their intellectual property. Any deficiency in the application, or any conflict with existing registered trade marks, shall be communicated to the applicant, who shall be afforded a period of thirty days to remedy the same. Failure to adequately address the registrar’s objections may result in the rejection of the application, and the applicant shall be notified accordingly. The registrar may, at their discretion, request further evidence or clarification from the applicant to facilitate a complete and accurate assessment.

The registration of an assignment of copyright under this Act shall be deemed conclusive evidence of the validity of such assignment, subject to judicial review on grounds of fraud or misrepresentation. Where a copyright owner desires to assign specific rights relating to a literary or dramatic work, including but not limited to reproduction, distribution, and adaptation, the instrument effecting such assignment shall clearly delineate the precise rights assigned. Such specification shall detail whether the assignment is exclusive or non-exclusive, and for what period it remains in effect. Any subsequent transfer of copyright, or any further assignments relating to the same work, must be registered separately as provided herein. Failure to accurately specify rights assigned may render the registration voidable at the discretion of the Registrar.

Where an applicant has failed to comply with a notice issued under this Act requiring him to amend his specification or drawings, or to furnish statements relating thereto, the Patent Office shall give him a further opportunity to do so within a period not exceeding two months, provided that such failure does not relate to a matter of substance affecting the patentability of the invention. If, after the expiry of that extended time, the applicant still fails to comply, the application for patents shall be deemed abandoned and all fees paid by the applicant shall be forfeited to the Government. Any person aggrieved by an order made under this provision may appeal to the Controller within sixty days from the date of such order; and the Controller’s decision shall be final. The grant of a patent in respect of any invention shall create offices patent conferring upon the patentee certain exclusive rights as provided herein.

Any person claiming an invention relating to a plant variety registered under this Act may apply to the Controller for authorization to use the registered variety for purposes other than those specified in the granted Plant Variety Protection. Such application shall include detailed justification demonstrating that the refusal of the right holder to grant permission constitutes an impediment to agricultural development or access to essential medicines derived from the plant variety. The Controller, after giving notice to the concerned right holder and providing them a reasonable opportunity to be heard, may determine whether a compulsory licensing is warranted, considering factors such as public interest, freedom to operate for research institutions, and the adequacy of remuneration proposed. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the terms and conditions, including duration and royalty rates, as provided herein.

The Registrar, upon receipt of an application for registration of a new plant variety claiming crop sciences indian expertise, shall conduct a preliminary examination to ascertain compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. Should the application satisfy the initial requirements, the Registrar may, subject to payment of the prescribed fee, initiate a substantive examination involving a detailed assessment of distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability. A variety shall be deemed distinct if it exhibits clearly distinguishable characteristics from any other variety commonly known or commercially available, taking into account essential botanical characteristics. Provided that, the applicant may submit evidence of prior art to demonstrate the novelty of the claimed variety. The examination process may include field trials conducted at designated testing centers, and the applicant shall bear the costs associated with such trials, unless otherwise determined by the Registrar. Any person aggrieved by the decision of the Registrar regarding the rejection of an application may file an appeal to the Appellate Board, as provided herein. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final and binding.

The holder of a certificate registration produced under this Act shall be entitled to grant non-exclusive licenses relating to the integrated circuit layout design for which such certificate has been issued. Such license may specify the field of use, duration, and geographical territory within which the licensee is permitted to exploit the registered layout design. Assignment of rights pertaining to a layout design, including any existing or future licenses, requires prior written consent from the Controller, subject to payment of prescribed fees. The Controller shall not withhold such consent without providing reasoned justification in writing to the assignor. Further, where an assignment occurs, the assignee shall be bound by all terms and conditions applicable to the certificate registration produced, as provided herein, including any restrictions on reverse engineering or unauthorized reproduction.

Any person desiring to seek a patent based on an international application shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a complete specification as prescribed, together with a statement of priority, if any, and the international application number with the Controller within thirty-six months from the date of the international application. Failure to furnish the statement of priority, where applicable, shall render the application incomplete and liable to be rejected. Any misrepresentation regarding the priority date in an international application, if discovered, may attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. The Controller may, however, allow a grace period of three months for rectifying any deficiency in the application, provided that a surcharge, not exceeding ten thousand rupees, is paid. All applications originating from an international application shall be subject to examination as provided herein, and any false claim made therein will be treated as an offence punishable with imprisonment.

Where an international registration designating India is subject to an opposition under this Act, the opponent shall serve a copy of the Notice of Opposition on the applicant for international registration within the prescribed period. The applicant may file a counterstatement in response to the opposition, as provided herein, and such counterstatement shall be accompanied by any evidence relied upon in support thereof. Failure to comply with these procedural requirements regarding service and filing may render the opposition vulnerable to challenge under this Act. If an objection is raised concerning acquired distinctiveness of the mark within India, the Registrar shall consider all relevant evidence presented by both parties. The applicant for international registration retains the right to appeal any decision made by the Registrar relating to such an international registration opposed.

A registered trade mark shall be subject to revocation on an application made to the Trade Marks Registry if, and only if, it has remained unused for a continuous period of five years, and there is no bona fide intention to use it in the future. However, non-use shall not be deemed to have occurred if circumstances beyond the control of the proprietor have prevented such use, provided that such circumstances are proven to the satisfaction of the Registry. Where a mark is registered in relation to specified goods or services, the determination of ‘use’ shall be assessed in relation to those goods or services only. 

Crucially, a finding of ‘use’ in relation to a mark requires a demonstrable connection between the mark and the goods or services offered, establishing a clear use mark relation in the minds of consumers. Any use by a licensee shall, for the purposes of this Act, be considered use by the proprietor. The Registry may require evidence of legitimate commercial activity to substantiate claims of use.

Where a patent has been granted for an invention and subsequently, the applicant seeks to claim an additional invention related to the subject matter of the original patent, such request shall be considered as an application for a validity patent addition. The Controller may grant this addition provided that the added invention is novel and non-obvious, and relates to the same or similar field of technology as the originally patented invention. Assignment of rights pertaining to both the primary patent and any subsequent patent additions thereto shall be governed by the provisions relating to assignment under this Act. Further, any license granted in respect of the original patent shall automatically extend to cover the scope of the validity patent addition unless explicitly excluded within the terms of the licensing agreement; such exclusion must be clearly stated and agreed upon by all parties involved, considering the effect registered trade marks may have on consumer perception.

An applicant seeking registration of a trade mark shall, upon filing the application, remit a prescribed fee as detailed in Schedule I. Where an objection is raised by the Trade Marks Registry under this Act concerning distinctiveness or any other ground, the applicant may respond within the time specified, accompanied by arguments and evidence addressing the concerns articulated. Following such response, if the Registrar remains unconvinced of the registrability of the trade mark, a fee payable notice shall be issued to the applicant, informing them of the continued objection and providing an opportunity for further representation or withdrawal of the application. Failure to comply with the requirements outlined in the fee payable notice within the stipulated period will result in the abandonment of the application.

The Chairperson of the Appellate Board shall be a person of eminence in the field of semiconductor technology or law, possessing not less than ten years of experience in either domain. The Central Government shall appoint the Chairperson, and any vacancy arising shall be filled in like manner. The Appellate Board Chairperson shall exercise administrative control over the Board and be responsible for ensuring the efficient and timely disposal of appeals. Subject to the provisions contained herein, the Chairperson may constitute Benches of the Appellate Board as deemed necessary to hear and decide on pending matters. All decisions of a Bench shall be made by majority vote, with the Chairperson having a casting vote in the event of a tie. The Chairperson shall also oversee the maintenance of records and the implementation of procedures established under this Act, and may, with the approval of the Central Government, formulate rules for the smooth functioning of the Appellate Board. Any person aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may seek review before the Chairperson, provided that such application is made within thirty days of the order’s issuance.

Any copyright owner desiring to grant a license for reproduction or adaptation of their work may execute an assignment, irrevocably transferring such rights to another party, subject to the terms stipulated within the agreement. Such assignments shall be registered with the Copyrights Appellate Board, and failure to register will render the assignee unable to enforce the assigned rights in any legal proceeding under this Act. The Board may, upon application by a third party demonstrating substantial reliance on an unregistered assignment, grant temporary relief pending registration, provided that such application includes evidence of good faith and demonstrable prejudice resulting from the lack of registration. Further, where a license is granted through a collective management organization, the terms governing royalty distribution shall be subject to review and approval by the Copyrights Appellate Board.

For the purposes of this Act, where a trade mark is designated for protection in India through an international application filed under the means madrid agreement, the designation shall be deemed to constitute a separate application relating only to India. Such application is subject to all requirements and procedures applicable under this Act to applications for registration as if it were an initial application made directly within India. The Registrar may require the deposit of any prescribed fees associated with such international designations. Provided that, where an international registration extends protection to India, subsequent amendments or renewals shall be processed in accordance with regulations pertaining to extensions of existing registrations and subject to compliance with all relevant provisions regarding distinctiveness and non-use.

An applicant seeking a patent under this Act shall file a request for institution of examination within six months from the date on which the application is deemed to have been made available for public inspection. Provided that, if an application has been published earlier than the date it is deemed to have been made available for public inspection, the time limit for filing the said request shall be reckoned from the date of such publication. Where the applicant fails to file a request within the stipulated period, the Controller may issue a notice requiring the applicant to show cause why the application should not be refused. The period specified in the notice shall not exceed thirty days. In cases where an invention is claimed to originate from research supported by funds received from outside India, the applicant must declare such funding and provide details of the grant agreement. It is further provided that india filed months after initial publication are considered for examination priority.

An application for registration as a registered user layout shall be made to the Controller within six months from the date of first commercial exploitation of the layout-design, or where such exploitation has not occurred, within three years from the date of its initial publication. The application must specify the nature and extent of the use sought by the applicant, and provide evidence demonstrating a substantial investment in resources directly attributable to the utilization of the registered layout-design. Upon receipt of an application, the Controller may require further information or clarification regarding the proposed usage. Any objection to the registration of a registered user layout shall be filed within thirty days from the date of publication of the application under this Act. The Controller shall afford all parties an opportunity for hearing before making any determination concerning the validity of the registration.

A geographical indication, when registered under this Act, shall confer upon the applicant and their successors in interest the exclusive right to use the geographical indication in relation to those goods in respect of which it is registered. The Registrar may, subject to such conditions as may be deemed necessary, grant a license to use a registered geographical indication to an applicant who demonstrates a legitimate interest and a need to use the indication for purposes consistent with the protection of the reputation of the geographical indication goods. Any association of producers or artisans concerned with the production of geographical indication goods may, with the prior approval of the Central Government, exercise the rights conferred by this Act on behalf of the producers. A false application of a geographical indication, or a representation that goods are of a particular geographical origin when they are not, shall be actionable under this Act and may result in injunction and damages. The Central Government shall maintain a register of all registered geographical indications and shall make it available for public inspection.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may be made by any association of persons, cooperative society, producer company or other body of persons engaged in production or processing of goods, or by collectives, but no person shall represent themselves as a legal practitioner person unless they are duly enrolled under the Advocates Act. Upon receiving an application, the Registrar shall issue a public notice inviting objections to the proposed registration, and any interested party may file such objections within the time specified therein. If, after considering all objections, the Registrar is satisfied that the applicant meets the criteria for eligibility as defined under this Act, and that the geographical indication qualifies as a defendant geographical indication signifying unique qualities attributable to its origin, then provisional registration shall be granted pending examination of distinctiveness.

Any proprietor seeking registration of a trade mark shall diligently maintain its distinctiveness and reputation following grant; failure to do so constitutes grounds for revocation under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving complaint from any interested party demonstrating material damage resulting from use contrary to accepted regulations concerning registration common regulations, initiate proceedings for rectification of the register. Such complaints must be substantiated with documentary evidence establishing ongoing misrepresentation or dilution of brand identity. Any person found guilty of knowingly employing a deceptively similar mark shall face penalties including fines up to five hundred thousand rupees and imprisonment extending to three years; repeat offences will attract enhanced sanctions as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against a proposed mark registration act on the grounds of likelihood of confusion with any existing mark registered under this Act, the Registrar shall provide both the applicant and the proprietor of the earlier mark with an opportunity for written submissions and oral hearing. The Registrar may, after considering such submissions and hearings, direct that the marks be accepted or refused, or impose limitations on the scope of either registration, provided that such limitations are demonstrably necessary to avoid a likelihood of confusion as assessed under this Act. Any party aggrieved by any direction issued by the Registrar may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, subject to payment of prescribed fees.

An application for registration of a layout design may be filed by the creator of the layout design or by any person authorized by him to make such an application. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the layout design, including its title and a concise description of its function. Where the layout design incorporates elements which are commonplace or readily accessible, the applicant must demonstrate that the overall arrangement constitutes original authorship. Registration shall confer upon the registered creator exclusive rights to exploit the layout design commercially for a period as provided herein. Any person seeking to utilize a registered creators layout designs without authorization may be subject to remedies available under this Act.

An applicant seeking to obtain a grant patent shall submit a complete specification detailing the invention, including its utility and mode of manufacture, accompanied by requisite drawings where applicable. The Controller may require further clarification or experimental data demonstrating non-obviousness over existing prior art, provided that such requests are reasonable and do not unduly delay processing. An invention shall be deemed obvious if it is readily deducible by a person skilled in the relevant field from knowledge available before the date of filing. Furthermore, any claim within the patent application must clearly define the scope of protection sought; ambiguous or overly broad claims may be rejected under this Act. The applicant’s entitlement to the grant shall also be verified against records maintained by the government.

The application for registration of a trade mark shall contain such particulars as may be prescribed, including a representation of the marks applied for and a list of goods or services associated therewith. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar shall examine it to ascertain whether it complies with the requirements of this Act. If the Registrar finds that the applicant has not furnished the requisite information or that the form is incomplete, he may require the applicant to submit such further particulars as are necessary for proper examination. The decision of the Registrar in respect of acceptance or rejection of an application shall be final, subject to appeal under this Act. Further, the registrar accordance with established practice may issue directions regarding procedural aspects of registration and renewals.

For the purposes of this Act, “person” shall include not only an individual, but also any body corporate or association of individuals, whether incorporated or unincorporated. Where a dispute arises concerning whether an entity qualifies as a "person" under this definition, the Controller may require submission of relevant constitutive documents and operational records for examination. An appeal against such determination by the Controller lies to the Appellate Board, subject to the condition that the appellant demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the initial assessment. Provided that, in cases involving foreign entities claiming “person” status, verification of domicile and principal place of business shall be mandatory, and any challenge to this verification may be raised before a designated tribunal as provided herein.

Any producer failing to remit the prescribed registry fee within thirty days from the date specified on the official demand notice issued under this Act shall be deemed to have committed an offence and is liable, upon conviction, to a fine not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated failure to pay such fees, or attempting to evade payment through fraudulent means, will attract further penalties as determined by the Controller. The Controller may, at his discretion, initiate proceedings for recovery of outstanding registry fees as arrears of land revenue. Any person found assisting a producer in circumventing these fee obligations shall also be subject to similar fines and potential prosecution under this Act.

The proprietor of a registered geographical indication relating to tea may grant non-exclusive licenses conferring the right to use the indication on tea products meeting specified quality standards as provided herein. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and filed with the Registrar within thirty days of their execution, detailing the scope of permitted usage, duration, and any royalties payable. Assignment of rights under a geographical indication registration may occur only with the prior consent of the Central Government, ensuring continued adherence to production norms established for that particular geographical indication goods. Any subsequent owner acquiring such assignment shall be bound by all conditions precedent applicable to the original proprietor’s license agreements. The Registrar may, after due inquiry and subject to principles of natural justice, refuse registration of an assignment deemed detrimental to the reputation or distinctiveness of the registered geographical indication.

A mark shall not be registered as a trade mark under this Act if it contains any indication likely to deceive consumers regarding the nature, quality or geographical origin of goods or services. Where a sign functions primarily as an indication customary in the relevant trade, and its use is prevalent and understood by those familiar with such trade practices, registration may proceed provided that evidence demonstrating non-distinctiveness has not been presented. The Registrar shall consider any submissions from interested parties regarding the customary nature of a mark and whether it serves solely to describe goods or services. Further, an application for registration shall be refused if the proposed mark comprises exclusively marks indications customary in relation to the goods or services concerned, unless the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive use over a significant period.

Where the proprietor of a registered trade mark, intending to grant a license for use of the mark, desires to assign the right to collect royalties arising from such licensed use, he shall submit a declaration to the Registrar detailing the terms and conditions governing both the license and the assignment. This declaration must specify the duration of the license, the geographical territory covered, and the nature of the goods or services in relation to which the mark may be used under the license. The Registrar may require further clarification regarding any aspect of these regulations before registering the assignment. Provided that the assignment is consistent with the terms initially stipulated within the licensing agreement, it shall be deemed valid. Any subsequent alteration to the license’s scope requires prior notification and approval from the Registrar, ensuring continued compliance as provided herein.

An international registration shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, confer on the proprietor the same rights as if the trade mark had been registered in India directly under this Act. Where an application for registration is pending before the Trade Marks Registry at the time of the international registration, and the applicant satisfies the Registrar that the application relates to the same trade mark and goods or services as those covered by the international registration, the pending application shall be deemed to have been withdrawn as from the date of the international registration. Provided that, the applicant may, within a period of three months from the date of such deeming, elect to proceed with the pending application, in which case the international registration shall not confer any rights in respect of the goods or services covered by the pending application. Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar under this provision may, within one month, prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board as provided herein. The Registrar may, at any time, require the proprietor of an international registration to furnish a certificate of renewal from the International Bureau.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Registrar relating to the registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit or any other matter under this Act may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. Such appeal shall be made within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order and shall state specifically the grounds on which the order is sought to be challenged, failing which the appeal shall be deemed void ab initio. The Tribunal may, after giving notice to all concerned parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, confirm, modify or reverse the order appealed against. Decisions of the Appellate Tribunal are final subject to further appeals under the relevant provisions concerning copyrights appellate jurisdiction. Any infringement of layout-design rights shall attract penalties as provided herein.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions of this Act, file a petition with the High Court contesting the validity of an international registration designating India, if such registration conflicts with a prior registered trade mark or a pending application for registration in India relating to identical or similar goods or services. The High Court shall, following notice to the proprietor of the international registration and any relevant parties, determine whether the grounds for contesting the registration are substantiated. Provided that, the international bureau’s refusal to grant protection in its country of origin shall be admissible evidence, but not conclusive. An appeal from any order of the High Court in respect of an international registration trade dispute may be made to the Supreme Court, subject to such conditions as the Supreme Court may prescribe. The burden of proving non-use, as provided herein, shall lie with the party alleging non-use.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark may, by instrument in writing and subject to such terms and conditions as they deem fit, grant a license to use the trade mark for specific goods or services. Such licenses shall be assignable, either wholly or partially, provided that any assignment is notified to the Registrar within thirty days of its execution. The provisions act relating to sub-licensing are governed by regulations framed under this Act and published in the Official Gazette; these will detail requirements regarding territorial limitations and duration. A manufactured notification specifying the precise scope of permitted use shall accompany every license agreement, and copies thereof must be filed with the Registrar within fourteen days of the grant. Any alteration to a licensed trade mark requires prior written consent from the proprietor and subsequent registration as a variation under this Act.

Subject to any directions issued under this Act, no person shall institute any proceedings for the enforcement of any right granted herein against the proprietor of a registered trade mark unless he has previously given the proprietor notice specifying the nature of the infringement and demanding that such infringement be stayed. Provided that where the infringement consists of the application of a false or deceptive indication relating to goods or services, the remedies available under this Act may be sought without prior demand. The proprietor shall have a right to apply to the relevant authority for an injunction restraining any act of infringement discovered after the notice has been served. Any damages recoverable in relation registered trade mark infringement shall be determined having regard to all relevant factors including loss suffered by the proprietor and profits made by the infringer.

Where, following the grant of a patent under this Act, it is demonstrated to the Controller, through presentation of verifiable *ii india document* and supporting affidavits, that the patented invention was commercially exploited by an unauthorized party within India without the consent of the patentee, the Controller may order such infringing entity to pay damages proportionate to the profits derived from said exploitation. Such damages shall be calculated considering the reasonable royalty which would have been payable had a license been granted to the patentee. Further, the Controller may, subject to due process and opportunity for both parties to present their case, issue an injunction restraining the infringer from further commercialization of the invention. The patentee shall bear the burden of proving unauthorized exploitation and resultant profits; provided that the Controller may consider evidence demonstrating a pattern of similar activity in determining reasonable royalty.

For the purposes of this Act, "plate" means any lithographic, photogravure, etching, or similar artistic work produced by mechanical means and intended for reproduction, whether singly or in combination with other works. A plate shall be deemed to include stereoscopic plates and electrotypes derived therefrom. The right of copyright subsists in a plate as if it were an engraving under this Act, subject to the condition that such plate is original in its creation. Reproduction of any substantial part of a plate without authorization from the owner of the copyright therein shall constitute infringement, provided that fair dealing for research or private study is permitted as provided herein.

Where a registered layout design is infringed by any act constituting certification trade, the aggrieved party may institute civil proceedings for redress. Such proceedings shall be before the relevant jurisdictional court, subject to its discretion regarding interim injunctions and other equitable remedies as provided herein. The court may grant relief including damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the copyright holder, or a reasonable royalty, whichever is greater. Furthermore, the infringing party shall be liable to pay costs of the litigation. Any application for rectification of registration alleging infringement under this Act must first be made before the Layout Design Registrar, who shall entertain such applications and conduct hearings as deemed appropriate. The registrar’s decision may then be appealed to the jurisdictional court.

Where any person makes use of a registered mark without authorization from the proprietor, and such use creates confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services offered under that unauthorized mark, then such person shall be deemed guilty of an offence. The penalty for this offence shall be imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, and with a fine which shall not be less than fifty thousand rupees. Further, any goods bearing the infringing mark are liable to seizure and destruction as provided herein. Nothing in this section shall prevent civil remedies available under this Act, including an injunction restraining further use of the mark. The proprietor is entitled to recover damages suffered due to the unauthorized *mark uses registered*.

Where a patent is jointly owned by multiple applicants, each owner shall hold an equal share patent in the invention, subject to any contractual agreements executed prior to the grant. Such agreements may specify varying percentages of ownership and define rights pertaining to exploitation of the patented invention. The Controller may, upon application from one or more joint owners, facilitate the transfer or assignment of a share patent to another party, provided that all other co-owners consent in writing or demonstrate an inability to participate in the commercialization efforts. Any license granted by one joint owner shall be deemed to bind all other joint owners unless explicitly excluded within the original agreement establishing the share patent arrangement. Further, any action taken concerning the patent’s enforcement requires the collective authorization of the holders of a majority share patent interest.

Where a patent application is filed claiming priority from a foreign application, and an objection is raised by any interested party alleging that the claimed invention was anticipated or rendered obvious by prior publication occurring before the date of the said foreign application, the Controller shall provide the applicant with a reasonable opportunity to demonstrate the validity of the claim based on the priority document. Such demonstration shall be considered in light of the evidence presented and the arguments advanced by both parties. The decision of the Controller regarding novelty and inventive step, as determined under this Act, may be appealed before an appellate authority. It is provided that any appeal must specify the grounds upon which it is founded, and failure to do so will render the appeal inadmissible.

For the purpose of this Act, a “trade marks registry” includes any office established under this Act for receiving applications for registration of trade marks, conducting hearings, and maintaining records pertaining to registered trade marks. The Registrar shall maintain at each trade marks registry a register of trade mark applications and registrations in that jurisdiction, accessible for public inspection subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. Any communication required or permitted to be made under this Act with the trade marks registry shall be deemed duly served when delivered at the appropriate office location, as notified by the Registrar. The term "jurisdiction" refers to the geographical area assigned to a particular trade marks registry.

The appeal against any decision rendered by the Controller General Patents relating to the grant, revocation or sealing of a patent shall be made within sixty days from the date of communication of such decision. Provided that where the appellant was prevented by act of God, public emergency or other cause beyond his control from filing an appeal within the said period, the Board may entertain the appeal if sufficient cause is shown for the delay. The Board may, subject to just considerations and after affording opportunity of being heard to all concerned parties, allow such delayed appeal. Any order made by the Board under this Act shall be final. Further, the Controller General Patents may, at his discretion, require a party seeking review of a decision to furnish security for costs.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a process for producing a substance defined by its chemical composition, the Controller may, upon application made by any person aggrieved, review the decision to grant said patent if it is demonstrated that the claimed subject matter lacks novelty or involves an obvious modification of existing knowledge. Such applications shall be accompanied by reasoned arguments and supporting documentation substantiating the grounds for challenge. The Patent Office shall provide a reasonable opportunity for both the applicant and the patentee to present their respective cases, including expert testimony. Patents shall entered in the register with notations reflecting any such review proceedings and their outcomes, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

The Registrar shall maintain a comprehensive register detailing the assignment and licensing of rights pertaining to registered trademarks, including provisions for collective mark schemes. Any proprietor seeking to assign or license their trademark, or any portion thereof, to another party shall file a formal notice with the Registrar within thirty days of such transaction. This notice must specify the precise index names proprietors involved in the transfer, the scope of the assigned rights, and the duration of any licensing agreement. The Registrar may require further documentation substantiating the validity of the assignment or license, as deemed necessary. Failure to comply with these notification requirements shall render the assignment or license unenforceable against third parties unless registered within a period of six months from the date of execution. Further provisions relating to sub-licensing are detailed under this Act.

The registered proprietor of a layout-design may, subject to the terms of any contract to the contrary, assign the right, title and interest in the layout-design, or any right therein, to any other person, and such assignment shall be in writing and shall be subject to such conditions, if any, as may be agreed upon between the parties. Any license granted under this Act, whether exclusive or non-exclusive, shall be in writing and shall specify the duration, scope, and territorial limits of the license, as well as the royalty or other consideration payable. Where a dispute arises concerning the validity of an assignment or the terms of a license, or any alleged infringement thereof, the aggrieved party may apply to the authority appellate board for redressal. The authority appellate board shall have the power to examine the evidence, hear the parties, and pass such orders as it deems fit, including orders for specific performance, injunction, or damages, subject to the provisions contained herein. Any decision of the authority appellate board shall be final and binding on all parties, unless appealed to the High Court.

A trade mark registered under this Act shall be taken as conclusive evidence of the proprietorship thereof and of the exclusive right to use the said trade mark subject to the provisions contained herein. However, such registration may be challenged on grounds including but not limited to a prior existing identical or deceptively similar trade mark, or where the registered trade mark is devoid of any distinctive character at the time of application. A collective trade mark, being a mark distinguishing goods or services of members of an association, shall confer rights only upon those authorized by the association and subject to its regulations as filed with the Trade Marks Registry. Any assignment of a registered trade mark requires written consent from the Registrar and adherence to prescribed procedures.

Any person applying for registration of a trade mark shall furnish a clear and unambiguous notice of such application to the Trade Marks Registry, failing which the application shall be deemed defective and liable to be rejected as provided herein. Such notice applicant registration shall include a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and the applicant’s name and address for service. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered in association with a pre-existing, relating trade mark, the applicant shall disclose the nature of the connection, if any, and provide evidence of lawful use. Failure to accurately disclose such relating trade mark or to provide supporting evidence shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Repeated non-compliance with these provisions may result in the Registrar refusing further applications from the offending party and initiating proceedings for fraud. The Registrar may, subject to due process, impose additional conditions as deemed necessary to ensure transparency and prevent undue advantage.

An application for registration of a Semiconductor Integrated Circuit Layout-Design shall be filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form and shall contain such information as is required under this Act. The applicant shall furnish particulars relating to the creator of the layout-design, including their address for service in India, and specify whether the applicant claims right to protection as the first maker or otherwise, providing supporting documentation where applicable. Upon receipt of an application, the Registrar may direct the applicant to rectify any defects or omissions therein. The Registrar shall publish a notice of the application in the Official Gazette and on the website maintained by the Office. Objections to the registration, if any, must be filed within three months from the date of such publication, detailing grounds for opposition as provided herein. The Registrar shall consider all objections received and may afford the applicant an opportunity to respond before proceeding with examination.

The applicant seeking registration of a trade mark for goods produced limits india shall, at the time of application, furnish a statement detailing the origin of such goods, specifying whether they are manufactured or produced within India or imported from outside India. Where goods are produced limits india, the applicant shall submit evidence establishing substantial local production, including details of manufacturing facilities, workforce employed, and value addition occurring within the territory of India. An applicant claiming use of a trade mark on goods produced limits india, but lacking demonstrable local production, may be required to provide a clear undertaking to establish such production within a specified timeframe, not exceeding two years, failing which the application may be subject to refusal. The Registrar may, subject to verification of submitted evidence, grant a conditional registration, contingent upon fulfillment of the production undertaking as provided herein. Any false declaration regarding the origin or production of goods shall render the registration liable to revocation.

For the purposes of this Act, the term ‘registered proprietor’ shall mean the person or entity entered in the Register as the holder of the registration for a trademark, and includes any assignee of that registration who has duly recorded their title with the Trade Marks Registry. A registered proprietor is entitled to exercise all rights conferred by virtue of such registration, subject to the provisions contained herein. Where a trade mark is jointly owned, each joint owner shall be deemed a registered proprietor, and may act independently in relation to the trademark unless otherwise agreed between them in writing. Any transfer of ownership or interest in a registered trade mark requires formal assignment as provided within this Act, failing which such transfer shall not confer rights equivalent to those of a registered proprietor.

Any person seeking to challenge the acceptance of a respect registered application shall file an objection with the Registrar within three months from the date of advertisement under this Act. Such objection must specify, with particularity, the grounds upon which the challenge is based and demonstrate demonstrable prejudice resulting from registration proceeding. Failure to adhere to these procedural requirements will render the objection inadmissible. The Registrar may, at his discretion, require further evidence substantiating the claims made in the objection. Where an objection is upheld, any fees paid towards the respect registered application shall be forfeited to the government. Deliberate submission of false information within an objection constitutes a cognizable offence punishable with imprisonment and fine.

The Registrar may accept an application for registration of a trade mark if he considers that the proposed trade mark is distinctive in its intended class and is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of the applicant from those of others. However, an application shall be refused if the representation of the trade mark includes any element which directly suggests the nature, quality or geographical origin of such goods or services. Where a trade mark is sought to be registered in relation to particular goods or services, evidence of the *trade mark used* in connection with those goods or services may be required by the Registrar as proof of its existence and reputation. The applicant shall furnish such evidence within the time specified under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee desiring to grant a license under his patent shall file with the Controller a request specifying the terms and conditions of such license, including royalty rates, duration, and geographical area of application. The Controller may, after giving notice to the patentee and interested parties and affording them an opportunity of being heard, approve or disapprove of the proposed license, provided that approval shall not be withheld solely on the grounds that the royalty rate is deemed inadequate. Assignment of a patent, or any interest therein, shall also require notification to the Controller, accompanied by prescribed fees. The Controller may record such assignments and provide certificates thereof, which shall be binding evidence of the transfer of rights as provided herein. Any subsequent dealing with the license or assignment requires similar notification.

Where a patentee grants a licence to any person, such grant shall be deemed to create an interest in property and subject to the provisions of this Act, may be assigned, mortgaged, or alienated in manner similar to other forms of movable property. The term "means licence patentee" signifies that for the purposes of revocation proceedings under this Act, a party holding a license granted by the original patentee shall possess standing to petition where such license explicitly confers upon them the right to enforce the patent against infringement. Further, any alteration or modification to the terms of a licence agreement affecting the scope of the patented invention requires prior notification to the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trademarks. This requirement applies irrespective of whether the alteration is undertaken by the patentee or the licensee. The Controller may issue directions regarding such alterations if deemed necessary to protect public interest.

Where a patent has lapsed due to non-payment of the prescribed renewal fee, any person aggrieved may institute proceedings before the relevant High Court seeking restoration of the patent. Such application shall be made within six months from the date on which the lapse occurred and must demonstrate reasonable cause for the failure to pay said fee. The Controller may, subject to satisfying himself that the applicant has a prima facie case, grant leave to file such an application. Failure to comply with any condition imposed by the Controller in granting such leave shall render the application liable to dismissal without further hearing. Any person found to have knowingly and willfully obstructed or hindered the renewal process shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years.

The gene fund shall be established and maintained by the Plant Variety Protection Authority, and shall be applied for the promotion of plant research and the welfare of farmers, particularly small and marginal farmers, as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the allocation of resources from the gene fund, or the eligibility of a claimant to receive benefits therefrom, may be raised before the Authority, which shall conduct a hearing and issue a reasoned order. An appeal from any such order shall lie to the High Court, subject to the provisions of this Act concerning limitation periods for appeals. Provided that, the Authority may, in cases of demonstrable urgency affecting livelihoods, authorize a temporary disbursement from the gene fund pending the resolution of any appeal. The Authority shall maintain detailed records of all contributions to, and disbursements from, the gene fund, and shall submit an annual report to the Central Government. Any allegation of mismanagement or misappropriation of funds shall be investigated by a committee appointed by the Central Government.

Any person who, without due authorization from the registered proprietor of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design, makes, imports, sells, or offers to sell any product in which the design is applied or embodied, shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be determined by the Court, taking into consideration the loss of profits suffered by the proprietor and reasonable royalty that such infringer would have paid had they obtained a license under this Act. The Court may also issue an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement, subject to conditions as it deems fit. Repeated or willful infringements shall attract enhanced penalties, including imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, and fines which may extend to ten times the value of goods produced or sold infringing the design act.

Where an applicant seeks to introduce alterations to a patent application beyond those permissible under this Act relating to clerical errors or obvious matters, such proposed amendments shall constitute an amendment claim specification. The Controller may allow such amendment only if he is satisfied that the alteration does not substantially alter the nature of the invention as originally disclosed and that the amended claims remain clear and concise. Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Controller permitting or refusing an amendment claim specification may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, demonstrating how the amendment fundamentally changes the scope of protection sought and prejudices their existing rights under this Act. The Board’s determination shall be final.

Where an application for patent is granted subject to a condition imposed under this Act, and such condition relates to the use of the invention in respect of any particular field, the Controller may, upon receiving a representation from any person aggrieved by the imposition of that condition, direct the revision thereof. Such direction shall be accompanied by notice served upon the patentee, affording them an opportunity to make representations against the proposed modification or removal of the condition. The Controller shall consider all submissions received and issue an order either confirming, modifying, or revoking the imposed condition. A condition declared unlawful under this Act due to its discriminatory effect on competition may be subject to immediate revocation without prior notice to the patentee if it is deemed a matter of urgency affecting public interest. Appeals against orders issued by the Controller concerning conditions shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Any patentee of a pharmaceutical substance, being a process or a product, may grant licenses to other persons to work the patented invention, subject to such terms and conditions as may be mutually agreed upon and recorded with the Controller. Where a license is granted in respect of a pharmaceutical substance essential to public health, the Controller may, upon application by any person, direct the patentee to grant a license to that person, if the patentee fails to do so within a reasonable time. Assignment of any right, title or interest in a patent for a pharmaceutical substance shall be subject to the provisions of this Act, and all instruments of assignment shall be in writing and registered with the Controller. The assignee shall, for the unexpired term of the patent, possess the same rights as the assignor, provided that the assignee demonstrates sufficient manufacturing capacity for the pharmaceutical substance. Any royalty payments due under an assignment or license agreement shall be determined as per the terms agreed between the parties, but shall not be manifestly unreasonable.

Any person aggrieved by the registration of a trade mark may apply to the Trade Marks Registry for rectification of the register, and such application shall be made in the prescribed manner and be accompanied by the prescribed fee. The Registry shall, upon receipt of such application, cause a notice to be served upon the proprietor of the trade mark, requiring him to state within a prescribed period whether he consents to the rectification sought. Should the proprietor consent, the Registry shall make the necessary alterations to the register and notify the applicant accordingly. If no consent is received, or if the proprietor disputes the grounds for rectification, the matter shall be referred to the High Court for determination. The High Court, acting as a rectification register court, shall consider the evidence presented and may, subject to the provisions of this Act, either confirm the registration, order its rectification, or dismiss the application. Evidence relating to prior use or inherent distinctiveness may be presented during such proceedings.

An international application form filed pursuant to this Act shall be accompanied by a certified true copy of the Indian registration certificate, or where such certificate has not been issued, evidence of prior use in India satisfactory to the Registrar. The Registrar may require any applicant submitting an international application form to furnish further documentation demonstrating compliance with applicable treaty obligations and regulations; failure to do so within thirty days shall render the application liable for rejection. Where a trade mark registered following an international application is subsequently found to infringe upon existing rights, or where evidence emerges of fraudulent misrepresentation in the initial application process, the High Court may order court directed forfeiture of the registration, subject to due process and opportunity for the registrant to be heard. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all international applications received, accessible for public inspection as provided herein.

For the purposes of this Act, a “producer” shall mean any person who undertakes or participates in the creation of a patented invention through manufacturing, processing, or other substantial modification resulting in a commercially viable product. Where such production involves reliance upon technical information disclosed within a patent specification, the producer shall be deemed to have exercised due diligence subject to demonstrating reasonable efforts to independently verify the accuracy and completeness of said information. Any person claiming status as a producer may submit evidence of their manufacturing process for inspection as provided herein. Acknowledged producers are entitled to certain benefits relating to royalty payments, contingent upon adherence to quality control standards established by the Controller. Failure to maintain such standards may result in revocation of producer status.

The Authority Appellate Board is constituted for adjudicating disputes arising under this Act concerning layout-design registrations or related matters. The Chairperson of the Board shall be a retired Judge of a High Court, appointed by notification in the Official Gazette. Members of the Board shall include individuals possessing specialized knowledge and experience in semiconductor technology, intellectual property law, or industrial design, as determined by the Central Government. Decisions of the Authority Appellate Board shall be binding on all parties involved, subject to appeal to such higher judicial forum as may be prescribed under this Act. The Board’s proceedings shall adhere to principles of natural justice.

Any person who, without authorization from the Geographical Indications Registry, uses a protected geographical indication in relation to goods for which that indication is registered, or applies it in a manner likely to deceive or cause confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin of those goods, shall be liable for damages. Such damages will be assessed based on the extent of misrepresentation and resultant loss suffered by authorized users. Further, any proprietor of a registered geographical indication may apply to the civil court for an injunction restraining such unauthorized use. The court may also order seizure and destruction of infringing materials. Penalties under this Act shall be without prejudice to any action that may be taken against the offender under other applicable laws concerning unfair trade practices or infringement or for passing off referred to in section 66.

Any goods or services a mark which is identical or confusingly similar to a registered geographical indication shall be guilty of an offence and liable to prosecution under this Act. It shall be a defence for the accused to prove that he had used the said mark in good faith prior to the registration of the geographical indication, provided that such use did not constitute an attempt to deceive consumers regarding the origin of the goods or services. An appeal against any order made by the Registrar determining whether a particular act constitutes falsify geographical indication may be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order to the appellant. The Appellate Board shall hear and dispose of such appeals expeditiously, subject to principles of natural justice.

Where a proprietor of a registered trade mark institutes proceedings for infringement under this Act, and demonstrates that an alleged infringing advertisement contains an express or implied acceptance of offer relating to goods or services identical or similar to those for which the trade mark is registered, such acceptance shall be deemed material for establishing passing off.
