The court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further use of the offending advertisement if it finds that the advertised acceptance relates directly to the distinctive character of the registered trade mark and creates a likelihood of confusion amongst consumers regarding the origin or quality of the goods or services. Damages, including loss of profits and account of profits, shall be awarded subject to principles of fairness and equity, considering the extent to which the defendant’s conduct has exploited the reputation associated with the registered trade mark.

Where an article patented process incorporates elements protected by copyright under this Act, and a license is granted permitting utilization of said patented process, the terms governing royalties manner shall be explicitly defined within the licensing agreement. Such agreements must detail the calculation methodology for royalty payments, specifying whether these are based on net sales revenue derived from products manufactured using the licensed process or another agreed-upon metric. Provided that the copyright owner retains all rights not expressly assigned under the license, any assignment of such rights relating to the patented process shall require a written instrument duly executed and registered as provided herein. Furthermore, sublicensing is permitted subject to conditions stipulated in the primary license agreement, ensuring continued adherence to the agreed royalties manner and safeguarding the integrity of copyright protection.

Any person who knowingly and without authorization makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any product incorporating a registered layout design shall be liable for damages. Such damages shall be assessed at an amount not less than five per centum of the cost of production of the infringing article nor more than ten per centum thereof, as determined by the relevant civil court. Further, where infringement is established, the Court may order the destruction or disposal of the infringing products and materials used in their manufacture. The registered layout design proprietor shall have the right to apply for interlocutory orders restraining any acts that would constitute an infringement under this Act, subject to just terms. Repeated contravention of these provisions may result in imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years.

Where a trade mark is registered in the name of a company, and any element thereof is also registered *mark separately registered*, the proprietor may, subject to an agreement in writing, grant a license to use the entire trade mark or any particular goods or services associated with that mark. Such licenses shall be assignable by the grantor, provided that the assignee complies with all conditions precedent to the original registration and subsequent licensing agreements. Further, a company may, through board resolution duly recorded in its minutes, irrevocably assign the right to use a *mark separately registered* element of its composite trade mark to another entity, including an individual or partnership, as it deems fit. Any such assignment shall be notified to the Trade Marks Registry within thirty days and shall become effective upon registration thereof.

Where an appeal lies against a determination made under this Act regarding the originality of a creators layout designs, the Appellate Authority shall consider whether the alleged copying constitutes substantial similarity, taking into account both the overall impression and any distinctive features. The appellant shall bear the burden of demonstrating that the finding of the original determining authority was erroneous; however, the respondent may present evidence to rebut such claims. It is provided that a determination regarding infringement shall not be invalidated solely on grounds of minor procedural irregularities. Further, the Appellate Authority may order discovery of relevant documents if it deems necessary for just resolution of the dispute and subject to reasonable restrictions as prescribed by regulations.

Any person possessing a registered layout-design shall, subject to the provisions of this Act, have the exclusive right to exploit the layout-design in India. A license to use a registered layout-design may be granted by the registered owner to another party, and such license shall be in writing and specify the duration, scope, and territorial limits of the permitted use. Assignment of the exclusive right to a layout-design shall also be in writing and registered with the appropriate authority as provided herein, failing which such assignment shall be void. 

The register sub section maintained by the Controller of Patents shall accurately reflect all current assignments and licensed uses of registered layout-designs. An applicant seeking to protect a layout-design incorporating a distinctive mark or sign may, concurrently with the application for registration, apply trade mark protection for such mark or sign, provided that the mark does not mislead regarding the origin of the layout-design itself. Any dispute concerning the validity of a license or assignment shall be subject to the jurisdiction of the High Court.

A trade mark shall mean a mark capable of being represented graphically including signs or combinations of signs, letters, numerals, figures, shape of goods or their packaging, colours, or combinations thereof, and shall include service marks and collective marks. For the purposes of this Act, a well-known trade mark means a mark which has become reputed among the relevant public by reason of the use thereof, and may, irrespective of the goods or services in relation to which it was originally used, be recognized as a distinctive mark. A descriptive trade mark, however, shall not be registrable unless it has acquired distinctiveness through use, subject to the provisions of this Act regarding the acquisition of secondary meaning. The register of trade marks maintained under this Act shall be the primary evidence of ownership.

Any aggrieved party may initiate a case proceeding before the Trade Marks Registry, subject to the provisions contained herein, by filing a notice of opposition against a pending application for registration or against an existing registered trade mark. The Registrar shall, upon receiving such notice, notify the applicant or registered proprietor, affording them an opportunity to submit a counter-statement. A member appointed bench, consisting of at least two officers of the Trade Marks Registry, shall be constituted to examine the evidence presented by both parties. The bench may, at its discretion, require further evidence or call for hearings. Decisions rendered following a case proceeding shall be communicated in writing, detailing the grounds for acceptance or rejection of the opposition, and may be subject to appeal as provided under this Act. The Registry shall maintain a complete record of all case proceedings and associated documentation.

Where an applicant seeks to obtain a patent for an invention relating to a process by which a substance is produced, and where that process involves complex scientific principles, the Controller may, at his discretion, require the assistance of an independent scientific adviser. Such an adviser shall be appointed from a panel maintained by the Patents Office, comprising individuals possessing demonstrable expertise in the relevant field. The costs associated with the engagement of this independent scientific adviser shall be borne equally by the applicant and the patent office, subject to regulations prescribed by the Central Government. Any party aggrieved by the appointment or findings of an independent scientific adviser may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days of the order being made, provided that such appeal does not operate as a stay on any subsequent proceedings under this Act.

A breeder variety registered under this Act shall confer upon the breeder the exclusive right to commercially exploit the protected variety in any manner, including by production, sale, marketing, distribution, import, and export, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, the farmer shall have the right to save, use, sow, re-sow and multiply any farm-saved seed of a registered variety, provided that the farmer does not sell, market or distribute such saved seed in a manner that infringes the breeder’s rights. Any person who contravenes the exclusive rights of the breeder, or the farmer’s limited rights as detailed herein, shall be liable to a penalty as prescribed, and may be subject to injunction restraining further infringement. The Authority may, upon application and subject to verification, grant compulsory licenses for the exploitation of a registered variety if it is determined to be necessary in the public interest. Any dispute relating to the infringement of rights, or the grant of compulsory licenses, shall be adjudicated by the designated Tribunal.

Where the Controller publishes an application registration notice, indicating acceptance of a patent application subject to any conditions specified therein, such acceptance shall not preclude assignment or licensing of the invention claimed. Any party possessing a relevant ground for opposition under this Act may file a pre-grant opposition with the Opposition Board within the prescribed period following publication of the application registration notice. The assignor of a patent application shall provide written notification to the Controller regarding any subsequent transfer, and such notification shall be recorded as provided herein. Further, licensees granted rights under an invention claimed in a pending patent application may, subject to the terms of their license agreement, participate in opposition proceedings before the Opposition Board relating to that application.

Where a proprietor registered trade mark is used in relation to goods or services not identical with those specified in the registration, an application for the removal of the mark from the Register may be made to the Registrar by any person claiming interest. Such application shall state the grounds upon which it is based and shall include evidence demonstrating non-use of the proprietor registered trade mark for a continuous period of five years immediately preceding the date of the application. The Registrar may, after giving notice to the applicant for removal and affording him an opportunity of being heard, direct that the mark be removed from the Register if satisfied that the grounds for removal have been established. Any person aggrieved by such direction may appeal under this Act to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. The mark registered goods shall remain subject to these provisions regarding potential removal from the register.

Where an act constitutes infringement registered of a trademark as provided herein, the aggrieved proprietor may institute suit for damages sustained by reason of such infringement. The measure of damages shall be not less than a sum equivalent to the lost profits reasonably attributable to the infringement and not more than three times the amount of such losses where the infringement was found to have been committed wilfully. Further, the Court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from any further act of infringement registered, subject to just terms. It is provided that in determining damages, the Court shall consider any measures taken by the proprietor to make known the trademark in India and the extent to which the infringing use has damaged the reputation or goodwill associated with the mark. Costs of the suit shall be awarded at the discretion of the Court.

A complete specification, submitted under this Act, shall fully and particularly describe the invention and the manner in which it is to be performed. The specification must disclose the best mode contemplated by the inventor for carrying out the invention. Every claim shall be supported by matter in the complete specification as filed; any claim not so supported shall be deemed invalid. A claim complete specification, for the purposes of determining inventive step, shall be construed in light of the common knowledge in the relevant field. Provided that, where an invention involves a process, the specification shall clearly define the process and its essential features, subject to the provisions relating to secrecy where applicable. The specification may contain diagrams or drawings to illustrate the invention.

The Registrar may register a collective mark upon application made by an association conforming to the requirements prescribed herein. Such application shall state the objects of the association, the geographical area of its operation and the rules governing the use of the collective mark by members. The applicant shall furnish evidence demonstrating that the association is a body corporate or a society registered under relevant legislation and possesses the requisite authority to regulate the quality and characteristics of goods or services associated with the mark. Registration of a collective mark does not grant exclusive rights to any individual member, but rather vests such rights in the association itself, subject to adherence to the prescribed usage guidelines. Any dispute concerning eligibility for membership or infringement of the collective mark’s standards may be referred to an Arbitrator appointed by the Registrar.

An application for registration of a layout-design shall accompany an affidavit verifying the originality of the design and confirming that no prior publication or unauthorized disclosure thereof has occurred. The Controller General may require such further documentation as is deemed necessary to ascertain compliance with these provisions, including detailed schematics and manufacturing processes. Upon receipt of an application, the established registry shall conduct a preliminary examination to determine if it meets the formal requirements under this Act. If any deficiency is identified, notice shall be served upon the applicant allowing for rectification within sixty days. Failure to rectify such deficiencies within the prescribed period will result in rejection of the application as provided herein.

A geographical indication, being an indication referring to a place and the goods which originate from that place, may be licensed by the registered proprietor to applicants fulfilling such conditions as may be prescribed. Any license granted under this Act shall specify the scope of permitted use, including territorial limitations and quality standards pertaining to the goods bearing the geographical indication. The registrar may maintain a public register of all licenses recorded, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Assignment of any right in a registered geographical indication shall be effected only through a written instrument duly executed by both parties and filed with the Geographical Indications Registry. Provided that no assignment shall prejudice the rights of existing licensees unless their consent is obtained or alternative arrangements are agreed upon as provided herein. The proprietor may revoke a license for cause, following due process and affording reasonable opportunity to be heard; however, such revocation shall not affect contracts entered into prior to notice of termination.

An application for registration of a layout-design may be filed by any person claiming to be the first inventor of the design, or by any other person entitled under this Act to make an application. Where a layout-design has been previously published outside India, the applicant shall disclose all particulars of such prior publication as provided herein. The Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application, issue a notification requiring objections to be filed within three months from the date of such notification. Any person may file an objection under this Act, subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Upon determination of any objections, if satisfied that the applicant is the design registered proprietor and that the layout-design is original and not infringing existing rights, registration shall be granted.

A registered layout is defined as a final or interim version of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout, irrespective of whether it is incorporated in a semiconductor chip. The layout shall be considered original if it demonstrates independent creative thought and is not derivative of any pre-existing layout or knowledge. A layout-design, to be eligible for registration under this Act, must be inherently capable of being distinctly identified and must not be identical with any other registered layout-design. Subject to the provisions herein, a registered layout confers upon the proprietor the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, and commercially utilize the layout. Any person dealing in semiconductor integrated circuits shall, prior to manufacture, ensure that the layout is not already subject to a valid registration.

The proprietor of a collective mark may grant licenses to use the mark to members of the association entitled to its benefit, subject to such terms and conditions as are specified in the license agreement. Such agreements shall clearly delineate the scope of permissible activities under the mark, including geographical limitations and product categories. Any assignment of rights relating to a collective mark requires prior approval from the Registrar, who may condition such assignments on maintaining the integrity and quality standards associated with the mark. The association shall provide the Registrar with details of all licenses granted and assignments made, as provided herein. Further, any sublicensee or assignee shall be bound by the original license terms and conditions, and remain subject to disciplinary action under the association’s internal regulations for misuse of the collective mark.

Subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, any person claiming damages for the use of a registered trade mark without consent shall be required to demonstrate that such use has resulted in actual financial loss attributable directly to the infringement. The Registrar may, upon receiving evidence of misleading similarity between an unregistered mark and a registered trade mark, issue a notice to the proprietor of the unregistered mark, affording them opportunity to submit their response within sixty days. Failure to adequately respond shall be deemed conclusive acceptance of the Registrar’s determination regarding likelihood of confusion. Further, any party aggrieved by such determination may petition the Tribunal for review, provided that the petitioner demonstrates demonstrable prejudice resulting from the Registrar's action.

Any registered trade mark shall be transmissible by way of assignment, mortgage or otherwise, subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder. An assignment shall not be valid unless it is in writing and duly executed by or on behalf of both the assignor and the assignee, and notice of the assignment is sent to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner. Where a trade mark is mortgaged, the mortgagee shall have the same rights and remedies as a mortgagee of other movable property, but no power to sell the trade mark without the leave of the court. A transmission by operation of law, including through inheritance or bankruptcy, shall vest in the successor-in-interest the same rights and obligations as the original proprietor, provided that the successor-in-interest duly notifies the Trade Marks Registry of such transmission. Any assignment or transmission not complying with these provisions shall be voidable at the option of the aggrieved party, and the Trade Marks Registry may refuse to record such assignment or transmission.

Applications for registration of geographical indications, duly completed in the prescribed form and accompanied by the requisite fee, shall be submitted to the Registrar. The Registrar may require the applicant to submit further information or clarification regarding the application, including particulars relating to the quality and characteristics of the goods for which the geographical indication is sought, and the area of production concerned. Upon receipt of such an application, the Registrar shall publish a notice thereof in the Geographical Indications Journal. Any person feeling aggrieved by the publication may, within the time specified therein, file objections with the Registrar, stating clearly the grounds upon which such objection is based. The central government shall determine the procedure for dealing with objections received and for affording interested parties an opportunity to be heard. Following due consideration of any objections, the Registrar shall proceed as provided herein.

A breeder shall be deemed to have obtained a valid certificate issued breeder when the Plant Variety Protection Authority has formally registered a plant variety in their name, as provided herein. For the purposes of this Act, a "certificate issued breeder" signifies the legal recognition conferred upon an individual or entity demonstrating creativity and expression in developing a new plant variety. The authority may, subject to due process and opportunity for hearing, review any certificate issued breeder if it is established that the claimed novelty was not demonstrable at the time of application, or if the applicant misrepresented essential characteristics of the registered variety.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any person holding a right to intellectual property in a registered variety shall be permitted to grant licenses conferring rights to use propagating material derived from that variety. Such licenses may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may specify conditions relating to royalty payments, geographical limitations, and duration. Assignment of such rights, including the entire registered variety or specific aspects thereof, is also permissible by way of written agreement, duly executed and recorded with the Plant Varieties Registry. Any licensee seeking to sub-license rights under this Act shall obtain prior consent from the original right holder, as provided herein. The Registrar may require submission of detailed documentation pertaining to any proposed assignment or license for review and approval to ensure compliance with the objectives of promoting farmer’s rights and preventing anti-competitive practices.

The Central Government shall establish and maintain a National Gene Fund for the purposes of supporting research relating to plant genetic resources and providing benefit-sharing compensation to traditional farming communities. Contributions to the Fund shall include levies collected from registered plant variety breeders, as determined by regulations framed under this Act, and any grants received from international organizations or philanthropic entities. The Central Government may also direct that a portion of royalties derived from licensed propagating material be credited into the National Gene Fund. An advisory committee shall be constituted to oversee the management and disbursement of funds; it shall prescribed chairperson appointed by the Central Government from amongst eminent scientists and agricultural economists. All accounts pertaining to the Fund shall be audited annually, and reports submitted to the Comptroller and Auditor General of India as provided herein.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Such appeal shall lie on a question of law, and the Board may entertain appeals relating to facts only if they involve questions of public importance or affect the interests of a large number of persons. Where a geographical indication is considered geographical indication and its registration has been cancelled or revoked, any proprietor who was using the mark immediately prior to such cancellation or revocation shall be entitled to compensation as determined by the Central Government. The Central Government may, in prescribing the amount of compensation, consider factors including investments made in good faith and losses incurred due to reliance upon the registered geographical indication. Further, remedies for unfair competition involving a considered geographical indication are available under this Act.

Applications for registration of plant varieties shall include detailed particulars regarding the proposed contribution to the sources gene fund. Such contributions are mandatory and reflect a commitment to preserving genetic diversity within registered varieties. The amount contributed shall be determined based on factors including, but not limited to, the commercial viability projections submitted by the applicant during the registration process, as assessed by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Further, applicants demonstrating significant investment in conservation efforts may petition the authority for adjustments to their contribution schedule. During each house parliament session, a review of the fund’s operational efficiency and allocation procedures shall be undertaken to ensure equitable distribution amongst deserving research institutions.

For the purposes of this Act, "threatened infringement" shall mean an instance where a party communicates, either directly or indirectly, to another party that they intend to pursue legal action alleging trade mark infringement, dilution, or passing off. Such communication must reasonably appear to convey an intention to enforce rights claimed under this Act against the recipient’s use of a sign, whether identical or similar to a registered trade mark. The threat may be explicit or implied and need not specify the precise nature of the alleged violation. Provided that such communication is made in bad faith or with the primary purpose of intimidation, it shall constitute threatened infringement as provided herein.

A proprietor of a service mark shall be entitled to restrain the use in India of any trade mark which is identical or confusingly similar to his registered service mark if such use is made in connection with goods or services identical or similar to those for which the registration is granted. Provided that where the alleged infringing use occurs in relation to goods or services not identical, the proprietor shall establish a likelihood of confusion on the part of the public, and that such use would be detrimental to the distinctiveness of the mark or the reputation connecting with it. Any person aggrieved by an infringement of a registered service mark may institute suit for damages sustained thereby, or for injunction relief as provided herein. The remedy of account shall also be available where the defendant has made profits attributable to the infringement.

For the purposes of this Act, a “layout design relation” exists where two or more persons jointly create a layout-design and their contributions are not severable for the purpose of determining ownership. Such joint creation shall be deemed to establish a layout design relation unless it is demonstrated that each contributor’s effort was independent and intended solely for individual benefit. The determination of whether a layout design relation exists shall consider the degree of collaboration, the sharing of information, and any agreements entered into by the contributors. Subject to this, rights in the layout-design shall be jointly held as provided herein.

Where a trade mark is registered for goods manufactured in India, the Registrar may, upon application by any interested person and after due inquiry, direct the registration proprietor to furnish, within a prescribed period, particulars relating to the geographical location of the manufacturing premises where such goods are produced. Failure to comply with this direction shall render the registration liable to be amended to reflect that the trade mark is registered for goods manufactured in India generally, rather than from a specific defendant geographical area. The Registrar may also issue a notification requiring all proprietors of trade marks registered for goods manufactured notification to provide updated details regarding their manufacturing locations annually, as provided herein.

Any party aggrieved by an order passed under this Act may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order. The Appellate Board shall consist of a Chairperson and two other members appointed by the Central Government, possessing expertise in intellectual property law or semiconductor technology. Appeals shall be heard expeditiously, and the Board may, subject to provisions relating to natural justice, dismiss frivolous appeals with costs. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during appeal proceedings may result in dismissal. The Appellate Board’s decision shall be final, but it may award compensation for demonstrable financial loss arising from an incorrect enforcement action.

A basic application, when filed in a convention country, shall confer a right to claim priority in India, provided that such right is explicitly asserted at the time of filing the complete specification as provided herein. The applicant shall submit a certified copy of the basic application, duly translated if necessary, within the prescribed period to demonstrate lawful origin and sufficient disclosure. Failure to furnish such documentation may result in the application being deemed incomplete and subject to rejection. Where the basic application is not in the name of the applicant, evidence of title or assignment demonstrating a clear chain of ownership shall be submitted. Any subsequent amendment to the basic application must be communicated to the Controller of Patents within one month of such amendment, failing which the priority claim may be invalidated. The Controller may, subject to due process, require additional evidence to verify the validity of the asserted priority.

Any person seeking to challenge the entry of a name in the application register relating to a trademark shall file an opposition within four months from the date of publication of the said application. Failure to do so shall render such objection unenforceable under this Act. The Registrar may, upon receiving a timely and duly supported opposition, issue a notice to both the applicant and the opponent, affording them opportunities for reasoned submissions. Where the Registrar determines that the entry of a name as an *application register proprietor* is detrimental to existing rights or contrary to public interest, he shall refuse registration, and any subsequent attempt by the applicant shall be subject to enhanced scrutiny and penalties for frivolous claims.

Any person deriving economic benefit from the exploitation of a registered plant variety, including through the commercial production or sale of seeds, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act regarding benefit sharing and royalty payments. Licensing of rights to exploit a variety shall be governed by agreements negotiated between the breeder and the licensee, specifying the scope of the license, duration, and royalty rates, and such agreements shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Assignment of breeder’s rights may be effected through a written instrument duly executed by both parties, and notification of such assignment shall be submitted to the Authority within thirty days of the transfer. 

The Authority may, subject to conditions, grant licenses to facilitate the utilization of crop sciences indian for research and breeding purposes, provided that the breeder receives equitable remuneration. Failure to comply with royalty obligations or terms of the licensing agreement shall constitute grounds for revocation of the license, as provided herein, and may result in legal proceedings for recovery of due payments.

Where a patent is granted for an invention relating to a process for producing a substance controlled under this Act, the Controller may, subject to appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal, direct that the patentee shall, prior to commencing commercial exploitation of the said process, enter into an agreement with such entities as the Central Government specifies, ensuring non-discriminatory access to the produced substance. This direction may be imposed where it is demonstrated that the invention significantly impedes research or development in a field of national importance. The patentee shall have the right to challenge this imposition on grounds of manifest arbitrariness or lack of reasoned justification; however, any such challenge does not preclude the Central Government from subsequently issuing further directives concerning acquiring restrict relating to similar inventions.

Where an appeal under this Act is preferred against any order passed by the Controller, the Appellate Tribunal shall hear such appeal and may pass such orders as it thinks fit, subject to the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder. The aggrieved party may further appeal from any decision of the Appellate Tribunal to the High Court within whose territorial jurisdiction the cause of action arose, provided that such appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order. Any order passed by the High Court shall be final. It is clarified that determination of originality for purposes of copyright act protection remains solely at the discretion of the Controller unless demonstrably arbitrary or perverse.

The Registrar shall, upon receiving an application for registration of a proposed trade mark, conduct such examination as is deemed necessary to ascertain whether the mark fulfills all requirements under this Act. Where the proposed trade mark comprises a geographical indication already registered or capable of being registered under this Act, the Registrar may proceed with registration only if satisfied that use by the applicant does not constitute misleading practices or unfair competition. Justified registration shall be granted where the applicant demonstrates acquired distinctiveness through extensive and continuous use following initial application, provided that such use has created a significant association between the mark and the goods or services for which it is proposed. The Registrar may require further evidence to substantiate claims of acquired distinctiveness as deemed appropriate.

The owner of a registered geographical indication relating to Darjeeling tea may grant non-exclusive licenses permitting the use of the indication on products other than Darjeeling tea, provided that such license explicitly restricts the licensed product’s marketing as originating from Darjeeling. Any assignment of rights in respect of a geographical indication shall require prior notification to the Registrar and registration of the transfer with the Geographical Indications Registry. The Registrar may refuse registration of an assignment if it appears that the proposed assignee lacks the capacity or intention to protect the geographical indication's distinctiveness and reputation, upholding its inherent geographical indication respect. Further, any licensee granted rights under this Act shall be bound by conditions ensuring continued adherence to quality standards associated with the Darjeeling tea geographical indication.

For the purposes of this Act, "semiconductor" means a material possessing semiconducting properties, exhibiting electrical conductivity between that of a conductor and an insulator, and which is utilized in the fabrication of integrated circuits. An “integrated circuit,” as defined under this Act, includes any arrangement of semiconductor devices or other components designed to perform a specific function or functions; provided that such arrangement is fixed permanently or semi-permanently on a substrate made of ceramic, glass, silicon, or another material suitable for such purpose. The term "layout design" shall mean the three dimensional representation of the integrated circuit’s structure.

Any commission offence attributable to a person involved in the production or distribution of a cinematographic film, as understood under the provisions relating to producer relation cinematograph, shall be investigated by an officer duly authorized by the Controller of Patents. Such officer may, subject to the obtaining of a warrant issued by a Judicial Magistrate of First Class, enter any premises where reasonable suspicion exists of evidence pertaining to the offence being retained. The Controller shall maintain a register of all such investigations, detailing the nature of the alleged offence, the particulars of the accused, and the evidence collected. Where the offence involves the unauthorized use of a patented invention in the creation of the cinematographic work, the rights holder may submit a detailed report to the Controller, outlining the extent of the infringement. Failure to comply with the requirements as provided herein regarding the submission of such reports shall render the rights holder liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand rupees. Any evidence obtained during the investigation shall be admissible in any subsequent legal proceedings.

The registered proprietor of a geographical indication may grant exclusive licenses under this Act, subject to such terms and conditions as are agreed upon between the proprietor and the licensee, provided that any such license shall not extend to dealings in counterfeit goods. Any assignment of rights pertaining to a geographical indication registered under this Act shall require prior approval from the Registrar, who may demand evidence demonstrating the assignee’s commitment to upholding the quality standards associated with the indicated product. Further, where a geographical indication is jointly owned by multiple producers, any licensing or assignment agreement must be executed by all joint proprietors or their duly authorized representatives. The Registrar may impose conditions on licenses and assignments to ensure continued adherence to the code of conduct applicable to the registered geographical indication.

Where any person aggrieved by an order passed under this Act relating to the determination of copyright infringement, or concerning the rectification of entries in the Register of Copyrights, believes that such order is manifestly unjust or perverse, he may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate court shall consider only questions of law arising out of the decision appealed from and may confirm, reverse, or modify the order under appeal. Provided that an appeal lies notwithstanding any technical objection, and the Parliament may, by notification in the Official Gazette, prescribe conditions for granting leave to appeal. Any party dissatisfied with the judgment of the High Court may further appeal to the Supreme Court on such grounds as are provided herein.

The grant of a breeder's right shall confer upon the registered breeder exclusive rights to propagate the plant variety, produce and condition harvested material, and market it. Any person who without authorization from the right holder engages in acts infringing these exclusive rights shall be liable for damages, which shall include compensation for loss of profits and reasonable royalty payments as determined by a civil court. Provided that, where an infringement arises directly from the exploitation of patents granted relating to traits incorporated into the plant variety, the remedies available under this Act shall not preclude claims arising under the patent legislation. Further, any party claiming entitlement to the breeder's right may apply to the relevant authority for redressal of grievances concerning alleged unauthorized propagation or marketing, subject to demonstrating a prima facie case of infringement.

The Trade Mark Registrar shall, upon receipt of an application for registration of a trade mark, conduct an examination as provided herein to ascertain the registrability of the mark in accordance with the provisions of this Act. Where the Trade Mark Registrar has reason to believe that a mark applied for includes or is connected with a geographical indication identifying a product originating from a specific region, the Registrar may, subject to rules, require the applicant to furnish evidence of lawful user of said geographical indication or consent from the producers associated with that region. Any objection raised by the Trade Mark Registrar shall be communicated to the applicant in writing, detailing the grounds for such objection and affording the applicant a reasonable opportunity to submit a response. The Trade Mark Registrar may, after considering the applicant’s response, either accept the application, require further evidence, or refuse registration, with a reasoned order. All decisions of the Trade Mark Registrar shall be subject to appeal to the Appellate Board. The Registrar shall maintain a register of all registered trade marks and geographical indications, accessible for public inspection.

Where any party believes that a patent has been granted in contravention of, or otherwise than in accordance with the provisions of this Act, such party may, within six months from the date of publication of grant of the patent, file a notice of opposition with the Controller. The notice shall specify the grounds upon which the opposition is based and shall be accompanied by a statement of facts relied upon to support the objection. Subject to any procedural direction issued by the Controller, the patentee shall be afforded an opportunity to respond to the notice of opposition within a prescribed period. Any appeal against an order passed by the Controller in respect of such opposition lies to the Appellate Board, and is subject to the provisions regarding limitation periods as provided herein.

Any person seeking registration of a trade mark, as provided herein, shall furnish a declaration confirming that the applicant is a citizen of, or is domiciled in, or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in India, or is a citizen of, or is domiciled in, or has a real and effective industrial or commercial establishment in a Contracting State or a Contracting Organisation. Where an application is made by a person resident outside India, but claiming rights through association to a Contract ing State or a Contracting Organisation, such applicant shall submit evidence of such association, including documentation establishing the legal standing of the applicant within that jurisdiction. The Controller may, subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed, require further verification of the applicant’s status and the nature of their connection to the relevant Contracting State or Organisation. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence of such association shall render the application liable to be refused, and the applicant shall have no recourse under this Act. Any false declaration made under this provision shall be punishable as contempt of this Act.

Any person intending to initiate a dispute regarding the validity of a registered layout-design, or alleging infringement thereof, shall submit a zm form petition to the appropriate authority designated for the purpose, and such petition shall be accompanied by a non-refundable fee as prescribed in Schedule III. The petition shall clearly and concisely state the grounds upon which the dispute is founded, identifying with particularity the registered layout-design in question and the alleged acts of infringement. Supporting documentation, including but not limited to, technical drawings, samples of the integrated circuit, and evidence of commercial exploitation, may be submitted to substantiate the claims made within the petition. 

Provided that, a petition lacking the requisite fee or failing to adequately specify the grounds for dispute may be rejected by the authority. The authority, upon receipt of a complete zm form petition, shall, subject to the provisions contained herein, notify the respondent and afford them an opportunity to submit a reply within thirty days. Failure to respond within the stipulated timeframe may result in ex parte proceedings.

For the purposes of this Act, a “claim” in a patent application shall define the scope of protection sought by the applicant and shall be construed according to the meaning ascribed thereto under established principles of legal interpretation. Claims must be clear, concise, and supported by the description as provided herein; failure to meet these requirements may render the claims invalid. The term "reprography," when used in relation to a claimed process or product, refers specifically to the reproduction of printed matter by mechanical means, including but not limited to photocopying and digital duplication. Claims incorporating reprographic processes shall be assessed for patentability subject to considerations of novelty and inventive step.

Any person claiming to be the owner of a trade mark capable of being represented graphically and distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings may apply for registration india in such manner as may be prescribed. An application for registration shall include a representation of the trade mark, a list of goods or services to which it relates, and a statement of the claim to ownership. The Trade Marks Registry may, subject to such conditions as it deems fit, require the applicant to limit the goods or services specified in the application. Provided that, where a trade mark is similar to an existing trade mark, the Registry may require evidence of distinctiveness to avoid confusion in the market. All applications shall be examined for compliance with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder, and any application found deficient may be rejected or amended as necessary. Failure to respond to official objections within the prescribed time shall be deemed a withdrawal of the application.

A layout-design shall be deemed original if it was created independently by the claimant or derived from a prior work with substantial modifications that constitute an original design. Subject to compliance with prescribed standards regarding technical documentation, registration of a layout-design is permissible only after a period of six months has elapsed from the date of its first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world. Any person claiming infringement under this Act must demonstrate that the infringing layout-design possesses a striking similarity to the registered design, considering both overall appearance and component arrangement. Provided that such similarity does not arise solely from features dictated by functional considerations or technical necessity, the claimant shall be entitled to seek injunctive relief and damages as provided herein.

Where an objection is raised against the grant of a certificate registration produced before the Registrar under this Act, the applicant shall be afforded a reasonable opportunity to submit written representations and counter-evidence in rebuttal. The Registrar may then proceed to either uphold the objection, requiring the applicant to rectify deficiencies or withdraw the application, or dismiss the objection and proceed with the examination process as provided herein. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar dismissing an objection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellate tribunal shall consider all relevant materials and evidence presented before it and issue a reasoned judgment, subject to judicial review under law.

Any person who contravenes any provision of this Act relating to the registration of a plant variety, including making false statements in an application or failing to disclose material information, shall be liable for a penalty not exceeding five hundred thousand rupees and may also face imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. Furthermore, where a registered plant variety is reproduced for sale by any person without authorization from the Registrar, that person shall be subject to damages assessed by the civil court, taking into account lost profits and reasonable expenses incurred. The indian council agricultural shall have the power to initiate investigations into suspected violations and report findings to the Central Government for appropriate action, including prosecution under this Act.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, where the owner of copyright in a literary or dramatic work has refused to grant a licence on reasonable terms for its utilization for adaptation into a cinematograph film, any person may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence. Such application shall specify the work in question and the purpose for which the applicant seeks authorization, demonstrating that the refusal constitutes an impediment to public access to artistic expression. The Controller may, after affording the copyright owner an opportunity of being heard, grant such a licence if satisfied that the terms offered by the owner were indeed unreasonable, considering factors including the extent of exploitation of the work and the nature of adaptation proposed.

A trade mark shall be deemed to be deceptively similar to another trade mark if, taking the whole mark as a whole, it is likely to cause confusion among the public, or a substantial section thereof, as to the goods or services in relation to which the marks are used. The assessment of deceptive similarity shall consider all relevant factors, including the visual, phonetic, and conceptual similarities between the marks, as well as the overall impression created by each. The India Registrar, when examining applications for registration, shall apply a comparative analysis, considering the distinctiveness of the earlier trade mark and the likelihood of association in the minds of consumers. Provided that, mere resemblance shall not, by itself, constitute deceptive similarity; the likelihood of confusion must be demonstrated. Any party opposing a trade mark application on grounds of deceptive similarity shall bear the burden of proving such likelihood to the satisfaction of the India Registrar.

An application for registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be accompanied by such particulars as may be prescribed, including a full and accurate representation of the layout-design. The Controller General shall examine each application in accordance with the provisions herein relating to examination and shall afford the applicant an opportunity of being heard if any objection is taken to the registration. Any person interested may, within sixty days from the date of publication of the acceptance of the application for registration, file a notice of opposition under this Act. The Controller General may require such further information or clarification as he deems necessary from the applicant or the opponent. Upon hearing all parties and considering any evidence submitted, the Controller General shall pass an order either allowing or refusing the registration, providing reasons for the decision. Appeals against such orders are subject to review by the Intellectual Property Appellate Board.

Where an appeal lies under this Act against a decision refusing registration of a trade mark on the ground that it is deemed to be generic, the Appellate Board shall consider whether, at the date of application for registration, use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified had become so prevalent as to have resulted in the mark losing its distinctive character and acquiring a common descriptive meaning within the relevant geographical area. The Board may, subject to just considerations, allow such appeal if it finds that the evidence presented does not establish beyond reasonable doubt that section 36e ixd has been contravened. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court on any question of law arising out of the decision.

Where a proprietor establishes that use by another person is likely to cause dilution of the distinctiveness of the Geographical Indication, or is otherwise detrimental to the interests of the registered proprietors or authorized users, the Registrar may, subject to appeal under this Act, issue an order injunction restraining such use. This power shall extend to preventing the application of the Geographical Indication in relation to goods or services not conforming to the standards prescribed herein. It is provided that a trade description denotes origin within the defined geographical area only if it accurately reflects production methods and characteristics as registered; any misleading portrayal constitutes actionable infringement, justifying injunctive relief. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both parties regarding potential consumer confusion and economic impact when determining the scope of such an order injunction.

Subject to this Act, a copyright case shall be deemed to arise where any person alleges infringement of rights vested under this Act. The determination of such a case requires examination of the work’s originality and substantial similarity to the claimed copyrighted material. Further, the aggrieved party may apply to the relevant High Court for rectification of entries in the court rectification register pertaining to copyright ownership or duration. Such applications shall be accompanied by an affidavit verifying the grounds for rectification and supporting documentation as provided herein. The Court may order correction if it finds the existing entry erroneous or misleading.

Every application patent shall be accompanied by a complete and clear description of the invention, sufficient to enable a person skilled in the relevant art to carry it into effect. The description shall disclose the best mode contemplated by the applicant for carrying out the invention. A provisional specification may be filed initially, subject to the requirement that a complete specification is filed within twelve months from the date of the provisional application, failing which the provisional application shall be deemed to be withdrawn. Where an application patent relates to a process, the specification shall clearly define the process and the manner in which it is performed. Any amendment to the complete specification shall not extend beyond the scope of the provisional specification, if any, and shall be subject to scrutiny as provided herein. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish further information or documents relating to the application patent, as deemed necessary for examination.

An applicant seeking registration of a patent shall furnish a detailed specification outlining the scope and boundaries of the claimed invention. The description must clearly articulate all elements encompassed within the claims, ensuring that any matter not explicitly described is understood to be excluded. Where an invention far claimed extends beyond the originally disclosed subject matter, the Controller may require further clarification demonstrating the inventive step relating to each additional element. Such requirements shall be considered met only upon submission of a revised specification and accompanying drawings, if applicable, accurately reflecting the broadened scope. The applicant’s compliance with these stipulations is essential for determining patentability under this Act and preventing subsequent challenges regarding claim interpretation.

Where any proprietor institutes legal proceedings against a person alleging infringement of a geographical indication registered under this Act and fails to substantiate such allegation before the relevant judicial authority, the Court shall have the power to order, as part of its judgment, court directed forfeiture of assets acquired or utilized by the complainant in connection with the aforementioned litigation. Such forfeiture shall be limited to those assets demonstrably employed for pursuing the unsuccessful claim, including but not limited to legal fees and associated expenses. Provided that, where the Court finds evidence of a bonafide belief in the existence of infringement, it may exercise discretion regarding the extent of such forfeiture, subject to ensuring fairness and proportionality between the frivolous nature of the allegation and the potential impact on the complainant’s livelihood.

An application for registration of a geographical indication may include a statement specifying the extent of the territory to which the applicant claims protection under this Act, subject to the provisions regarding reference use geographical indications. Where an applicant seeks to limit the scope of protection afforded by registration to a specific area within the defined geographical unit, such limitation shall be clearly delineated in the application and supported by verifiable documentation demonstrating the distinct characteristics attributable solely to that restricted territory. The Geographical Indications Registry may require further evidence establishing the connection between the quality or other characteristic of the goods and the specified reference use geographical area. Failure to provide satisfactory evidence may result in rejection of the application or limitation of protection as determined by the Registrar. Any subsequent alteration of this defined area requires a separate application and approval process, as provided herein.

Any person initiating proceedings against an authorized breeder or research institution alleging infringement of plant variety rights shall be required to remit a non-refundable application fee as determined by the Central Government, such amount subject to periodic revision. Failure to pay this initial fee within thirty days of filing the complaint will result in automatic dismissal of the claim without further notice. Further, should any party found to have acted vexatiously or maliciously in pursuing a legal action under this Act shall be liable to pay compensatory costs, including fees in any proceeding incurred by the respondent. The Registrar may, at his discretion, order recovery of such costs through attachment of assets.

A variety registered act under this Act shall vest in the applicant, subject to the provisions relating to research and experimentation and the rights of farmers as provided herein. Any person desiring to commercially exploit a registered variety, including propagation, multiplication, distribution, sale, and import or export, shall obtain a license from the breeder or his duly authorized agent, upon terms mutually agreed upon, or failing such agreement, determined by the Central Government. The licensing agreement may include provisions for royalty payments, quality control, and duration of the license, and shall be registered with the Plant Variety Protection Authority. Where a licensee sub-licenses rights relating to a variety, such sub-license shall be subject to the terms and conditions of the original license and require prior written consent of the breeder. In cases involving section 36e ixd concerning the transfer of rights to a corporate entity, due diligence regarding the original breeder’s claim shall be mandatory before approval. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in penalties as prescribed.

An application for registration of a geographical indication shall include particulars as prescribed, including details regarding the quality, reputation or other characteristics of the goods attributable to its origin. Where any person believes that the acceptance of an application for registration is erroneous, or that any registered geographical indication is being used in contravention of this Act, such person may, relating plaintiff forthwith to the Geographical Indications Registry, file a representation against the proposed registration or the existing registration. The Registry shall consider such representations and provide an opportunity for all interested parties to be heard under this Act. Any decision made by the Registry regarding a representation is subject to appeal before the Appellate Board.

A reference geographical indication, for the purposes of determining a conflict under this Act, shall extend to include not only the registered geographical indication itself but also any colourable variation thereof likely to cause confusion or deception amongst the public, or to unfairly compete with the proprietor of the registered geographical indication. Such determination of colourable variation shall be made according to the principles governing comparative advertising and unfair trade practices as understood in the ordinary course of civil procedure. Provided that, a mere similarity in appearance or sound shall not, by itself, constitute a colourable variation, unless accompanied by evidence of actual confusion or intent to deceive. Any party alleging infringement based on a reference geographical indication may initiate proceedings before the competent court, subject to the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908.

For the purposes of this Act, “registration respect” means the legal entitlement afforded to a registered trade mark holder by virtue of its registration and shall include the exclusive right to use, license, and otherwise exploit the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. This right extends to preventing the use by any person of an identical or confusingly similar sign in relation to identical or similar goods or services without due cause, subject to principles of fair dealing as provided herein. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to grant registration respect beyond the scope of the specific goods and services listed in the trade mark register.

The owner of a registered trade mark shall, subject to this Act, be entitled to grant licences allowing others to use the trade mark in relation to goods for which the register respect goods are specified. Such licences may be exclusive or non-exclusive and may be granted for a fixed term or during the subsistence of the registration. Any assignment of the registered trade mark shall include any existing licences relating thereto, unless the assignee expressly declines such inclusion in writing at the time of assignment. Provided that, where a licence is assigned separately from the registered trade mark itself, the assignor remains bound by the terms of the original licensing agreement until the expiry or termination thereof. The Registrar may require evidence of consent from affected licensees prior to registering an assignment which includes their licences, as provided herein.

Any person who applies for registration of a mark registered trade deceptively similar to an existing registered trademark shall be liable to a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Where a fraudulent application is made, intending to deceive or mislead, such applicant shall be punishable with imprisonment which may extend to one year, or with fine, or with both. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions of this Act and upon sufficient cause being shown, direct rectification of the register in cases where a mark has been registered improperly. Any person aggrieved by an order refusing registration, or directing rectification, may appeal to the Appellate Board within ninety days from the date of such order; provided that any delay exceeding said period may be condoned if reasonable cause is demonstrated. Failure to comply with directions issued under this Act shall attract daily penalties as determined by the Registrar.

A person seeking protection under this Act, who has filed an application for a patent in a convention country, shall submit a declaration verifying the priority claim within the prescribed period. The declaration must identify the first filing date and the name of the convention country where such initial application was made. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in forfeiture of the claimed priority date. Where the subject matter of the invention includes a cinematograph film, the applicant shall furnish details regarding its production, including dates and locations of principal photography, as part of the complete specification. Provided that an applicant claiming convention priority based on an application disclosing a cinematograph film must also submit certified copies of any official documentation relating to said film from the competent authority in the convention country. Any misrepresentation or omission concerning these details shall be subject to penalties as provided herein.

Any use of a registered trade mark by a person other than the registered proprietor, or a duly authorized user, shall constitute an infringement of the exclusive right conferred by registration under this Act, subject to the provisions contained herein. However, a use which does not create a likelihood of confusion, or cause damage to the reputation of the mark, may be permissible, provided that such use is bona fide and in accordance with honest practices in industrial or commercial matters. The determination of whether a use creates a likelihood of confusion shall be made with reference to all relevant factors, including the similarity of the marks, the similarity of the goods or services for which they are used, and the overall impression created on the public. A crucial element in assessing infringement is the ‘use mark relation’, wherein the court shall consider the manner in which the allegedly infringing mark is presented and used in relation to the registered mark. Where a registered trade mark is a well-known mark, the scope of protection extends beyond identical goods or services, and any use that takes unfair advantage of, or is detrimental to, its distinctive character shall be actionable.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board concerning the revocation of a breeder variety registered under this Act may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. Such an appeal shall be only on grounds specified in sub-section (1) of section forty-seven, relating to errors apparent on the face of the record or violation of principles of natural justice. The appellate court may allow a party to present additional evidence if it considers such evidence relevant and could not reasonably have been produced before the Board. Failure to comply with this provision shall be grounds for dismissal of the appeal. Further, any infringement of farmers’ rights associated with a breeder variety, including unauthorized sale or distribution, is actionable under this Act and may attract penalties as provided herein.

An application for registration of a trade mark shall include particulars sufficient to identify clearly the goods or services with which the index registered trade is associated, and such identification must conform to classes as prescribed by the Regulations. The Registrar may require any applicant to furnish further details concerning the nature and extent of use of the proposed trade mark prior to acceptance, particularly where there exists a likelihood of confusion with an earlier registration. Where an application relates to multiple goods or services, the fees payable shall be determined according to the number of classes involved. Any alteration to the representation of a registered trade mark must be notified to the Registrar and approved as provided herein before it takes effect.

Any person being the owner of copyright, or having an exclusive license to do so, may assign the copyright or any part thereof by writing under his hand, or that of his duly authorized agent. Such assignment shall be subject to the provisions contained herein regarding duration, scope, and territorial extent, and must clearly identify the work assigned. An assignee acquiring rights as provided herein shall be entitled to all remedies available to the original owner against infringement of copyright in the assigned portion, save where expressly restricted by the terms of the assignment itself. Where an assignment is made for a defined period, any failure to exercise rights within that period does not constitute abandonment unless explicitly stated in the instrument of assignment. The assignor retains the right to seek accounting of royalties paid, and may petition a competent court for redressal should discrepancies arise concerning amounts due as per the terms of the assignment. An assignment lacking these specifications shall be voidable at the option of either party.

An application patent shall be deemed invalid if it is determined, under this Act, that the invention was not novel at the time of filing. The Controller may require the applicant to furnish evidence demonstrating prior publication disclosure has been adequately addressed, provided that such requirement shall only arise where a credible challenge regarding novelty is presented by an interested party. Further, an application patent will be rejected if it contains subject matter which is solely comprised of a discovery relating to living organisms or naturally occurring substances, unless it incorporates a process by which the substance can be extracted or produced. The applicant bears the responsibility for demonstrating compliance with these conditions throughout the examination procedure.

Any person aggrieved by an entry relating to a trademark in the register, or by any matter affecting the registrability thereof, may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date on which such entry was made or became known to him, whichever is earlier. The Board shall have power to entertain and determine appeals against orders of the Registrar refusing registration, directing deletion from the *matters included register*, or concerning rectification of entries. Failure to comply with prescribed procedures during appeal proceedings may result in dismissal. Any party dissatisfied with an order of the Appellate Board may further appeal to the High Court within ninety days, subject to a penalty of five thousand rupees for delay beyond that period. The Registrar shall enforce these provisions diligently.

The registered proprietor of a trade mark shall have the exclusive right to use the trade mark in relation to the goods or services for which it is registered. Any assignment of the registration, or any interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and require written instrument duly executed by both parties, specifying clearly the goods or services in respect of which the transfer applies. A co-ownership of a registered trade mark may be permissible, provided that all co-owners are jointly responsible for ensuring lawful use and preventing infringement. Where a registered proprietor fails to exercise reasonable diligence to maintain control over the quality of certified goods associated with a collective trade mark, the Registrar may initiate proceedings as deemed appropriate. The rights conferred by registration shall not extend to goods or services unrelated to those specified in the register, nor shall it prejudice the lawful use of prior marks.

Subject to appeal under Chapter X, any person who, knowing that a particular trade mark is registered in the name of a valid registered proprietor, uses such trade mark or a deceptive imitation thereof in connection with goods or services shall be guilty of an offence and liable to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or both. Further, where a holder licence patent relating to a process incorporates a protected trademark without express authorization from the registered proprietor, such use constitutes infringement subject to remedies as provided herein. The Court may also order the seizure and destruction of goods bearing the infringing mark, and impose costs reflective of the damages suffered by the proprietor.

Any individual or entity utilizing a layout design in commerce without formally registering it under this Act shall be deemed to have availed of impliedly registration, subject to verification by the Layout Design Registrar. Such utilization constitutes an infringement actionable at the instance of the rightful owner. Where the infringing party demonstrates demonstrable commercial gain attributable to the unregistered use, they shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to three times the value of profits earned, or rupees five hundred thousand, whichever is greater. Furthermore, repeat offenders found exploiting layout designs without registration may face prosecution and a prohibition from applying for registration under this Act for a period not exceeding two years, as determined by the Layout Design Registrar.

A person who is the registered proprietor of a registered layout-design shall have the exclusive right to reproduce, exploit, or import the layout-design in any manner, subject to the provisions of this Act. Any act undertaken without the express license of, or contrary to the directions of, the registered proprietor shall constitute an infringement of their exclusive right. Where a person, being the manner registered proprietor, reasonably believes that an infringement of their registered layout-design has occurred or is about to occur, they may apply to the High Court for a prohibitory injunction. The Court, upon being satisfied of the prima facie case, may grant an injunction restraining the infringing party from further acts of infringement. Provided that, the registered proprietor shall not be entitled to relief where the alleged infringement relates to a layout-design that is demonstrably not novel or is otherwise ineligible for registration as provided herein. Any damages awarded shall be commensurate with the actual loss suffered, or the reasonable royalty due, whichever is higher.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and any rules made thereunder, a Plant Variety Protection Licensee may grant licenses for the commercial use of protected plant varieties, including rights relating to seed production, sale, distribution, and import. Such licenses shall be documented in writing and specify the scope of permitted activities, duration, geographical area, and royalty payments payable to the original breeder or their assignee. The Agriculture Commissioner government may, upon application by an interested party demonstrating a public interest concern regarding access to protected varieties for research or conservation purposes, authorize non-exclusive licenses under conditions it deems appropriate. Any assignment of rights in a plant variety protection license requires prior notification to and registration with the Agriculture Commissioner government, accompanied by details of the assignee’s qualifications and intended use of the assigned rights. Failure to register an assignment shall render such assignment voidable.

Where an infringement of copyright has occurred outside India, but the infringer or authorising agent thereof had a place of business within India at the time of the infringement, proceedings for enforcing any right under this Act may be instituted in India as if the infringement had occurred within India. The Appellate Tribunal shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals arising from orders passed by the Registrar relating to requests for transborder rights enforcement. Any person found guilty of an offence involving copyright infringement, whether acting alone or jointly with others, shall be liable to prosecution under this Act. This liability extends to corporate entities where the act was committed with the knowledge or consent of its officers. A commission offence notwithstanding any other provision contained herein, a person assisting in the commission of such an offence shall be deemed as guilty and subject to penalties equivalent to those applicable for direct infringement.

A geographical indication shall, for the purposes of registration under this Act, identify goods originating from a specific geographical area where a particular quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such good is essentially attributable to its place of origin. An application for registration seeking protection as a geographical indication must include a clear and concise definition of the geographical area with demarcated boundaries, alongside a detailed specification outlining the qualities or characteristics linked to that origin. Where an applicant seeks international registration prescribed by the Madrid Protocol, compliance with all requirements of this Act is mandatory prior to filing such request through the International Bureau. The Register shall maintain a public register of all registered geographical indications and associated specifications, accessible for inspection subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any alteration affecting the defined geographical area or good specification requires formal amendment duly recorded in the Register.

Any person aggrieved by the Registrar’s decision refusing an application for registration of a geographical indication, or rejecting a statement of proposed use as an authorised user, may file an appeal to the Appellate Board within a period of ninety days from the date of the order appealed against, subject to the payment of such fees as may be prescribed. The Appellate Board shall, after giving the applicant and the Registrar a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and considering the evidence presented, either confirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Where an application for registration is refused due to a lack of proper documentation establishing origin or quality, the Appellate Board may direct the applicant to submit additional evidence, provided that such evidence is submitted within a timeframe stipulated by the Board. A finding of the Appellate Board regarding the status of an application registrati authorised shall be final and binding, except where grounds of fraud are demonstrably proven before a court of competent jurisdiction.

The Trade Marks Registry shall maintain a register of all trade marks applied for and registered under this Act, and such register shall be open to inspection by any person subject to payment of the prescribed fee. Any application for registration, to be considered complete, shall be accompanied by a clear representation of the trade mark and a statement as to the goods or services for which registration is sought. The Registry may, where an application is found to be deficient in any respect, require the applicant to amend it within a period not exceeding thirty days from the date of such requirement. All correspondence with the Trade Marks Registry shall be addressed to the appropriate branch office, and any notice served upon the Registry shall be deemed to have been duly served upon actual delivery.
