Provided that, the Registry reserves the right to reject any application not complying with the provisions as provided herein, and such rejection shall be communicated to the applicant in writing with reasons.

Any enterprise found to have used a registered geographical indication in relation to goods not conforming to the standards as defined under this Act, or which creates a false or misleading impression regarding the origin of such goods, shall be liable for penalties as prescribed. Such penalty may extend to imprisonment of up to three years and a fine not less than fifty thousand rupees, and may be further increased incrementally for subsequent offences. Where an indication falsified results in demonstrable financial loss to registered proprietors, compensation may be awarded by the relevant adjudicating authority. The authorised user shall have the right to initiate civil proceedings against any party violating these provisions, subject to limitations provided herein regarding frivolous claims.

An application for registration may be rejected if the proposed denomination is deemed deceptively similar to an existing denomination already in use for another plant variety, subject to the proviso that the Registrar shall provide the applicant with written reasons for such rejection and afford them a reasonable opportunity to submit representations against the finding. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar rejecting an application on grounds of denominational similarity may appeal to the Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order, provided that the appeal shall be accompanied by a fee as prescribed. The burden of proving distinctiveness and freedom from deceptive similarity in respect of an assignment denomination shall lie upon the applicant.

The Controller of Designs may, if satisfied that the disclosure of any design registration information or application details would be prejudicial to the security of India, refuse to permit inspection or grant of copies of such information as provided herein. Any application for registration of a design which incorporates elements demonstrably impacting national security shall be subject to a mandatory review by a designated authority within the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion. Provided that, such review shall be completed within a period of sixty days from the date of application. The Controller shall, notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, act in accordance with the recommendations of said authority regarding designs affecting security india. Failure to comply with the requirements of this review may result in the rejection of the design application.

Any person cultivating a commercially viable entitled produce variety, and claiming a right therein, shall maintain a record of all transactions relating to the said variety, including but not limited to seed production, sales, and distribution, for a period of not less than five years, subject to inspection by officers authorized under this Act. Failure to maintain such records, or provision of false or misleading information during inspection, shall attract a penalty not exceeding fifty thousand rupees. Furthermore, any farmer demonstrating independent development of an essentially derived variety, and subsequently commercializing it without acknowledging the initial breeder, shall be liable to a fine up to one hundred thousand rupees, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years, or both. The Authority may, however, consider extenuating circumstances such as traditional knowledge and customary practices in determining the appropriate penalty. Any appeal against a penalty imposed as provided herein shall lie before the designated Appellate Tribunal.

The Registrar may, upon application by any proprietor of a registered trade mark, extend the period of registration thereof for further periods of ten years each, subject to payment of the prescribed fees. Such extension shall be granted only if the applicant demonstrates continued use of the trade mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the register during the immediately preceding five-year period. However, this requirement is not applicable where the non-use can be attributed directly to actions taken by a third party without the proprietor’s consent. The limitations on extending registration apply equally if the applicant has entered into a licensing agreement affecting the mark's use, as provided herein.

An exclusive licensee of a copyright in any work shall, subject to the terms of the license agreement, possess the right to sue for infringement of the copyright as if they were the owner of the copyright, and to recover all damages and costs as are recoverable by the copyright owner under this Act. However, such right shall be conditional upon the exclusive licensee providing notice to the copyright owner of any intended legal action, and affording the owner the opportunity to join as a party to the proceedings, at the licensee’s expense. Where the copyright owner declines to join such action, the exclusive licensee may proceed independently, but any recovery shall be subject to any pre-existing contractual obligations regarding profit-sharing or royalty payments. A non-exclusive licensee shall not have the right to sue for infringement, but may be entitled to claim damages from the copyright owner to the extent of any loss suffered due to the owner’s failure to enforce their rights. Any assignment of the license shall be subject to the prior written consent of the copyright owner, unless otherwise provided in the license agreement.

Any person desiring to commercially exploit a copyrighted work through licensing or other means, shall register the terms of such exploitation with the Registrar of Copyrights to ensure proper accounting of remuneration due to the owner. Registration of royalty rates is mandatory for all licenses exceeding a period of one year, and shall include details regarding the basis of calculation, frequency of payment, and any deductions permissible as provided herein. The copyright owner may, subject to mutual agreement, specify different royalty structures for various modes of exploitation including reproduction, distribution, public performance, or adaptation. Provided that where a license is terminated prematurely by either party, final accounting of all accrued royalties shall be completed within ninety days from the date of termination and any dispute regarding such accounting shall be resolved through arbitration. Failure to register the terms may result in penalties as determined by the Registrar.

Any person being a breeder, or a successor of such breeder, desiring to obtain a breeder’s right in respect of a new, distinct, uniform and stable variety, shall make an application to the Plant Variety Protection Authority in the prescribed manner, clearly stating the claims purposes for which protection is sought, including but not limited to commercial exploitation, propagation, and the marketing of propagating material. The application shall be accompanied by the prescribed fee and a detailed description of the variety, demonstrating its novelty and distinctiveness. Where a variety is essentially derived from another variety, as established through prescribed testing procedures, the applicant shall disclose the initial variety and the breeder thereof, and may be subject to a royalty arrangement determined by the Authority. Assignment of breeder’s rights shall be permissible, provided that the assignee undertakes to adhere to the obligations stipulated under this Act, and any such assignment shall be registered with the Authority to be legally effective. Failure to comply with these provisions may result in the revocation of the breeder’s right.

Subject to the provisions of this Act and rules made thereunder, an Integrated Circuit shall be deemed to be protected if it incorporates original features which reveal the author's intellectual conception and are fixed therein. Protection under this Act shall not extend to any Integrated Circuit that is substantially similar to an earlier Integrated Circuit already registered, unless such similarity arises directly from reverse engineering conducted in compliance with prescribed conditions. The right of layout-design protection conferred by this Act may be assigned or licensed, provided that the terms of assignment or license are documented and readily accessible for inspection as per regulations. Any person desiring to utilize a protected Integrated Circuit for commercial purposes shall obtain prior authorization from the registered proprietor, subject to exceptions outlined herein regarding analysis for defensive purposes.

A new variety, for the purposes of registration under this Act, shall be considered distinct if it demonstrates the clearly distinguishable characteristics from any other variety whose existence is a matter of common knowledge. Such distinctness shall be established through a detailed description of the plant’s morphological, physiological, and, where applicable, molecular characteristics, conforming to the guidelines established by the Plant Variety Protection Authority. However, a variety which is essentially derived from another variety, as defined herein, shall not be considered a new variety unless the applicant demonstrates significant characteristics differentiating it from the initial variety. Provided that, the applicant fulfills the requirements regarding novelty, distinctness, uniformity, and stability, and submits evidence of the variety’s origin and breeder’s entitlement, registration may be granted subject to payment of the prescribed fees and compliance with all other provisions of this Act. Any false representation regarding the new variety’s characteristics shall render the registration voidable.

Registration of a semiconductor integrated circuit layout-design shall be deemed to have been granted in error, and consequently, provided cancelling registration may occur, if it is established that the layout-design was substantially similar to an already registered design under this Act. The determination of substantial similarity shall consider the overall impression created by the designs, irrespective of minor variations. An application for cancellation must specify the grounds upon which it is based and identify the prior registered design. The Registrar may require further evidence supporting the claim of substantial similarity before proceeding with a hearing concerning the validity of the design registry registration.

Any person desiring to register a trade mark under this Act shall apply to the Trade Marks Registry in the prescribed manner, furnishing the requisite particulars and statement of use. The application for registration shall include a clear representation of the trade mark, specifying the goods or services for which registration is sought, and shall be subject to the provisions relating to inherent distinctiveness and deceptive similarity. Where multiple applicants seek registration of identical or similar trade marks for related goods or services, the Registry may, considering the date of application and bona fide use, determine priority in accordance with established principles of registration common regulations. A registered trade mark shall be maintained on the Register provided that the prescribed renewal fees are paid and the mark continues to be used in relation to the goods or services specified. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the removal of the trade mark from the Register, as provided herein.

The determination regarding whether an application constitutes a convention application, and consequently qualifies for priority under this Act, shall be subject to rigorous scrutiny during the examination process. Where the Controller finds that the claimed priority date is demonstrably invalid due to discrepancies in filing dates or applicant details compared to the original application filed in a convention country, such finding may be challenged by the applicant. An appeal section shall exist specifically for addressing disputes concerning the validity of claimed priorities and the determination of convention status. The Appellate Board shall consider evidence presented by both the Controller and the applicant when adjudicating these appeals, ensuring due regard is given to international treaties and established legal precedent relating to patent applications from a convention country.

An application for registration of a plant variety shall include particulars specifying the name and address of the applicant, whether the applicant is the breeder or not, and if not, the relationship of the applicant to the breeder. Where an application relates to a *breeder registered variety*, the application must further state the details of the original registration under this Act, including the registering authority and date of such prior registration. The Registrar may require the applicant to furnish evidence establishing their right to make the application, particularly where the applicant is not the initial breeder or a successor company deriving rights through assignment. Any challenge to the validity of the claimed relationship shall be adjudicated according to procedures as provided herein. The Registrar shall publish notice of the application and any objections received will be considered before proceeding with examination.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, a compulsory license may be granted by the Controller permitting the manufacture and sale of a patented invention solely for export purposes where the patentee has failed to adequately satisfy reasonable demands concerning availability within India, or where such failure demonstrably prejudices public health. An application for such a compulsory licence shall include detailed justification regarding the necessity for export, including evidence of unmet needs in importing nations and an assessment of potential impact on domestic production. The Controller may require the applicant to provide security as deemed appropriate. Any appeal against the decision of the Controller granting or refusing a compulsory licence export shall lie before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of such order.

Where an application for registration of a trademark is refused under this Act, the applicant shall have the right to appeal against such refusal. The Registrar person act shall be recorded and made available for inspection by any interested party within thirty days of the order being passed. Any party aggrieved by an order of the Registrar may prefer an appeal to the Appellate Board, provided that the appeal is filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the said order. The Appellate Board shall consider all relevant evidence presented before it and may affirm, modify, or reverse the decision of the Registrar. Further, any interlocutory order made by the Registrar or the Appellate Board may be challenged under this Act through a writ petition in the High Court.

Any visual recording, whether expressed by means of a cinematograph film or other process, shall be deemed a work under this Act, subject to the provisions herein contained regarding originality. A claim of authorship in a visual recording may be disputed on grounds of substantial derivation from a pre-existing work, and the burden of proving independent creation shall lie with the claimant. Where a dispute arises concerning the ownership of rights in a visual recording made for purposes of private use, the court may, considering the nature of the recording and the circumstances of its creation, determine equitable ownership. An appeal from any decision regarding such ownership shall lie before the High Court, provided that the aggrieved party demonstrates irreparable harm. Furthermore, any alteration of a visual recording that prejudices the author’s reputation may constitute infringement, unless such alteration is demonstrably transformative and does not diminish the original work’s expressive qualities.

Where an application for the registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the Registrar may, subject to appeal before the Intellectual Property Appellate Board, direct that the reasons for such refusal be recorded in writing and made available to the applicant. Further, if any marks registered are subsequently found to be deceptively similar to other existing marks, or where confusion likely arises due to similarity between marks registered associated with different proprietors, the Registrar shall issue a notice requiring the proprietor of the potentially infringing mark to submit representations within a prescribed period. Failure to respond adequately may result in an order directing the amendment of the register, including the removal of the offending mark from the register and consequential adjustments to any related classifications. The Registrar’s decision on such matters is final, subject to appeal as provided herein.

Where an application for registration of a trade mark includes a reference to any other trade mark owned by the applicant, and such other trade mark is not identical to the mark applied for, the Registrar may require the applicant to declare whether they desire those marks to be registered as associated trade marks. Such declaration shall specify the nature of the association between the trade marks, which may include common ownership, a parent-subsidiary relationship, or a contractual arrangement for joint marketing purposes. The registrar shall publish notice of such requirement and any subsequent registration of associated trade marks in the Trade Marks Journal. Any party may object to the registration of associated trade marks under this Act within the prescribed period, subject to conditions as provided herein.

Subject to the provisions of this Act, any patentee may grant an exclusive license to use or exercise their patented invention relating to a particular field of application described within the specification. Such licenses shall be assignable by the patentee, either wholly or partially, and may include the right to make, sell, hire, or import the patented article. The scope of such assignment shall not extend beyond the boundaries defined by the original specification claim, unless expressly agreed upon in writing between the parties involved. Further, any sub-license granted under an exclusive license is deemed an assignment for the purposes of revocation proceedings under this Act. A licensee may enforce the patent against infringement, provided that they adhere to the terms stipulated within the licensing agreement and do not act contrary to the interests of the patentee as determined by a competent authority.

Any farmer who, in good faith and without knowledge of an extant registered variety of like kind, propagates or multiplies any variety protected under this Act, for purposes of propagation and sale, shall be subject to a penalty not exceeding two thousand rupees for each such propagation or multiplication. Provided that, if the farmer can demonstrate reasonable efforts to ascertain the existence of a registered variety prior to such propagation or multiplication, the penalty may be waived at the discretion of the Authority. Furthermore, a farmer knowingly selling seed of a protected variety without authorization, or falsely representing seed as a registered variety, shall be liable to a fine not exceeding five thousand rupees, and may be subject to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year. Any seed so sold, or represented, shall be deemed forfeited to the Central Government. The Authority may, however, consider extenuating circumstances relating to traditional farming practices when determining penalties applicable to a farmer.

Where a patentee elects to license the manufacture or use of a patented article, such license shall be assignable in accordance with the provisions under this Act relating to assignment of patents, subject to the conditions stipulated within the original licensing agreement. Any subsequent assignee of such a license shall be deemed to hold the rights and obligations as if they were the initial licensor, provided that the patentee retains the right to revoke the license upon demonstrating substantial breach of contract by either the licensee or any assignee. The patentee may grant multiple licenses relating to the same patented article, but where such licenses are non-exclusive, priority shall be determined according to the date of execution of each respective agreement. A requirement exists that all assignments and sub-licenses concerning a requires patented article must be registered with the Controller within three months of their creation.

Applications for rectification of entries relating to copyright ownership shall be filed with the office of the Registrar of Copyrights. Upon receipt of such application, the Registrar shall serve notice thereof upon all parties whose interests are affected by the proposed rectification, affording them a reasonable opportunity to submit objections under this Act. Any party aggrieved by an order made by the Registrar concerning the rectification of copyright entries may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of that order. The High Court shall have the same jurisdiction in respect of such appeals as it has in relation to appeals under other provisions of this Act. Provided that, where an objection is raised regarding the validity of a copyright itself, the High Court may determine the matter de novo.

Where a patentee desires to grant a license conferring specific rights relating to their invention, they shall execute a written instrument detailing the scope of such license, including but not limited to territorial limitations, field of use restrictions, and royalty arrangements. Such instruments must be filed with the Controller within thirty days of execution; failure to do so renders the license unenforceable against third parties. The Controller may, upon application by any interested party, require further clarification regarding the terms of a license agreement. Patents shall entered in the Register detailing all assignments, transmissions, and licenses granted under this Act, along with the date of such actions and the names and addresses of the relevant parties involved. Any subsequent modification or revocation of a license must also be recorded as provided herein to maintain transparency and facilitate public access to patent information.

For the purpose of this Act, a design registry is defined as an official record maintained by the Office, containing particulars relating to registered designs and applications for registration. The design registry shall include, but not be limited to, information regarding the applicant’s name and address, the date of application, representations of the design, claims made in respect thereof, and any subsequent modifications or renewals. Access to the design registry may be granted to members of the public subject to payment of prescribed fees and adherence to regulations as provided herein. The Registrar shall ensure that information within the design registry is accurate and readily accessible for inspection.

Where an invention is rejected under this Act based on grounds specified in section 35, the applicant shall have the right to prefer an appeal to an *order appellate* within three months from the date of communication of the refusal. Such appeal may be directed against any decision or direction made by the Controller relating to the grant of a patent, including but not limited to objections raised during examination or opposition proceedings. The Appellate Board shall hear parties de novo and may confirm, vary, or reverse the order appealed from. 

Provided that, if the appellant fails to deposit the prescribed fee within the time specified by the Appellate Board, the appeal shall be deemed abandoned. Further, any party aggrieved by an order of the Appellate Board may prefer further appeals as provided herein, subject to limitations on successive appeals and costs awarded at the discretion of the appellate forum.

Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Authority regarding the acceptance or rejection of a request for surrender of a plant variety protection may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days from the date of communication of the order. The appellate board shall, after giving notice to all parties concerned and affording them an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders as it deems fit, which may include directing the Authority to reconsider its decision or substituting the same with a new decision. Provided that where the surrender is sought due to non-compliance with conditions stipulated under this Act concerning farmers’ rights, the Board shall consider evidence pertaining to such non-compliance before entertaining an appeal and may dismiss the appeal ab initio if it finds merit in the Authority's findings.

Where an application for a patent is refused by the Patent Office, the applicant may appeal to the Controller. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of communication of the order of refusal. The appeal shall specify the grounds on which it is based and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed. The Controller shall give notice to any interested party who has raised an objection to the grant of patent, affording them an opportunity of being heard. The Controller’s decision on an appeal shall be final, subject to further appeal under this Act.

Provided that where a patent is granted and subsequently challenged in proceedings before a civil court seeking an order injunction restraining the applicant from exercising his patent rights, the Patent Office may intervene as a party to such proceedings at its discretion. The Controller may require production of documents or other evidence relevant to the determination of any question arising under this Act.

A services trade mark, distinct from marks used for goods, shall be registrable under this Act, subject to the provisions herein concerning distinctiveness and descriptiveness. An applicant seeking registration of a services trade mark shall clearly designate the class of service according to the prescribed classification, and the application shall specify the geographical area in which the services are, or are proposed to be, rendered. The Registrar may, prior to accepting an application, require clarification regarding the nature of the services claimed, or evidence of genuine use of the mark in relation to those services. Where a mark is identical with or deceptively similar to an existing registered services trade mark, and the services offered are identical or closely related, registration shall be refused, unless the proprietor of the earlier mark has consented in writing. However, a mark shall not be deemed deceptively similar merely due to the inclusion of descriptive matter necessary to indicate the nature, quality, or kind of service. Any appeal against the Registrar’s decision concerning the registration of a services trade mark shall lie to the Appellate Board, as constituted under the relevant rules.

Any person who knowingly makes, uses, imports, or offers to sell any integrated circuit layout-design infringing a registered design shall be liable to pay damages equivalent to the loss suffered by the proprietor of the design, and may also be subject to a further penalty not exceeding five times the value of such infringing goods. The Central Government may, upon receiving a complaint from the proprietor of a registered design, issue an injunction restraining any person from engaging in acts that constitute infringement as provided herein. Failure to comply with such an injunction shall render the offender liable for contempt of court and subject to imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year. A design apply registration is deemed invalid if it does not meet the novelty requirements outlined under this Act.

Any assignment of a registered trade mark, or any interest therein, shall be subject to the provisions of this Act and shall be effected by an instrument in writing signed by the assignor and the assignee, and shall include a clear and unambiguous disclosure of the register disclosed particulars relating to the mark, including but not limited to the class of goods or services, the date of registration, and any limitations or conditions recorded against it. The instrument of assignment may provide for the transfer of the right to renew the trade mark, subject to the assignee fulfilling all obligations pertaining to renewal fees as provided herein. Where an assignment involves a partial transfer of interest, the instrument shall delineate with precision the scope of rights transferred and retained by the assignor. Failure to adequately disclose the register disclosed information may render the assignment unenforceable against third parties. Any license granted under the trade mark shall be construed as an interest in property.

For the purposes of this Act, “breeder complied provisions” shall mean the conditions stipulated within a Plant Variety Registration Certificate pertaining to the sharing of breeder’s material and derived varieties. These stipulations are binding upon any person conducting activities involving the registered variety, including but not limited to commercialization, propagation, or research. Failure to adhere to these breeder complied provisions, as determined by the Board under this Act, constitutes an infringement of the rights granted to the plant breeder. Such infringements may result in penalties and injunctive relief, provided that farmers’ rights relating to saved seed are unaffected.

A broadcasting organisation shall, upon intending to utilise any copyrighted work for transmission via radio or television signals, obtain a license from the owner of copyright therein, provided that such licensing fees are determined according to guidelines established by the Central Government. Where a member of staff within the broadcasting organisation undertakes the adaptation of a literary work prior to broadcast, ensuring compliance with fair dealing principles as provided herein, the broadcasting organisation shall remain ultimately responsible for any infringement claims arising from said adaptation. Any member found to have acted in contravention of these stipulations may be subject to disciplinary action by their employer and potential civil liability under this Act. The Central Government may issue further directives regarding permissible uses and limitations concerning copyrighted material broadcasted by such organisations.

Any party aggrieved by a decision of the Registrar relating to the rectification of a trade mark, or concerning any matter arising under this Act where no other right of appeal is specifically provided, may dispose th appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Tribunal. Such an appeal must be filed within ninety days from the date of communication of the order sought to be appealed against. The appellant shall deposit such fees as are prescribed for appeals before the Tribunal. Provided that, if the aggrieved party can demonstrate reasonable cause for delay, the Tribunal may entertain the appeal notwithstanding the lapse of the stipulated period, subject to its satisfaction regarding the justification for the delay. Further, the Tribunal shall consider any counter-claims filed by other interested parties in relation to the trade mark concerned.

A proposed registered proprietor, seeking registration of a trade mark under this Act, shall furnish an address for service within the territory of India, which address shall be deemed to be the address to which all communications relating to the application and subsequent proceedings shall be sent. Should the proposed registered proprietor fail to maintain a valid address for service, the Registrar may, after reasonable notice, strike the application from the register. Furthermore, any registered proprietor intending to assign or transfer their rights in a trade mark, shall provide written notice to the Registrar, detailing the particulars of the assignee or transferee. Subject to the provisions herein, a transfer of ownership shall not invalidate any existing registrations, provided that the assignee or transferee demonstrates sufficient legal capacity to hold and utilize the trade mark. The Registrar may require evidence of title from the assignee or transferee to satisfy themselves as to the legitimacy of the transfer.

The Controller may, upon receiving an objection from a third party challenging the validity of a patent, direct the patentee to furnish such information and clarification as the Controller deems necessary to substantiate the inventive step and industrial applicability claimed in the patent. Such direction shall not preclude the patentee from subsequently presenting counter-arguments or evidence refuting the grounds for objection. Where an addition validity patent is granted based on modifications to a previously patented invention, any challenge asserting that these modifications do not constitute a novel and non-obvious improvement over the prior art may be considered by the Controller; however, it shall be presumed that the claimed subject matter possesses inventive step unless proven otherwise through clear and convincing evidence presented under this Act. The patentee shall have the right to appeal any decision of the Controller relating to such objections.

Any application for registration of a trade mark shall be accompanied by a statement of use, demonstrating bona fide adoption and continuous use of the mark in relation to the goods or services specified in the application, and shall be submitted in the prescribed form. An applicant seeking registration shall also furnish evidence, acceptable under this Act, of the mark’s distinctiveness, and shall not include descriptive terms or common trade names unless such terms have acquired secondary meaning through extensive use and public recognition. Provided that, where the applicant is not the owner of the trade mark, a duly executed power of attorney or assignment document shall be submitted along with the application. The Registrar may, subject to the provisions herein, require further clarification or evidence regarding the applicant registration if the initial submission is deemed insufficient or ambiguous. Failure to comply with these requirements may result in the rejection of the application.

Where an application for registration of a mark is refused under this Act, the applicant may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board. Such appeal shall be filed within sixty days from the date of receipt of the order of refusal by the applicant. The Board shall give notice to all parties who appeared in the proceedings before the Registrar and afford them an opportunity of being heard. If the mark applied for is a *mark registered different* from a previously registered trade mark, the Appellate Board shall consider whether use of the applied-for mark would constitute passing off or otherwise infringe any right conferred by registration under this Act. The Board’s decision shall be final, subject to appeal to the High Court within a further period of sixty days.

A product originating from a defined geographical area shall be considered a geographical indication if its qualities, reputation or other characteristics are essentially attributable to its geographical origin and, in consequence, possess a special quality, reputation or other characteristics which distinguish it from other goods of the same category. The applicant seeking registration of a considered geographical indication shall demonstrate a clear link between the specified geographical area, the qualities of the goods, and the reputation enjoyed by those goods. Evidence of traditional production methods consistently practiced within the geographical area, and contributing to the unique characteristics, may be submitted as supporting documentation. Provided that the geographical area is not a country, but a region, locality, or even an identifiable sub-region within a country. The Registrar may, subject to verification of the submitted evidence, accept the application and proceed with the registration process as provided herein. Any dispute regarding the authenticity of the link shall be resolved through established procedures.

Where an invention is granted patent protection under this Act and a condition attached to the grant restricts competition in a manner deemed detrimental to public interest, the Controller may, following due inquiry and notice to the patentee, declare such condition unlawful. Any party aggrieved by a declaration made under this provision may appeal to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board within sixty days of receipt of notification of the order. The Board shall consider representations from all interested parties before affirming, reversing or modifying the Controller’s determination. Further, where a condition declared unlawful involves an unreasonable tying arrangement for a complementary product, the patentee shall be liable to pay damages proportionate to the loss suffered by affected licensees and consumers. This liability is without prejudice to any other remedies available under contract law.

A certificate of registration, once granted for a new plant variety, shall be valid for a period of nine years from the date of notification, subject to the continued payment of annual fees as prescribed. The renewal of such certificate may be permitted for two successive terms of six years each, provided that the applicant demonstrates the continued distinctiveness, uniformity, and stability of the variety. Any farmer who has bred or developed a new variety, or essentially derived variety, shall be eligible to apply for registration, subject to compliance with the requirements regarding novelty, distinctiveness, stability, and uniformity. Where a variety is registered, the breeder shall have the exclusive right to commercially exploit the variety, except as otherwise provided herein. The Authority may, however, revoke the certificate registration if it is proven that the variety lacks the essential characteristics or that the information furnished during the application process was materially misleading. A register of all registered plant varieties shall be maintained and open for public inspection.

Where a proprietor institutes proceedings for the recovery of damages for the infringement of a trade mark under this Act, the court shall cognizance of such suit subject to the provisions regarding limitation as provided herein. The measure of damages recoverable shall be proportionate to the loss suffered by the proprietor and may include compensation for injury to reputation or goodwill arising from the use of the infringing mark. Further, where the infringement is established, the court may grant an injunction restraining the defendant from further infringing acts, and may order the delivery up or destruction of goods bearing the infringing trade mark, as it deems fit. Provided that any counterclaim alleging validity challenges to the registered trade mark shall be adjudicated concurrently with the main suit.

Any person aggrieved by an order passed by the Plant Variety Protection Appellate Board may appeal to the High Court within sixty days from the date of such order. The appellant shall be liable to pay such fees in any proceeding before the High Court as determined by the rules framed under this Act, provided that a default in payment of such fees shall not automatically preclude the appellate authority from considering the merits of the case if the appellant demonstrates sufficient financial hardship and satisfies the court that payment would cause undue burden. The Board may, at its discretion, waive or reduce any applicable fees for applicants who are smallholder farmers or belong to scheduled castes or tribes, as a measure to promote equitable access to justice. Further, costs incidental to the appeal shall be determined by the High Court in its discretion, taking into account the complexity of the matter and the conduct of the parties.

Any person intending to commercially exploit audio-visual works through broadcasting shall first register a Declaration of Intent with the designated Copyright Office. Such declaration must specify the title of the work, the name and address of the copyright owner, and the intended method of broadcasting, differentiating clearly whether it is via terrestrial radio, satellite transmission, or internet streaming platforms. The registration shall be deemed incomplete until all requisite fees are remitted and supporting documentation verifying ownership is submitted. Broadcasting shall different from mere public performance; a separate license is required for each distinct broadcast event involving copyrighted material. Provided that, works falling under the domain of fair dealing as provided herein are exempt from this requirement.

Any aggrieved person may, subject to the provisions herein, appeal to the Appellate Board against any decision of the Controller relating to an application for a patent, or the amendment or revocation thereof, or against any order made by the Controller refusing to grant a patent or dismissing an application for the restoration of a patent. The grounds for such appeal shall be limited to questions of law, and the Appellate Board shall not review findings of fact unless such findings are demonstrably based on no evidence or are manifestly erroneous. Provided that no appeal shall lie from a decision of the Controller relating to an interim order concerning the preservation of evidence or the conduct of proceedings. All appeals shall be filed within a period of sixty days from the date of the Controller’s decision, and a prescribed fee shall accompany the filing. The Appellate Board may, at its discretion, require the appellant to furnish security for the payment of costs. Any party to an appeal may, with leave of the Appellate Board, appear in person or be represented by a patent agent or legal practitioner.

Any person who, without obtaining requisite licenses as provided herein, engages in the commercial exploitation of a sound recording shall be guilty of an offence punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both. The unauthorized duplication of any sound recording for purposes of sale or distribution constitutes prima facie evidence of such commercial exploitation and shifts the burden of proof onto the accused to demonstrate lawful authorization. Furthermore, any instrumentality used in the making of an infringing sound recording, including but not limited to mixing consoles and digital audio workstations, shall be liable to seizure by a Magistrate First Class. A copyright owner may initiate proceedings for recovery of damages sustained due to such infringement, which shall include actual losses suffered as well as statutory damages not less than five thousand rupees per infringing unit. Provided that, legitimate licensees operating under compulsory license provisions are excluded from the ambit of this prohibition.
